title: Lecture 1: Course Introduction
subtitle: How can a natural-language question about the brain be converted into a closed loop linking variables, models, computable predictions, and testable data?
text: Course Introduction How can a natural-language question about the brain be converted into a closed loop linking variables, models, computable predictions, and testable data? Brain and behavior question → variables and hypotheses → mathematical model → simulation / analysis → data and estimation → testing and revision Explain computational neuroscience as a cycle of questions, data, models, and inference, rather than equating it with programming or the application of machine-learning algorithms. Distinguish descriptive, mechanistic, and normative models, and select an appropriate level of model for a given neuroscience question. Starting from a minimal input–output model, write testable predictions, residuals, and a parameter-estimation objective, and explain how each quantity is obtained experimentally. Organize the mathematical, programming, and neuroscience prerequisites into an actionable learning loop: know when to calculate, when to plot, and when to return to the biological hypothesis. This lecture presents computational neuroscience as a research strategy, not a particular software package, algorithm, or job title. The strategy may start from data and estimate neural representations, or start from a mechanistic hypothesis and build a model for simulation. Its essential standards are clear variables, computable predictions, falsifiable assumptions, and results that answer a neuroscience question. Later lectures apply this language to single neurons, population coding, vision, movement, decision-making, reinforcement learning, and memory. Equating computational neuroscience with “using computers” or “training neural networks.” Assuming that a good fit proves the proposed mechanism; different models can make similar predictions. Choosing a tool before defining the question, leaving variables, units, and falsifiable predictions unspecified. Treating firing rate as a directly observed continuous quantity even though it is usually a statistical estimate. Treating course logistics as permanent academic content; Page 3 belongs to the 2025 course archive. This lecture establishes only the concepts and dependencies needed by the next 26 lectures; it is not a general survey of computational neuroscience. Minimal threshold-linear input–output model \(r(s) = [ws + b]\)+ Static, one-dimensional stimulus; nonnegative rate Generative model: distribution of the data given inputs and parameters \(P (y | x, \theta )\) Conditioning variables and random variables are defined explicitly Maximum-likelihood parameter estimate θb = arg \(\max P (y | x, \theta )\) \(\theta \) The model class and assumptions about data independence hold Prediction from a fitted model for a new input b yb = \(f (x; \theta )\) The relationship between the new input and the training distribution is stated Residual between observation and prediction error = y − yb Must have the same units as y computational neuroscience The study of computation in nervous systems using quantitative models, algorithms, and data analysis. model An explicit, simplified representation of variables, relationships, and assumptions. simulation Generation of state trajectories or synthetic data by applying a model's rules. inference Using data to constrain unknown states, parameters, or models. prediction A model's quantitative output for data not used in fitting, under specified conditions. falsifiability The property that some possible observation could conflict with a model's prediction. machine learning A family of methods that optimize predictive functions from data; it overlaps with computational neuroscience but is not identical to it. data science The broad practice of organizing, analyzing, computing with, and interpreting data. mechanistic model A model whose variables and interactions are interpreted as candidate biological processes. parameter A quantity held fixed during one model run but potentially estimated from data. Researchers record firing rate r at several sound intensities s. Identify the input and output, and propose a minimal testable hypothesis. Naming the variables is not enough: a testable hypothesis must specify their relationship and allow data to contradict it. If firing rate saturates as intensity rises, for example, the threshold-linear relationship will leave systematic residuals. The input is sound intensity s and the output is firing rate r. One testable hypothesis is \(r=\max(0,ws+b)\), where w is the intensity gain and b is the baseline offset. “A more complex model is closer to the truth, so it must be better.” What is wrong with this claim? A complex model can fit more shapes, but it can also be harder to interpret, estimate, and falsify. Compare out-of-sample prediction, parameter uncertainty, and whether the omitted mechanisms matter for the current question. Model quality depends on the question, the amount of data, and testability. Extra degrees of freedom may merely memorize noise without improving predictions on new data. If ten repetitions of the same stimulus produce ten different responses, does that directly refute a deterministic input–output model? First specify whether the model predicts a single-trial response or an average response. Only after separating the mean trend from the fluctuations can you decide whether a discrepancy belongs to the mean model or the noise model. No. A deterministic model may describe the conditional mean response, while observation noise or a probabilistic model describes trial-to-trial variation. If a model underestimates firing rate for every large stimulus, what pattern should the residuals show, and what should you do next? A systematic dependence of residuals on input is diagnostic. A residual-versus-stimulus plot usually localizes model failure more clearly than a single score. Residuals remain positive at large stimulus values, so the errors are not scattered randomly. Examine the gain, nonlinear shape, or missing variables instead of reporting only an overall mean squared error. Why is “this brain region activates during the task” not yet a mechanistic explanation? It reports only that activity and task co-occur. It does not specify the variables, connections, or dynamics that generate the activity, nor does it predict quantitatively how an intervention should change it. This is the distinction tested in From interdisciplinary backgrounds to answerable questions. Worked example — Split a perception problem into two tests: Present 50 motion trials in each direction. A neuron produces an average of 12 spikes for rightward motion and 5 for leftward motion. A threshold \(n\ge 9\) predicts “right”; 38 rightward trials and 7 leftward trials cross threshold. Calculate accuracy and identify which part of the model this rule tests. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Present 50 motion trials in each direction. A neuron produces an average of 12 spikes for rightward motion and 5 for leftward motion. A threshold \(n\ge 9\) predicts “right”; 38 rightward trials and 7 leftward trials cross threshold. Calculate accuracy and identify which part of the model this rule tests. The rule correctly classifies 38 rightward trials; the remaining 12 are incorrectly labeled left. For leftward motion, \(50-7=43\) trials remain below threshold, so 43 trials are classified correctly. The total is \(38+43=81\) correct trials out of 100, for an accuracy of 81%. The difference in means supports an effect of stimulus on response. The 81% accuracy tests whether a specific readout rule can convert the response into a stimulus judgment. Accuracy must lie between 0 and 1. Swapping every left/right label would give 19%, and the two accuracies sum to 100%. When applying “From interdisciplinary backgrounds to answerable questions” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Interdisciplinary value comes from a testable chain of work, not a list of disciplinary labels. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Turn a verbal question into a testable chain”? Probability is dimensionless and lies between 0 and 1. A count n is dimensionless, but its counting window must be stated explicitly in seconds or milliseconds. If n is completely unrelated to s, \(P(n|s)\) is identical for every s, so the response cannot discriminate stimuli. If \(P(y|n,s)\) still changes substantially with s after conditioning on n, the simplified \(s\to n\to y\) Markov chain fails and must include a missing neural state or direct stimulus pathway. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why does computational neuroscience require neuroscience, physics, mathematics, and engineering together rather than any one discipline alone? The first page uses the instructor's background across neurobiology, physics, and applied mathematics to reveal the field's working pattern. Experiments define the nervous-system objects and constraints. Mathematics compresses verbal hypotheses into relationships that can be derived. Computation extends those derivations beyond hand-calculable scales. Engineering forces models to produce operational outputs. These are not four unrelated labels; they form a chain from observation to explanation to test. Consider the question “How does an animal judge motion direction?” Neuroscience selects the area to record and the stimulus and behavioral measures. Mathematics defines stimulus direction s, neural response n, and choice y. A model proposes \(P(n|s)\) or \(P(y|n)\). A program estimates parameters and compares predictions. Code without a well-defined question cannot generate a scientific explanation automatically; biological description without quantitative relationships cannot distinguish competing mechanisms. A model fits its training set well but predicts new stimuli poorly. What does that tell you most directly? The model or estimation procedure has not captured a generalizable relationship. It may have too many degrees of freedom, inadequate training coverage, or omitted variables that change under the new stimuli. This is the distinction tested in Four core questions and the model–data loop. Worked example — Calculate threshold, predictions, and residuals by hand: Let \(w=4 \mathrm{Hz}/unit\) and \(b=-8 \mathrm{Hz}\). At stimuli \(s=1\), 3, and 5, the observed mean firing rates are 1, 5, and 15 Hz. Calculate the threshold, predictions, and residuals. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(w=4 \mathrm{Hz}/unit\) and \(b=-8 \mathrm{Hz}\). At stimuli \(s=1\), 3, and 5, the observed mean firing rates are 1, 5, and 15 Hz. Calculate the threshold, predictions, and residuals. The threshold is \(s_{0}=-b/w=8/4=2\), so \(s=1\) is below threshold while \(s=3\) and 5 are above it. The predictions are \(\max(0,4-8)=0\), \(\max(0,12-8)=4\), and \(\max(0,20-8)=12 \mathrm{Hz}\). The residuals \(r-\hat{r}\) are \(1-0=1\), \(5-4=1\), and \(15-12=3 \mathrm{Hz}\). Residuals increase with stimulus, suggesting that the true gain may exceed 4 or that the relationship bends upward at high stimulus values. Every prediction is nonnegative, the linear segment begins at zero at threshold, and units remain Hz throughout. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Four core questions and the model–data loop”? Reduce a broad question to an executable one by specifying the object, time window, manipulated variable, and observable. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Four core questions and the model–data loop”? After parameter estimation, evaluate predictions on data that were not used for fitting. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Four core questions and the model–data loop” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? After parameter estimation, evaluate predictions on data that were not used for fitting. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Minimal prediction and diagnosis with a threshold-linear model”? ws and b must both have units of Hz before they can be added. The residual \(r-\hat{r}\) is also measured in Hz. If \(w=0\), response does not vary with stimulus. If \(b\ge 0\) and \(w>0\), the nonnegative stimulus range may contain no visible threshold. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why begin with a hand-calculable example before running a large simulation? It provides an independent expectation and quickly exposes errors in indices, signs, units, and boundary conditions. A smooth-looking large plot does not prove that an implementation matches its equations. This is the distinction tested in Course map, tool choice, and sustainable self-study. Worked example — Design a twenty-minute model-learning loop: You need to study \(r=\max(0,3s-6)\) with only paper, pencil, and any programming environment. Give a short verifiable workflow and calculate the response for \(s=0\), 1, 2, and 4. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: You need to study \(r=\max(0,3s-6)\) with only paper, pencil, and any programming environment. Give a short verifiable workflow and calculate the response for \(s=0\), 1, 2, and 4. State in words: below threshold the response is zero; above threshold each additional stimulus unit raises the response by 3 Hz. By hand, the linear term 3s−6 equals −6, −3, 0, and 6. After nonnegative rectification, the responses are 0, 0, 0, and 6 Hz. Enter only these four inputs in the program and print the outputs, confirming exact agreement with all four hand calculations. Then plot the curve from \(s=0\) to 5, mark threshold \(s=2\), and note two boundaries: the model has no saturation and no trial-to-trial variability. At \(s=2\) the linear term is exactly zero. For every increase of 1 in s above threshold, response should rise by 3 Hz. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Course map, tool choice, and sustainable self-study”? Verify code against a small hand-worked example before increasing scale or changing parameters. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Completion means being able to reconstruct, calculate, interpret, and state the model's boundaries. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Model–data feedback loop”? Fitting parameters is only the middle of the loop. A model must first predict data that were not used for fitting; systematic stimulus-dependent residuals then determine whether the hypothesis should be retained, revised, or replaced. title: From interdisciplinary backgrounds to answerable questions
subtitle: Lecture 1 · Lecture1-Course-Introduction.pdf, p. 1
text: Why does computational neuroscience require neuroscience, physics, mathematics, and engineering together rather than any one discipline alone? The first page uses the instructor's background across neurobiology, physics, and applied mathematics to reveal the field's working pattern. Experiments define the nervous-system objects and constraints. Mathematics compresses verbal hypotheses into relationships that can be derived. Computation extends those derivations beyond hand-calculable scales. Engineering forces models to produce operational outputs. These are not four unrelated labels; they form a chain from observation to explanation to test. Consider the question “How does an animal judge motion direction?” Neuroscience selects the area to record and the stimulus and behavioral measures. Mathematics defines stimulus direction s, neural response n, and choice y. A model proposes \(P(n|s)\) or \(P(y|n)\). A program estimates parameters and compares predictions. Code without a well-defined question cannot generate a scientific explanation automatically; biological description without quantitative relationships cannot distinguish competing mechanisms. Interdisciplinary work often breaks at the level of terminology. “Encoding,” for example, might mean that mean firing rate changes with a stimulus, or that a full conditional distribution carries information. Repair the ambiguity by replacing nouns with observables and operations: hold stimulus s fixed, repeat the trial to obtain responses n, ask whether the distribution of n changes with s, and measure how accurately s can be estimated after observing n. Once the claim is operationalized, the disagreement has a calculable target. Three levels of explanation recur in this field. A descriptive model summarizes a pattern in data, such as a tuning curve. A mechanistic model proposes components that generate the pattern, such as ion channels or network connections. A normative model asks for the best strategy for a task, such as maximum-likelihood decoding. The three levels may give different answers for the same phenomenon; choose among them according to the question, not the length of the equation. Interdisciplinary value comes from a testable chain of work, not a list of disciplinary labels. Rewrite a scientific question in terms of inputs, outputs, repeatable conditions, and comparable predictions. Descriptive, mechanistic, and normative models answer questions at different explanatory levels. Present 50 motion trials in each direction. A neuron produces an average of 12 spikes for rightward motion and 5 for leftward motion. A threshold \(n\ge 9\) predicts “right”; 38 rightward trials and 7 leftward trials cross threshold. Calculate accuracy and identify which part of the model this rule tests. This threshold decoder has accuracy 0.81. That does not prove that the brain uses the same threshold, but it supplies a comparable decoding baseline. Why is “this brain region activates during the task” not yet a mechanistic explanation? It reports only that activity and task co-occur. It does not specify the variables, connections, or dynamics that generate the activity, nor does it predict quantitatively how an intervention should change it. Treating “uses a computer” as a sufficient definition of computational neuroscience while ignoring models and scientific questions. Inferring a causal mechanism from correlated activity without proposing predictions that an intervention or new data could test.

title: Four core questions and the model–data loop
subtitle: Lecture 1 · Lecture1-Course-Introduction.pdf, p. 2
text: How can broad questions about sensory extraction, body control, memory, and intelligence be reduced to one computable and falsifiable study? The second page groups the field's targets into extracting information from sensation, controlling the body, forming memories, and producing intelligent behavior. Each is too broad until an object, time scale, and observable are specified. “How does vision work?” can become “How does the spike count of an MT neuron change with coherence during a 200 millisecond random-dot-motion stimulus?” Narrowing the question does not diminish it; it links theory to experiment. The model–data loop has five repeatable actions: define variables, write relationships, estimate parameters, predict held-out data, and inspect the error structure. In \(r(s)=\max(0,ws+b)\), s is stimulus intensity, r is mean firing rate, w controls slope, and b is the extrapolated intercept at zero stimulus. Data must constrain the parameters, and predictions must target observations that were not used for fitting. Error is evidence for what to do next, not a nuisance outside the model. For stimulus \(s_{i}\), define residual \(e_{i}=r_{i}-\hat{r}_{i}\). Residuals scattered without pattern around zero reveal no obvious systematic bias in the mean relation. Persistently positive residuals at large stimuli suggest missing upward curvature or another input. Residual magnitude that grows with the mean suggests that the noise model must change. Different shapes motivate different revisions. Simulation, data analysis, machine learning, and mathematical modeling play distinct roles in the loop. Simulation generates consequences of a specified model. Data analysis summarizes and displays observations. Machine learning can uncover high-dimensional predictive relationships. Mathematical modeling emphasizes the logical path from assumptions to results. A study may use all four, but each step needs explicit inputs, outputs, and evaluation criteria so that a high prediction score does not conceal a wrong interpretation. Reduce a broad question to an executable one by specifying the object, time window, manipulated variable, and observable. After parameter estimation, evaluate predictions on data that were not used for fitting. Residual structure tells you whether to revise the mean relationship, the noise model, or the set of variables. Let \(w=4 \mathrm{Hz}/unit\) and \(b=-8 \mathrm{Hz}\). At stimuli \(s=1\), 3, and 5, the observed mean firing rates are 1, 5, and 15 Hz. Calculate the threshold, predictions, and residuals. The threshold is 2; predictions are 0, 4, and 12 Hz; residuals are 1, 1, and 3 Hz. A model fits its training set well but predicts new stimuli poorly. What does that tell you most directly? The model or estimation procedure has not captured a generalizable relationship. It may have too many degrees of freedom, inadequate training coverage, or omitted variables that change under the new stimuli. Reporting only a correlation coefficient or training error without plotting predictions and residuals against stimulus. Interpreting machine-learning prediction accuracy automatically as discovery of a neural mechanism.

title: Course map, tool choice, and sustainable self-study
subtitle: Lecture 1 · Lecture1-Course-Introduction.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture1-Course-Introduction.pdf, p. 4
text: How can mathematics and programming serve understanding instead of becoming two additional subjects detached from neuroscience? The schedule on the third page and the mathematics and programming guidance on the fourth page define a learning path: establish model language, study single-neuron dynamics, then move to neural coding, populations, and networks. Every stage reuses earlier tools. Vectors become population responses, differential equations become membrane voltages and synaptic currents, and probability becomes spike counts and decoding. The foundational lectures are not isolated units to discard after an exam. MATLAB or Python can serve as the programming language; syntax preference is secondary to performing the same scientific actions: create variables with units, calculate from equations, plot a check, vary parameters, and save a reproducible experiment. For a first implementation, verify the code with a hand-calculable example. Predictions for three points should match pencil-and-paper results before you expand the grid or the number of trials. Small examples guard against mistakes in symbols, indices, and units. Flipped learning requires exposure before class, but “I watched it” is not a completion criterion. A stronger standard is to perform four tasks without prompts: answer the guiding question in your own words, reconstruct one derivation, solve one numerical example, and identify at least one condition under which the model fails. If one step breaks, return to the corresponding section and repair it rather than replaying everything from the beginning. Keep a model card in your own notes: scientific question, variables and units, equations, parameter meanings, initial conditions, outputs, testable predictions, and known limitations. When the next lecture introduces a model, compare it directly with the previous one. Perfect integrate-and-fire and leaky integrate-and-fire differ by one leak term, yet that term creates a steady state and rheobase current. Also record an experimental manipulation that could distinguish the two. Repeated comparison builds transferable understanding better than isolated memorization. Foundational tools recur at the levels of single neurons, coding, and networks. Verify code against a small hand-worked example before increasing scale or changing parameters. Completion means being able to reconstruct, calculate, interpret, and state the model's boundaries. You need to study \(r=\max(0,3s-6)\) with only paper, pencil, and any programming environment. Give a short verifiable workflow and calculate the response for \(s=0\), 1, 2, and 4. The verified prediction is \([0,0,0,6]\) Hz, accompanied by a verbal explanation, hand calculation, code check, plot, and limitation check. Why begin with a hand-calculable example before running a large simulation? It provides an independent expectation and quickly exposes errors in indices, signs, units, and boundary conditions. A smooth-looking large plot does not prove that an implementation matches its equations. Treating executable code as correct without checking it against independent values or limiting cases. Rereading in page order without attempting to reconstruct derivations, examples, and failure conditions.

title: Lecture 2: Vectors, Matrices, and Probability
subtitle: How can shape reasoning guarantee that a linear-algebra operation is defined, and how can probability distributions turn uncertainty in neural data into a computable object?
text: Vectors, Matrices, and Probability How can shape reasoning guarantee that a linear-algebra operation is defined, and how can probability distributions turn uncertainty in neural data into a computable object? Objects and shapes → linear-algebra operations → probability distributions → joint / marginal / conditional distributions → Bayesian updating Determine the shape of each scalar, vector, or matrix before carrying out addition, inner products, outer products, matrix multiplication, or element-wise multiplication, and explain what the result represents. Use a determinant to decide whether a given two-by-two matrix is invertible, calculate its inverse by hand, and verify that the product is the identity matrix. From a probability mass function or density, calculate normalization, means, variances, marginals, and conditional distributions, and distinguish “uncorrelated” from “independent.” Derive Bayes' rule from the two factorizations of a joint probability and distinguish the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior clearly. This lecture establishes the grammar used by almost every later formula: first identify whether each object is a scalar, vector, or matrix and determine its shape; then decide whether the operation is defined. The probability material moves from univariate Bernoulli and exponential distributions to bivariate Gaussians, marginals, conditionals, and Bayes' rule. An expression that MATLAB can execute is not necessarily an operation defined in abstract mathematics, so program output must be interpreted separately from the meaning of its objects. Mistaking MATLAB scalar expansion for scalar+matrix addition in abstract linear algebra. Confusing * with .*: the former is matrix multiplication, whereas the latter is a Hadamard product. Calculating entries before checking shape and thereby assigning a result to an undefined operation. Treating a density value as the probability of one exact value of a continuous variable. Assuming that uncorrelated variables are always independent; this implication holds only in special cases such as a Gaussian distribution. Reversing the conditioning directions of posterior, likelihood, and prior. Interpreting clear all and inv in the MATLAB source literally as best practices. Numerical work generally favors solving a linear system over forming an explicit inverse. Keep MATLAB's scalar-plus-matrix behavior distinct from abstract linear algebra. Shape rule for matrix–vector multiplication Am×n \(xn\times 1 \to  ym\times 1\) The inner dimensions are equal Inner product uT \(v = u_{i} v i i\) The vectors have the same dimension Outer product uv T The output shape is len(u)×len(v) Euclidean norm \(\Vert w\Vert 2 = w_{\mathrm{T}} w A\) consistent row/column convention is used Variance identity \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[X 2 ] - E[X]2\) The second moment exists Definition of the CDF FX (x) = P (X ≤ x) Applies to both discrete and continuous variables Exponential PDF \(fX (x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} 1x\ge 0\) \(\lambda >0\) Bivariate Gaussian density 1 −1 (x−µ) e− 2 (x−µ) C 1 T \(p(x) = \sqrt  2\pi  \det C C\) is symmetric positive definite Bayes' rule \(P (B | A)P (A)\) \(P (A | B) = P (B)\) \(P(B)>0\) scalar A single number; it may be represented as a \(1\times 1\) object when the context is stated. vector An ordered set of components; this course uses column vectors by default. matrix A two-dimensional array organized by rows and columns that represents a linear map. inner product The sum of componentwise products of two vectors with the same dimension. outer product The matrix produced by multiplying a column vector by a row vector. Hadamard product Elementwise multiplication of objects with the same shape. singular matrix A square matrix that is not invertible and has determinant zero. probability mass function, PMF The probability assigned to each possible outcome of a discrete random variable. probability density function, PDF Probability density per unit interval for a continuous random variable. marginal distribution The distribution of one variable after summing or integrating over the others. conditional distribution A distribution renormalized after another event or variable is known. likelihood A function of model parameters that measures their relative support with the observations held fixed. prior A distribution over an unknown quantity before observing the current data. posterior The updated distribution obtained by combining likelihood and prior. A has shape \(4\times 2\) and v has shape \(2\times 1\). Are both Av and vA defined? If so, what is the shape? Check the inner dimensions first. In Av, 2 matches 2 and the outer dimensions \(4\times 1\) remain. Reversing the order changes both compatibility and meaning. Av is defined and has shape \(4\times 1\). vA is undefined because the 1 column of v does not match the 4 rows of A. Why is \(C=[[3,4],[6,8]]\) not invertible? Give a reason that does not depend on a software error. Dependent rows mean that distinct inputs collapse to the same output. Once that information is lost, the output cannot recover a unique input. A zero determinant is the algebraic statement of the same fact. The second row is 2 times the first, so the rows are linearly dependent. Equivalently, \(\det(C)=3\cdot 8-4\cdot 6=0\), and no inverse exists. An exponential distribution has rate \(\lambda =5 \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). What is the probability that the waiting time exceeds 0.2 s? The exponential survival function is \(\exp(-\lambda x)\). The product of \(\lambda\) and time is dimensionless, as an exponential argument must be. \(P(X>0.2)=\exp(-\lambda \cdot 0.2)=\exp(-1)\approx 0.368\). When does “zero covariance implies independence” hold, and why is it false in general? For example, let X be symmetric about zero and let \(Y=X^{2}\). Then \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[X^{3}]-E[X]E[X^{2}]=0\) even though knowing X determines Y exactly. It holds for jointly Gaussian variables. For a general distribution, zero covariance rules out only linear co-variation; nonlinear dependence may remain. Why can each output of A v be read as a weighted sum of one row of weights and the input? By definition, matrix multiplication gives \(y_{i}=\sum _j A_{ij} v_{j}\). Once output row i is fixed, the sum runs only over input index j, so that row lists how the output weights each input. This is the distinction tested in Start with shape: scalars, vectors, matrices, and products. Worked example — Distinguish the inner product, outer product, and norm: Given \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), calculate u+v, \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\), \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\), and \(||v||_{2}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), calculate u+v, \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\), \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\), and \(||v||_{2}\). Component-wise addition gives \(u+v=(2,6)^{\mathrm{T}}\). The inner product is \(0\cdot 2+1\cdot 5=5\), a scalar. The outer product is \([[0\cdot 2,0\cdot 5],[1\cdot 2,1\cdot 5]]=[[0,0],[2,5]]\), with shape \(2\times 2\). The norm is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(2^{2}+5^{2})=\operatorname{sqrt}(29)\approx 5.385\). The norm must exceed the largest component magnitude 5 and be smaller than the sum of component magnitudes 7; 5.385 satisfies both bounds. The likelihood fixes the observed data and compares how well parameter values explain them. The parameter posterior must also incorporate a prior and normalize across every candidate parameter; the two expressions condition in opposite directions. This is the distinction tested in From Bernoulli and exponential distributions to joint Gaussians and Bayes. Worked example — Two normalizations: a conditional Gaussian and low-base-rate Bayes: A: \(\mu _{1}=0\), \(\mu _{2}=1\), \(\sigma _{1}=0.5\), \(\sigma _{2}=1\), \(c=0.7\), and \(x_{2}=0.75\). Find the conditional mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(X_{1}\). B: disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity is 0.9, and false-positive rate is 0.05. Find the probability of disease after a positive result. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A: \(\mu _{1}=0\), \(\mu _{2}=1\), \(\sigma _{1}=0.5\), \(\sigma _{2}=1\), \(c=0.7\), and \(x_{2}=0.75\). Find the conditional mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(X_{1}\). B: disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity is 0.9, and false-positive rate is 0.05. Find the probability of disease after a positive result. For A, the conditional mean is \(0+0.7\cdot 0.5\cdot (0.75-1)=-0.0875\). The conditional variance is \(0.5^{2}(1-0.7^{2})=0.25\cdot 0.51=0.1275\), so the conditional standard deviation is approximately 0.3571. Because correlation is positive and \(x_{2}\) is below \(\mu _{2}\), the conditional mean falls below \(\mu _{1}\). The conditional variance 0.1275 is also smaller than the marginal variance 0.25. For B, the joint probability of a true positive is \(0.9\cdot 0.01=0.009\), and that of a false positive is \(0.05\cdot 0.99=0.0495\). The total probability of a positive result is \(0.009+0.0495=0.0585\). The posterior probability after a positive result is \(0.009/0.0585\approx 0.1538\), or about 15.4%. For jointly Gaussian variables, zero covariance implies independence; general distributions do not share this guarantee. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Multiplying \(\sigma _{1}/\sigma _{2}\) by \((x_{2}-\mu _{2})\) yields units of \(X_{1}\). Conditional variance and \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) both have squared \(X_{1}\) units. As \(|c|\to 1\), the nondegenerate model approaches a line, conditional variance approaches zero, and the covariance matrix becomes singular. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Conditioning a joint Gaussian shifts the mean and reduces the variance”? When two variables are correlated, fixing \(X_{2}\) takes a slice through the joint density. The conditional mean shifts along the correlation direction, while conditional variance decreases from \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}(1-c^{2})\). title: Start with shape: scalars, vectors, matrices, and products
subtitle: Lecture 2 · Lecture2-FC_NEUROSCI_366_F2025.pdf, p. 1
text: Why should a matrix calculation begin by writing every object's shape and the meaning of its rows and columns, rather than by substituting numbers? The first exercise page defines \(s=2\), \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(w=(0,1,2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), and matrices A, B, and C. These are more than arithmetic exercises: a vector may represent responses from several neurons, and a matrix may represent a linear map from stimulus to response. Shape records the input and output slots. If you ignore it, you may swap neuron and condition indices even when the arithmetic itself is correct. Vector addition requires equal lengths and proceeds component by component. The inner product \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\) maps two equal-length vectors to a scalar and can measure overlap in a common coordinate system. The norm \(||w||_{2}\) is the square root of \(w^{\mathrm{T}}w\) and gives Euclidean distance from the origin. The outer product \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\) maps two vectors to a matrix whose i,j entry is \(u_{i}\) \(v_{j}\), retaining every pairwise combination. Do not confuse it with the inner product. Interpret Av as the inner product of each row of A with v. If A is \(4\times 2\) and v is \(2\times 1\), the result is \(4\times 1\), with each output component a weighted sum of two input components. Matrix product BC pairs every row of B with every column of C. Matrix multiplication is generally noncommutative: even when BC and CB have the same shape, they may have different values and represent transformations in different orders. Keep the abstract rule separate from language behavior. In MATLAB, `B*C` is matrix multiplication and `B.*C` is element-wise multiplication; for a real vector, `v'` produces a row vector. Some versions permit s+A by implicitly adding the scalar to each entry. That is an array-language convention, not ordinary addition between linear-algebra objects of different shapes. State explicitly which meaning your code uses. Matrix multiplication requires matching inner dimensions and retains the outer dimensions. An inner product is a scalar; an outer product is a matrix. They retain different information. Software implicit expansion must be distinguished conceptually from abstract matrix addition. Given \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), calculate u+v, \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\), \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\), and \(||v||_{2}\). The sum is \((2,6)^{\mathrm{T}}\), the inner product is 5, the outer product is \([[0,0],[2,5]]\), and the norm is approximately 5.385. Why can each output of A v be read as a weighted sum of one row of weights and the input? By definition, matrix multiplication gives \(y_{i}=\sum _j A_{ij} v_{j}\). Once output row i is fixed, the sum runs only over input index j, so that row lists how the output weights each input. Multiplying whenever two objects have the same number of entries, without checking the inner dimensions required by matrix multiplication. Confusing `*` with `.*`, which can produce the expected shape but a different scientific meaning.

title: Identity, transpose, inverse, and singularity
subtitle: Lecture 2 · Lecture2-FC_NEUROSCI_366_F2025.pdf, p. 2
text: When can a matrix recover the input uniquely from the output, and why does a zero determinant prevent that recovery? The identity matrix I has 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere and plays the role of scalar 1: \(Ix=x\). Transpose \(A^{\mathrm{T}}\) swaps rows and columns. Thus, if A maps a two-dimensional input to a four-dimensional output, \(A^{\mathrm{T}}\) has shape \(2\times 4\), but it is generally not the inverse of A. An inverse \(A^{-1}\) must satisfy \(A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I\) and exists only for a square, one-to-one mapping. For a two-by-two matrix \(B=[[a,b],[c,d]]\), \(\det(B)=ad-bc\). Geometrically, the determinant is the signed area scale factor of the linear map. A zero determinant means that a two-dimensional region is compressed into a line or point, so distinct inputs yield the same output. Once the map flattens information, output alone cannot identify the original input and no inverse exists. This is the same fact as linear dependence among rows or columns. For \(B=[[4,4],[8,9]]\), \(\det(B)=36-32=4\), so \(B^{-1}=(1/4)[[9,-4],[-8,4]]\). Verification matters more than calling `inv`: multiplying by B should give 1 on the diagonal and 0 off the diagonal. In numerical work, a nonzero determinant that is very close to zero may still produce an inverse that amplifies tiny errors dramatically. Check the condition number instead of stopping at “the software returned an answer.” The Hadamard product B⊙C multiplies corresponding entries and requires equal shapes; the matrix product BC sums along a shared index. The first may represent channel-wise gain, while the second composes transformations. Calling both simply “multiplication” erases model structure. In a code audit, describe the objects on both sides of every multiplication sign and verify the first entry by hand. An inverse recovers the input uniquely from the output; a transpose does not serve that purpose. A zero determinant means that a map compresses dimensions and loses recoverable information. A Hadamard product is element-wise, whereas a matrix product sums over the shared dimension. Let \(B=[[4,4],[8,9]]\) and \(C=[[3,4],[6,8]]\). Calculate BC and B⊙C. \(BC=[[36,48],[78,104]]\), whereas \(B\odot C=[[12,16],[48,72]]\). Which distinct inputs does \(C=[[3,4],[6,8]]\) map to the same output, and how does that demonstrate noninvertibility? Because \(C(4,-3)^{\mathrm{T}}=(0,0)^{\mathrm{T}}\), any x and \(x+a(4,-3)^{\mathrm{T}}\) have the same output. The output cannot determine a, so it cannot recover a unique input. Treating a nonzero determinant as sufficient for numerical stability and ignoring error amplification near singularity. Using `inv(B)*y` instead of a more stable linear solve and failing to verify the result.

title: From Bernoulli and exponential distributions to joint Gaussians and Bayes
subtitle: Lecture 2 · Lecture2-FC_NEUROSCI_366_F2025.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture2-FC_NEUROSCI_366_F2025.pdf, p. 4
text: How do we move from uncertainty in one variable to dependence between two variables, then use observations to infer a hidden cause? A Bernoulli variable X takes only 1 or 0 with probabilities p and 1−p. Its mean is \(E[X]=p\) because \(1\cdot p+0\cdot (1-p)=p\). Since \(X^{2}=X\), its variance is \(E[X^{2}]-E[X]^{2}=p-p^{2}=p(1-p)\). This can represent whether a spike occurs in a time window or whether a choice is correct. Counts across multiple windows form a binomial distribution only if trials are independent and share the same p. The exponential density \(f(x)=\lambda \exp(-\lambda x)\), \(x\ge 0\), describes waiting times in a constant-rate Poisson process. Integration gives \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\), so the survival probability is \(\exp(-\lambda x)\). The mean and standard deviation are both \(1/\lambda\), the median is \(\ln 2/\lambda\), and the mode is 0. A mean larger than the median reflects the long right tail. Treating \(\lambda\) as the mean waiting time gives both a dimensional and numerical error. A bivariate Gaussian is determined completely by its mean vector and covariance matrix. Integrating out one variable gives a Gaussian marginal; fixing an observation and renormalizing gives a Gaussian conditional distribution. Conditioning shifts the mean and reduces variance to the uncertainty left after accounting for the correlation. The derivation below gives the conditional mean, conditional variance, and Bayesian reweighting, allowing you to calculate the complete distribution rather than merely infer the tilt of an ellipse. Bayes' rule follows from two factorizations of one joint probability: \(P(A,B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A)\). Rearrangement gives \(P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)\). In parameter inference, A may be parameter \(\theta\) and B the data D. Then \(P(D|\theta )\) is the likelihood, \(P(\theta )\) the prior, \(P(D)\) the normalizing evidence, and \(P(\theta |D)\) the posterior. A likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameter unless it is multiplied by a prior and normalized. Bernoulli variance \(p(1-p)\) is zero at \(p=0\) or 1 and maximal at \(p=1/2\). Exponential rate \(\lambda\) and mean waiting time \(1/\lambda\) are reciprocals. For jointly Gaussian variables, zero covariance implies independence; general distributions do not share this guarantee. Bayes' rule is a rearrangement of two factorizations of the joint probability. A: \(\mu _{1}=0\), \(\mu _{2}=1\), \(\sigma _{1}=0.5\), \(\sigma _{2}=1\), \(c=0.7\), and \(x_{2}=0.75\). Find the conditional mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(X_{1}\). B: disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity is 0.9, and false-positive rate is 0.05. Find the probability of disease after a positive result. A: conditional mean −0.0875, variance 0.1275, and standard deviation about 0.357. B: probability of disease after a positive result about 15.4%. Why is \(P(D|\theta )\), viewed as a function of \(\theta\), called a likelihood but not equal to \(P(\theta |D)\)? The likelihood fixes the observed data and compares how well parameter values explain them. The parameter posterior must also incorporate a prior and normalize across every candidate parameter; the two expressions condition in opposite directions. Treating a continuous density \(f(x)\) as a point probability \(P(X=x)\), even though probability comes from integration over an interval. Confusing \(P(A|B)\) with \(P(B|A)\), especially by ignoring the prior in a low-base-rate setting. Generalizing zero correlation to independence for arbitrary distributions.

title: Lecture 3: Differential Equations and Euler Simulation
subtitle: How can an instantaneous law of state change be turned into a time trajectory, and how can Euler's method approximate it safely when no analytic solution is available?
text: Differential Equations and Euler Simulation How can an instantaneous law of state change be turned into a time trajectory, and how can Euler's method approximate it safely when no analytic solution is available? State \(x(t)\)→ derivative / ODE → initial condition → analytic solution → Euler discretization → stability and error Translate the statement “the rate of change depends on the current state and input” into a first-order differential equation, and explain why an initial condition is part of a complete prediction. Derive the exact constant-input solution of \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\) by hand and verify it using the initial value, long-time limit, and units. Derive the Euler update from the definition of a derivative, state the step-size condition for stability, and distinguish discrete numerical error from continuous-system behavior. Rewrite a second-order oscillator as two first-order equations, interpret its state-space trajectory, and audit the piecewise boundaries and indices in the supplied MATLAB code. A differential equation defines a full time trajectory through a local rate of change, while an initial condition selects one member of the solution family. An analytic solution exposes exact structure and enables limiting checks; Euler's method turns the derivative definition into an iterative update. A numerical result is trustworthy only when the step size is appropriate relative to the time constant, not merely because the code runs. Higher-order equations can be rewritten as coupled first-order systems by adding state variables, which is foundational for later network dynamics. Treating a derivative as the total change over a finite interval instead of the instantaneous rate obtained as \(\Delta t\to 0\). Dropping the initial condition or integration constant when solving by separation of variables. Assuming that executable code implies a sufficiently small \(\Delta t\). An Euler update evaluates \(I(t_{n})\), not the unknown \(I(t_{n+1})\); an off-by-one index changes the algorithm. Confusing the exact oscillatory dynamics with the outward spiral produced by explicit Euler. Confusing the time constant \(\tau\) with the simulation step \(\Delta t\). A code explanation must connect every MATLAB line to its differential equation, discrete update, and plotted result; potential bugs and incorrect source comments must be listed separately. First-order initial-value problem \(\dot{x} = f (x, t)\), \(x(0) = x_{0} f\) is regular enough to guarantee a solution Integral form of an ODE \(x(t) = x_{0} + f (x(t' ), t' )dt'\) 0 The integral follows the actual trajectory First-order system with constant input \(x(t) = I + (x_{0} - I)e^{-t/\tau } I\) is constant and \(\tau >0\) Explicit Euler method xn+1 = xn + ∆tf (xn , tn ) \(\Delta t\) is sufficiently small Euler stability interval for the decay equation 0 < ∆\(t/\tau  < 2\) Linear first-order test equation First-order form of the harmonic oscillator \(\dot{x} = y\), \(\dot{y} = -x\) Undamped, with unit angular frequency Conserved quantity of the exact oscillator, up to a constant factor \(E = x_{2} + y 2\) Exact continuous dynamics differential equation An equation that constrains an unknown function through its derivatives. initial condition A state specified at the starting time that selects one trajectory from a family of solutions. analytic solution An exact expression written in terms of known functions. numerical solution An approximation to the state at discrete time points. time constant The timescale over which a first-order exponential process removes about 63% of its initial gap. steady state A solution whose state no longer changes with time. Euler method Numerical integration by taking a small forward step along the current derivative. truncation error Local error caused by omitting higher-order Taylor terms in a finite-difference approximation. numerical stability Whether small perturbations decay during a discrete iteration instead of being amplified. coupled equations Equations in which the derivatives of multiple states depend on one another. phase space A space whose coordinates are all state variables and in which a trajectory is represented. Both \(x=e^t\) and \(x=2e^t\) solve \(dx/dt=x\). What information is still missing? The differential equation constrains local slopes; the initial condition selects one trajectory from the allowed family. An equation without an initial value usually cannot make a unique numerical prediction. An initial condition is missing. Once \(x(0)=x_{0}\) is given, the coefficient is fixed at \(x_{0}\) and the solution becomes unique. For \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\), what is the sign of the derivative when \(x>I\), and in which direction does the state move? A slope field gives the direction without solving the equation. The state rises when \(x<I\), falls when \(x>I\), and has zero slope at \(x=I\). Because \(-x+I<0\), \(dx/dt<0\): x decreases toward the steady state I. For the no-input Euler update \(x_{n+1}=(1-\Delta t/\tau )x_{n}\), when does the sequence decay instead of diverging? Each discrete step multiplies the state by amplification factor a. Convergence of the magnitude requires \(|a|<1\), while \(a<0\) creates sign alternation that the continuously decaying system does not have. Require \(|1-\Delta t/\tau |<1\), or \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\). If sign alternation must also be avoided, require \(0<\Delta t/\tau \le 1\). A forward-Euler simulation of an undamped oscillator spirals outward. Does that prove that the physical amplitude grows? Compare a continuous invariant, results at different step sizes, and a numerical method better suited to oscillators. A simulation plot reflects both the equation and the algorithm; it is not the equation alone. No. The continuous system conserves energy, whereas the forward-Euler update matrix has a modulus greater than 1 at every finite step. The outward spiral is introduced by the numerical method. If the input switches suddenly from \(I=5\) to \(I=-2\), which part of the solution changes? Does x jump instantly to −2? The new steady state is −2, and the value of x at the switching time becomes the new initial condition. A continuous first-order state does not jump; it approaches −2 exponentially with time constant \(\tau\). This is the distinction tested in From a rate of change to the exact solution of a first-order system. Worked example — Calculate a step response over several time constants: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x_{0}=0\), with input held at \(I=5\) after \(t=0\). Calculate x at \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\) and 30 ms, and find the first time x reaches 4. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x_{0}=0\), with input held at \(I=5\) after \(t=0\). Calculate x at \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\) and 30 ms, and find the first time x reaches 4. The exact solution is \(x(t)=5+(0-5)e^{-t/10}=5(1-e^{-t/10})\). At \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x=5(1-e^{-1})\approx 5\cdot 0.6321=3.1605\). At \(t=30 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x=5(1-e^{-3})\approx 5\cdot 0.9502=4.751\). Set \(4=5(1-e^{-t/10})\), giving \(e^{-t/10}=0.2\) and \(t=-10 \ln 0.2\approx 16.09 \mathrm{ms}\). The trajectory must rise monotonically from 0 without exceeding 5. All three results satisfy that condition, and reaching 80% of steady state takes about \(1.61\tau\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From a rate of change to the exact solution of a first-order system”? A differential equation determines a trajectory only when paired with an initial condition. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion.
