title: From a rate of change to the exact solution of a first-order system
subtitle: Lecture 3 · Lecture3-Differential-Equations.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture3-Differential-Equations.pdf, p. 2
text: How can a local slope rule determine a complete time trajectory, and how can we verify that the resulting function satisfies both the equation and the initial value? The first page uses \(dx/dt=x\) and \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) to show that a differential equation specifies a dynamical rule. A candidate solution is checked by substitution, not by visual resemblance. The derivative of \(x=e^t\) is \(e^t\), satisfying the first equation; the second derivative of \(x=\sin t\) is \(-\sin t\), satisfying the second. Initial conditions then select the amplitude and phase. In \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\), \(\tau\) is the response time constant and I is constant input. Write the right-hand side as −(x−I): the steady state is \(x^{*}=I\), with positive slope below I and negative slope above I. Let \(y=x-I\) be the deviation from steady state. The equation becomes \(\tau  dy/dt=-y\), converting a constantly driven problem into pure exponential decay. Separate variables to obtain \(dy/y=-dt/\tau\). Integration gives \(\ln|y|=-t/\tau +C\), and exponentiation gives \(y=Ae^{-t/\tau }\). Since \(y(0)=x_{0}-I\), \(A=x_{0}-I\) and \(x(t)=I+(x_{0}-I)e^{-t/\tau }\). The expression combines the steady state I with a fading memory of the initial condition; understanding those two terms matters more than memorizing the formula. Apply three independent checks to the exact solution. Initial value: at \(t=0\) the exponential is 1, giving \(x_{0}\). Equation: differentiation gives \(\tau  dx/dt=-(x_{0}-I)e^{-t/\tau }\), equal to −x+I. Long time: as \(t\to \infty\) the exponential vanishes and \(x\to I\). You can also verify the initial slope \((I-x_{0})/\tau\). Failure of any check rules out the candidate for this initial-value problem. A differential equation determines a trajectory only when paired with an initial condition. For constant input, the steady state is I and the deviation x−I decays exponentially. The initial value, substitution into the equation, and the long-time limit provide three independent checks of the exact solution. Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x_{0}=0\), with input held at \(I=5\) after \(t=0\). Calculate x at \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\) and 30 ms, and find the first time x reaches 4. \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\approx 3.16\), \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\approx 4.75\), and x reaches 4 after approximately 16.1 ms. If the input switches suddenly from \(I=5\) to \(I=-2\), which part of the solution changes? Does x jump instantly to −2? The new steady state is −2, and the value of x at the switching time becomes the new initial condition. A continuous first-order state does not jump; it approaches −2 exponentially with time constant \(\tau\). Dropping the integration constant and thereby losing the ability to satisfy an arbitrary initial condition. Treating \(\tau\) as a finite deadline at which steady state is reached; an exponential approaches its limit only asymptotically.

title: Euler's method: from the derivative definition to a stable step size
subtitle: Lecture 3 · Lecture3-Differential-Equations.pdf, p. 3
text: How does a discrete update approximate continuous dynamics, and why can step size determine stability as well as accuracy? The derivative definition gives \(dx/dt\approx [x(t+\Delta t)-x(t)]/\Delta t\). Substitute it into \(dx/dt=f(x,t)\) and evaluate the right-hand side at the current time to obtain forward Euler: \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t f(x_{n},t_{n})\). The method extends the current tangent by one step, so error arises because the true slope changes during that interval. Local error per step is usually of order \(\Delta t^{2}\); over a fixed total time, global error is of order \(\Delta t\). For \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\), Euler gives \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+(\Delta t/\tau )(-x_{n}+I)\). Define \(\alpha =\Delta t/\tau\) and \(y_{n}=x_{n}-I\) to obtain \(y_{n+1}=(1-\alpha )y_{n}\). The continuous deviation always decays smoothly; the discrete deviation is controlled by amplification factor \(a=1-\alpha\). Its magnitude shrinks only when \(|a|<1\). Solving \(|1-\alpha |<1\) gives \(0<\alpha <2\). For \(0<\alpha \le 1\), the deviation keeps its sign and approaches steady state monotonically. For \(1<\alpha <2\), it alternates sign while decaying. At \(\alpha =2\), its magnitude does not shrink; for \(\alpha >2\), it grows. This is a property of the algorithm, not the biology of the original differential equation. Choose the step size relative to the system's fastest time constant. To verify a numerical implementation, compare the Euler trajectory with a known exact solution at the same times and repeat the calculation with \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta t/2\). Roughly halving the error is consistent with a first-order method. Also check that the first array entry is the initial value, whether an update uses \(I_{n}\) or \(I_{n+1}\), and whether time and state arrays have matching lengths. These choices matter at segment boundaries. An Euler step is the current state plus the step size times the current slope. The stability interval for first-order decay is \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\); the monotonic interval is narrower. Doubling or halving the step size helps separate discretization error from model behavior. Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\), \(I=0\), and \(x_{0}=1\). For \(\Delta t=5\), 15, and 25 ms, calculate the first three updates and classify the behavior. 5 ms gives stable monotonic decay, 15 ms gives stable oscillatory decay, and 25 ms gives unstable divergence. Why does a discrete trajectory that alternates across steady state not immediately imply an oscillatory mechanism in the continuous system? This first-order continuous equation has only a real negative decay rate. Alternation may come from a negative Euler amplification factor. Reduce \(\Delta t\) and compare with the exact solution before calling it model dynamics rather than a numerical artifact. Accepting a trajectory because the program ran without error, without checking \(\Delta t\) relative to \(\tau\). Changing total duration or input sampling together with step size, making the error comparison uninterpretable.

title: Second-order oscillator, state space, and code-boundary audit
subtitle: Lecture 3 · Lecture3-Differential-Equations.pdf, p. \(4 \cdot  Lecture3_{\mathrm{Diff},\mathrm{Eq},\mathrm{MATLAB}}\).pdf, p. 1
text: How can a system involving “acceleration” be rewritten as first-order state updates, and how can we recognize artifacts introduced by a numerical method or piecewise code? The second-order equation \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) needs both position x and velocity \(v=dx/dt\) to determine the future. Defining v gives \(dx/dt=v\) and \(dv/dt=-x\), so state \(z=(x,v)^{\mathrm{T}}\) evolves in a two-dimensional plane. For the continuous system, \(E=(x^{2}+v^{2})/2\) has derivative \(x\cdot dx/dt+v\cdot dv/dt=xv-vx=0\). The trajectory is therefore a closed curve of fixed radius, not an inward or outward spiral. A physical oscillator must retain angular frequency \(\omega\). Under forward Euler, an energy-like quantity is multiplied by \(1+(\omega \Delta t)^{2}\) on every step. No finite \(\Delta t\) conserves it exactly, so a long simulation drifts outward. This does not mean Euler fails to converge: with total duration fixed and \(\Delta t\to 0\), cumulative amplification approaches 1 and the numerical trajectory approaches the continuous solution. Only after setting \(\omega =1\) and nondimensionalizing time can the factor be shortened to \(1+\Delta t^{2}\) as in the notes. The accompanying code also simulates a first-order system with \(\tau =0.01 \mathrm{s}\), step 0.001 s, and duration 0.250 s. Inputs are 0, 2, 1, a cosine, and 0 in sequence. Each update reads the previous input \(I(t-1)\), as expected for the current-time slope in explicit Euler. The final condition is `time<0.250`, but the time vector includes the endpoint 0.250 exactly. Consequently, \(I(end)\) remains NaN and the last input point is not plotted normally. That NaN does not immediately contaminate \(x(end)\), because the final state update reads \(I(end-1)\), not \(I(end)\). This demonstrates why “the output looks normal” does not prove that an array is complete. A second semantic error concerns \(t_{0}=0.150\) in \(\cos(\omega (t-t_{0}))\): this is a phase-reference time, so a comment calling it a frequency conflicts with its units. The actual frequency parameter is angular frequency \(\omega =220 \mathrm{rad}/s\). Audit comments, formulas, units, and indices together. A second-order system can be represented by two coupled first-order equations for position and velocity. Forward Euler multiplies an undamped oscillator's energy-like quantity by \(1+(\omega \Delta t)^{2}\) each step; only the nondimensional \(\omega =1\) form becomes \(1+\Delta t^{2}\). Array endpoints, strict inequalities, and use of a previous index jointly determine whether NaN propagates. The time vector is 0:0.001:0.250. The last input branch assigns 0 only when \(t<0.250\); all other values remain preallocated as NaN. How many time points exist, which one is NaN, and does it enter the final x update? There are 251 points, and \(I(251)\) is NaN. It does not enter the final explicit update here, but it exposes a gap in the boundary conditions. What two checks, at minimum, distinguish an outward spiral caused by the continuous model from one caused by the numerical method? First calculate a continuous invariant such as the energy derivative, or the system's eigenvalues. Then vary the step size and compare with an energy-preserving method or an exact solution. If continuous energy is constant while Euler energy grows, the artifact is localized. Interpreting a spiral in a phase portrait as damping or self-excitation before checking the discrete update matrix. Trusting variable comments without checking how the variable appears in equations and what units it carries. Missing the final array assignment because the time vector includes the right endpoint while the branch uses a strict inequality.

title: Lecture 4: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire
subtitle: How can ion diffusion, electric fields, and membrane structure be mapped to a circuit, and how does charge conservation produce integrate-and-fire dynamics?
text: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire How can ion diffusion, electric fields, and membrane structure be mapped to a circuit, and how does charge conservation produce integrate-and-fire dynamics? Concentration gradient → electrochemical equilibrium → Nernst potential → membrane capacitance / channels → Kirchhoff's law → IF / LIF Build a consistent sign convention from the definitions of force, potential energy, electric potential, and membrane voltage, and explain how a concentration gradient and an electric field jointly determine net ionic flux. Derive the Nernst equation from the electrochemical equilibrium of a single ion, handling the valence z, the inside-to-outside concentration ratio, temperature, and voltage sign correctly. Map the lipid membrane, ion channels, and applied current onto a capacitor, conductance–battery branches, and a current source, then derive the membrane equation from charge conservation. Distinguish the perfect integrate-and-fire model from the leaky integrate-and-fire model, and calculate their slopes, time constants, steady-state voltages, rheobase currents, and first-spike times. State what the equivalent circuit, integrate-and-fire model, and action-potential mechanism each retain and omit, without interpreting model components as literal biological parts. The neural membrane is both a capacitor that separates charge and a conductance network formed by ion-selective channels. Diffusion drives ions down concentration gradients, while the electric field drives charged particles toward lower electric potential energy. Their balance defines each ion's reversal potential. The circuit equivalent is not a decorative analogy: it combines charge conservation, Ohm's law, and channel selectivity into a solvable equation for membrane voltage. Treating an equilibrium potential as the cell's actual instantaneous membrane voltage. Forgetting the sign convention V_m=inside−outside. Applying a cation's sign intuition to Cl−. Conflating current direction, positive-charge motion, and voltage change. Assuming that ions cross the membrane through the capacitor branch; an ideal capacitor represents redistribution of charge on the two sides of the membrane. Treating threshold and reset as an action potential generated naturally by the LIF differential equation. This lecture stops at the LIF equation. Do not fold in Lecture 5's full closed-form LIF solution or HH gating dynamics prematurely, though a clear preview at the end is useful. Membrane-voltage sign convention Vm = \(\varphi _{\mathrm{in}} - \varphi _{\mathrm{out}}\) Inside minus outside Nernst equilibrium potential kB \(T [c]_{\mathrm{out}}\) Ec = ln qc \([c]_{\mathrm{in}}\) Single-ion equilibrium at fixed temperature Definition of capacitance \(Q = CV C\) is approximately constant Capacitive current \(I = C \dot{V}\) \(Q=CV\) Leak current IL = GL (V − EL ) Linear passive conductance Subthreshold LIF equation C V̇ = Ie − GL (V − EL ) Threshold and reset are specified separately F-I slope of the pure IF model Ie \(r= C(VT - VR )\) Constant current, no refractory period, and no leak membrane voltage Electric potential inside the cell minus electric potential outside the cell. diffusion Net random motion driven by a concentration gradient. electric potential energy The energy \(q\phi\) of a charged particle in an electric potential. equilibrium potential The voltage at which the net flux of one ion is zero. reversal potential The voltage at which current through a channel changes direction; in the simplest case, it equals the equilibrium potential. conductance The reciprocal of resistance, \(G=1/R\). capacitance Charge stored per unit voltage, Q/V. Kirchhoff current law The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving a node is zero. integrate-and-fire model An abstract model that integrates input, emits a spike at threshold, and resets. leaky integrator A state driven by input while exponentially relaxing toward a baseline. If \(V_{m}=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\), which side has the lower electric potential? On which side does a cation have lower electric potential energy? First use the voltage definition to order the electric potentials, then multiply by the sign of the charge to order potential energies. The ordering reverses for anions, so “negative inside” alone cannot determine the direction of every ion. The intracellular electric potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential. For a cation with \(q>0\), \(U=q\phi\), so its electric potential energy is also lower inside. Intracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration exceeds extracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration, and the Nernst equation uses \(\ln([K]_{\mathrm{out}}/[K]_{\mathrm{in}})\). Is the equilibrium potential positive or negative? The \(K^{+}\) concentration gradient drives efflux. Preventing net efflux requires a negative intracellular potential that attracts \(K^{+}\) inward, so the inside-minus-outside equilibrium potential is negative. Because \(z=+1\) and the concentration ratio is less than 1, the logarithm is negative; therefore \(E_{K}\) is negative. A membrane capacitor has \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\) and receives a constant inward current of 100 pA. Ignoring all ion channels, what is \(dV/dt\)? The \(10^{-12}\) factors in pA/pF cancel to give V/s, whose numerical value equals mV/ms. A constant current therefore produces a linear voltage ramp across an ideal capacitor. \(dV/dt=I/C=0.5 \mathrm{V}/s=0.5 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\). In a leaky integrate-and-fire model, \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). What minimum constant current places the subthreshold steady state exactly at threshold? At threshold, \(dV/dt=0\) requires the applied current to exactly balance the leak current. Because \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), any smaller current leaves the steady state below threshold. \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\). If \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of \(K^{+}\)? In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge. This is the distinction tested in Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium. Worked example — Calculate the \(K^{+}\) equilibrium potential at body temperature: Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM. The initial concentration ratio is \(5/140\approx 0.035714\), and \(\ln(0.035714)\approx -3.332\). \(E_{K}\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\cdot (-3.332)=-88.96 \mathrm{mV}\), or about −89 mV. After extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises, the ratio is \(10/140\approx 0.071429\) and its logarithm is ≈−2.639. The new value is \(E_{K}\approx 26.7\cdot (-2.639)=-70.46 \mathrm{mV}\), about 18.5 mV more positive than before—a depolarizing shift. In both cases \(c_{\mathrm{out}}<c_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(z>0\), so \(E_{K}\) must be negative. Raising the external concentration moves the ratio toward 1 and reduces the magnitude of the potential. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium”? Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium”? Nernst equilibrium is a zero-net-flux state in which chemical and electrical driving forces cancel. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From the Boltzmann ratio on the source page to the Nernst equation”? RT has units J/mol and F has units C/mol, so \(RT/F=J/C=V\). The concentration ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless; \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is measured in volts. If \(c_{\mathrm{out}}=c_{\mathrm{in}}\), the logarithm is zero and \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=0\). Increasing \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}\) for a cation makes \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) more positive. The ideal formula tends toward zero voltage as \(T\to 0\), but a physiological model is not valid at absolute zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: When an ion moves across a membrane down its concentration gradient, how does charge separation create an opposing electric field, and at what voltage does net flux vanish? The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. The first page introduces the electrical sign convention through \(F=-\nabla U\) and \(\phi =U/q\), then defines \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\). A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams. A concentration gradient supplies the diffusive drive. Suppose only \(K^{+}\) channels are open and \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}>[K]_{\mathrm{out}}\). Random motion produces net \(K^{+}\) efflux and leaves the inside relatively negative. As charge separation grows, the negative intracellular potential attracts \(K^{+}\) back inward. The chemical drive remains outward while the electrical drive points inward. At equilibrium, their contributions to the electrochemical-potential difference cancel, yielding zero net flux—not an end to microscopic ion exchange. Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach? It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\), which reduces the membrane time constant \(C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\); voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster. This is the distinction tested in The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL. Worked example — Instantaneous slope and steady state of a two-branch membrane: Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\). The outward leak current is \(10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+65)\mathrm{mV}=50 \mathrm{pA}\). The outward K current is \(20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+85)\mathrm{mV}=500 \mathrm{pA}\), so net inward current is \(300-50-500=-250 \mathrm{pA}\). Thus \(dV/dt=-250 \mathrm{pA}/200 \mathrm{pF}=-1.25 \mathrm{V}/s=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\), so voltage is falling at this instant. The steady-state numerator is \(300 \mathrm{pA}+10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-65 \mathrm{mV})+20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-85 \mathrm{mV})=300-650-1700=-2050 \mathrm{pA}\). Total conductance is 30 nS, so \(V^{*}=-2050/30 \mathrm{mV}\approx -68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(\tau =C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}=200 \mathrm{pF}/30 \mathrm{nS}\approx 6.67 \mathrm{ms}\). The steady state should reflect competition among the two branches after the current-induced shift. Substituting \(V=-68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) makes the total outward branch current approximately 300 pA. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL”? The lipid membrane maps to capacitance, ion channels to conductance, and concentration gradients to reversal-potential batteries. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL”? \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\) follows from \(Q=CV\) and \(I=dQ/dt\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\) follows from \(Q=CV\) and \(I=dQ/dt\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive the multichannel membrane equation from charge conservation”? C·dV/dt has units \(F\cdot V/s=C/s=A\), and G·(V−E) has units \(S\cdot V=A\), so every term can be added in one KCL equation. If all \(G_{x}=0\), the equation reduces to the ideal capacitor \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no finite steady state. If one \(G_{k}\) greatly exceeds all other conductances while \(I_{e}\) remains finite, \(V^{*}\) approaches \(E_{k}\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above? Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold. This is the distinction tested in From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire. Worked example — Compare subthreshold behavior and repetitive firing with the same parameters: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period. The membrane time constant is \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}=200 \mathrm{pF}/10 \mathrm{nS}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), and the rheobase is \(I_{T}=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\). At 100 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65 \mathrm{mV}+100 \mathrm{pA}/10 \mathrm{nS}=-55 \mathrm{mV}\), below −50 mV, so the trajectory never crosses threshold. At 200 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65+20=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), above threshold. The threshold-time ratio is \((V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})=20/5=4\). Therefore \(t_{sp}=20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot \ln 4\approx 20\cdot 1.3863=27.73 \mathrm{ms}\). Each reset returns to the same voltage under the same input, so every cycle has the same duration. Without a refractory period, \(f=1/0.02773 \mathrm{s}\approx 36.1 \mathrm{Hz}\). Because 200 pA is only slightly above the 150 pA rheobase, the rate should be finite and modest. Ignoring leak, perfect IF gives \(15 \mathrm{mV}/(1 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms})=15 \mathrm{ms}\), correctly predicting a faster crossing. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire”? Perfect IF ramps linearly under constant current; every positive current eventually produces a spike. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire”? The leak branch introduces \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The LIF rheobase current is \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “LIF steady state, rheobase, and first-spike time”? \(C/G_{L}\) has units \(F/S=s\); \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units \(A/S=V\); the logarithm contains a dimensionless ratio of voltage differences; \(t_{sp}\) is a time. As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\) from above, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T}\to 0\), \(t_{sp}\to \infty\), and firing \(\mathrm{rate}\to 0\). For very large \(I_{e}\), leak matters less during the short ramp and the result approaches the perfect-IF value \(C(V_{T}-V_{R})/I_{e}\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Current conservation in the membrane equivalent circuit”? Node conservation divides the applied current into two parts: C \(dV_{m}/dt\) changes the charge stored across the membrane, while \(\sum G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\) flows through ionic branches. \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage of a branch, and \(G_{x}\) sets how strongly that branch pulls \(V_{m}\) toward \(E_{x}\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “diffusion” mean in this lecture? diffusion: Net random motion driven by a concentration gradient. title: Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium
subtitle: Lecture 4 · Lecture4-Neurons1.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture4-Neurons1.pdf, p. 2
text: When an ion moves across a membrane down its concentration gradient, how does charge separation create an opposing electric field, and at what voltage does net flux vanish? The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. The first page introduces the electrical sign convention through \(F=-\nabla U\) and \(\phi =U/q\), then defines \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\). A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams. A concentration gradient supplies the diffusive drive. Suppose only \(K^{+}\) channels are open and \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}>[K]_{\mathrm{out}}\). Random motion produces net \(K^{+}\) efflux and leaves the inside relatively negative. As charge separation grows, the negative intracellular potential attracts \(K^{+}\) back inward. The chemical drive remains outward while the electrical drive points inward. At equilibrium, their contributions to the electrochemical-potential difference cancel, yielding zero net flux—not an end to microscopic ion exchange. For a dilute solution, the molar electrochemical potential of an ion is \(\mu =\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c+zF\phi\). This is equivalent to the single-particle Boltzmann form in the source: \(q_{c}=z e\), \(R=N_{Ak,B}\), and \(F=N_{Ae}\), so \(RT/(zF)=k_{\mathrm{BT}}/q_{c}\). At equilibrium, \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}=\exp(q_{c}E/k_{\mathrm{BT}})\); taking the logarithm gives \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_{\mathrm{out}}=(RT/zF)\ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\). For a cation, \(z>0\) preserves the logarithm's sign. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses it. An equilibrium potential is not the voltage that a membrane must have at every instant. It is the voltage at which the net current carried by one ionic species is zero. Away from \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\), current direction depends on the driving force \(V_{m}-E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) together with channel conductance. The source values—about +55 mV for \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), −75 mV for \(K^{+}\), +125 mV for \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), and −60 mV for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\)—are illustrative physiological values, not universal constants. Nernst potentials vary with concentration, temperature, and activity, while the actual \(V_{m}\) depends on multiple permeabilities and dynamic gating. This framework also explains the direction of an action-potential trajectory. Rapid Na⁺-channel opening pulls \(V_{m}\) toward the positive \(E_{\mathrm{Na}}\). \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) inactivation and a delayed rise in \(K^{+}\) conductance then pull \(V_{m}\) back toward \(E_{K}\), after which channel recovery and leak currents return the membrane to rest. Approaching a reversal potential does not instantaneously equalize ion concentrations: only a small fraction of the cellular ion reservoir crosses the membrane during one action potential. Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral. Nernst equilibrium is a zero-net-flux state in which chemical and electrical driving forces cancel. The sign of \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is set jointly by the definition \(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_{\mathrm{out}}\), the concentration ratio, and the signed valence z. A reversal potential is the zero-current voltage for one ionic branch, not the membrane voltage at every instant. Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM. Initially \(E_{K}\approx -89 \mathrm{mV}\); doubling extracellular \(K^{+}\) shifts \(E_{K}\) to ≈−70.5 mV. If \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of \(K^{+}\)? In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge. Mixing \([ion]_{\mathrm{in}}/[ion]_{\mathrm{out}}\) with \([ion]_{\mathrm{out}}/[ion]_{\mathrm{in}}\) without changing the sign to match the voltage convention. Using \(z=+1\) for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) and thereby obtaining an equilibrium potential with the wrong sign. Interpreting zero net flux as no microscopic exchange, or interpreting a reversal potential as equal concentrations.

title: The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL
subtitle: Lecture 4 · Lecture4-Neurons1.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture4-Neurons1.pdf, p. 4
text: How does each biological membrane feature map onto a circuit element, and how does charge conservation combine those elements into a membrane-voltage equation? The lipid bilayer separates conducting solutions and allows opposite charges to accumulate on its inner and outer surfaces, so it acts as a capacitor C. Ion channels provide selective conducting pathways; the number of open channels and their single-channel conductance combine into a conductance G. Each ion's concentration gradient sets a reversal potential E, represented by a battery in series with the conductance. An external electrode or synaptic input injects charge and is represented by a current source \(I_{e}\). This equivalent circuit preserves relationships among charge flow and voltage; it does not claim that the membrane contains metal components. For fixed C, \(Q=CV\) means that changing voltage requires changing surface charge. Differentiating gives \(dQ/dt=C dV/dt\), and the definition \(I=dQ/dt\) therefore gives \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\). Injecting 100 pA into a 200 pF capacitor produces a slope of 0.5 mV/ms. A capacitor alone does not set a steady state: as long as a nonzero constant net current persists, voltage continues to change linearly. Under a linear conductance approximation, an ionic branch obeys \(I_{x}=G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\). Net current is zero at \(V_{m}=E_{x}\), and the driving force grows with the distance from \(E_{x}\). \(G_{x}\) may be constant, as for a passive leak \(G_{L}\), or vary with voltage and time, as do \(G_{\mathrm{Na}}(t,V)\) and \(G_{K}(t,V)\) in the Hodgkin–Huxley model. The battery \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage; conductance determines the current produced by a given driving force. Apply Kirchhoff's current law at the membrane node: net current entering the capacitor equals applied current minus the outward ionic currents, giving C \(dV_{m}/dt=I_{e}-\sum _x G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\). Every term has units of current. A positive net sum deposits positive charge on the inner capacitor plate and raises \(V_{m}\); a negative sum lowers \(V_{m}\); a zero sum makes voltage momentarily stationary. This equation is the common backbone of the IF, LIF, and Hodgkin–Huxley models. The Hodgkin–Huxley equivalent circuit on the third page contains the membrane capacitor, a leak branch, and variable Na and K branches. Conductance changes during an action potential make those branches compete: increasing \(G_{\mathrm{Na}}\) pulls V more strongly toward \(E_{\mathrm{Na}}\), whereas increasing \(G_{K}\) pulls V toward \(E_{K}\). “Pull toward” does not mean setting voltage instantaneously to a reversal potential; capacitance and every other open branch determine the rate and trajectory. The lipid membrane maps to capacitance, ion channels to conductance, and concentration gradients to reversal-potential batteries. \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\) follows from \(Q=CV\) and \(I=dQ/dt\). KCL combines applied current and all ionic branches into one voltage-dynamics equation. Conductance sets the strength of attraction toward a reversal potential; capacitance sets how quickly voltage can change. Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\). At −60 mV, \(dV/dt=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\); the steady state is approximately −68.3 mV and the time constant is approximately 6.67 ms. Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach? It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\), which reduces the membrane time constant \(C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\); voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster. Memorizing C dV/dt without declaring current directions, then mixing sign conventions across ionic branches. Treating reversal potential E as if conductance created it. E comes from an electrochemical gradient; G sets current magnitude. Forgetting that \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), or reporting pA/pF as mV/s instead of V/s or mV/ms.

title: From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire
subtitle: Lecture 4 · Lecture4-Neurons1.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture4-Neurons1.pdf, p. 6
text: What firing behavior follows from threshold and reset alone, and why does adding a leak branch create a steady state, a rheobase current, and a nonlinear F–I curve? The perfect integrate-and-fire model retains capacitance C and applied current \(I_{e}\), with subthreshold equation \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\). A constant positive current produces a linear ramp with slope \(I_{e}/C\). When V reaches threshold \(V_{T}\), the model records a spike and resets V to \(V_{R}\). Spike times stand in for action potentials; the model does not reproduce waveforms generated by Na and K conductances. It converts input current into interspike intervals but has no resting attractor. Moving from \(V_{R}\) to \(V_{T}\) requires \(\Delta V=V_{T}-V_{R}\). Under constant current, the ramp time is \(\Delta t=C\Delta V/I_{e}\), so without a refractory period \(f=1/\Delta t=I_{e}/[C(V_{T}-V_{R})]\). Every \(I_{e}>0\) eventually produces a spike, so the perfect model has no positive rheobase current and its F–I curve rises linearly from the origin. Real neurons, by contrast, may remain at rest under a weak constant input. Adding a leak branch gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Leak grows with the displacement of V from \(E_{L}\) and always pulls voltage toward \(E_{L}\). With \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\), the equation becomes \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant input, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\); voltage approaches a finite steady state exponentially instead of rising without bound. Spiking requires \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) to lie above threshold. The boundary condition \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=V_{T}\) gives \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). If \(I_{e}\le I_{T}\), the steady state remains subthreshold and sustained current produces no periodic spikes. If \(I_{e}>I_{T}\), the exponential solution gives the travel time from \(V_{R}\) to \(V_{T}\). This threshold current emerges from the balance between input and leak; it is not an extra current rule inserted by hand. LIF still omits the action-potential waveform, channel gating, adaptation, and absolute refractoriness, but it links biophysical circuit elements to spike events. Compare models term by term: perfect IF and LIF both contain capacitance, threshold, and reset; only LIF contains \(E_{L}\), \(G_{L}\), a finite steady state, and a positive rheobase. Identifying the responsible term lets you interpret an F–I change as a mechanistic consequence. Perfect IF ramps linearly under constant current; every positive current eventually produces a spike. The leak branch introduces \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\). The LIF rheobase current is \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). Threshold and reset are event rules, not a simulation of the action-potential waveform. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period. At 100 pA, voltage approaches −55 mV without spiking. At 200 pA, the first interval is about 27.7 ms and the repetitive rate is about 36.1 Hz. Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above? Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold. Treating \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) as the voltage immediately after reset, or treating threshold \(V_{T}\) as a reversal potential. Applying the logarithmic crossing-time formula when \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\le V_{T}\) and assigning physical meaning to the resulting number. Mistaking the model's zero-width spike event for the voltage waveform of a biological action potential.

title: Lecture 5: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley
subtitle: How does exponential charging in an LIF neuron determine threshold crossing and its F-I curve, and how does the Hodgkin–Huxley model generate a real spike through dynamic conductances?
text: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley How does exponential charging in an LIF neuron determine threshold crossing and its F-I curve, and how does the Hodgkin–Huxley model generate a real spike through dynamic conductances? LIF ODE → steady state → threshold time → exact F-I relation → HH conductances → gating / refractory period Rewrite the LIF equation in time-constant–steady-state form and explain the exponential trajectory after a current step begins and ends. Derive the exact interspike interval and F–I curve of the LIF model from the threshold condition, and analyze behavior near rheobase and in the strong-input limit. Interpret current direction and maximal conductance in the leak, \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), and \(K^{+}\) branches of the Hodgkin–Huxley membrane equation. Derive a gating variable's steady state and time constant from the transition rates of a two-state channel, and explain activation, inactivation, and refractoriness. Explain how area normalization, multicompartment propagation, and cellular diversity extend a point-neuron model without confusing passive subthreshold decay with active action-potential regeneration. An LIF model treats each spike as a threshold-and-reset event, so its threshold-crossing time and firing rate can be derived analytically. The HH model instead explains the spike waveform through feedback among dynamic Na/K conductances. The two models answer different questions: LIF provides a tractable abstraction for networks and coding, whereas HH addresses ionic mechanisms and waveform shape. Membrane time constant, interspike interval, and refractory period must remain distinct. Confusing \(\tau _{m}\), the ISI, and refractory interval \(\delta\). Assuming that \(V_{\infty }=V_{T}\) leads to a threshold crossing in finite time; the voltage only approaches threshold asymptotically. Treating the threshold-linear F-I relation as the exact LIF result. Treating m, h, and n as numbers of ion channels. Forgetting that current=conductance×driving force; increasing a gate does not by itself determine current direction. Treating HH as the unique model of every neuron. Keep membrane time constant, interspike interval, and refractory period separate. Likewise distinguish channel activation probability, conductance, and ionic current. title: LIF time constant, steady state, and current-step response
subtitle: Lecture 5 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 3
text: How do capacitance and leak convert a constant current into an exponential voltage response, and why does voltage return to rest with the same time constant after the step ends? The first two pages rebuild the circuit from an ideal capacitor to a leaky integrate-and-fire membrane. An ideal capacitor obeys \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no steady state under constant current. Adding leak gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Above \(E_{L}\), outward leak current is positive and opposes further depolarization; below \(E_{L}\), current reverses and drives voltage upward. Thus \(E_{L}\) is the stable point with no input. Define \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) to write \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant current, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\). The solution contains its final target \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and an initial deviation that decays over time. After one \(\tau _{m}\), 36.8% of the deviation remains; after three \(\tau _{m}\), about 5% remains. At current-step onset, voltage cannot jump: a finite current cannot change the finite charge on a capacitor instantaneously. The initial slope is \([I_{e}-G_{L}(V_{0}-E_{L})]/C\). Starting from \(V_{0}=E_{L}\) makes initial leak zero and slope \(I_{e}/C\). As V rises, leak grows, net current falls, and the trajectory flattens. This curvature is the direct signature of competition between capacitive charging and leak. After the step ends at \(t_{\mathrm{off}}\), input becomes zero and the new steady state changes immediately to \(E_{L}\). Voltage itself remains continuous and takes its value at step offset as the new initial value, then decays as \(V(t)=E_{L}+[V(t_{\mathrm{off}})-E_{L}]e^{-(t-t_off)/\tau _{m}}\). Rise and recovery use the same \(\tau _{m}\) because C and \(G_{L}\) have not changed. Different experimental time constants imply at least one voltage-dependent conductance or changing parameter. \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) controls speed, while \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) sets the steady state under constant current. Capacitor voltage is continuous; a current step changes its slope immediately, not its value. With fixed C and \(G_{L}\), the onset and offset exponentials share one time constant. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\). Starting at rest, inject 100 pA for 40 ms, then remove it. Find voltage at 40 ms and again 20 ms later. Voltage is approximately −56.35 mV at pulse offset and −61.82 mV 20 ms after removal. If C and \(G_{L}\) both double, how do \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and \(\tau _{m}\) change? \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) remains unchanged. For the same total current \(I_{e}\), \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) is halved, so \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) moves closer to \(E_{L}\). If input also doubles in proportion to area, the steady-state offset can remain unchanged. Combining \(\tau _{m}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) into one parameter effect instead of distinguishing response speed from steady state. Forcing V to reset to \(E_{L}\) when current ends, which violates continuity of capacitor voltage.

title: Derive the exact F–I curve from threshold crossings
subtitle: Lecture 5 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 4
text: How does constant current become firing rate through an exponential threshold-crossing time, and why do the near-threshold and strong-input regimes have different shapes? After each spike, reset voltage to \(V_{R}\). With constant input and no additional state variables, each subthreshold trajectory repeats the previous cycle. Threshold can be crossed only if \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\). The critical current follows from \(E_{L}+I_{T}/G_{L}=V_{T}\): \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). At or below this value, voltage approaches a subthreshold steady state asymptotically and firing rate is zero. Set \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{R}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\) equal to \(V_{T}\) to obtain period \(\Delta t=\tau _{m} \ln[(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})]\) and frequency \(f=1/\Delta t\). This relation is not linear. As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\), the denominator voltage difference approaches zero and \(\Delta t\) diverges. At larger \(I_{e}\), the period shortens and approaches the linear strong-input approximation of a perfect integrator. Add an absolute refractory period \(\delta\): after each spike, no integration occurs during a fixed wait, so total period is \(\delta +\Delta t\) and \(f=1/(\delta +\Delta t)\). For very large input, \(\Delta t\to 0\) and firing rate approaches \(1/\delta\) instead of increasing without bound. This is a falsifiable limit. A model with no refractory period cannot consistently claim a finite maximum rate. The notes also introduce the common biased threshold-linear approximation \(f\approx [wI+b]_{+}\). It can summarize an F–I curve over a limited operating range, but it does not preserve the logarithmic onset near rheobase and does not generate \(1/\delta\) saturation automatically. Report the fitted range and determine w and b from the exact curve or data; do not mistake the approximation for the exact LIF solution. LIF fires periodically only when \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), equivalently \(I_{e}>I_{T}\). The exact period contains the natural logarithm of a ratio of voltage differences. The refractory period limits the strong-input firing rate to \(1/\delta\). A threshold-linear F–I curve is a local approximation and does not retain the full dynamics. Let \(\tau _{m}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(\delta =2 \mathrm{ms}\). For \(I_{e}=200 \mathrm{pA}\), calculate \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), charging time, total period, and firing frequency. \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), charging time 27.73 ms, total period 29.73 ms, and frequency approximately 33.6 Hz. Why can a complex or negative time returned by the crossing formula when \(I_{e}<I_{T}\) not be interpreted as an unusual form of spiking? The derivation assumes \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), making the logarithmic ratio a positive number greater than 1. At a subthreshold steady state, the trajectory never crosses threshold; an expression outside its domain simply signals that the assumption failed. Applying the logarithmic formula without first checking \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\). Confusing charging time with total period and omitting the absolute refractory interval. Interpreting the intercept of a threshold-linear approximation as one specific biological membrane parameter.

title: Hodgkin–Huxley gating, area normalization, and spatial propagation
subtitle: Lecture 5 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 6 · Lecture5-Neurons2.pdf, p. 7
text: How do variable ionic conductances produce action potentials and refractory periods, and how does a point-neuron equation extend across membrane area and axonal space? The Hodgkin–Huxley membrane equation is \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})-\bar{G}_\mathrm{Na} m^{3}h(V-E_{\mathrm{Na}})-\bar{G}_K n^{4}(V-E_{K})\). \(\bar{G}\) is maximal conductance when every relevant gate is open; \(m^{3}h\) and \(n^{4}\) are open fractions. Each branch still has the form “conductance × driving force,” but voltage-dependent gating variables now modulate conductance dynamically. A two-state gate n obeys \(dn/dt=\alpha _{n}(V)(1-n)-\beta _{n}(V)n\). The first term is closed fraction times opening rate; the second is open fraction times closing rate. Rearranging gives \(dn/dt=-(\alpha +\beta )n+\alpha\). Define \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\) and \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) to obtain \(\tau _{n} dn/dt=-n+n_{\mathrm{inf}}\). At fixed voltage, n approaches that voltage's steady-state open fraction exponentially. During the action-potential upstroke, rapid growth of Na activation m produces inward Na current and positive feedback. Na inactivation h falls with depolarization while K activation n rises more slowly; together they terminate the upstroke and repolarize the membrane. After a spike, h has not recovered and n remains elevated, making another depolarization difficult. This is the kinetic origin of refractoriness. It differs from the fixed \(\delta\) imposed in LIF, although \(\delta\) can approximate its rate-limiting effect. To compare cell sizes, substitute \(C=c_{m}A\), \(\bar{G}_x=\bar{g}_xA\), and \(I=iA\) and divide by A to obtain an area-normalized membrane equation. Doubling area while keeping current density and channel density fixed leaves voltage dynamics unchanged. Keeping total injected current fixed gives a larger cell lower current density and a smaller voltage response. State whether an experiment controls total current or current density. A single-compartment model assumes uniform voltage throughout the cell. A multicompartment model writes one membrane equation per segment and couples neighbors by axial currents. Passive subthreshold perturbations decay with distance because axial current continually leaks across the membrane. An action potential, however, activates voltage-gated Na channels in the next segment and regenerates. Different combinations of channel type, density, morphology, and time constant produce diverse firing patterns, while charge conservation and gating logic remain reusable. HH current still equals conductance times driving force; gating variables regulate the instantaneous conductance. \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\) sets speed, while \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) sets the target at fixed voltage. Na activation, Na inactivation, and delayed K activation together generate the action potential and refractory period. Area normalization separates total parameters from densities; multicompartment coupling separates passive decay from active regeneration. At a fixed voltage, \(\alpha =0.3 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), \(\beta =0.1 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), and \(n(0)=0.2\). Find \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\), \(\tau _{n}\), n after 5 ms, and the change in \(n^{4}\). \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=0.75\), \(\tau _{n}=2.5 \mathrm{ms}\), \(n(5 \mathrm{ms})\approx 0.676\), and \(n^{4}\) rises from 0.0016 to about 0.208. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both double, why does \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\) remain fixed while \(\tau _{n}\) is halved? Steady state depends only on the ratio \(\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\), so the common factor cancels. The time constant is the reciprocal of total transition rate; doubling both rates halves the relaxation time. Treating m, h, and n as currents or voltages instead of gate-open fractions between 0 and 1. Judging current magnitude from reversal potential alone while ignoring an instantaneous gated conductance that may be nearly zero. Mixing total current, total conductance, and per-area density when comparing cells of different membrane area.

title: Lecture 6: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood
subtitle: How can trial-to-trial spike variability be expressed as a Poisson encoding model, and how can a stimulus be decoded from the population likelihood?
text: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood How can trial-to-trial spike variability be expressed as a Poisson encoding model, and how can a stimulus be decoded from the population likelihood? Stimulus / task → voltage → spikes → raster / PSTH → Poisson variability → encoding \(P(n|s) \to  MLE\)/ Fisher information Explain how the analysis moves from the mechanisms that generate action potentials to observable spike sequences, and identify which single-cell details are retained or averaged away in a coding analysis. Interpret the stimulus, MT recording, spike train, raster, and PSTH in a random-dot motion experiment, and calculate firing rates by hand from raw counts. Use the Fano factor and the coefficient of variation of interspike intervals to distinguish count variability from interval variability, and state the statistical object measured by each. Derive the window-count and waiting-time distributions of a homogeneous Poisson process, and explain how a constantly driven LIF neuron differs from Poisson spiking. Write the likelihood, log-likelihood, maximum-likelihood estimate, and Fisher information for a population of independent Poisson neurons, and relate likelihood curvature to estimation uncertainty. Neural encoding requires more than drawing a tuning curve: it specifies the full response distribution conditional on the stimulus. A Poisson model jointly predicts count variance≈mean, exponential ISIs, and independent increments. These are testable assumptions, not universal facts. A population likelihood multiplies the evidence from neurons; the log-likelihood turns that product into a sum, and its curvature connects decoding precision to Fisher information. Treating firing rate as a continuous signal measured directly by the electrode. Treating a raster, a count, a PSTH, and a rate as the same object. Concluding that a spike train is fully Poisson merely because \(\mathrm{Fano}\approx 1\). Ignoring observation window T and thereby confusing the units of rate and count. Reversing \(P(n|s)\) and \(P(s|n)\). Assuming independence in a population likelihood without stating it. Firing rate is not a directly observed continuous signal; it is generally a statistical model quantity or estimate. Neuropixels and head-direction-cell data are useful transfer examples, while MT remains the original example. Fisher information Local sensitivity of a probability distribution to a small parameter change. A 20 ms PSTH bin contains a total of 8 spikes across 10 trials. What is the firing rate in that bin? The PSTH denominator includes both the number of trials and the bin width. Dividing only by 20 ms would yield a rate based on the count pooled across trials, not the mean rate per trial. The total observation time is \(10\times 0.020=0.20 \mathrm{s}\), so the rate is \(8/0.20=40 \mathrm{Hz}\). At a fixed stimulus, the count mean is 4 and the variance is 6. What is the Fano factor, and how should it be interpreted relative to a Poisson process? Slow state changes, uncontrolled stimulus variables, correlated inputs, and nonstationary rates can all increase count variance. Distinguishing them requires additional experiments or model comparisons. \(\mathrm{Fano}=6/4=1.5\), which is above the Poisson reference value of 1 and is called overdispersion. This number alone does not identify the underlying mechanism. A homogeneous Poisson process has rate \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\). What is the probability of observing zero spikes in \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\)? Window counts follow \(a \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda )\) distribution, where \(\lambda\) must equal rate times time. Exponential waiting times and Poisson window counts are two views of the same process. \(\lambda =rT=2\), so \(P(N=0)=e^{-2}\approx 0.1353\). A deterministic LIF neuron receives constant current and is reset to the same \(V_{R}\) after every spike. Why does it not naturally generate exponentially distributed ISIs? The Poisson assumption is a statistical model of event generation; it does not follow automatically from the use of an integrate-and-fire neuron. Every cycle has the same initial value, input, and dynamics, so threshold is crossed after a fixed time and the ISI is nearly constant. Random ISIs require stochastic input, a fluctuating threshold, or another source of noise. Why does an accurate count model not establish that precise spike timing contains no additional information? It establishes only that counts suffice for the chosen task. To determine whether timing adds predictive information beyond counts, compare the count model with a model that retains timing on independent data. This is the distinction tested in From channel dynamics to coding observables. Worked example — Checking a proposed firing rate against the refractory period: A neuron has an absolute refractory period of at least 2 ms. A model predicts a mean of 80 spikes in a 100 ms window. Use an upper-bound calculation to decide whether the prediction is possible. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A neuron has an absolute refractory period of at least 2 ms. A model predicts a mean of 80 spikes in a 100 ms window. Use an upper-bound calculation to decide whether the prediction is possible. An absolute refractory period of 2 ms means adjacent spikes must be separated by at least 0.002 s. The idealized maximum sustained rate is \(1/0.002=500 \mathrm{Hz}\). In 100 ms, the neuron can emit at most about \(0.1\times 500=50\) spikes. Conventions about the endpoints of the window can change this by only about one event. A predicted mean of 80 already exceeds the physical maximum, so the model is missing an essential constraint even before it is fit to data. Shortening the window should reduce the maximum event count in direct proportion to its duration. Because 100 ms is one tenth of 1 s, its upper bound is about one tenth of the per-second bound. Refractoriness and the history of gating variables impose physiological bounds on spike statistics. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. These mechanisms constrain observable spike sequences: the absolute refractory period imposes a lower bound on adjacent interspike intervals, recovery of gating variables introduces history dependence, and conductances and morphology shape the stimulus-to-spike transformation. Thus, even a coding model that uses only counts cannot permit unbounded firing rates or negative counts. Compressed mechanisms remain present as boundary conditions on the statistical description. The second source page reviews parameters per unit area, axonal propagation, and cell diversity. Applying the same total current to cells with different areas produces different current densities, while different channel combinations produce tonic, bursting, or adapting response patterns. If multiple cell types are pooled into one “average neuron” category, count variance may reflect differences among cell types rather than intrinsic randomness within a cell. Experimental grouping is therefore a necessary step before specifying a probabilistic model. Why can concatenating all trials into one long spike train before making a histogram conceal important structure? Concatenation discards alignment to each stimulus onset and the identity of each trial. It can no longer separate time-locked changes in the mean, trial-to-trial count variability, and slow state drift, and it may create artificial intervals at concatenation boundaries. This is the distinction tested in Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability. In a separate analysis of the full 200 ms window, the ten trial counts are \([1,2,3,2,2,1,4,2,1,2]\). Calculate the bin rate, the mean full-window count, the variance defined with 1/K, and the Fano factor. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Across 10 trials, one 20 ms bin contains a total of 8 spikes. In a separate analysis of the full 200 ms window, the ten trial counts are \([1,2,3,2,2,1,4,2,1,2]\). Calculate the bin rate, the mean full-window count, the variance defined with 1/K, and the Fano factor. The bin's total exposure time is \(10\times 0.020=0.20 \mathrm{s}\), so its PSTH rate is \(8/0.20=40 \mathrm{Hz}\). The full-window counts sum to 20, so \(\mu =20/10=2\). The squared deviations from the mean are \([1,0,1,0,0,1,4,0,1,0]\), whose sum is 8. Using 1/K gives variance \(8/10=0.8\). \(\mathrm{Fano}=0.8/2=0.4\), below the Poisson reference. An unbiased sample variance would instead use denominator K−1, so the convention must be reported. An average of 2 spikes over the full 200 ms window corresponds to 10 Hz. This does not conflict with a 40 Hz instantaneous bin because the PSTH can vary over time. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability”? A raster retains individual-trial events; a PSTH estimates the time-varying rate averaged across trials. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability”? The PSTH denominator is trial count times bin duration in seconds, giving a result in Hz. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The PSTH denominator is trial count times bin duration in seconds, giving a result in Hz. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Constructing a PSTH rate estimate from total bin counts”? Counts are dimensionless, so division by \(K\Delta t\) gives \(s^{-1}=\mathrm{Hz}\). The standard-deviation expression also reduces to Hz. As K grows, fluctuations in the estimate shrink as \(1/\sqrt K\). Making \(\Delta t\) too small leaves most bins empty and increases variance, although temporal resolution improves. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does taking the logarithm of a product of likelihood terms leave the location of the maximum-likelihood estimate unchanged? The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on positive numbers, so it preserves the ordering of candidate likelihoods. Taking logs only changes products into sums and improves numerical stability; it does not change the maximizer. This is the distinction tested in Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature. Worked example — Estimating a constant Poisson rate from repeated counts: The same condition is presented 5 times. Each trial lasts \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\), and the counts are \([1,3,2,0,4]\). Assuming a shared constant Poisson rate r, find its maximum-likelihood estimate and the probability of zero spikes in one 0.2 s window. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The same condition is presented 5 times. Each trial lasts \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\), and the counts are \([1,3,2,0,4]\). The total count is \(1+3+2+0+4=10\), and the total exposure is \(5\times 0.2=1.0 \mathrm{s}\). Because the total observation time is exactly 1 second and the total count is 10, the intuitive count rate is 10 Hz. With \(\lambda =2\), the zero-count probability should be less than \(e^{-1}\).
