title: From channel dynamics to coding observables
subtitle: Lecture 6 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 2
text: When the question changes from “How are spikes generated?” to “What do spikes represent?”, which mechanisms still constrain the code, and which details can temporarily be compressed? The first source page reviews Na activation, Na inactivation, K activation, and the refractory period. These mechanisms constrain observable spike sequences: the absolute refractory period imposes a lower bound on adjacent interspike intervals, recovery of gating variables introduces history dependence, and conductances and morphology shape the stimulus-to-spike transformation. Thus, even a coding model that uses only counts cannot permit unbounded firing rates or negative counts. Compressed mechanisms remain present as boundary conditions on the statistical description. The second source page reviews parameters per unit area, axonal propagation, and cell diversity. Applying the same total current to cells with different areas produces different current densities, while different channel combinations produce tonic, bursting, or adapting response patterns. If multiple cell types are pooled into one “average neuron” category, count variance may reflect differences among cell types rather than intrinsic randomness within a cell. Experimental grouping is therefore a necessary step before specifying a probabilistic model. A coding problem must define the stimulus variable s and response variable n. The stimulus s might be motion direction, coherence, or sound frequency; n might be a single-window count, a complete spike train, or a vector of counts across neurons. Different choices retain different information. Keeping only the total count over 200 ms prevents testing whether the stimulus mainly alters precise within-window timing; retaining every event time increases both model complexity and data requirements. Moving from a mechanistic model to a statistical model does not declare channel details “unimportant”; it marginalizes them for a specified task and timescale. Once spikes can be detected reliably, for example, event times can replace action-potential shape, and a conditional firing rate can summarize fast intracellular variables. If the statistical law fails systematically, return to the mechanistic level to investigate refractory effects, adaptation, common input, or nonstationary stimuli. Productive analysis moves back and forth between these levels. Refractoriness and the history of gating variables impose physiological bounds on spike statistics. The response can be represented by counts, event times, or population vectors; that choice determines which questions can be answered. A statistical model is a task-directed compression of mechanistic variables, not a denial that those mechanisms exist. A neuron has an absolute refractory period of at least 2 ms. A model predicts a mean of 80 spikes in a 100 ms window. Use an upper-bound calculation to decide whether the prediction is possible. 80 spikes/100 ms equals 800 Hz, exceeding the approximately 500 Hz upper bound imposed by a 2 ms refractory period. Why does an accurate count model not establish that precise spike timing contains no additional information? It establishes only that counts suffice for the chosen task. To determine whether timing adds predictive information beyond counts, compare the count model with a model that retains timing on independent data. Compressing each action-potential waveform to an event and then claiming that the model explains channel dynamics. Mistaking variance caused by pooling cell types or stimulus states for intrinsic randomness under a fixed condition.

title: Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability
subtitle: Lecture 6 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 4
text: How can repeated extracellular voltage recordings be converted into a time-dependent mean response without erasing variability across trials? A random-dot motion stimulus controls motion direction and coherence: some dots move together while the rest move randomly. When recording an MT neuron, an extracellular electrode measures fast voltage waveforms that are converted into spike times by a consistent detection rule. Motion direction, coherence, recording window, and behavioral task are all conditioning variables. If they change across trials, the spikes cannot simply be pooled into one “average response.” Each row of a raster represents one trial, each tick represents one spike, and the horizontal axis is time relative to stimulus onset. A raster displays both mean temporal structure and trial differences. If many rows become denser around 100 ms after stimulus onset, the conditional rate has increased during that period; variation in event counts and times across rows shows that repeated responses are not deterministic trajectories. A raster is not a rate curve: visual density must be converted to a normalized count before experiments can be compared. A PSTH partitions time into bins, totals the spikes in each bin across all trials, and divides by the number of trials K and bin width \(\Delta t\): \(\hat{r}_{b}=N_{b}/(K\Delta t)\). It estimates the trial-averaged rate under that condition. Narrow bins localize fast changes but have small, noisy \(N_{b}\) values; wide bins are smoother but mix distinct temporal phases. Choose and report a bin width that matches the timescale of the hypothesis being tested. Trial-to-trial variability can be quantified in a fixed window using the count \(\operatorname{mean} \mu _{N}\) and variance \(\sigma _{N}^{2}\), with Fano \(\mathrm{factor}=\sigma _{N}^{2}/\mu _{N}\). The Poisson reference is 1; values greater than 1 are relatively overdispersed, and values less than 1 are relatively regular. The Fano factor changes with window length, stimulus alignment, and latent state, so it should never be reported without its condition. Plot the count distribution as well, because identical means and variances can arise from very different tails or mixture structures. A raster retains individual-trial events; a PSTH estimates the time-varying rate averaged across trials. The PSTH denominator is trial count times bin duration in seconds, giving a result in Hz. The Fano factor compares count variance with count mean, but its interpretation depends on a fixed condition and window. Across 10 trials, one 20 ms bin contains a total of 8 spikes. In a separate analysis of the full 200 ms window, the ten trial counts are \([1,2,3,2,2,1,4,2,1,2]\). Calculate the bin rate, the mean full-window count, the variance defined with 1/K, and the Fano factor. PSTH-bin rate: 40 Hz; window-count mean: 2; variance: 0.8; Fano factor: 0.4. Why can concatenating all trials into one long spike train before making a histogram conceal important structure? Concatenation discards alignment to each stimulus onset and the identity of each trial. It can no longer separate time-locked changes in the mean, trial-to-trial count variability, and slow state drift, and it may create artificial intervals at concatenation boundaries. Dividing a PSTH only by bin width and omitting trial count, thereby inflating the rate by a factor of K. Entering 20 ms as 20 s, producing a factor-of-1000 unit error. Examining only the smooth PSTH average and ignoring the trial distribution visible in the raster.

title: Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature
subtitle: Lecture 6 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 6 · Lecture6-Neurons3-NeuralCoding1.pdf, p. 7
text: When neural responses are stochastic, how can a decoder be built from stimulus-conditional distributions, and how does likelihood curvature quantify the precision with which the stimulus can be localized? A homogeneous Poisson point process assumes that the probability of one event in any very short interval dt is approximately r dt, disjoint intervals are independent, and the probability of two or more events is of higher order. It follows that the count N in a window of length T is Poisson with \(\operatorname{mean} \lambda =rT\). The probability that a waiting time exceeds t is the probability of no preceding event, \(e^{-rt}\), so the ISI density is r \(e^{-rt}\). Its mean and standard deviation are both 1/r, giving \(CV=1\). An encoding model should specify the conditional distribution \(P(n|s)\), not merely a mean relation \(n=f(s)\). For MT neuron i, a tuning curve \(f_{i}(\theta )\) can specify the mean rate at direction \(\theta\), with \(N_{i}|\theta \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(f_{i}(\theta )T)\) in a window T. Two directions may produce the same mean in one neuron and therefore be ambiguous; a population with different preferred directions can break this degeneracy through its joint response. If neurons are conditionally independent given \(\theta\), the population likelihood is a product of neuron-wise terms. Its log-likelihood is ℓ(θ)=Σ_i[N_i ln(f_i(θ)T)−f_i(θ)T−ln(N_i!)]. The maximum-likelihood estimate \(\theta _{\mathrm{hat}}\) is the direction under which the observed counts are most probable. Factorial terms that do not depend on \(\theta\) may be omitted when finding the maximum, but they still matter when calculating normalized probabilities or comparing different datasets. Near the true \(\theta _{0}\), the log-likelihood can be approximated by a downward-opening quadratic. Fisher information is the negative expected second derivative, \(J(\theta )=-E[\ell ''(\theta )]\). A large J means a sharp peak and good discrimination among nearby directions. Under regularity conditions and with large samples, the maximum-likelihood estimate is approximately normal with variance about 1/J. This is an asymptotic scaling relation; with finite data, use repeated simulation or bootstrap analysis to examine bias and tails. Poisson spiking is a useful baseline, not a default truth. Real neurons have refractory periods, adaptation, nonstationary rates, and correlations across neurons, all of which violate independent homogeneous assumptions. A useful diagnostic sequence proceeds from single-unit count distributions and ISI survival curves to Fano/CV measures and population noise correlations. The form of model failure should guide revision, instead of using a more complicated distribution to conceal inadequate experimental control. A homogeneous Poisson process produces both Poisson window counts and exponential ISIs. An encoding model specifies \(P(n|s)\); decoding holds the response fixed and compares likelihoods across s. For an independent population, the log-likelihood is the sum of the evidence contributed by individual neurons. Fisher information is expected negative curvature, and asymptotic estimation variance is approximately its reciprocal. The same condition is presented 5 times. Each trial lasts \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\), and the counts are \([1,3,2,0,4]\). Assuming a shared constant Poisson rate r, find its maximum-likelihood estimate and the probability of zero spikes in one 0.2 s window. The maximum-likelihood rate is 10 Hz; the model assigns a probability of about 13.5% to zero spikes in one window. Why does taking the logarithm of a product of likelihood terms leave the location of the maximum-likelihood estimate unchanged? The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on positive numbers, so it preserves the ordering of candidate likelihoods. Taking logs only changes products into sums and improves numerical stability; it does not change the maximizer. Interchanging \(P(n|s)\) and \(P(s|n)\) without specifying a prior or normalization. Declaring that all assumptions of an independent homogeneous Poisson process hold merely because \(\mathrm{Fano}\approx 1\) and \(CV\approx 1\). Applying the Fisher-information formula directly near \(f_{i}(\theta )=0\) without checking regularity and differentiability.

title: Lecture 7: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes
subtitle: How does the Fisher information of a population code grow with neuron count and observation time, and how do correlated noise, bias, and a prior alter decodable precision?
text: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes How does the Fisher information of a population code grow with neuron count and observation time, and how do correlated noise, bias, and a prior alter decodable precision? Population likelihood → Fisher information → CRLB → noise covariance → information limitation → bias–variance tradeoff Explain how a population with diverse preferred directions resolves ambiguities in single-neuron tuning, and write the population Poisson likelihood. Derive Fisher information from the population log-likelihood, distinguishing the contributions of neuron count N, observation time T, and tuning-curve shape. State the assumptions of the Cramér–Rao lower bound and relate perceptual error to neural decoding precision without treating the bound as achieved performance. Calculate the variance of pooled correlated counts, use the inverse covariance matrix to explain harmful noise along the signal direction, and distinguish the existence of correlation from a limitation on information. Derive the bias–variance decomposition and explain how biased or Bayesian decoders can trade prior-induced bias for reduced variance. A single tuning curve often gives similar rates for multiple stimuli, but a population response pattern can resolve the ambiguity. Under ideal assumptions of independent Poisson neurons and uniformly distributed preferred directions, Fisher information grows linearly with N and T. Noise correlations, decoder mismatch, and behavioral constraints can make real-population performance saturate. A Bayesian prior trades a controlled bias for reduced variance. Treating the CRLB as the observed error of every decoder instead of a conditional lower bound. Assuming that positive correlation is always harmful and negative correlation is always beneficial. Conflating three levels: the encoding distribution, the decoding algorithm, and behavior. Automatically attributing saturation of Fisher information to one biological mechanism. Ignoring the modified bound for a biased decoder. Treating a prior as extra data instead of an assumption about stimulus frequency or structure. Keep three levels explicit: the neural encoding distribution, the decoder algorithm, and behavioral performance. The existence of correlation does not establish whether a particular decoder uses or ignores it. title: Population decoding and the N and T scaling of Fisher information
subtitle: Lecture 7 · Lecture7-NeuralCoding2.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture7-NeuralCoding2.pdf, p. 2
text: How do neurons with translated tuning curves jointly localize a stimulus, and why do adding neurons and lengthening the observation time increase information in the same way? A single bell-shaped tuning curve can give the same firing rate on either side of its peak, so count \(k_{i}\) may have equal likelihood under directions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Neuron i in a population has preferred direction \(\theta _{i}\) and tuning \(f_{i}(\theta )=f(\theta -\theta _{i})\). Although the two stimuli are degenerate for one neuron, they produce different count patterns across other neurons. The joint probability compares the entire pattern, allowing distributed preferences to resolve a single neuron's ambiguity. In a window T, the independent Poisson likelihood is Π_i[(f_i(θ)T)^{k_i}e^{−f_i(θ)T}/k_i!]. Taking the logarithm converts the product to a sum, whose derivative is the score. At the true \(\theta\), the negative expected second derivative contains terms with \(f_{i}''\) that vanish because \(E[k_{i}]=f_{i}T\), leaving \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i[f_{i}'(\theta )]^{2}/f_{i}(\theta )\). Each neuron's local evidence is nonnegative and the contributions add. Suppose N preferred directions \(\theta _{i}=2\pi _{i}/N\) are uniformly spaced on the circle and N is large. The sum can be approximated by a Riemann integral: \(\sum _i F(\theta _{i})\approx N\int _{0}^{2\pi }F(\vartheta )d\vartheta /(2\pi )\). Because every tuning curve is a translation of the same shape, a change of variables makes the integral independent of the current \(\theta\). Thus J equals N T times a constant determined only by tuning shape, and a uniform population has approximately equal local precision at all directions. For large samples, the maximum-likelihood estimate is approximately \(N(\theta _{0},1/J)\). Information therefore grows linearly with N and T, variance falls as 1/(NT), and standard deviation falls as \(1/\sqrt{NT}\). Observation time must be multiplied by four to halve the standard deviation. This scaling relies on independence and stable tuning; common noise, drift, and neural redundancy can alter additivity. If a model predicts that information grows without bound with N but behavioral or neural performance saturates, at least three explanations are possible: correlation structure is information-limiting, the recorded neurons do not represent the population actually read out, or the biological decoder is suboptimal. Saturation alone cannot select among these explanations; discriminating covariance and decoding experiments are needed. A population resolves single-neuron tuning ambiguity through the joint pattern of neurons with different preferred directions. Independent Poisson information is \(T\sum _i(f_{i}')^{2}/f_{i}\). For a large uniform population, replacing a sum with an integral gives \(J\propto NT\) and error standard deviation∝\(1/\sqrt{NT}\). Suppose the mean shape constant contributed by one uniformly tuned neuron is \(j_{f}=0.8 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}s^{-1}\). For \(N=100\) and \(T=0.5 \mathrm{s}\), calculate J and the asymptotic standard deviation; then increase N to 400. Increasing N from 100 to 400 raises J from 40 to 160 and lowers error standard deviation from about 9.1° to 4.5°. Why need a high firing rate at the peak of a tuning curve not contribute the greatest local Fisher information? The Poisson information term is \((f')^{2}/f\). Although f is large at the peak, the slope f' is generally zero, so the mean barely changes under an infinitesimal stimulus change and local information may be zero. Equating information with total spike count and ignoring tuning slope. Replacing a sum with an integral for a very small or nonuniform population without checking the approximation error. Inferring directly from \(J\propto N\) in an independent model that biological performance must improve without limit.

title: The CRLB, noise correlations, and information limits
subtitle: Lecture 7 · Lecture7-NeuralCoding2.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture7-NeuralCoding2.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture7-NeuralCoding2.pdf, p. 5
text: When do correlated fluctuations disappear through population averaging, and when do they persist along the signal direction and constrain every decoder? For a differentiable model with regular support and an unbiased estimator, the Cramér–Rao lower bound gives \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{s})\ge 1/J(s)\). It constrains any decoding method, not only maximum likelihood, but it does not guarantee attainability at finite sample size and does not directly apply to biased estimators. Comparing \(1/\sqrt J\) with a psychophysical discrimination threshold can test whether the recorded population contains enough information; it cannot prove that the animal uses an optimal readout. First distinguish two kinds of “correlation.” Signal correlation compares conditional means or tuning shapes across stimuli. Noise correlation fixes the stimulus and compares trial-wise deviations from each neuron's conditional mean. Only the latter enters the present pooling variance. Suppose the \(N_{R}\) residuals in a right-choice pool each have variance \(\sigma _{R}^{2}\) and every distinct pair has correlation \(c_{R}\). The variance of the pool average R is \(c_{R}\sigma _{R}^{2}+(1-c_{R})\sigma _{R}^{2}/N_{R}\). The independent component disappears as \(N_{R}\) grows, but the shared residual remains. This saturation of pooling demonstrates that correlations can limit a particular readout; it does not establish that optimal population information must also saturate. With a uniform correlation structure, simple averaging may discard discriminable differences along with noise, whereas an optimal linear or nonlinear decoder may exploit other directions. The fifth source page therefore distinguishes information-limiting correlations, models that saturate only for extremely large N, and performance saturation caused by a suboptimal decoder. More generally, suppose a count vector k at stimulus s is approximately Gaussian, \(N(\mu (s),C)\), and C is temporarily assumed independent of s. The stimulus-dependent part of the log-likelihood is \(-(k-\mu )^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}(k-\mu )/2\), and Fisher information is \(J=\mu '^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}\mu '\). This is Mahalanobis geometry: changes in the mean along high-noise eigen-directions are downweighted, while changes along low-noise directions are amplified. Information-limiting noise specifically means shared fluctuations that are indistinguishable from a change in the signal. For example, a noise component along \(\mu '(s)\) makes the population response appear as if the stimulus itself shifted slightly. Adding more similar neurons cannot readily average away that component. Neither positive nor negative correlation is a sufficient criterion. Compare the eigenvectors of the covariance with \(\mu '\), and keep biological information, the recorded subpopulation, and the actual decoder conceptually distinct. The CRLB is a variance lower bound under explicit regularity and unbiasedness assumptions, not an automatic equality with observed error. The variance of an equicorrelated pool average retains the \(c\sigma ^{2}\) term, so simple pooling can saturate as N grows. Under a Gaussian approximation, \(J=\mu '^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}\mu '\); the effect of correlation depends jointly on noise direction and signal direction. There are \(N=100\) similar neurons, each with count variance \(\sigma ^{2}=4\), and every pair has correlation \(c=0.1\). Calculate the variance of their pool average and compare it with the independent case. The correlated pool-average variance is 0.436, compared with 0.04 for the independent pool; most error comes from the 0.4 term that does not disappear with N. Why does saturation of performance in a simple left-versus-right pooling model not prove that the Fisher information of the full neural population saturates? Simple pooling uses only one projection of response space and may discard other decodable directions. To determine whether the population itself is information-limited, analyze the full covariance and mean derivative or compare stronger decoders. Calling every nonzero correlation an information-limiting correlation. Writing the CRLB as an equality achieved by every finite-sample estimator. Inverting a covariance matrix without checking sample size, positive definiteness, and the effect of regularization.

title: Biased decoding, bias–variance tradeoffs, and Bayesian priors
subtitle: Lecture 7 · Lecture7-NeuralCoding2.pdf, p. 6
text: When data are limited or stimuli have a well-defined prior, why can allowing estimates to favor common values reduce total error? At true stimulus \(s_{0}\), write the estimator's mean output as \(s_{e}=E[\hat{s}|s_{0}]\) and its bias as \(b(s_{0})=s_{e}-s_{0}\). Unbiasedness requires \(b=0\), but behavioral and neural estimates often show central bias, shrinkage, or category priors. Variance alone cannot evaluate a biased estimator: a decoder that always emits one constant has zero variance yet may be far from the truth. Use the mean-squared error \(E[(\hat{s}-s_{0})^{2}]\). Write the error as \((\hat{s}-s_{e})+(s_{e}-s_{0})\). After squaring and taking the expectation, the cross term is \(2bE[\hat{s}-s_{e}]=0\), so \(MSE=\operatorname{Var}(\hat{s})+b^{2}\). Thus, reduced variance can compensate for some bias. The best tradeoff depends on the true \(s_{0}\) and the loss function. A shrinkage estimator that improves mean MSE near common stimuli may incur greater bias for rare, extreme stimuli. The biased Cramér–Rao bound is \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{s})\ge [1+b'(s)]^{2}/J(s)\). If the estimator's mean response changes more slowly than the true stimulus, b' is negative and the variance bound may lie below the unbiased value 1/J; squared bias is the price. This bound still requires regularity conditions and is not a prescription for choosing a bias function. Compare full MSE or a task-relevant loss. A Bayesian decoder combines the likelihood of the current response with an environmental prior through \(P(s|n)\propto P(n|s)P(s)\). The MAP estimate maximizes \(\ell (s)+\ln P(s)\), whereas the posterior mean minimizes expected error under squared loss. When data are weak, the prior exerts more influence and pulls the estimate toward common stimuli. When the likelihood is sharp, the observation dominates the posterior. Bias induced by a prior can be a useful adaptation or a mismatch. If the experimental environment changes before the internal prior updates, estimates will be systematically drawn toward the old environment. Distinguishing prior effects from likelihood changes and readout noise requires manipulating stimulus frequency, response reliability, or training history; a single bias curve cannot identify a unique mechanism. \(MSE=\mathrm{variance}+squared\) bias; low variance alone does not imply accurate estimation. The biased CRLB includes the derivative of bias and permits response compression to exchange bias for lower variance. A Bayesian posterior is likelihood times prior; MAP and posterior mean correspond to different loss choices. For an observation X at true \(s_{0}=2\), suppose \(E[X]=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\). Compare the unbiased estimate \(\hat{s}=X\) with the shrinkage estimate \(\widetilde{s}=0.8X\) in terms of bias, variance, and MSE. At \(s_{0}=2\), 0.8X trades a bias of −0.4 for lower variance, reducing MSE from 1 to 0.8. Why does a reasonable Bayesian posterior usually depend less on the prior when data are highly reliable? Reliable data produce a sharp likelihood whose relative variation in the posterior product greatly exceeds that of a smooth prior. After normalization, probability concentrates near the likelihood peak, and the prior makes only a small correction. Comparing only estimator variance and failing to calculate squared bias. Treating MAP, posterior mean, and maximum likelihood as the same estimator. Inferring a specific prior from a behavioral bias without ruling out changes in the sensory likelihood or readout rule.

title: Lecture 8: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance
subtitle: How are discrete spike times converted into synaptic currents, and how do the mean, variance, and E/I balance scale differently in a large network?
text: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance How are discrete spike times converted into synaptic currents, and how do the mean, variance, and E/I balance scale differently in a large network? Spike-train δ-sum → kernel / convolution → coupled network → \(\operatorname{Poisson} E/I\) input → mean versus variance → failure of 1/N scaling Interpret the direction and shape of recurrent weights \(W_{ij}\) and input weights \(U_{ij}\), and explain their roles in coupled membrane equations. Distinguish excitation-dominated, inhibition-dominated, and balanced fluctuation-driven firing from voltage trajectories, and explain why dynamic balance does not mean that the current is exactly zero at every instant. The Dirac delta makes each spike time an integrable event, and convolution of a synaptic kernel with a spike train produces a continuous current. In the large-N limit, a proposed weight scaling must be checked for both mean and variance. Scaling as 1/N keeps the mean finite but suppresses fluctuations to zero. Balanced \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling lets large excitation and inhibition cancel in the mean while preserving \(O(1)\) fluctuations. Treating \(\delta (t)\) as an ordinary infinite number at \(t=0\). Reversing the time direction of \(K(t-t')\) and \(K(t')\) in a convolution. Forgetting to square the weight when calculating variance. Forgetting that inhibition contributes negatively to the mean but positively to the variance. Checking only mean scaling and not variance scaling. Interpreting E/I balance as exact equality of excitation and inhibition at every instant. The scaling derivations in this lecture are easy to distort by skipping steps. Calculate mean and variance separately and state the independence assumption explicitly. If \(W_{ij}\) denotes \(j\to i\) and the voltage vector of N network neurons is V, does the input to neuron i use row i or column i of W? Fixing receiver i while varying sender index j selects incoming connections. Transposing the convention would mistake outgoing connectivity for incoming connectivity. Neuron i receives input from every j, so it uses row i of W and sums along j. For spike train \(\Delta (t)=\delta (t-1)+\delta (t-3)\), what is the convolution \(K*\Delta\) at \(t=4\)? The sifting property of \(\delta\) converts a convolution integral into a sum over events. If the kernel is causal, future spikes make no contribution. It is \(K(4-1)+K(4-3)=K(3)+K(1)\): every preceding spike contributes the kernel evaluated at its elapsed time. There are N independent Poisson inputs, each with weight W. How do the mean and variance of the total input scale with N and W? Variance depends on squared weight. This is why the 1/N and \(1/\sqrt N\) scalings have different fluctuation limits. The mean scales as NW, the variance as \(NW^{2}\), and the standard deviation as √N|W|. Why do trial-to-trial fluctuations in Poisson input disappear as \(N\to \infty\) when \(W\sim 1/N\)? The downstream neuron receives an almost deterministic mean drive, so this limit is not ideal for producing Poisson-like irregular spiking. The total variance is \(NW^{2}\sim N/N^{2}=1/N\to 0\), even though the total mean remains finite because \(NW\sim 1\). Why should \(\delta (t_{k})\) not be treated as an infinite number that must be stored directly in code? \(\delta\) is defined by how it acts under integration. Numerical implementations usually store event indices and add a discrete kernel afterward, or approximate the event with area 1 in a finite bin. Storing infinity directly would break units and arithmetic. This is the distinction tested in Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution. Worked example — Superposition of exponential kernels from two spikes: Spikes occur at 1 ms and 3 ms. This example calculates only the kernel shape, using the dimensionless, peak-normalized causal kernel \(K(u)=e^{-u/2 ms}H(u)\); an external weight supplies the physical current amplitude. Find the dimensionless total kernel response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) and 4 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Spikes occur at 1 ms and 3 ms. This example calculates only the kernel shape, using the dimensionless, peak-normalized causal kernel \(K(u)=e^{-u/2 ms}H(u)\); an external weight supplies the physical current amplitude. Find the dimensionless total kernel response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) and 4 ms. At \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\), the delay from the 1 ms spike is 1 ms, contributing \(e^{-1/2}\approx 0.6065\). The 3 ms spike has not yet occurred and contributes 0. Thus the total response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) is approximately 0.6065. At \(t=4 \mathrm{ms}\), the two delays are 3 ms and 1 ms, contributing \(e^{-3/2}\approx 0.2231\) and \(e^{-1/2}\approx 0.6065\). Adding them gives \(0.2231+0.6065=0.8296\). After the second spike, the total response can rise; each individual exponential contribution is at most 1, its value at the event. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution”? The first index of \(W_{ij}\) is receiver i; the second is sender j. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution”? A \(\delta\) spike train is an event distribution that becomes an ordinary time process after convolution with a kernel. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The first index of \(W_{ij}\) is receiver i; the second is sender j. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Using the sifting property of \(\delta\) to reduce a convolution to a sum of kernels”? \(\Delta\) has units 1/s, while the convolution integral contributes dt' with units s, so \(K_{s}*\Delta\) has the same units as \(K_{s}\). Multiplication by W must then produce the current units required by the membrane equation. With no spikes, the sum is empty and the response is zero. As the kernel approaches \(\delta\), the convolution approaches the unsmoothed spike train. Responses add in amplitude when identical spikes coincide. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can a consistent index and convolution notation incorporate the complete spike history of every neuron into N coupled membrane equations? The network contains N interconnected neurons and M external inputs. \(W_{ij}\) is the recurrent weight \(j\to i\), and \(U_{ij}\) is the weight from external input j→network neuron i. For each i, the membrane equation contains leak, every network sender, and every external sender. Whether diagonal entries of W allow self-connections is a modeling choice. A network is recurrent when W contains feedback paths, not because of where nodes happen to be drawn. The spike train of neuron j is \(\Delta _{j}(t)=\sum _k\delta (t-t_{k}^{(j)})\). The area of \(\delta\) is 1, so for any smooth g, \(\int \delta (t-t_{k})g(t)dt=g(t_{k})\). Event times \(t_{k}\) are preserved while waveform details are omitted. If time is measured in seconds, \(\Delta\) has units \(s^{-1}\) and cannot be sampled directly as a finite current value. Why does inhibition enter the mean with a negative sign but still enter the independent variance with a positive sign? Variance measures squared deviations from the mean. Multiplication by −W only reverses the direction of a fluctuation; its squared magnitude remains \(W^{2}\), so independent uncertainty from both excitation and inhibition increases total variance. This is the distinction tested in Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input. Worked example — Fluctuations under 1/N scaling with ten thousand inputs: Let \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r_{E}=r_{I}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(W_{E}=W_{I}=1/N\) in arbitrary units. Calculate each population's mean magnitude, the net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r_{E}=r_{I}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(W_{E}=W_{I}=1/N\) in arbitrary units. Calculate each population's mean magnitude, the net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. \(W=1/10000=10^{-4}\). The mean of either population is NWr\(\Delta t=10000\cdot 10^{-4}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=0.01\). E/I symmetry makes the net \(\operatorname{mean} 0.01-0.01=0\). The variance of either population is \(N W^{2}\) \(r\Delta t=10000\cdot 10^{-8}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=10^{-6}\). Total variance is \(2\times 10^{-6}\), and standard deviation is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(2\times 10^{-6})\approx 0.001414\). Variance must remain positive even when E/I means cancel exactly. The standard deviation is about 14% of the single-population \(\operatorname{mean} 0.01\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input”? The E/I mean is a signed difference, whereas independent variances add through squared weights. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input”? With \(W\sim 1/N\), the mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(1/N)\), so stochastic fluctuations vanish at large N. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? With \(W\sim 1/N\), the mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(1/N)\), so stochastic fluctuations vanish at large N. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Mean and variance of convergent Poisson input”? If W is charge per spike, Q is charge. Because \(r\Delta t\) is dimensionless, the mean has units of charge and the variance has units of charge squared. When \(N_{E}=N_{I}\), \(W_{E}=W_{I}\), and \(r_{E}=r_{I}\), the mean is zero but the variance is the sum of two positive population contributions. As \(N\to \infty\) with \(W\sim 1/N\), this variance approaches zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is a net input mean near zero insufficient evidence that the network is in a strongly balanced state? Weak inputs can also give zero net mean. Strong balance additionally requires large separate E and I means that cancel at leading order, finite net variance, and the predicted scaling as connectivity changes. This is the distinction tested in Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking. Worked example — Balancing the same ten thousand inputs under \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling: Continue with \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), but set \(W=1/\sqrt N=0.01\). The E/I means are exactly equal. Calculate each population mean, net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Continue with \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), but set \(W=1/\sqrt N=0.01\). The E/I means are exactly equal. Calculate each population mean, net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. The mean of either population is \(10000\cdot 0.01\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=1\). By symmetry the net mean is \(1-1=0\), but each term is 100 times larger than its value 0.01 under 1/N scaling. The variance of either population is \(10000\cdot 0.01^{2}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=0.01\). Total variance is 0.02, and standard deviation is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(0.02)\approx 0.1414\), remaining finite to leading order as N changes. Changing from 1/N to \(1/\sqrt N\) makes a single weight 100 times larger and variance 10000 times larger, from \(2\times 10^{-6}\) to 0.02. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking”? \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\) keeps variance \(O(1)\) but makes the separate E and I means \(O(\sqrt N)\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking”? Balance cancels the leading-order mean while retaining instantaneous fluctuations; it is not zero current at every moment. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Recurrent feedback can dynamically adjust E/I rates and place a strongly coupled network in an irregular balanced state. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Finite variance and the balance condition under \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling”? a and N are dimensionless; \(w/\sqrt N\) inherits the units of a single-synapse weight. Mean and variance units are as in the preceding module. If the balance difference is a fixed nonzero constant, the net mean diverges as \(\sqrt N\). If the weights are changed to 1/N, the variance again approaches zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A strongly coupled network retains finite fluctuations after balance”? Under \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), the conditional means of excitatory and inhibitory input are each \(O(\sqrt N)\) and must cancel at leading order. Their instantaneous difference remains \(O(1)\), so net input is not zero at every instant and can continue to drive irregular spiking. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “Dirac delta” mean in this lecture? Dirac delta: A generalized function, or distribution, that samples a function under integration. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “convolution” mean in this lecture? convolution: An operation that shifts a kernel across the input history, weights it, and sums the result. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “synaptic kernel” mean in this lecture? synaptic kernel: The time-dependent response caused by one presynaptic spike. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “recurrent weight” mean in this lecture? recurrent weight: The connection strength from neuron \(j\to i\) within a network. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “input weight” mean in this lecture? input weight: The connection from an external input neuron→recurrent-network neuron. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “excitation-inhibition balance” mean in this lecture? excitation-inhibition balance: A state in which large excitatory and inhibitory currents approximately cancel in their means. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “dynamic balance” mean in this lecture? dynamic balance: Balance generated online by recurrent feedback rather than imposed as moment-by-moment equality. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “order of magnitude” mean in this lecture? order of magnitude: The leading scaling as N grows, such as \(O(1)\) or \(O(\sqrt N)\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term.
