title: Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution
subtitle: Lecture 8 · Lecture8-NeuralNetworks1.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture8-NeuralNetworks1.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture8-NeuralNetworks1.pdf, p. 3
text: How can a consistent index and convolution notation incorporate the complete spike history of every neuron into N coupled membrane equations? The network contains N interconnected neurons and M external inputs. \(W_{ij}\) is the recurrent weight \(j\to i\), and \(U_{ij}\) is the weight from external input j→network neuron i. For each i, the membrane equation contains leak, every network sender, and every external sender. Whether diagonal entries of W allow self-connections is a modeling choice. A network is recurrent when W contains feedback paths, not because of where nodes happen to be drawn. The spike train of neuron j is \(\Delta _{j}(t)=\sum _k\delta (t-t_{k}^{(j)})\). The area of \(\delta\) is 1, so for any smooth g, \(\int \delta (t-t_{k})g(t)dt=g(t_{k})\). Event times \(t_{k}\) are preserved while waveform details are omitted. If time is measured in seconds, \(\Delta\) has units \(s^{-1}\) and cannot be sampled directly as a finite current value. A synaptic kernel \(K_{s}(t)\) describes how current or conductance changes after one spike. The convolution \((K_{s}*\Delta _{j})(t)=\int K_{s}(t-t')\Delta _{j}(t')dt'\) reduces by the \(\delta\) property to \(\sum _kK_{s}(t-t_{k}^{(j)})\). A causal kernel is zero at negative times, so only past events \(t_{k}\le t\) contribute. Under a linear-synapse approximation, responses to overlapping events add directly. The coupled equation can be written compactly as C \(dV_{i}/dt=-G_{L}(V_{i}-E_{L})+\sum _jW_{ij}(K_{s}*\Delta _{j})+\sum _jU_{ij}(K_{s}*X_{j})\). Because \(\Delta _{i}\) is itself generated by the threshold–reset dynamics of \(V_{i}\), the system combines continuous voltage states with feedback through discrete events. A network trajectory is fully specified only after initial values, external spike trains, kernels, weights, and event rules are given. Convolution notation separates “sum over all past spikes” from “the time course after a spike,” so the kernel can be changed without altering network indices. It also exposes the linearity assumption. If synapses saturate, facilitate over the short term, or have inhibitory conductance that depends on V, a single fixed kernel and simple superposition may fail; additional synaptic state variables or conductance-based currents are then needed. The first index of \(W_{ij}\) is receiver i; the second is sender j. A \(\delta\) spike train is an event distribution that becomes an ordinary time process after convolution with a kernel. Network equations combine continuous membrane states with discrete feedback events generated by thresholds. Spikes occur at 1 ms and 3 ms. This example calculates only the kernel shape, using the dimensionless, peak-normalized causal kernel \(K(u)=e^{-u/2 ms}H(u)\); an external weight supplies the physical current amplitude. Find the dimensionless total kernel response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) and 4 ms. The response is approximately 0.6065 at 2 ms and 0.8296 at 4 ms. Why should \(\delta (t_{k})\) not be treated as an infinite number that must be stored directly in code? \(\delta\) is defined by how it acts under integration. Numerical implementations usually store event indices and add a discrete kernel afterward, or approximate the event with area 1 in a finite bin. Storing infinity directly would break units and arithmetic. Reading \(W_{ij}\) as \(i\to j\) and thereby transposing the direction of network connections. Allowing future spikes to affect the present state by using a noncausal kernel. Treating the height of \(\delta\) as a physical current amplitude and ignoring conventions for area and weight units.

title: Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input
subtitle: Lecture 8 · Lecture8-NeuralNetworks1.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture8-NeuralNetworks1.pdf, p. 5
text: When many independent Poisson inputs converge on one LIF neuron, how do the mean and fluctuations of total input scale, and why does keeping the mean finite make fluctuations disappear? Consider \(N_{E}\) excitatory inputs, each with rate \(r_{E}\) and weight \(W_{E}>0\), and \(N_{I}\) inhibitory inputs, each with rate \(r_{I}\) and magnitude \(W_{I}>0\) that is subtracted from total charge. Temporarily ignore kernel shape and let the count of each input during \(\Delta t\) be Poisson. Total charge is \(Q=\sum _E W_{E} K_{j}-\sum _I W_{I} K_{j}\). The sign affects the mean, but squared weights make excitatory and inhibitory fluctuations both contribute positively to variance. Using \(E[K]=\operatorname{Var}(K)=r\Delta t\) gives \(E[Q]=(N_{\mathrm{EW},Er,E}-N_{\mathrm{IW},Ir,I})\Delta t\). Independence gives \(\operatorname{Var}(Q)=(N_{\mathrm{EW},E}^{2}r_{E}+N_{\mathrm{IW},I}^{2}r_{I})\Delta t\). E/I contributions can cancel in the mean, but their variances cannot cancel merely because their signs differ. If inputs are correlated, pairwise covariance terms must be added and the independent formula may underestimate or otherwise alter the fluctuations. First try \(W_{E}\),\(W_{I}\sim 1/N\). Each population \(\operatorname{mean} N W\) remains \(O(1)\), so it does not diverge even without precise cancellation. But variance \(N W^{2}\sim 1/N\to 0\) and standard deviation∼\(1/\sqrt N\to 0\). Input to a large network becomes almost a deterministic mean current. A deterministic downstream LIF neuron then fires regularly if the mean is above threshold and remains silent if it is below, rather than preserving Poisson-like trial variability. This does not mean fluctuations are exactly zero at finite N; it means that they systematically shrink as connectivity grows. Kernel smoothing further averages rapid fluctuations in time without changing the essential appearance of squared weights in the variance. To identify the simulated limit, measure means and variances across several N values instead of inspecting a voltage trace at one network size. Same-sign independent input alone cannot keep both mean and fluctuations finite. \(W\sim 1/N\) preserves the mean but loses the variance, whereas \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\) preserves the variance but makes each population mean grow as \(\sqrt N\). The solution is cancellation between the large excitatory and inhibitory means, which leads to the balanced state on the next page. This cancellation affects the signed first moment, not the variance created by independent events. Precisely because means and variances obey different addition rules, balance can prevent divergence while retaining fluctuations. The E/I mean is a signed difference, whereas independent variances add through squared weights. With \(W\sim 1/N\), the mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(1/N)\), so stochastic fluctuations vanish at large N. Finite fluctuations require stronger \(1/\sqrt N\) weights and cancellation between E/I means. Let \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r_{E}=r_{I}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(W_{E}=W_{I}=1/N\) in arbitrary units. Calculate each population's mean magnitude, the net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. The two population means are each 0.01 and cancel. Total standard deviation is only about 0.00141 and continues to decrease as N grows. Why does inhibition enter the mean with a negative sign but still enter the independent variance with a positive sign? Variance measures squared deviations from the mean. Multiplication by −W only reverses the direction of a fluctuation; its squared magnitude remains \(W^{2}\), so independent uncertainty from both excitation and inhibition increases total variance. Keeping the inhibitory minus sign in the variance formula and obtaining a potentially negative variance. Applying weight scaling only to the mean and failing to use \(W^{2}\) in the variance. Inferring from one irregular trajectory in a finite network that the large-N limit must also remain irregular.

title: Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking
subtitle: Lecture 8 · Lecture8-NeuralNetworks1.pdf, p. 6
text: How can a large network retain finite stochastic fluctuations from many inputs without letting the mean excitatory or inhibitory drive diverge as \(\sqrt N\)? If weights scale as \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), variance \(N W^{2}\sim O(1)\), so total-input standard deviation remains finite as N grows. The cost is that each population \(\operatorname{mean} N W\sim \sqrt N\) becomes large. For the net mean to stay \(O(1)\), leading-order balance \(N_{\mathrm{EW},Er,E}\approx N_{\mathrm{IW},Ir,I}\) is required: two \(O(\sqrt N)\) terms cancel and leave only a finite residual. Balance does not require excitatory and inhibitory currents to be exactly equal in every millisecond. It constrains conditional means or leading terms at a large scale; instantaneous differences between independent spikes retain \(O(1)\) fluctuations. Those differences make LIF voltage wander irregularly and occasionally cross threshold. With excitation dominance, the mean slope remains upward and firing is more regular. With inhibition dominance, voltage stays below threshold. In the balanced state, fluctuations drive threshold crossings at irregular intervals. The balance condition is sensitive to relative mismatch. Each canceled term is \(O(\sqrt N)\), so if their relative mismatch remains constant, the net input also grows as \(\sqrt N\). Through \(E\to I\), \(I\to E\), recurrent connections, and external drive, network dynamics must adjust firing rates so that mean inhibition tracks mean excitation. Dynamic balance is a network-generated state, not merely a manual choice of equal external rates. The dynamic-balance framework cited in the source lecture shows that recurrent E/I networks can maintain this cancellation spontaneously and produce nearly Poisson variability. “Nearly” should be tested using ISIs, Fano factors, correlations, and state dependence. Irregular firing can also arise from external noise or slow modulation, so a balanced network is a candidate mechanism, not something uniquely identified by one jagged voltage trace. Scaling analysis gives testable simulation predictions. Change K or N while scaling weights as \(1/\sqrt K\), and record the mean absolute E and I magnitudes, net mean, variance, and firing CV. In the correct balanced limit, E and I means grow as \(\sqrt K\) and cancel, while net mean and variance remain \(O(1)\). Plotting only net current hides the large underlying cancellation. \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\) keeps variance \(O(1)\) but makes the separate E and I means \(O(\sqrt N)\). Balance cancels the leading-order mean while retaining instantaneous fluctuations; it is not zero current at every moment. Recurrent feedback can dynamically adjust E/I rates and place a strongly coupled network in an irregular balanced state. Continue with \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), but set \(W=1/\sqrt N=0.01\). The E/I means are exactly equal. Calculate each population mean, net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. The strong E/I means are each 1 and cancel, leaving net \(\operatorname{mean} 0\). Total standard deviation is about 0.141, preserving fluctuations that can drive voltage. Why is a net input mean near zero insufficient evidence that the network is in a strongly balanced state? Weak inputs can also give zero net mean. Strong balance additionally requires large separate E and I means that cancel at leading order, finite net variance, and the predicted scaling as connectivity changes. Interpreting balance as exact equality of E and I current at every instant and therefore predicting zero fluctuations. Plotting only the net E+I curve without separately verifying the two large components and their N scaling. Treating a balanced network as the unique cause of irregular firing without comparing external noise and nonstationary drive.

title: Lecture 9: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models
subtitle: How is a linear system's exponential memory equivalent to a synaptic ODE, and how does timescale separation turn a spiking network into a firing-rate model?
text: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models How is a linear system's exponential memory equivalent to a synaptic ODE, and how does timescale separation turn a spiking network into a firing-rate model? Integrating factor → causal exponential kernel → synaptic-current ODE → spike averaging → F-I nonlinearity → rate dynamics Use an integrating factor to derive the causal solution of \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I(t)\), and recognize it as the convolution of the input with an exponential kernel. Explain the area, time constant, and causality of a normalized exponential kernel, and calculate its response to a step or impulse input. Rewrite convolution with an exponential synapse as a first-order synaptic-current ODE, and count the 2N continuous states and discrete events in a network of N neurons. Approximate spike trains by firing rates through Poisson averaging, and distinguish the dynamical assumptions and relevant timescales of three rate models. Write the feedforward layer \(h^{(\ell )}=F(U^{(\ell )}h^{(\ell -1)})\), check weight shapes, and explain why nonlinearity prevents a multilayer composition from collapsing to one linear map. The solution of a first-order linear ODE is the causal exponential convolution of its past input; conversely, exponential convolution can be implemented by an ODE with one additional state variable. This equivalence turns a spiking network into a coupled voltage-and-current system and, under temporal averaging and timescale separation, produces rate models. Different rate-model forms make different assumptions about which variables are fast or slow and cannot be interchanged merely because they look similar. Omitting the \(1/\tau\) normalization of the exponential kernel. Conflating membrane \(\tau\), synaptic \(\tau _{s}\), and rate-response \(\tau _{r}\). Automatically equating a statistical firing-rate estimate with a dynamical rate variable. Making a fast-variable approximation without writing the derivative that is set to zero. Ignoring the biological problem of negative rates when using a tanh or linear F-I function. Conflating feedforward architecture with backpropagation training. Distinguish a statistical description of spike rate from a dynamical firing-rate variable. They are related, but they are not automatically the same object. Causal exponential kernel \(K\tau  (t) = e^{-t/\tau } H(t)/\tau \) \(\tau >0\) Linear low-pass solution \(x = K\tau  \ast  I\) The transient has been handled Exponential-synapse ODE \(\tau s\) I˙ = \(-I + u(t)\) Single-exponential kernel Instantaneous F-I approximation \(h = F(I)\) Rate response is fast Dynamic rate response \(\tau r\) \(\dot{h} = -h + F(I)\) Smooth population rate Feedforward layer h(ℓ) = F(W (ℓ) h(ℓ−1) ) Shape-compatible weights integrating factor A function that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into a product derivative. causal kernel A filter that is zero at negative times and depends only on past input. synaptic time constant The timescale of synaptic-current integration or decay. firing-rate response time The timescale on which a population rate approaches \(F(I)\). time-scale separation A regime in which one variable is much faster than another and can be approximately eliminated. F-I function A nonlinearity mapping input current to steady firing rate. threshold-linear Zero below threshold and increasing linearly above threshold. \(\operatorname{sigmoid} A\) smooth S-shaped function with lower and upper saturation. feedforward network An architecture in which information moves in one direction across layers without a recurrent loop. What is the integral of \(K_\tau (t)=\tau ^{-1}e^{-t/\tau }H(t)\), and what does it imply for a constant input? Under the area-normalized, unit-DC-gain convention used in this lecture, omitting \(1/\tau\) changes the kernel area from 1 to \(\tau\) and alters both weight units and steady-state gain. Peak normalization is not inherently wrong, but it requires a simultaneous redefinition of the weights. Its integral from 0 to \(\infty\) is 1. The long-run convolution output for a constant input equals the input amplitude and does not acquire an extra factor of \(\tau\). How many continuous ODE states are in a network with N membrane voltages \(V_{i}\) and N exponential synaptic currents \(I_{i}\)? The spike train is not an additional continuous state. Voltage-threshold crossings generate it, and its impulses change synaptic currents. There are 2N continuous states, plus discrete events such as thresholds, resets, and spike arrivals. If \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h}\), why can the synaptic current I be approximated by its instantaneous steady state? This is a timescale-separation approximation that must be checked against parameters and trajectories; it is not license to delete a derivative under all conditions. I relaxes rapidly before h changes appreciably, making \(\tau _{s} dI/dt\) relatively small. Setting \(0=-I+Wh+Ux\) approximately gives \(I\approx Wh+Ux\). Both layers are linear, with no bias or nonlinearity: \(h=U_{1}x\) and \(y=U_{2}h\). Why does depth add no expressive power? Componentwise nonlinearities prevent this complete collapse by making different input regions experience different effective linear relations. Because \(y=U_{2}U_{1}x\), the matrix product can be defined as a single \(U_{\mathrm{eff}}\) and the entire network is still one linear map. If the kernel is incorrectly written \(e^{-t/\tau }H(t)\), omitting \(1/\tau\), what happens to the long-run response to a constant input? If the weight units from this lecture's area-normalized convention are retained, the kernel area changes from 1 to \(\tau\) and the steady-state response becomes \(\tau I_{0}\). If peak normalization is intentional, weights must instead be interpreted as amplitudes and their units checked again. This is the distinction tested in Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution. Worked example — A step response at three times: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x(0)=0\), with \(I(t)=6\) for \(t\ge 0\). Calculate \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\), \(x(20 \mathrm{ms})\), and \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\), and identify the long-run value. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x(0)=0\), with \(I(t)=6\) for \(t\ge 0\). Calculate \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\), \(x(20 \mathrm{ms})\), and \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\), and identify the long-run value. The step response is \(x(t)=6(1-e^{-t/10 ms})\). At \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x=6(1-e^{-1})\approx 6\times 0.6321=3.793\). At \(t=20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x=6(1-e^{-2})\approx 5.188\); at \(t=30 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x\approx 6(1-e^{-3})=5.701\). As \(t\to \infty\), the exponential vanishes and \(x\to 6\), consistent with gain 1 for a unit-area kernel under constant input. The response should rise monotonically from 0 and remain below 6. After each \(\tau\), the remaining error is multiplied by \(e^{-1}\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution”? An integrating factor converts the left side of a first-order linear equation into the exact derivative of a product. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution”? The solution consists of an initial transient plus the causal convolution of past input. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An integrating factor converts the left side of a first-order linear equation into the exact derivative of a product. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Integrating-factor solution of a first-order system with arbitrary input”? \(K_\tau\) has units 1/time, so \(K_\tau I\) dt' has the same units as I. The equation requires x and I to share units, and \(t/\tau\) is dimensionless. When \(I=0\), only exponential decay of the initial condition remains. Under a constant input, \(x\to I\) in the long run. As \(\tau \to 0\), \(x(t)\to I(t)\) when the input is sufficiently smooth. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How does an arbitrary time-varying input leave a gradually decaying memory in a first-order linear system, and why can that memory be written as a normalized causal convolution? Consider \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I(t)\). Moving terms and dividing by \(\tau\) gives \(dx/dt+x/\tau =I(t)/\tau\). After multiplication by \(e^{t/\tau }\), the left side becomes \(d[xe^{t/\tau }]/dt\) by the product rule. Integrating from initial time \(t_{0}\) to the present t retains both an initial-condition term and a forced integral. If the system is assumed to have been stable since the distant past and the initial transient has vanished, the lower limit can instead be written as \(-\infty\). The general solution is \(x(t)=x(t_{0})e^{-(t-t_{0})/\tau }+\int _{t_{0}}^{t}\tau ^{-1}e^{-(t-t')/\tau }I(t')dt'\). The first term is memory of the initial state, and the second is the input history. Older inputs have larger elapsed time t−t' and receive exponentially smaller weight. Future times \(t'>t\) are excluded from the integration interval, so the response is causal. Why is an event-driven implementation less sensitive to dt than approximating \(\delta\) as a single bin of fixed height? An event-driven implementation applies the jump derived by integration and preserves impulse area. Unless fixed height is scaled by 1/dt, changing the time step changes both the area and total input. This is the distinction tested in ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states. Worked example — Synaptic jump and decay after one impulse: Let \(\tau _{s}=5 \mathrm{ms}\), the event term be \(q\delta (t)\), \(q=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\), and \(I(0^{-})=0\) just before the event. Find \(I(0^{+})\) and the current at 5 ms and 10 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau _{s}=5 \mathrm{ms}\), the event term be \(q\delta (t)\), \(q=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\), and \(I(0^{-})=0\) just before the event. Find \(I(0^{+})\) and the current at 5 ms and 10 ms. Integrate \(\tau _{s} dI/dt=-I+q\delta\) across the event. As event width approaches zero, the integral of the finite −I term vanishes, leaving \(\tau _{s}[I(0^{+})-I(0^{-})]=q\). The jump is \(q/\tau _{s}=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}/5 \mathrm{ms}=10 \mathrm{pA}\), so \(I(0^{+})=10 \mathrm{pA}\). With no new input after the event, \(I(t)=10e^{-t/5 ms}\) pA. \(I(5 \mathrm{ms})=10e^{-1}\approx 3.679 \mathrm{pA}\); \(I(10 \mathrm{ms})=10e^{-2}\approx 1.353 \mathrm{pA}\). After each \(\tau _{s}\), amplitude is multiplied by \(e^{-1}\). The response area \(10 \mathrm{pA}\times 5 \mathrm{ms}=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\) equals q. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states”? Convolution with a normalized exponential is equivalent to a first-order synaptic-state ODE. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states”? N membrane voltages plus N synaptic currents give 2N continuous states, in addition to threshold events. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? N membrane voltages plus N synaptic currents give 2N continuous states, in addition to threshold events. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Proving that exponential convolution satisfies a first-order synaptic ODE”? If I is a current, S must also have units of current. When \(S=q\delta\), q has units current×time because \(\delta\) has units 1/time. When \(S=0\), I decays exponentially. Under sustained constant \(S_{0}\), \(I\to S_{0}\). When \(\tau _{s}\) is very small, I follows sufficiently smooth S rapidly. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h} a\) mathematical justification for deleting the synaptic derivative, whereas “the model should be simpler” is not? The timescale ratio supplies a testable small parameter and an expected error: the fast variable relaxes before the slow variable changes. Without timescale separation, deleting the derivative changes delay, stability, and transients and must be tested against data. This is the distinction tested in From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers. Worked example — Calculating a two-layer threshold-linear feedforward network by hand: Input \(x=(1,2)^{\mathrm{T}}\), first-layer \(U^{1}=[[1,-1],[0.5,1]]\), and \(F(z)=\max(0,z)\) applied componentwise. Second-layer weight \(U^{2}=[2,-1]\), with a linear output layer. Find the hidden layer and output, and verify all shapes. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Input \(x=(1,2)^{\mathrm{T}}\), first-layer \(U^{1}=[[1,-1],[0.5,1]]\), and \(F(z)=\max(0,z)\) applied componentwise. Second-layer weight \(U^{2}=[2,-1]\), with a linear output layer. Find the hidden layer and output, and verify all shapes. \(U^{1}\) has shape \(2\times 2\) and multiplies a \(2\times 1\) input to give a \(2\times 1\) vector: \(z^{1}=(1\cdot 1-1\cdot 2,0.5\cdot 1+1\cdot 2)^{\mathrm{T}}=(-1,2.5)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Componentwise threshold-linear activation gives \(h^{1}=(0,2.5)^{\mathrm{T}}\). \(U^{2}\) has shape \(1\times 2\) and can multiply the \(2\times 1\) hidden vector, giving scalar \(y=2\cdot 0-1\cdot 2.5=-2.5\). If the second layer also used a nonnegative threshold-linear activation, the final output would be \(\max(0,-2.5)=0\). The output nonlinearity must be stated explicitly. The inner dimensions match in every matrix multiplication. The first hidden unit's negative preactivation is clipped to zero, while the second retains 2.5. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers”? Spike-to-rate averaging gives conditional-mean dynamics and discards single-trial event fluctuations. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers”? The three rate models respectively assume fast rate, retain both timescales, or assume fast synapses. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A feedforward steady-state layer is \(h=F(Ux)\), and weight shape is determined by the widths of adjacent layers. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving the common single-state form from a two-timescale rate model”? h has units Hz. If F maps current to Hz, W h and U x must have units of current; \(\tau _{h} dh/dt\) and h both have units Hz. If \(\tau _{s}\) is not sufficiently small, the quasi-steady approximation introduces phase and amplitude errors. \(W=0\) at steady state gives a feedforward layer. If F is the identity, stacked layers remain linear. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The synaptic time constant determines how long one spike is retained”? For a peak-normalized exponential response, larger \(\tau _{s}\) makes the effect of a spike decay more slowly and preserves a longer memory. Under the area-normalized kernel \(K_{s}=\tau _{s}^{-1}e^{-t/\tau _{s}}\), the peak also changes as \(1/\tau _{s}\), so the normalization convention must be checked before curves are compared. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “integrating factor” mean in this lecture? integrating factor: A function that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into a product derivative. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “causal kernel” mean in this lecture? causal kernel: A filter that is zero at negative times and depends only on past input. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “synaptic time constant” mean in this lecture? synaptic time constant: The timescale of synaptic-current integration or decay. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “firing-rate response time” mean in this lecture? firing-rate response time: The timescale on which a population rate approaches \(F(I)\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “time-scale separation” mean in this lecture? time-scale separation: A regime in which one variable is much faster than another and can be approximately eliminated. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “F-I function” mean in this lecture? F-I function: A nonlinearity mapping input current to steady firing rate. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “threshold-linear” mean in this lecture? threshold-linear: Zero below threshold and increasing linearly above threshold. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “sigmoid” mean in this lecture? sigmoid: A smooth S-shaped function with lower and upper saturation. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feedforward network” mean in this lecture? feedforward network: An architecture in which information moves in one direction across layers without a recurrent loop. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Causal exponential kernel” be used? Causal exponential kernel: \(K\tau  (t) = e^{-t/\tau } H(t)/\tau \). \(\tau >0\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Linear low-pass solution” be used? Linear low-pass solution: \(x = K\tau  \ast  I\). The transient has been handled This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Exponential-synapse ODE” be used? Exponential-synapse ODE: \(\tau s\) I˙ = \(-I + u(t)\). Single-exponential kernel This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Instantaneous F-I approximation” be used? Instantaneous F-I approximation: \(h = F(I)\). Rate response is fast This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Dynamic rate response” be used? Dynamic rate response: \(\tau r\) \(\dot{h} = -h + F(I)\). Smooth population rate This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Feedforward layer” be used? Feedforward layer: h(ℓ) = F(W (ℓ) h(ℓ−1) ). Shape-compatible weights This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution
subtitle: Lecture 9 · Lecture9-NeuralNetworks2.pdf, p. 1
text: How does an arbitrary time-varying input leave a gradually decaying memory in a first-order linear system, and why can that memory be written as a normalized causal convolution? Consider \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I(t)\). Moving terms and dividing by \(\tau\) gives \(dx/dt+x/\tau =I(t)/\tau\). After multiplication by \(e^{t/\tau }\), the left side becomes \(d[xe^{t/\tau }]/dt\) by the product rule. Integrating from initial time \(t_{0}\) to the present t retains both an initial-condition term and a forced integral. If the system is assumed to have been stable since the distant past and the initial transient has vanished, the lower limit can instead be written as \(-\infty\). The general solution is \(x(t)=x(t_{0})e^{-(t-t_{0})/\tau }+\int _{t_{0}}^{t}\tau ^{-1}e^{-(t-t')/\tau }I(t')dt'\). The first term is memory of the initial state, and the second is the input history. Older inputs have larger elapsed time t−t' and receive exponentially smaller weight. Future times \(t'>t\) are excluded from the integration interval, so the response is causal. Define \(K_\tau (u)=\tau ^{-1}e^{-u/\tau }H(u)\). The forced term is then \((K_\tau *I)(t)\). The kernel area is \(\int _{0}\infty \tau ^{-1}e^{-u/\tau }du=1\), and its mean delay is \(\tau\). Small \(\tau\) concentrates the response on the recent past and follows input quickly; large \(\tau\) gives a longer smoothing window. The kernel is not simply a “delay of \(\tau\),” but a continuous weighting of an entire history. Convolution and an ODE are two representations of the same linear filter. Convolution displays the weighting of history directly and is useful for analyzing input contributions; an ODE stores only the current x and is efficient for stepwise simulation. Their equivalence requires the same kernel normalization, initial condition, and boundary convention. When numerical convolution and ODE results disagree, first check the discrete dt factor and the initial transient. For step input \(I(t)=I_{0}H(t)\) with \(x(0)=0\), integration gives \(x(t)=I_{0}(1-e^{-t/\tau })\); for a brief impulse \(q\delta (t)\), the response is \(qK_\tau (t)\). More complex inputs can be assembled from these building blocks. The long-run step output \(I_{0}\) verifies area normalization, while impulse-response area q verifies that the linear system preserves total input amount. An integrating factor converts the left side of a first-order linear equation into the exact derivative of a product. The solution consists of an initial transient plus the causal convolution of past input. A normalized exponential kernel has area 1; \(\tau\) controls memory width, not steady-state gain. Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x(0)=0\), with \(I(t)=6\) for \(t\ge 0\). Calculate \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\), \(x(20 \mathrm{ms})\), and \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\), and identify the long-run value. The values at the three times are approximately 3.79, 5.19, and 5.70, and the long-run value is 6. If the kernel is incorrectly written \(e^{-t/\tau }H(t)\), omitting \(1/\tau\), what happens to the long-run response to a constant input? If the weight units from this lecture's area-normalized convention are retained, the kernel area changes from 1 to \(\tau\) and the steady-state response becomes \(\tau I_{0}\). If peak normalization is intentional, weights must instead be interpreted as amplitudes and their units checked again. Multiplying only part of the equation by the integrating factor and failing to verify the product rule. Extending the integration limit to \(\infty\) without a causal Heaviside factor, allowing future input to affect the present. Omitting dt in a discrete convolution sum and making the result depend on sampling rate.

title: ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states
subtitle: Lecture 9 · Lecture9-NeuralNetworks2.pdf, p. 2
text: Why does a single-exponential synapse require only one additional current state per neuron instead of revisiting the complete spike history at every time step? The preceding lecture wrote synaptic current as the convolution of \(K_{s}\) with a spike train. Real synapses often have a biexponential shape with a fast rise and slower decay. When rise time is much shorter than the timescale of interest, a single exponential is a useful approximation. The normalized kernel \(K_{s}(t)=\tau _{s}^{-1}e^{-t/\tau _{s}}H(t)\) is exactly the impulse response of the first-order filter \(\tau _{s} dI/dt=-I+S(t)\). For network neuron i, the input events are \(S_{i}(t)=\sum _jW_{ij}\Delta _{j}(t)+\sum _jU_{ij}X_{j}(t)\). The synaptic state therefore obeys \(\tau _{s} dI_{i}/dt=-I_{i}+S_{i}(t)\), while the membrane state obeys C \(dV_{i}/dt=-G_{L}(V_{i}-E_{L})+I_{i}\). Each i has two continuous variables, \(V_{i}\) and \(I_{i}\), so N neurons have 2N ODE states in total. The threshold–reset remains a discrete event. When \(V_{j}\) reaches \(V_{T}\), record \(t_{k}^{(j)}\), reset \(V_{j}\), and use \(W_{ij}\) to impose an impulse jump in \(I_{i}\) for every receiver. If the right side contains \(W\delta\), integrating over an infinitesimal event gives \(\tau _{s}\Delta I_{i}=W\), so W has units current×time. If W is intended to be the current jump amplitude itself, write the event term as \(\tau _{s}W\delta\). Unit conventions must agree with kernel normalization. The ODE representation has recursive memory. In the absence of new spikes, the current \(I_{i}\) is simply decayed from its present value, so every \(t_{k}\) need not be stored. A time-step simulation must still treat impulses correctly, often by applying the jump directly at an event and integrating the ODE between events. Treating \(\delta\) as an ordinary array height without division by dt or an equivalent jump rule makes results depend on the time step. The limits of the single-exponential approximation can be judged from data. If synaptic current has a visible rising phase, one state cannot match both peak time and decay; rise and decay states can be added to form a biexponential response. If the actual current is \(G_{s}(t)(V-E_{s})\), reversal potential and voltage dependence must also be retained, and a fixed current kernel cannot be generalized across all membrane voltages. Convolution with a normalized exponential is equivalent to a first-order synaptic-state ODE. N membrane voltages plus N synaptic currents give 2N continuous states, in addition to threshold events. The coefficient of a \(\delta\) term determines the event-induced jump and its units; numerical implementation must respect the normalization convention. Let \(\tau _{s}=5 \mathrm{ms}\), the event term be \(q\delta (t)\), \(q=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\), and \(I(0^{-})=0\) just before the event. Find \(I(0^{+})\) and the current at 5 ms and 10 ms. The current jumps to 10 pA and then decays to approximately 3.68 pA and 1.35 pA at 5 ms and 10 ms. Why is an event-driven implementation less sensitive to dt than approximating \(\delta\) as a single bin of fixed height? An event-driven implementation applies the jump derived by integration and preserves impulse area. Unless fixed height is scaled by 1/dt, changing the time step changes both the area and total input. Treating W simultaneously as kernel area and current-jump amplitude, thereby omitting a factor of \(\tau _{s}\). Counting only N voltage states and forgetting that an exponential synapse adds one continuous state per receiver. Assuming that one exponential can represent a finite rise time and conductance reversal effects.

title: From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers
subtitle: Lecture 9 · Lecture9-NeuralNetworks2.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture9-NeuralNetworks2.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture9-NeuralNetworks2.pdf, p. 5
text: On what timescale can continuous firing rates replace discrete spikes, how do three rate equations arise from different fast–slow assumptions, and how does the result reduce to a feedforward network layer? In a short window \(\Delta t\) that contains many spikes while the input rate remains approximately constant, the mean count of a Poisson spike train divided by \(\Delta t\) gives firing rate \(h_{j}\). Taking a conditional mean of the synaptic equation replaces \(\Delta _{j}\) with \(h_{j}\) and external \(X_{j}\) with \(x_{j}\), yielding \(\tau _{s} dI_{i}/dt=-I_{i}+\sum _jW_{ij}h_{j}+\sum _jU_{ij}x_{j}\). This replacement describes the mean; it does not retain single-trial spike fluctuations. Closing the model requires an F–I curve \(h_{i}=F(I_{i})\). The source lecture lists threshold-linear, sigmoid, linear, and tanh choices. Threshold-linear is appropriate for nonnegative rates near threshold; sigmoid has lower and upper saturation; a purely linear function is analytically convenient but permits negative rates; tanh has positive and negative outputs and better represents a centered activity variable. Function choice determines the number of steady states, gain, and saturation and cannot be changed merely for plotting convenience. The first approximation assumes that the rate responds rapidly, sets \(h=F(I)\) directly, and retains only synaptic dynamics. A more complete second model adds \(\tau _{h} dh/dt=-h+F(I)\), keeping separate response times for I and h. If synapses are much faster than rate, \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h}\), set \(I\approx Wh+Ux\) to obtain the common form \(\tau _{h} dh/dt=-h+F(Wh+Ux)\). Every deleted derivative must be justified by an explicit timescale separation. With recurrent weight \(W=0\) at steady state, a single-layer map becomes \(h=F(Ux)\). Repetition gives \(h^{(\ell )}=F(U^{(\ell )}h^{(\ell -1)})\), with input \(x=h^{(0)}\) and an output y connected after the final layer. Each matrix has one row per unit in the current layer and one column per unit in the previous layer. If a bias is included, write U h+b and check its shape as well. If F is the identity, the full multilayer map is \(U^{(L)}\)⋯\(U^{(1)}x\), still one linear transformation. Nonlinearities allow different layers to select different effective slopes in different input regions and thereby construct richer functions. This establishes a feedforward computational architecture, not a rule for learning weights from data. Training objectives, gradients, and generalization require additional assumptions and do not follow from the layered equations alone. Spike-to-rate averaging gives conditional-mean dynamics and discards single-trial event fluctuations. The three rate models respectively assume fast rate, retain both timescales, or assume fast synapses. A feedforward steady-state layer is \(h=F(Ux)\), and weight shape is determined by the widths of adjacent layers. Without nonlinearities, multiple linear layers can be combined, so depth does not enlarge the function class. Input \(x=(1,2)^{\mathrm{T}}\), first-layer \(U^{1}=[[1,-1],[0.5,1]]\), and \(F(z)=\max(0,z)\) applied componentwise. Second-layer weight \(U^{2}=[2,-1]\), with a linear output layer. Find the hidden layer and output, and verify all shapes. Hidden activity is \((0,2.5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), and the linear output is −2.5. Why is \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h} a\) mathematical justification for deleting the synaptic derivative, whereas “the model should be simpler” is not? The timescale ratio supplies a testable small parameter and an expected error: the fast variable relaxes before the slow variable changes. Without timescale separation, deleting the derivative changes delay, stability, and transients and must be tested against data. Claiming that a model retains single-trial Poisson fluctuations after averaging its spike trains. Setting \(I=Wh+Ux\) while also retaining independent I dynamics without stating which approximation is being used. Relying on implicit broadcasting when matrix shapes do not match and thereby computing a different architecture. Equating the existence of a feedforward stack with having specified a learning algorithm.

title: Lecture 10: Synaptic Plasticity
subtitle: How does Hebbian plasticity alter a synapse through spike timing and receptor mechanisms, and how can its firing-rate and matrix descriptions select statistical input structure without runaway weight growth?
text: Synaptic Plasticity How does Hebbian plasticity alter a synapse through spike timing and receptor mechanisms, and how can its firing-rate and matrix descriptions select statistical input structure without runaway weight growth? \(LTP/LTD/STDP \to  NMDA-\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\)→ Hebbian/covariance rule → covariance eigenmodes → positive feedback → Oja/BCM stabilization Connect Hebb's hypothesis, LTP/LTD, the STDP timing window, and the NMDA–Ca2+–AMPA mechanism into a conditional explanatory sequence, distinguishing empirical regularities from proposed mechanisms. Derive the expected weight dynamics \(E[dw/dt]=Cw\) from a centered firing-rate Hebbian rule, explaining vector orientation, matrix shape, and why mean subtraction permits depression. Use a quadratic form to prove that a covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, then use an eigenbasis to explain why the direction of greatest variance grows fastest. Compare how synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and the BCM sliding threshold regulate overall magnitude, local normalization, and the boundary between LTP and LTD. Distinguish unsupervised, supervised, and reward-based learning, and explain how an error, reward, or reward-prediction error can gate plasticity as a third factor. This lecture joins three levels of synaptic plasticity: experimental phenomena (LTP/LTD/STDP), proposed molecular mechanisms (NMDA-dependent \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) signaling and AMPA trafficking), and abstract learning rules. A basic Hebbian rule amplifies high-variance eigenmodes of input covariance but also creates positive feedback and unbounded growth. Synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and BCM stabilize the system through global normalization, local weight-dependent decay, and a dynamic threshold, respectively. Equating LTP/LTD with one \(NMDA/\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) pathway even though mechanisms vary across synapses and contexts. Using only coincident high activity in basic Hebbian learning and overlooking centered covariance and depression. Treating an eigenvector as a particular neuron. Claiming that covariance “must be positive” without writing a quadratic-form proof of PSD. Confusing directional selection with stabilization of the norm. Equating Hebbian learning with PCA without stating its assumptions. Assuming dopamine is the third factor in every form of reward learning. The Hebbian-learning/PCA relationship holds only under particular linear, statistical, and stabilizing assumptions; “Hebbian = PCA” is not a universal identity. title: From Synaptic Timing and Receptor Mechanisms to a Firing-Rate Hebbian Rule
subtitle: Lecture 10 · Lecture10-SynapticPlasticity.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture10-SynapticPlasticity.pdf, p. 2
text: How can a local synapse convert the timing relation between pre- and postsynaptic activity into a lasting weight change, and how can that phenomenon be abstracted into a computable rate rule? Hebb's original proposal links coincident activity to stronger connectivity. Experimentally, high-frequency stimulation of the CA3-to-CA1 pathway can induce long-term potentiation (LTP), whereas a low-frequency protocol can induce long-term depression (LTD). Both describe persistent changes in synaptic efficacy after induction. Neither is the same as transient facilitation, and a single response curve cannot establish one unique molecular mechanism. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) makes relative timing part of the update. Let \(\Delta t=t_{\mathrm{post}}-t_{\mathrm{pre}}\). A classical pair-based window is often written as \(\Delta w=A_{+}e^{-\Delta t/\tau _{+}}\) for \(\Delta t>0\) and \(\Delta w=-A_{-}e^{\Delta t/\tau _{-}}\) for \(\Delta t<0\). The exponential terms encode weaker local coincidence at longer intervals. A_± and τ_± depend on the experimental protocol; they are not constants shared by every brain region. The canonical mechanism in the lecture notes is conditional: the presynaptic terminal releases glutamate; AMPA current helps depolarize the postsynaptic membrane; depolarization relieves the Mg2+ block of the NMDA pore; and NMDA-mediated Ca2+ influx converts pre/post coincidence into an intracellular signal. The first page of the source notes abbreviates Mg2+ unblock as if presynaptic release triggered it, so the distinction must be explicit: presynaptic release provides glutamate, whereas postsynaptic depolarization relieves the block. A stronger Ca2+ signal, or one with a different time course, can favor kinase activity and AMPA insertion; another range can favor phosphatase activity and AMPA removal. The point is this conditional sequence, not a one-way description of Ca2+ as an LTP switch. A rate model discards millisecond timing of individual spikes and retains activity strength over a window. The basic rule \(\tau _{w} dw_{i}/dt=h x_{i}\) produces only potentiation when h,\(x_{i}\ge 0\). The three covariance rules listed in the lecture notes center the output, the input, or both. Each separates co-fluctuation above a variable's own baseline from merely having a large absolute value. Centering both variables is especially direct statistically because its expectation yields the input covariance. LTP and LTD are experimentally observed lasting changes in efficacy; an STDP window summarizes an empirical result for a particular timing protocol. NMDA coincidence detection requires glutamate together with postsynaptic depolarization, after which Ca2+ can influence AMPA trafficking. A basic nonnegative Hebbian rule can only increase weights; centering activity allows negative covariance to produce depression. An input has \(\operatorname{mean} 5 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the postsynaptic output has \(\operatorname{mean} 10 \mathrm{Hz}\). Compare state A, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=14\), with state B, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=7\), taking one update to be proportional to the product of deviations. The centered rule assigns the sign from co-fluctuation relative to baseline, not from the absolute firing-rate magnitude. Why is a classical STDP window not interchangeable with a firing-rate covariance rule? STDP preserves millisecond relative timing between pre- and postsynaptic spikes, whereas a covariance rule averages activity fluctuations over a longer window. They can be related under specific statistical and timescale assumptions, but they use different state variables, experimental protocols, and levels of mechanistic interpretation. Treating the NMDA–Ca2+ sequence as the sole mechanism at every synapse while ignoring neuromodulation, dendritic voltage, and burst context. Saying only “fire together, wire together” without specifying baseline centering, the sign of the update, or the learning timescale.

title: Covariance Geometry, the PSD Proof, and Hebbian Eigenmode Blow-Up
subtitle: Lecture 10 · Lecture10-SynapticPlasticity.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture10-SynapticPlasticity.pdf, p. 4
text: Why do covariance eigenvectors provide the natural coordinates for Hebbian learning, and why does the largest eigenvalue cause both directional selection and unstable growth? The expected dynamics \(\tau _{w} E[dw/dt]=Cw\) form a linear dynamical system. An eigenvector \(v_{k}\) of C satisfies \(Cv_{k}=\lambda _{k}v_{k}\), so if w lies along \(v_{k}\), the update remains in that direction and changes only its magnitude. For a symmetric covariance matrix, the eigenvectors can be chosen as an orthogonal basis, allowing any initial w to be written as \(\sum _k a_{k}v_{k}\). Covariance is symmetric because \(C_{ij}=E[(x_{i}-\mu _{i})(x_{j}-\mu _{j})]\), and exchanging the two scalar factors leaves their product unchanged. It is also positive semidefinite (PSD): for every v, the quadratic form \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) is the expected square of the projection \(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu )\). PSD does not require every off-diagonal entry to be positive. Anticorrelated variables may have negative covariance while the full quadratic form remains nonnegative. In the eigenbasis, each coefficient obeys \(\tau _{w} da_{k}/dt=\lambda _{k}a_{k}\), with solution \(a_{k}(t)=a_{k}(0)e^{\lambda _{k}t/\tau _{w}}\). The mode with the largest \(\lambda\) grows faster than the others, so the normalized direction approaches the principal eigenvector. This produces the formal link to PCA while exposing the defect of basic Hebbian learning: because PSD eigenvalues are nonnegative, no existing component is actively reduced by these expected dynamics. A direction approaching PC1 is not the same as a weight vector converging to a stable PC1 solution. Under the basic rule the norm keeps increasing until the assumptions of a linear neuron, stationary statistics, and a fixed learning rate fail. A stable PCA-like solution can be discussed only after normalization or competition controls magnitude. A nonlinear output, nonstationary input, or several similar eigenvalues can alter both convergence and the resulting direction. The central evidence that covariance is symmetric PSD is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv=E[(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu ))^2]\ge 0\). The eigenbasis decomposes coupled weight dynamics into independent exponential modes, with \(\lambda _{k}\) setting each mode's growth rate. Selection of a principal direction does not imply norm stability; Hebbian learning equals PCA only under additional assumptions. Let \(C=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(\tau _{w}=1 \mathrm{s}\), and \(w(0)=(1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute the two components and their ratio at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). The direction of greatest variance rapidly dominates while the total weight magnitude explodes; both consequences arise from the same positive-feedback dynamics. Why does a negative off-diagonal covariance entry not violate positive semidefiniteness? Positive semidefiniteness constrains the variance \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) along every complete direction, not each matrix entry separately. Two variables can be anticorrelated, giving \(C_{ij}<0\), while every linear combination still has a variance equal to an expected square. Interpreting an eigenvector as one particular neuron or synapse; it is a direction in the full input or weight space. Noticing that the principal direction dominates but overlooking that every component still grows exponentially, and therefore claiming incorrectly that basic Hebbian learning is stable.

title: Stabilizing Rules and Third-Factor Learning
subtitle: Lecture 10 · Lecture10-SynapticPlasticity.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture10-SynapticPlasticity.pdf, p. 6
text: How can a system retain Hebbian feature selection while preventing weight blow-up, and how can learning be restricted to appropriate moments when a target or reward is required? Synaptic scaling slowly rescales a group of synapses together so that total weight or postsynaptic activity returns to a target range. It can preserve the relative weight pattern, but it requires some cell-wide measurement. As the lecture notes emphasize, restoring the norm to a fixed value after each Hebbian change still allows the direction to rotate toward the principal covariance eigenvector while preventing unbounded amplitude growth. Oja's rule incorporates normalization into a local approximation: \(dw/dt\propto hx-h^2w\). The first term is Hebbian correlation; the second grows with output energy and the current weight, creating weight-dependent decay. For centered, linear, stationary input, the expected fixed point can align with the principal eigenvector while retaining a finite norm. That result belongs to these simplifying assumptions, not to every variant of Oja's rule. The BCM rule changes the sign of plasticity using a postsynaptic sliding threshold, for example \(dw_{i}/dt\propto h x_{i}(h-\theta )\), while \(\theta\) adapts to recent \(h^2\). With \(h<\theta\), the same presynaptic activity tends toward LTD; with \(h>\theta\), it tends toward LTP. Sustained higher activity raises \(\theta\) and makes potentiation harder to trigger. Unlike Oja's explicit weight decay, BCM creates competition and stability through an activity-dependent sign switch. Unsupervised learning uses only input and neural activity to discover statistical structure. Supervised learning additionally requires a target-output error, whereas reward learning selects advantageous behavior through reward or deviation from expected reward. A three-factor rule multiplies pre-activity, post-activity, and a modulatory third signal. That factor controls when or in which direction a local eligibility trace is consolidated, but it need not always be dopamine and is not equivalent to a backpropagated gradient assigned precisely to every weight. Scaling rescales synapses globally; Oja's rule combines a Hebbian term with local weight-dependent decay; BCM uses a dynamic postsynaptic threshold. The connection between Oja's rule and PCA requires centered, linear, stationary input and a suitable learning rate. Three-factor learning supplements pre/post coactivity with an error, reward, or contextual gate. Let \(x_{i}=2\) and use \(x_{i}\) \(h(h-\theta )\) as the core update. Set \(\theta =5\), compare \(h=3\) with \(h=8\), and then explain how sustained high activity changes \(\theta\). BCM uses the postsynaptic operating point to determine the sign of plasticity and uses slow threshold feedback to counteract runaway growth from persistently high activity. Why is it inadequate to reduce a reward-based three-factor rule to “Hebbian learning multiplied by dopamine”? The third factor may encode reward, reward-prediction error, an error signal, context, or another neuromodulatory gate. Its timing, receptors, eligibility trace, and specificity for the target weight all affect learning, so dopamine is only one candidate implementation in some systems. Treating synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and BCM as interchangeable names for normalization, despite their different measured variables and feedback locations. Taking a formal resemblance to a three-factor rule as proof of a complete biological mechanism for backpropagation or a reward circuit.

title: The Components of Supervised Learning and Gradient Descent
subtitle: Lecture 11 · Lecture11-MachineLearning.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture11-MachineLearning.pdf, p. 2
text: How is a prediction task formulated as an optimizable mathematical problem, and how does local loss geometry imply a parameter update? Supervised learning supplies input-target pairs. In handwritten-digit recognition, x is an image and y is a discrete digit label, making the task classification. In optic-flow estimation, x may be two adjacent frames and y a continuous motion vector at each location, making it regression. Both require a clear account of how training examples are sampled and whether test examples follow the same distribution. The architecture specifies the prediction function. A multilayer network can be written \(z^{(0)}=x\), \(h^{(\ell )}=W^{(\ell -1)}z^{(\ell -1)}\), \(z^{(\ell )}=\phi (h^{(\ell )})\), and finally \(\hat{y}=g(W^{(L)}z^{(L)})\). If layer ℓ contains \(N_\ell\) units, then \(W^{(\ell -1)}\in \mathbb{R}^{N_\ell \times N_{\ell -1}}\). Writing every shape exposes most transpose errors before the derivation begins. A loss compresses the discrepancy between prediction and target into a scalar. Squared error is common for regression and cross-entropy for classification; choosing a loss embeds assumptions about noise and task priorities. An optimization rule then determines how W changes. Conflating architecture, loss, and learning rule makes it impossible to identify whether a performance change arose from representation, objective, or optimizer. In a parameter plane, squared-loss contours are ellipses. The gradient is perpendicular to a contour and points locally uphill. A first-order Taylor approximation is reliable only for a sufficiently small step, so the learning rate \(\eta\) must be neither so large that it jumps across the valley nor so small that training stalls. The negative gradient is a local descent direction; it does not take a deep network to a global optimum in one step. The dataset supplies the evidence defining the problem, the architecture defines the hypothesis class, the loss defines error, and the optimizer defines the search path. A gradient has the same shape as its parameter and points in the locally steepest ascent direction; gradient descent applies the negative sign. The Taylor argument is local. With an excessively large learning rate, the loss can rise instead of fall. Let \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(y=5\), \(w=(0,0)^\mathrm{T}\), \(L=1/2(y-w^\mathrm{T}x)^2\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Compute the update and the new loss. The negative-gradient step moves the prediction toward the target and reduces the loss by a factor of four. Why is the statement “the gradient points toward the minimum” inaccurate? The gradient points in the locally steepest ascent direction at the current point; its negative is the local descent direction. It uses only first-order information at that location and does not directly identify a distant global minimum. Classifying a task as classification or regression only by the model's name instead of examining target support and loss. Turning the negative gradient's local descent guarantee into a global guarantee for every learning rate and every nonconvex network.

title: Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization
subtitle: Lecture 11 · Lecture11-MachineLearning.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture11-MachineLearning.pdf, p. 4
text: Why does linear regression offer both an interpretable local learning rule and a closed-form solution, while optimization becomes more complicated after linear layers are stacked? Adopt the source notes' orientation: every column of \(X\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times P}\) is a sample, \(w\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}\), \(y\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\), and the prediction is \(X^\mathrm{T}w\). The batch loss is \(L=||y-X^\mathrm{T}w||^2/P\). Its gradient aggregates the correlation between each feature and the residual, so the update contains the data-dependent Hebbian-like term Xy. Expanding the gradient gives \(\nabla L=(2/P)(XX^\mathrm{T}w-Xy)\). Thus \(-\nabla L\) contains \(+(2\eta /P)\)Xy and \(-(2\eta /P)XX^\mathrm{T}w\). The first term writes input-target coactivity into the weights; the second grows with the current weights and input covariance, providing stabilization. Its form resembles biological Hebbian learning, but a target y, batch access, and signed error are not ordinary local coactivity. Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) yields the normal equation \(XX^\mathrm{T} \hat{w}=Xy\). If \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is invertible, \(\hat{w}=(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\)Xy. Redundant features or \(P<N\) can make the matrix singular, so its inverse must not be forced. The pseudoinverse selects a minimum-norm solution, while ridge regression replaces \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) with \(XX^\mathrm{T}+\lambda I\), exchanging a small bias for numerical stability. If every activation in a deep linear network is the identity, its overall map \(M=W^{(L)}\cdots W^{(0)}\) remains linear: \(\hat{y}=Mx\). Yet many layer factorizations represent the same M, and the loss contains products of individual layer weights. Consequently, the parameter landscape and learning dynamics are nonlinear. A linear represented function does not make the optimization problem ordinary convex regression. A least-squares update decomposes into input-target correlation and weight-dependent covariance stabilization. A closed form requires a stated orientation for X and invertibility; use a pseudoinverse or regularization when the system is singular. The function class of a deep linear network is still linear, but factorized parameters create nonconvexity and nonunique scaling. Let \(X=[[1,0],[0,2]]\), so its columns are \((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \((0,2)^\mathrm{T}\), and let targets \(y=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\). Find \(\hat{w}\). Because the sample value of feature 2 is 2, a weight of only 2 predicts target 4; the closed form respects feature scaling. Why can training every layer of a deep linear network not be treated as ordinary convex linear regression, even though the overall mapping is linear? The product \(W^L\cdots W^0\) defines a linear mapping, but it is a multilinear product of the component layer parameters. Scale and factorization are nonunique, and updates to different layers depend on one another, so optimization in parameter space is generally nonconvex. Applying a closed-form formula without declaring whether samples are columns or rows, thereby misplacing transposes and dimensions. Directly inverting a singular or ill-conditioned matrix instead of considering a pseudoinverse, ridge regularization, and feature scaling.

title: Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients
subtitle: Lecture 11 · Lecture11-MachineLearning.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture11-MachineLearning.pdf, p. 6
text: How is an output error re-expressed, through local derivatives, as the sensitivity of each layer's preactivation and then converted into a gradient with the same shape as each weight matrix? The forward pass stores each preactivation \(h^{(\ell )}=W^{(\ell -1)}z^{(\ell -1)}\) and activation \(z^{(\ell )}=\phi (h^{(\ell )})\). Backpropagation does not physically send the target backward through the network; it computes derivatives of the scalar loss with respect to intermediate variables. Define \(\delta ^{(\ell )}=\partial L/\partial h^{(\ell )}\), whose dimension equals the number of units in that layer. Looking backward from layer ℓ+1, \(h^{(\ell +1)}=W^{(\ell )}z^{(\ell )}\). One hidden activation influences every downstream preactivation, so the sensitivity is first multiplied by \((W^{(\ell )})^\mathrm{T}\) to aggregate downstream error and then multiplied elementwise by \(\phi '(h^{(\ell )})\). The transpose follows from the coordinate mapping; it is not optional notation. Each weight \(W^{(\ell -1)}_{ij}\) contributes presynaptic activation \(z^{(\ell -1)}_j\) to postsynaptic preactivation \(h^{(\ell )}_i\). Therefore \(\partial L/\partial W_{ij}=\delta _{i} z_{j}\), and the complete matrix gradient is the outer product \(\delta ^{(\ell )}(z^{(\ell -1)})^\mathrm{T}\). Batch training averages these outer products. The derivative of the nonlinear activation determines whether error can pass through a unit. A saturated sigmoid has a very small derivative and can cause vanishing gradients, whereas large weights can cause exploding gradients. ReLU has derivative 1 in its positive region and 0 in its negative region, which can also produce inactive units. Backpropagation is an exact chain-rule algorithm. Its outer-product form can be compared with biological three-factor rules, but weight transport, a global target, and update timing remain mechanistic differences. \(\delta\) denotes the derivative of loss with respect to a preactivation, not a directly observed biological firing error. The hidden-error recurrence contains the transpose of the downstream weights and the derivative of the local activation. A weight gradient is the outer product of postsynaptic sensitivity and presynaptic activation. Take \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(W^0=[[1,0],[0,1]]\), identity \(\phi\), \(W^1=(1,-1)\), target \(y=0\), and loss=\(1/2(\hat{y}-y)^2\). The two gradient shapes are \(1\times 2\) and \(2\times 2\), and every entry can be verified from its local outer product. Why does the backpropagated error recurrence use the transpose of the downstream weight matrix? The forward map W carries hidden coordinates into downstream coordinates. The chain rule must aggregate downstream scalar sensitivities back into each hidden coordinate, which is exactly the reverse Jacobian product \(W^\mathrm{T}\delta\); its shape also returns from the downstream dimension to the hidden dimension. Describing \(\delta\) as an error molecule that literally propagates backward through biological neurons, without separating a computed derivative from its possible implementation. Memorizing the recurrence without labeling h, z, \(\delta\), and W shapes at every layer, which invites errors at transposes and elementwise derivatives.

title: Lecture 12: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models
subtitle: How does the visual system use linear filters, nonlinearities, and hierarchical feature maps to turn luminance patterns into selectivity for position, orientation, and motion?
text: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models How does the visual system use linear filters, nonlinearities, and hierarchical feature maps to turn luminance patterns into selectivity for position, orientation, and motion? Retina→V1→streams → contrast → LNP → DoG center-surround → rectified feature maps → Gabor orientation Use the course-level photoreceptor–RGC–V1–MT/IT/LIP diagram to explain the visual hierarchy while separating anatomical pathways, receptive-field computations, and functional labels. Explain every stage of the LNP model—linear filter, static nonlinearity, and conditional Poisson output—and why early vision is commonly modeled in terms of contrast rather than raw luminance. Construct ON and OFF Difference-of-Gaussians receptive fields through spatial convolution and predict the response signs for a uniform field, a center spot, and surround illumination. Decompose a Gabor kernel into its Gaussian envelope, carrier frequency, orientation, and phase; then explain how the subsequent static nonlinearity introduces thresholding and saturation in V1 simple-cell orientation tuning. Extend receptive fields into space-time, distinguish separable from nonseparable kernels, and infer direction selectivity from slope in an x-t diagram. The visual hierarchy is not merely an anatomical list but a computational organization in which receptive-field size, feature complexity, history dependence, and invariance change by stage. LNP first projects a stimulus onto a linear receptive field, maps the drive through a nonlinearity to a rate, and uses a Poisson process to describe spikes. DoG, Gabor, and nonseparable spatiotemporal kernels summarize center-surround, orientation, and motion selectivity. Treating a receptive field only as a geometric region in visual space. Using raw luminance and contrast interchangeably. Leaving the sign or flip convention of a convolution kernel unstated. Assuming a feature map is a copy of the original image rather than a map of filter responses. Confusing Gabor orientation, phase, and spatial frequency. Assuming a separable spatiotemporal receptive field is automatically direction-selective. Equating an anatomical hierarchy with one purely feedforward computation. Do not describe a receptive field only as a screen “location”; it is a stimulus-response relationship. Distinguish a linear receptive field, classical receptive field, and experimental definition. Sparse-noise receptive-field mapping provides a useful transfer example. Visual contrast \(s = (I - I_{0} )/I_{0}\) \(I_{0}>0\) Linear receptive-field drive \(L=K \ast s\) Linear shift-invariant approximation Static nonlinearity \(r = F(L)\) A nonnegative or saturating rate, as specified LNP spike generation \(n \sim  \operatorname{Poisson}(rT )\) Conditional Poisson process Center-surround receptive field KDoG = Gcenter − Gsurround A wider surround Simple-cell orientation filter KGabor = G(x′ , y ′ ) cos(kx′ + ϕ) Localized sinusoid Separable receptive field \(K(x, y, t) = Ks\) Kt Rank-1 space-time structure receptive field A local or functional relation between a stimulus pattern and a response, not merely a screen location. feature selectivity A preferential response to a class of stimulus structures. dorsal stream A broad visual pathway associated with motion- and action-related processing. ventral stream A broad visual pathway associated with processing related to object identity. linear-nonlinear-Poisson model, \(\ln P A\) cascade of a linear filter, nonlinearity, and Poisson spike-count variability. center-surround A receptive-field organization with opposite signs in the center and periphery. feature map The rectified response of one filter at every location. Gabor kernel A Gaussian-windowed sinusoid. separable Having space and time components that can be written as a product. direction selectivity A preferential response to one direction of motion. For \(I_{0}=100\) and local \(I=120\), what is the contrast? If \(I_{0}=200\) and local \(I=220\), how does contrast change even though the raw increment is the same? Contrast measures relative change. The same 20-unit luminance increment is proportionally smaller on the brighter background, so an early-vision model should not compare raw differences alone. The first contrast is 0.2; the second is 0.1. If an ON-center kernel has zero total integral, what should its linear response be when uniform positive contrast covers both center and surround? A zero-integral center-surround filter removes the common luminance component while preserving spatial differences. A real cell may deviate from exactly zero because of imperfect balance, nonlinearity, and adaptation. Approximately zero, because the positive center contribution cancels the negative surround contribution. If k increases in a Gabor kernel while the Gaussian envelope stays fixed, which aspect of tuning changes? k determines phase change per unit distance along x', \(\theta\) determines the carrier coordinate's direction, and \(\phi\) translates the light and dark lobes. The carrier's spatial frequency increases and its ON/OFF lobes become more closely spaced; rotation \(\theta\) sets the preferred orientation. Why can a fully separable kernel \(K(x,t)=K_{x}(x)K_{t}(t)\) generally not distinguish two moving edges with equal speeds and opposite directions using only its linear response? Direction selectivity requires coupling spatial position to temporal delay. In a nonseparable kernel the preferred position changes with lag, matching a trajectory in one direction while rejecting the reverse trajectory. Its spatial preference has the same shape and position at every time lag, so it contains no tilted x-t structure encoding the order of locations. Why is “ON cells prefer light and OFF cells prefer dark” an incomplete account of a center-surround receptive field? The response depends on contrast location and surround context. A bright spot in an ON center can excite, whereas a bright surround can cancel it. A balanced kernel may not respond to the same global luminance, so both polarity and spatial pattern must be specified. This is the distinction tested in Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation. Worked example — Predicting Signs in a Discrete Three-Position Center-Surround Filter: Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify. \(L_{A}=(-0.5)0+1\times 1+(-0.5)0=1\), so \([L_{A}]_{+}=1\) after rectification. \(L_{B}=-0.5+1-0.5=0\); the balanced kernel cancels uniform contrast. With the OFF-center kernel -K, stimulus A gives -1 and therefore 0 after [L]_+. A zero sum of kernel weights is exactly the discrete condition for uniform cancellation. A nonzero sum leaves a residual response to a uniform field. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation”? The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion.
