The visual hierarchy mixes anatomy with computational abstraction; a region label is not an exclusive function. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From Contrast and Convolution to an ON-Center DoG”? Contrast is dimensionless. If x,y are measured in degrees of visual angle, a normalized Gaussian has units degree^{-2}, and integration leaves L with the drive units of A and B. If \(\sigma _{s}=\sigma _{c}\) and \(A=B\), the entire kernel is zero. If the surround is broad but B is not scaled for its area, comparing peak heights misrepresents total inhibitory strength. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How does the visual system turn a luminance image into local contrast features and connect a receptive field to spikes through a minimal probabilistic model? The source notes place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This course-level computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow. Along the hierarchy, classical receptive fields generally become larger, the selected features more complex, and history dependence and context stronger. Higher-level cells may also become more invariant to position, phase, or local detail. Feature selectivity asks which stimulus pattern changes the response; a receptive field additionally asks which positions and time lags matter. A single heat-map color cannot capture both questions. Why does changing Gabor phase \(\phi\) not change preferred orientation \(\theta\)? \(\phi\) translates positive and negative lobes along a fixed carrier axis and determines whether a bright or dark edge aligns with the filter. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinate system and determines which edge or grating direction aligns with the elongated lobes. This is the distinction tested in Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning. Worked example — Simple-Cell Responses at One Orientation and Different Phases: Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\). At difference 0, \(L=10cos0=10\) and \(r=10\). At difference \(\pi /2\), \(L=10\cos(\pi /2)=0\) and \(r=0\). At difference \(\pi\), \(L=10\cos\pi =-10\) and rectification gives \(r=0\). Without rectification, the response at phase \(\pi\) is -10 rather than no response; nonnegativity of firing rate comes from the nonlinear stage. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning”? Each location in a feature map stores a filter response, not a copy of the input image. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning”? For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How a Rotated Gabor Filter Produces Orientation-Selective Drive”? Both kx' and \(\phi\) must be dimensionless, so k has units inverse distance. The exponential argument \(x'^2/\sigma _{x}^2\) is dimensionless as well. As \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\to \infty\), localization is lost. As \(k\to 0\), the carrier approaches a constant and the kernel resembles a Gaussian blob rather than an oriented alternating filter. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does a biphasic temporal kernel not automatically guarantee direction selectivity? If the kernel still factors into a fixed spatial profile and a temporal waveform, it only reweights one spatial feature over time and never pairs distinct locations with particular lags. Direction selectivity requires space-time nonseparability or an equivalent multichannel nonlinear computation. This is the distinction tested in Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation. Worked example — Matching a Discrete Three-Frame Trajectory: Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0. The rightward sequence matches at all three lags, giving total linear drive \(1+1+1=3\). The leftward sequence matches only at middle position 1; the other two frames mismatch, so total drive is 1. With threshold 2, the rightward response passes and the leftward response is clipped to 0. If the three frames are averaged without order, both sequences contain positions \({0,1,2}\), and the distinction disappears. Temporal order is therefore indispensable. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation”? Spatiotemporal convolution uses past stimulus history, so the orientation of the time-lag axis must be explicit. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. A separable kernel's spatial profile does not move with lag; a tilted nonseparable kernel can encode the sign of velocity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. The spatiotemporal integral also includes dx \(d\tau\), so kernel normalization must preserve the drive units. At \(v=0\) the ridge is untilted and selects a static feature. With an extremely short temporal window, opposite-direction trajectories have not separated enough and direction discrimination weakens. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field”? ON/OFF center-surround filters first recode absolute luminance as local contrast. Arranging several polarity-specific subfields along one axis makes signed contributions add for the matching direction and cancel for an orthogonal direction, creating an elongated, orientation-selective Gabor-like linear receptive field. The diagram distinguishes local DoG contrast computation from the later subfield arrangement that creates orientation tuning. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feature map” mean in this lecture? feature map: The rectified response of one filter at every location. title: Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation
subtitle: Lecture 12 · Lecture12-IntroToVision.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture12-IntroToVision.pdf, p. 2
text: How does the visual system turn a luminance image into local contrast features and connect a receptive field to spikes through a minimal probabilistic model? The source notes place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This course-level computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow. Along the hierarchy, classical receptive fields generally become larger, the selected features more complex, and history dependence and context stronger. Higher-level cells may also become more invariant to position, phase, or local detail. Feature selectivity asks which stimulus pattern changes the response; a receptive field additionally asks which positions and time lags matter. A single heat-map color cannot capture both questions. The LNP model has three ordered stages: linear, nonlinear, and Poisson. The linear stage \(L=K*s\) measures the match between a stimulus and a receptive-field template. The nonlinearity \(r=F(L)\) rectifies, thresholds, or saturates the drive to produce a plausible rate. Finally, n~\(\operatorname{Poisson}(rT)\) describes count variability conditional on the stimulus. LNP is descriptive; it does not claim that each stage occupies a separate anatomical box. A Difference of Gaussians (DoG) often approximates an RGC center-surround receptive field. An ON-center filter subtracts a broad negative Gaussian from a narrow positive one; an OFF-center filter reverses every sign. If their integrals nearly balance, a uniform field cancels while center-surround differences are amplified. Threshold-linear rectification \([L]_{+}=\max(L,0)\) then separates ON and OFF drives into nonnegative feature maps. The visual hierarchy mixes anatomy with computational abstraction; a region label is not an exclusive function. An LNP linear drive may have either sign, the nonlinearity makes rate nonnegative, and a conditional distribution then generates spike count. A DoG center-surround filter suppresses common luminance and highlights local contrast and edges. Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify. The ON-center filter has positive drive for a local bright spot and no linear drive for a uniform bright field; the OFF-center channel is suppressed by that same bright spot. Why is “ON cells prefer light and OFF cells prefer dark” an incomplete account of a center-surround receptive field? The response depends on contrast location and surround context. A bright spot in an ON center can excite, whereas a bright surround can cancel it. A balanced kernel may not respond to the same global luminance, so both polarity and spatial pattern must be specified. Treating a receptive field as a purely geometric boundary without defining its internal positive and negative weights, time lags, and response measure. Comparing Gaussian centers and surrounds only by peak height while ignoring width, integrated strength, and the kernel sign convention.

title: Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning
subtitle: Lecture 12 · Lecture12-IntroToVision.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture12-IntroToVision.pdf, p. 4
text: How can one localized sinusoidal filter jointly select position, orientation, spatial frequency, and phase, and how do its responses form a feature map? Convolving one kernel over all retinal locations produces a feature map. Each map pixel records how well the surrounding image patch matches the feature template; it is not the original image intensity. ON and OFF kernels yield two polarity-specific maps, and rectification retains positive drive for each filter's preferred polarity. This resembles shared filters in convolutional neural networks mathematically, but it does not make biological wiring, learning rules, or boundary treatment identical. V1 simple-cell receptive fields often contain alternating elongated ON and OFF lobes. A Gabor kernel uses a Gaussian envelope to localize position and size and a cosine carrier to create the alternating lobes. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinates, k controls spatial frequency, and \(\phi\) controls phase. Orientation tuning arises because positive contributions add when an edge aligns with the lobes, whereas an orthogonal edge straddles positive and negative regions and cancels. Changing \(\theta\) rotates the preferred orientation. Changing \(\phi\) translates the bright-dark lobe pattern along the carrier direction without changing orientation or frequency. Increasing k packs more lobes into each unit distance. Collapsing all three parameters into a single “direction” label prevents predictions about phase reversal or different bar widths. A rectifying, saturating nonlinearity can turn linear Gabor drive into firing rate, for example \(r=r_{\mathrm{max}}[L]_{+}^2/(\alpha ^2+[L]_{+}^2)\). The response rises for small positive L, approaches \(r_{\mathrm{max}}\) for large L, and clips negative L. Localized sinusoidal analysis is mathematically related to wavelets and JPEG because all represent images with local scale-orientation components; this does not mean cortex implements the same codec. Each location in a feature map stores a filter response, not a copy of the input image. For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase. The nonlinearity determines sign handling, threshold, and saturation, so a single linear kernel can produce different tuning amplitudes. Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\). Simple-cell firing depends on both orientation/frequency matching and alignment of the light-dark phase. Why does changing Gabor phase \(\phi\) not change preferred orientation \(\theta\)? \(\phi\) translates positive and negative lobes along a fixed carrier axis and determines whether a bright or dark edge aligns with the filter. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinate system and determines which edge or grating direction aligns with the elongated lobes. Confusing the grating wave-vector direction with bar orientation without noting that they usually differ by 90°. Treating rectification or saturation as part of the linear receptive field rather than distinguishing linear drive L from firing rate r.

title: Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation
subtitle: Lecture 12 · Lecture12-IntroToVision.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture12-IntroToVision.pdf, p. 6
text: Why must direction selectivity link “where” with “how long ago” instead of using independent spatial and temporal filters? After time is included, the linear drive integrates past stimulus history: \(K(x',y',\tau )\) multiplies \(s(x-x',y-y',t-\tau )\), with \(\tau \ge 0\) denoting look-back time. Temporal lobes may be biphasic so that sustained components of a static image cancel. Because center and surround can have different time courses, an RGC receptive field is commonly nonseparable. Every time slice of a separable kernel \(K(x,y,t)=K_{s}(x,y)K_{t}(t)\) has the same spatial pattern, differing only by a scalar amplitude. It can express a fixed-location feature that excites and then inhibits, but it cannot move the preferred location. In a nonseparable kernel, positive and negative lobes shift with lag, binding spatial position to temporal order. A vertical edge moving rightward at velocity v satisfies \(x(t)=x_{0}+vt\). In an x-t diagram it is an oblique line of slope \(dx/dt=v\). If the positive lobes of a receptive field lie along the same line, the edge traverses every positive zone in sequence and produces a large inner product. An edge moving the other way follows the opposite slope and encounters mismatched positive and negative zones. The rightward-motion receptive field on page 6 of the lecture notes has precisely this tilted pattern. Direction selectivity can also be built from multiple filters, quadratic motion energy, or recurrence, so a tilted linear receptive field is a testable minimal description. Eye movements, coordinate transformations, and finite display refresh alter the stimulus trajectory; experiments must state the reference frame. Spatiotemporal convolution uses past stimulus history, so the orientation of the time-lag axis must be explicit. A separable kernel's spatial profile does not move with lag; a tilted nonseparable kernel can encode the sign of velocity. Motion is an orientation in the x-t plane, and velocity corresponds to trajectory slope. Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0. The same three positions produce different responses when their temporal order differs; direction selectivity arises from a space-time conjunction. Why does a biphasic temporal kernel not automatically guarantee direction selectivity? If the kernel still factors into a fixed spatial profile and a temporal waveform, it only reweights one spatial feature over time and never pairs distinct locations with particular lags. Direction selectivity requires space-time nonseparability or an equivalent multichannel nonlinear computation. Mixing time lag with absolute time, thereby flipping the receptive field on the temporal axis and reversing the inferred preferred direction. Explaining motion tuning from a single-frame spatial receptive field without checking the joint pattern across positions and lags.

title: Lecture 13: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification
subtitle: Under white-noise stimulation, why can the spike-triggered average estimate an LNP linear filter, and under which conditions can it fail fundamentally?
text: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification Under white-noise stimulation, why can the spike-triggered average estimate an LNP linear filter, and under which conditions can it fail fundamentally? White-noise stimulus → spike-triggered ensemble → matrix notation → least squares/Hessian → white covariance → STA proportionality Organize white-noise stimuli, spike trains, and the spike-triggered ensemble into a system-identification workflow, distinguishing a descriptive STA, a filter estimator, and a complete LNP component. Move among continuous convolution, pixel-index summation, and matrix notation while tracking the shapes of S, K, L, and the count vector and the orientation of the time-lag axis. Derive the normal equation and Hessian from mean-squared loss for a linear neuron, and explain circular versus elongated loss contours through stimulus covariance. Starting from \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), derive the proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and the STA while retaining the scaling by spike count, bin width, and stimulus variance. Recover a static nonlinearity with the small-bin Poisson approximation and diagnose STA failure caused by multiple features, an even nonlinearity, colored stimuli, or insufficient data. STA is both a descriptive average and, under a linear model, Gaussian white stimulation, and a suitable nonlinearity, a filter estimator. Matrix least squares reveals why: white stimulation makes the design covariance approximately a scalar identity, reducing the normal equation to a stimulus-response correlation. Recovering the nonlinearity yields an LNP model that can predict new stimuli, but multiple relevant dimensions, even-symmetric nonlinearities, or correlated stimulation can make the STA zero or biased. Treating the STA only as an image average without specifying time-lag alignment. Leaving matrix orientation unstated and confusing \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) with KS. Omitting the large-sample and equal-variance assumptions behind white covariance. Equating STA amplitude unconditionally with physical filter gain. Concluding from \(STA=0\) that a neuron has no receptive field. Forgetting to divide by bin width when recovering F. Evaluating a model on its training fit instead of held-out prediction. Distinguish the STA as a descriptive average, linear-filter estimator, and LNP-model component. They are related under particular assumptions, not unconditionally equivalent. Pixelized linear drive \(L = ST K S\):P×T Least-squares filter K̂ = (SS T )−1 Sh Invertible \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) Loss Hessian \(H = SS T /T\) Linear squared loss White-noise covariance SS \(T \approx  T \sigma s_{2} I\) Large T with independent equal-variance pixels Spike-triggered average 1 X \(ST A = st\) nsp t∈spikes Aligned stimulus histories STA/filter relation \(\hat{K} \propto  ST A\) White Gaussian single-filter assumptions Small-bin nonlinearity estimate P (spike|L) ≈ ∆\(tF (L)\) \(\Delta t\) rate≪1 system identification Inferring a system model from input-output data. white noise An ideal random stimulus with uncorrelated dimensions or time bins and uniform power. spike-triggered ensemble The collection of stimulus histories preceding all spikes. spike-triggered average, STA The mean of the spike-triggered ensemble. design matrix A matrix organizing stimulus vectors by examples or time bins. Hessian The matrix of second derivatives of loss with respect to parameters. isotropic Having equal curvature or variance in every direction. whitening Removing covariance correlations to obtain variables near unit covariance. correlated stimulus A stimulus whose dimensions have nonzero covariance. relevant dimension A stimulus-projection direction on which the response depends. What does column t of \(S\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times T}\) represent, and why is K^TS_{:t} a scalar? Each time bin is one high-dimensional regression example. Placing time in rows while retaining the original formulas misaligns the orientations of K, S, and the response. It is the stimulus history preceding time t, flattened in a fixed lag order. K and that column are both P-dimensional, so their inner product is one linear drive. What experimental problem is indicated by a small eigenvalue of the least-squares Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\)? Many K values displaced along that direction give almost identical predictions, leaving the estimate dominated by measurement noise or regularization. Identifiability improves only by adding stimulus variation in that direction. The stimulus varies little along that eigenvector direction, so loss curvature is weak and the data constrain that filter component poorly. Why are loss contours nearly circular, rather than tilted ellipses, for large-sample equal-variance white noise? The identity matrix favors no coordinate direction. Finite samples still create off-diagonal fluctuations, so circularity is an approximation rather than exact geometry in every experiment. Because \(H\approx \sigma _{s}^2I\), all orthogonal filter directions have equal curvature and cross-terms are nearly zero. A neuron fires strongly when \(|K^\mathrm{T}s|\) is large and responds identically to positive and negative projections. Why can its linear STA be nearly zero? A zero first moment does not imply an absence of stimulus dependence. Spike-triggered covariance can reveal increased variance along K, and an energy model can represent this even response. Stimuli resembling +K and -K both precede spikes, and the two groups cancel in their vector average. Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs? Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure. This is the distinction tested in White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations. Worked example — Matrix Prediction with Two Pixels and Four Time Bins: Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry. At t1 the stimulus is (1,1), so \(L_{1}=2\times 1+1\times 1=3\); at t2 it is (-1,1), so \(L_{2}=-2+1=-1\). At t3 the stimulus is (1,-1), so \(L_{3}=2-1=1\); at t4 it is (-1,-1), so \(L_{4}=-2-1=-3\). Therefore \(L=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). The first pixel has the larger weight, so changing its coordinate affects the drive more strongly. S is \(2\times 4\) and \(S^\mathrm{T}\) is \(4\times 2\); multiplication by \(2\times 1\) K must yield \(4\times 1\). A 2-dimensional result signals that the orientation has been reversed. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations”? An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations”? Continuous convolution, a pixel sum, and \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) are alternative representations of the same calculation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Discretizing Spatiotemporal Convolution as \(S^\mathrm{T}K\)”? If continuous K has units drive/(contrast·area·time), multiplying by contrast and dx dy \(d\tau\) gives drive. If discrete K absorbs grid volume, its numerical units depend on binning. A frame rate that is too low aliases fast temporal structure. A history window that is too short truncates the kernel; one that is too long increases P and reduces statistical power per dimension. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Given a complete stimulus movie and spike times, how can the stimulus history before each spike be converted into a dataset for estimating a filter? System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. The standard protocol in the source notes presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first. The spike-triggered ensemble contains every stimulus vector that preceded a spike, and its mean is the STA. For an ON-center RGC, the most recent lag may show a bright center and dark surround, while an earlier lag may differ in sign or shape, producing a biphasic temporal kernel. Every history must be aligned to its spike; otherwise alignment error artificially smears the filter in addition to true latency variation. Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably? Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially. This is the distinction tested in Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy. Worked example — Recovering a Known Filter from a White Design: Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares. \(SS^\mathrm{T}=[[4,0],[0,4]]=4I\), showing that the two stimulus dimensions have isotropic sample covariance. \(Sh=(8,4)^\mathrm{T}\); for example, its first entry is \(1\times 3+(-1)\times (-1)+1\times 1+(-1)\times (-3)=8\). \(\hat{K}=(4I)^{-1}(8,4)^\mathrm{T}=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), exactly recovering the true filter. If the second stimulus row is replaced by a copy of the first, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\operatorname{rank} 1\). Only the sum of the two filter weights affects prediction, so the weights cannot be identified separately. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy”? The normal equation expresses filter estimation as inverse covariance applied to stimulus-response correlation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy”? A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The Normal Equation and an Isotropic Hessian”? \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has units stimulus^2 and Sh has units stimulus×response. The resulting estimate therefore has units response/stimulus, as required for linear-filter gain. If \(T\le P\) or stimulus dimensions are linearly dependent, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) may be singular and the inverse expression cannot be used directly. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts? Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there. This is the distinction tested in From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics. Worked example — How an Even Nonlinearity Makes the STA Vanish: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance. The total spike probability is \((0.4+0.1+0.4)/3=0.3\). Bayes' rule gives \(P(s=-1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\), \(P(s=0|\mathrm{spike})=1/9\), and \(P(s=+1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\). The positive and negative endpoints have equal conditional weight, so \(STA=E[s|\mathrm{spike}]=(-1)(4/9)+0+(+1)(4/9)=0\). The spike-triggered second moment is \(E[s^2|\mathrm{spike}]=(4/9)+(4/9)=8/9\). Because the conditional mean is zero, this is also the spike-triggered variance. The original stimulus has zero mean and variance \(E[s^2]=2/3\). Spike-triggered variance increases by \(8/9-2/3=2/9\), revealing a preference for large |s|. The three conditional probabilities sum to 1. If the spike probabilities at ±1 are changed to equal that at \(s=0\), the spike-triggered distribution returns to the prior and the variance difference becomes zero. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics”? The proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and STA contains \(n_{sp}\), T, \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and \(\Delta t\); their directional relation is more robust than raw amplitude. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics”? Estimate the nonlinearity by dividing projection-conditioned spike probability by bin width. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An even response, multiple relevant dimensions, and colored stimulation can bias an STA or make it zero. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “STA Proportionality with All Scale Factors Retained”? \(n_{sp}/(T\Delta t)\) has units 1/time; dividing by \(\sigma _{s}^2\) and multiplying by stimulus gives rate/stimulus, as required for a linear rate filter. If bins are too wide, \(k_{t}\) can exceed 1 and the Bernoulli simplification fails. With too few spikes, STA variance is large even when the expectation relation holds. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow”? A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “white noise” mean in this lecture? white noise: An ideal random stimulus with uncorrelated dimensions or time bins and uniform power. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. title: White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations
subtitle: Lecture 13 · Lecture13-SpikeTriggeredAverage-UPDATE.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture13-SpikeTriggeredAverage-UPDATE.pdf, p. 2
text: Given a complete stimulus movie and spike times, how can the stimulus history before each spike be converted into a dataset for estimating a filter? System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. The standard protocol in the source notes presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first. The spike-triggered ensemble contains every stimulus vector that preceded a spike, and its mean is the STA. For an ON-center RGC, the most recent lag may show a bright center and dark surround, while an earlier lag may differ in sign or shape, producing a biphasic temporal kernel. Every history must be aligned to its spike; otherwise alignment error artificially smears the filter in addition to true latency variation. Continuous notation writes \(L(t)=\int dx'\) dy' dt' \(K(x',y',t')s(x',y',t-t')\). After discretization, combine (x,y,t') into index p to obtain \(L_{t}=\sum _pK_{p}S_{pt}\). Matrix notation is \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\). All three forms express the same inner product. Matrix form is convenient for least squares, whereas continuous form shows spatial location and causal lag directly. Each column of S is an entire stimulus history, not just the current frame; the p entries of K follow the same flattening order. Reversing the lag index flips the estimated kernel in time. A white-noise protocol matters not because the pattern merely looks random, but because different dimensions have nearly diagonal sample covariance on a common scale, reducing estimator bias and uneven uncertainty. An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient. Continuous convolution, a pixel sum, and \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) are alternative representations of the same calculation. The defining benefit of white noise is covariance isotropy, not an arbitrarily generated noisy picture. Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry. One matrix multiplication computes the filter projections for all four time bins while preserving the pairing with each stimulus column. Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs? Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure. Flattening the stimulus without recording pixel and lag order, so the resulting vector cannot be reshaped correctly into a receptive field. Calling a stimulus white merely because it looks random, without checking its mean, variance, cross-correlations, and finite-sample covariance.

title: Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy
subtitle: Lecture 13 · Lecture13-SpikeTriggeredAverage-UPDATE.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture13-SpikeTriggeredAverage-UPDATE.pdf, p. 4
text: Why does stimulus covariance control uncertainty in a filter estimate, and how does white noise place different feature directions on a common scale? First consider a linear neuron \(h_{t}\approx K^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\), where h may be a measured firing-rate estimate. Mean-squared loss averages prediction error over T bins. Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) gives the normal equation \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\): stimulus covariance scale times the filter equals stimulus-response cross-correlation. Identifiability depends on whether S spans the relevant directions. For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially. In ideal Gaussian white stimulation, every \(S_{pt}\) has zero mean and variance \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and different p dimensions are uncorrelated. At large T, \((SS^\mathrm{T})_{pq}=\sum _tS_{pt}S_{qt}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2\delta _{pq}\). Consequently \(H\approx \sigma _{s}^2I\), the loss contours are nearly circular, and every filter dimension has equal curvature. A finite dataset never has covariance exactly equal to the identity: off-diagonal sample covariances fluctuate around zero. Unequal pixel variances produce a diagonal but anisotropic H. With colored stimuli, correlations in H cause raw cross-correlation to mix the true filter with the stimulus spectrum. One must then apply the covariance inverse explicitly, whiten the stimulus, or fit a regularized likelihood model. The normal equation expresses filter estimation as inverse covariance applied to stimulus-response correlation. A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction. White-noise isotropy is a large-sample approximation; colored stimuli require covariance correction. Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares. For orthogonal equal-variance stimuli, the covariance inverse supplies only a common rescaling, so the direction of the cross-correlation is the filter direction. Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably? Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially. Interpreting a circular loss contour as a circular receptive field; the contour describes curvature in parameter space, not spatial shape. Using the white-noise approximation without the large-T, equal-variance, and independence assumptions.

title: From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics
subtitle: Lecture 13 · Lecture13-SpikeTriggeredAverage-UPDATE.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture13-SpikeTriggeredAverage-UPDATE.pdf, p. 6
text: Under which scaling and probabilistic assumptions does the stimulus average before spikes point along a linear filter, and what kinds of selectivity can this average cancel completely? The data contain spike counts \(k_{t}\) rather than a continuous rate \(h_{t}\). Choose bin width \(\Delta t\) small enough that \(k_{t}\in {0,1}\) usually holds and define rate estimate \(h_{t}=k_{t}/\Delta t\). Then Sh=(1/Δt)Σ_{t:k_t=1}\(s_{t}\), the sum of spike-triggered stimulus vectors scaled by bin width. Because \(STA=(1/n_{sp})\sum _{spikes}s_{t}\), a white design gives \(\hat{K}\approx [n_{sp}/(T\sigma _{s}^2\Delta t)]STA\). STA and K point in the same direction, but absolute amplitude depends on spike count, recording duration, stimulus variance, and bin width. Comparing raw STA amplitudes across cells or conditions can therefore mistake a firing-rate change for a filter-gain change. After estimating \(\hat{K}\), compute \(L_{t}=\hat{K}^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\) in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical \(P(\mathrm{spike}|L)\). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives \(P(k=1|L)\approx \Delta tF(L)\), hence \(\hat{F}(L)=P(\mathrm{spike}|L)/\Delta t\). Finally combine \(\hat{K}\), \(\hat{F}\), and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test. STA succeeds when one linear dimension dominates, the stimulus distribution is suitable, and spike count is adequate. Colored stimulation biases its direction; non-Gaussian input breaks the simple proportionality; multiple relevant dimensions collapse into one average; an even nonlinearity \(F(L)=F(-L)\) cancels +K and -K ensembles; and history dependence or adaptation contaminates the stimulus filter. Thus \(STA=0\) is not evidence for “no receptive field.” The proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and STA contains \(n_{sp}\), T, \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and \(\Delta t\); their directional relation is more robust than raw amplitude. Estimate the nonlinearity by dividing projection-conditioned spike probability by bin width. An even response, multiple relevant dimensions, and colored stimulation can bias an STA or make it zero. A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance. The STA is zero, yet spike-triggered variance rises from 2/3 to 8/9. STC or a quadratic model can detect the relevant direction hidden by symmetric averaging over signs. Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts? Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there. Comparing raw STA amplitudes across conditions without correcting for spike rate, stimulus variance, duration, and bin width. Reading \(STA=0\) as proof that a neuron is not stimulus-selective while ignoring even nonlinearities and multiple-feature coding.

title: Lecture 14: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
subtitle: When one linear feature is insufficient, how does STC reveal a multidimensional stimulus subspace, and how do GLMs unify Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli response models?
text: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models When one linear feature is insufficient, how does STC reveal a multidimensional stimulus subspace, and how do GLMs unify Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli response models? Multiple features → STC eigenspace → stimulus correction → GLM distribution → linear predictor → link Explain why one STA cannot describe an H1-like or complex-cell-like response driven by multiple features, and use spike-triggered covariance eigenvectors to find stimulus directions whose variance changes. Define the response distribution, linear predictor, and link function of a GLM, including the relation between the canonical parameter and the mean. Write the log likelihoods for Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli probability models and explain the supports enforced by identity, log, and logit links. Strictly separate Poisson counts, small-bin Bernoulli spike/no-spike observations, and logistic classification so their likelihoods and interpretations are not conflated. Reconstruct the stimulus, self-history, and coupling filters of a retinal population GLM, and explain why fitted coupling provides conditional prediction rather than proof of a direct synapse. STC compares spike-triggered covariance with raw stimulus covariance to find directions in which pre-spike variance expands or contracts; colored stimulation requires whitening or correction. A GLM unifies several regressions through a response distribution, linear predictor, and link. A retinal population GLM can fit stimulus filters, self-history, and cross-neuron coupling together, but remains a statistical model: a coupling filter is not automatically a direct synapse. Concluding from \(STA=0\) that there is no relevant feature. Applying ordinary eigendecomposition directly to \(\Delta C\) under colored stimulation. Interpreting “linear” in GLM as requiring a linear response mean. Using an identity link for Poisson data and thereby allowing a negative rate. Conflating Bernoulli logistic classification with a Poisson small-count model. Treating fitted coupling filters as direct anatomical synapses. Ignoring history dependence and thereby biasing the apparent stimulus filter. Do not read “linear” in GLM as a requirement that the response mean be linear. The predictor is linear; the link determines its relation to the mean. STC covariance change ∆C = Cspike − Cstim Centered ensembles GLM linear predictor \(\eta  = X\beta \) Shape-compatible design Link function \(g(E[y|x]) = \eta \) Chosen response family Inverse Poisson log link \(\lambda  = e\eta \) Positive mean Inverse logistic link \(q = (1 + e^{-\eta } )-1\) \(0<q<1\) Poisson log likelihood ℓP ois = (yη − eη − log y!) Conditionally independent bins or counts Logistic loss −ℓBern = cross-entropy Bernoulli outcomes spike-triggered covariance, STC Analysis of covariance in the spike-triggered ensemble. relevant subspace The response-sensitive subspace spanned by several stimulus filters. exponential family A family of distributions expressible in a specified canonical statistic-parameter form. linear predictor \(\eta =X\beta\). link function The mapping between a conditional mean and \(\eta\). Poisson regression A log-link GLM for a count or rate. logistic regression A logit-link GLM for a Bernoulli outcome. log odds \(\log[q/(1-q)]\). history filter The linear effect of past spikes on the current conditional response. coupling filter A predictive filter applied to the histories of other units. If \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\), what are the two eigenvalues of \(\Delta C\), and what does each mean? STC measures conditional covariance relative to raw stimulus covariance. Both positive and negative changes may reveal relevant dimensions, so keeping only the largest positive eigenvalue is unjustified. The eigenvalues are 3 and -0.75. Variance before spikes increases in the first direction and decreases in the second. Which part of a GLM is linear? Is the mean response of \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\) linear? The distribution and link determine mean support and curvature. Treating a GLM as ordinary linear regression would incorrectly permit a negative mean count. The predictor \(\eta =X\beta\) is linear. Through the inverse log link, the Poisson mean is \(\lambda =e^\eta\) and is nonlinear in the predictor. What mean count does \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\) predict for \(\eta =\log 2\)? What probability does a Bernoulli-logit model predict for \(\eta =0\)? The two inverse links map any real \(\eta\) into a positive real mean and a probability in (0,1), respectively. Enforcing this support is central to link selection. The Poisson mean is \(\lambda =e^{\log 2}=2\); the Bernoulli probability is \(q=1/(1+e^0)=0.5\). If the coupling filter from neuron j to neuron i has a positive coefficient in a retinal GLM, does that prove a direct excitatory connection from j to i? Shared input, unobserved cells, stimulus-model mismatch, and common network state can all produce fitted coupling. Establishing a causal synapse requires perturbation or a stronger identification design. No. It says only that, conditional on the included covariates, past spikes of j improve the prediction of i's conditional rate. Why cannot the sign of an STC eigenvector say whether a stimulus is excitatory or inhibitory? Covariance describes an unoriented axis. v and -v have identical squared projections and covariance. To learn how projection sign affects rate, fit or inspect the nonlinearity along that axis. This is the distinction tested in Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance. Worked example — Positive and Negative Directions in Two-Dimensional STC: Let \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\). Find \(\Delta C\) and its eigenvectors, then interpret them. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\). Find \(\Delta C\) and its eigenvectors, then interpret them. \(\Delta C=\operatorname{diag}(3,-0.75)\). It is already diagonal, with eigenvectors \(e_{1}=(1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(e_{2}=(0,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Along \(e_{1}\), spike-conditioned variance rises from 1 to 4, a change of +3, suggesting that large \(|s_{1}|\) is associated with spiking. Along \(e_{2}\), variance falls from 1 to 0.25, a change of -0.75, suggesting that spiking favors \(s_{2}\) within a narrow range. \(\operatorname{trace} \Delta C=2.25\) is the total variance change, but the trace alone erases the axis-specific combination of one positive and one negative change. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance”? STC finds spike-conditioned changes in variance and can reveal dimensions that symmetry hides from the STA. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance”? Both positive and negative covariance changes are informative; an eigenvector's sign is not an excitation sign. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? STC finds spike-conditioned changes in variance and can reveal dimensions that symmetry hides from the STA. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From a Covariance Difference to Relevant Axes”? Covariance and \(\Delta C\) have units stimulus^2, as do their eigenvalues. In normalized or whitened space they can be interpreted as dimensionless relative changes. If \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=C_{\mathrm{stim}}\), the second moment does not change and STC reveals no feature; the neuron may still depend on higher-order statistics. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: When a neuron responds to both signs of a projection or to several directions, how can features be recovered from the shape, rather than the mean, of the pre-spike stimulus distribution? The source notes use the blowfly H1 neuron, whose stimulus \(s(t)=v(t)\) is image velocity rather than a two-dimensional light pattern. The response may depend on projections through several temporal filters \(K_{1}\cdots K_{n}\) followed by a multidimensional nonlinearity F. Thus stimulus-vector coordinates are defined by the question: they may be pixels, velocity history, past spikes, or other measured covariates. If the nonlinearity is symmetric for +K and -K, the spike-triggered mean cancels. If the response depends on several relevant filters, one STA supplies at most one mean direction. It may consistently point toward one linear combination but cannot recover the full relevant subspace. Symmetry cancellation and dimensional limitation are distinct and should not both be dismissed as a noisy or unstable average. STC computes \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) and compares it with \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\). Eigenvectors of \(\Delta C\) give directions of altered variance, and eigenvalue signs show whether variance grew or shrank. Why is the identity link \(\lambda =\eta\) structurally unsuitable for \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\)? The linear predictor \(\eta\) may be any real number, so an identity link permits negative expected counts. The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) maps the whole real line to positive means and yields the convenient residual gradient of the canonical Poisson likelihood. This is the distinction tested in The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods. Worked example — The Direction of a One-Coefficient Poisson Update: For one observation \(x=2\) and \(\beta =0\), \(\eta =0\) and \(\lambda =1\); the observed count is \(y=3\). Find this observation's contribution to the log-likelihood gradient with respect to \(\beta\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For one observation \(x=2\) and \(\beta =0\), \(\eta =0\) and \(\lambda =1\); the observed count is \(y=3\). Find this observation's contribution to the log-likelihood gradient with respect to \(\beta\). \(\eta =x\beta =0\), and the inverse log link gives \(\lambda =e^0=1\). The count residual \(y-\lambda =2\). The gradient contribution is \(x(y-\lambda )=2\times 2=4\), which is positive; gradient ascent raises \(\beta\) and therefore the predicted count. If \(y=0\), the same sample gives gradient \(2(0-1)=-2\), lowering \(\beta\) and \(\lambda\) while the prediction remains positive. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods”? The linear component of a GLM is the predictor; the inverse link may make the mean nonlinear. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods”? A Gaussian identity link corresponds to squared error, while a Poisson log link enforces a positive count mean. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A Gaussian identity link corresponds to squared error, while a Poisson log link enforces a positive count mean. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving the Poisson Log Likelihood and Gradient from the Probability Mass”? Both \(\eta\) and log\(\lambda\) must be dimensionless. An expected event count is dimensionless; a continuous-time rate enters the Poisson mean only after multiplication by \(\Delta t\). If data variance greatly exceeds its mean, the Poisson model may be overdispersed; a negative-binomial or latent-state model may fit better. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does fitting stimulus and coupling filters jointly still not justify interpreting a coupling coefficient as a causal synapse? The model controls only measured covariates. Unobserved common input, global state, model mismatch, and indirect network paths can still create conditional dependence. Establishing a causal synapse additionally requires intervention, anatomy, or stronger identifiability assumptions. This is the distinction tested in Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence. Worked example — Combining History Filters into a Conditional Spike Probability: A bin's predictor consists of bias -2, stimulus contribution +1.5, refractory self-history -3, and coupling from another neuron +0.5. Compute \(\eta\) and q, then remove the refractory term and compare. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A bin's predictor consists of bias -2, stimulus contribution +1.5, refractory self-history -3, and coupling from another neuron +0.5. Compute \(\eta\) and q, then remove the refractory term and compare. With every term, \(\eta =-2+1.5-3+0.5=-3\) and \(q=1/(1+e^3)\approx 0.047\). Without the refractory term, \(\eta =0\) and \(q=0.5\). Thus a strong negative filter from the neuron's recent spike can suppress immediate spike probability even in the presence of stimulus and coupling drive. Contributions add in log-odds space, not as probabilities. Directly adding probabilities can exceed 1. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence”? A population predictor may include stimulus, self-history, cross-neuron history, and a bias simultaneously. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence”? A coupling filter is a conditional statistical coefficient, not automatically a direct excitatory or inhibitory synapse. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Bernoulli logit maps to probability; the small-bin Poisson approximation requires a very small expected count. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From Bernoulli Likelihood to the Sigmoid and Cross-Entropy”? \(\eta\) and log odds are dimensionless. A covariate with physical units therefore needs a reciprocal-unit coefficient so \(x_{j}\beta _{j}\) is dimensionless. As q approaches 0 or 1, sigmoid slope \(q(1-q)\) becomes small. Complete separation can make unregularized logistic coefficients diverge. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor”? A population GLM adds a stimulus filter, self-history filter, and cross-neuron coupling filters in predictor \(\eta _{i}(t)\), then uses a log or logit inverse link to produce a nonnegative rate or binary spike probability. Simultaneous fitting reduces omitted-covariate confounding, but a coupling coefficient still denotes predictive dependence conditional on the included variables, not an anatomical synapse. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “relevant subspace” mean in this lecture? relevant subspace: The response-sensitive subspace spanned by several stimulus filters. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “link function” mean in this lecture? link function: The mapping between a conditional mean and \(\eta\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Poisson regression” mean in this lecture? Poisson regression: A log-link GLM for a count or rate. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “logistic regression” mean in this lecture? logistic regression: A logit-link GLM for a Bernoulli outcome.
