title: Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance
subtitle: Lecture 14 · Lecture14-STC-GLM.pdf, p. 1
text: When a neuron responds to both signs of a projection or to several directions, how can features be recovered from the shape, rather than the mean, of the pre-spike stimulus distribution? The source notes use the blowfly H1 neuron, whose stimulus \(s(t)=v(t)\) is image velocity rather than a two-dimensional light pattern. The response may depend on projections through several temporal filters \(K_{1}\cdots K_{n}\) followed by a multidimensional nonlinearity F. Thus stimulus-vector coordinates are defined by the question: they may be pixels, velocity history, past spikes, or other measured covariates. If the nonlinearity is symmetric for +K and -K, the spike-triggered mean cancels. If the response depends on several relevant filters, one STA supplies at most one mean direction. It may consistently point toward one linear combination but cannot recover the full relevant subspace. Symmetry cancellation and dimensional limitation are distinct and should not both be dismissed as a noisy or unstable average. STC computes \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) and compares it with \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\). Eigenvectors of \(\Delta C\) give directions of altered variance, and eigenvalue signs show whether variance grew or shrank. A positive eigenvalue means that the spike-conditioned ensemble is broader along that feature direction, as when a large projection magnitude triggers spikes. A negative eigenvalue means that spikes require the projection to lie in a narrower range. An eigenvector's sign is arbitrary—v and -v are the same axis—so response sign must be inferred from the multidimensional nonlinearity. For white stimulation \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\approx \sigma ^2I\), so \(\Delta C\) can be analyzed directly. Colored stimulation allows intrinsically high-variance input directions to dominate even when irrelevant to the neuron. One should whiten first or solve \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) \(v=\lambda  C_{\mathrm{stim}} v\). STC remains sensitive to finite spike count, high dimension, and non-Gaussian input, requiring a null distribution, regularization, and held-out validation. STC finds spike-conditioned changes in variance and can reveal dimensions that symmetry hides from the STA. Both positive and negative covariance changes are informative; an eigenvector's sign is not an excitation sign. Colored stimuli require whitening or a generalized-eigenvalue correction relative to \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\). Let \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\). Find \(\Delta C\) and its eigenvectors, then interpret them. One neuron can simultaneously require a large magnitude in one projection and constrain another projection; one STA cannot express both conditions. Why cannot the sign of an STC eigenvector say whether a stimulus is excitatory or inhibitory? Covariance describes an unoriented axis. v and -v have identical squared projections and covariance. To learn how projection sign affects rate, fit or inspect the nonlinearity along that axis. Selecting the largest eigenvector of \(\Delta C\) under colored stimulation and mistaking the stimulus's own high variance for a neural feature. Reporting only positive eigenvalues and missing directions in which the spike-conditioned ensemble narrows.

title: The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods
subtitle: Lecture 14 · Lecture14-STC-GLM.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture14-STC-GLM.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture14-STC-GLM.pdf, p. 4
text: How can the same linear covariates model a continuous response or spike count, and how does the probability model determine the objective? A GLM has three components: response distribution \(p(y|\theta )\), linear predictor \(\eta =X\beta\), and link \(g(m)=\eta\) connecting \(\eta\) with conditional \(\operatorname{mean} m\). The exponential-family canonical form \(p(y|\theta )=\exp[y\theta +H(y)-D(\theta )]\) separates the data term, base measure, and log-partition function. D normalizes the distribution and determines its mean and variance. For a unit-variance Gaussian model with identity link, \(m=\eta =x^\mathrm{T}\beta\). The β-dependent part of the log likelihood is \(-1/2\Sigma (y-m)^2\), so likelihood maximization equals mean-squared-error minimization. Unknown or heteroscedastic variance requires an extension; squared loss is not the only model for continuous responses. For a nonnegative integer count \(y\ge 0\), the Poisson model is \(p(y|\lambda )=\lambda ^ye^{-\lambda }/y\)!. Its canonical parameter is \(\theta =\log\lambda\), predictor \(\eta =\theta\), and inverse link \(\lambda =e^\eta\). The exponential maps every real predictor to a positive mean and gives log likelihood Σ[yη-e^η-log(y!)], whose gradient is the covariate times observed minus predicted count. Poisson conditional independence says that bins or samples are independent after conditioning on all included covariates; it does not say that real spike trains lack refractoriness or coupling. Adding past spikes to the design matrix models history dependence conditionally. Bin size also sets response support: a longer window permits count>1, while a very small bin is closer to Bernoulli. The linear component of a GLM is the predictor; the inverse link may make the mean nonlinear. A Gaussian identity link corresponds to squared error, while a Poisson log link enforces a positive count mean. Likelihood assumptions include response support and conditional independence and must match the binning scheme. For one observation \(x=2\) and \(\beta =0\), \(\eta =0\) and \(\lambda =1\); the observed count is \(y=3\). Find this observation's contribution to the log-likelihood gradient with respect to \(\beta\). A Poisson gradient uses observed minus expected count to set direction, scaled by the covariate magnitude that determines this sample's influence on the coefficient. Why is the identity link \(\lambda =\eta\) structurally unsuitable for \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\)? The linear predictor \(\eta\) may be any real number, so an identity link permits negative expected counts. The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) maps the whole real line to positive means and yields the convenient residual gradient of the canonical Poisson likelihood. Treating Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli as merely three loss names without checking response support and variance assumptions. Inferring from a conditional Poisson model that real spikes have no refractory period or shared network fluctuation.

title: Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence
subtitle: Lecture 14 · Lecture14-STC-GLM.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture14-STC-GLM.pdf, p. 6
text: How can one predictor include external stimulus, a neuron's own history, and the past spikes of other neurons, while choosing appropriately between count and binary observations? For each neuron i, a retinal population GLM forms η_i(t)=k_i*s(t)+h_i*y_i(t-past)+Σ_{j≠i}c_{ij}*y_j(t-past)\(+b_{i}\). Stimulus filter \(k_{i}\) describes receptive-field drive. Self-history filter \(h_{i}\) may be negative at short post-spike lags for refractoriness and positive later for burst tendency. Coupling filter \(c_{ij}\) describes how past spikes of other neurons affect the conditional rate of i. All filters should be fit jointly. Omitting self-history can make the stimulus filter absorb refractory structure; omitting shared stimulus can make a coupling filter mislabel common stimulus drive as interaction. Even with simultaneous fitting, unobserved neurons and global state can leave residual coupling. A coefficient therefore measures predictive conditional dependence, not an anatomical synapse. In a very small bin, \(y_{t}\in {0,1}\) and a Bernoulli likelihood is suitable. Use log odds \(\theta =\log[q/(1-q)]\) as predictor \(\eta\), with inverse link \(q=e^\eta /(1+e^\eta )\). At \(\eta =0\), \(q=0.5\); increasing \(\eta\) by one multiplies the odds by e. That statement is more accurate than a fixed probability increment because sigmoid slope differs near 0 and near 1. Bernoulli negative log likelihood is binary cross-entropy. It can model either small-bin spike/no-spike observations or behavioral classification, but their observation units and covariates differ. For continuous-time rate r, the Poisson bin mean is \(\lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}=r\Delta t\). When \(\lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}\ll 1\), \(q=1-e^{-\lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}}\approx \lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}\approx r\Delta t\). If \(\lambda\) in the previous module already denotes expected count per bin, do not multiply by \(\Delta t\) again. Bernoulli loses count information once multiple spikes per bin are appreciable. Before selecting a model, state whether each observation is a count window, binary bin, or behavioral trial. A population predictor may include stimulus, self-history, cross-neuron history, and a bias simultaneously. A coupling filter is a conditional statistical coefficient, not automatically a direct excitatory or inhibitory synapse. The Bernoulli logit maps to probability; the small-bin Poisson approximation requires a very small expected count. A bin's predictor consists of bias -2, stimulus contribution +1.5, refractory self-history -3, and coupling from another neuron +0.5. Compute \(\eta\) and q, then remove the refractory term and compare. A GLM adds evidence from different sources in predictor space, then uses a sigmoid to convert the total into a valid probability. Why does fitting stimulus and coupling filters jointly still not justify interpreting a coupling coefficient as a causal synapse? The model controls only measured covariates. Unobserved common input, global state, model mismatch, and indirect network paths can still create conditional dependence. Establishing a causal synapse additionally requires intervention, anatomy, or stronger identifiability assumptions. Including current or future spikes in a history design matrix, causing information leakage and falsely high predictive performance. Interpreting a log-odds coefficient as a fixed additive change in probability and ignoring the sigmoid operating point.

title: Lecture 15: Efficient Coding and Information Theory
subtitle: How does the efficient-coding hypothesis formalize redundancy reduction with entropy, mutual information, and a noisy linear channel, and how can it predict retinal center-surround filters?
text: Efficient Coding and Information Theory How does the efficient-coding hypothesis formalize redundancy reduction with entropy, mutual information, and a noisy linear channel, and how can it predict retinal center-surround filters? Barlow hypotheses → surprise \(-\log p\)→ entropy → mutual information → Gaussian channel → redundancy/capacity Distinguish Barlow's three hypotheses accurately and present efficient coding as a normative proposal constrained by noise and resources. Explain surprise=\(-\log p\) from the additivity of information for independent events, and compute entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information. Derive the joint-distribution form of mutual information, show that \(I=0\) under independence, and explain why differential entropy can be negative and depends on coordinate units. Starting from \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), derive input and output covariance while distinguishing signal, input noise, and output noise by their locations in the encoder. Explain the Gaussian-MI determinant formula, fixed-information constraints, channel capacity, decorrelation, and orthogonal nonuniqueness, and show how added symmetries can select center-surround filters. Barlow's efficient coding is a normative hypothesis: under resource and noise constraints, a sensory system should reduce predictable redundancy while retaining useful information. Information theory quantifies predictability and transmission through surprise, entropy, and mutual information. Atick and Redlich model the retina as a noisy linear encoder and decoder that lowers redundancy under fixed-information and output-capacity constraints. Decorrelation is nonunique; rotational symmetry together with locality and related constraints can select a center-surround form. Treating efficient coding as a uniquely established mechanism rather than a normative hypothesis. Equating entropy unconditionally with useful information. Calling a negative differential entropy an error. Assuming \(MI=0\) means only zero linear correlation; when well-defined, it means independence. Optimizing only decorrelation while ignoring noise and output capacity. Assuming that the whitening solution is unique. Presenting the normative center-surround prediction as singular causal evidence. Distinguish entropy, differential entropy, mutual information, redundancy, and channel capacity. Avoid unconditional claims such as “more entropy is better.” Surprise \(S(x) = - \log p(x)\) Chosen logarithm base Entropy \(H(X) = E[- \log p(X)]\) Discrete distribution Mutual information \(I(X; Y ) = H(X) - H(X|Y )\) Known joint distribution Dependence form of MI \(\sum  p(x, y)\) \(I= p(x, y)\) \(\log p(x)p(y)\) Support handled correctly Linear Gaussian covariance propagation Cy = ACx \(AT + \sigma y_{2}\) I Independent additive output noise Gaussian-MI determinant form 1 det Cy \(I(X; Y ) = \log 2 \det Cy|x\) Jointly Gaussian variables Decorrelation objective Cout ≈ diagonal Second-order redundancy efficient coding A normative principle for optimizing an information representation under resource and noise constraints. redundancy Structure that is predictable from other components and transmitted repeatedly. surprise The −log probability of an event. entropy Average surprise or uncertainty. conditional entropy Residual uncertainty after another variable is given. mutual information The reduction in uncertainty about one variable supplied by another. differential entropy An entropy-like quantity for a continuous density that can be negative and depends on units. channel capacity The maximum mutual information attainable under input constraints. decorrelation Making off-diagonal covariance entries approach zero. normative model A model of what a system should optimize rather than a direct specification of mechanism. With logarithms base 2, what is the surprise of an outcome with probability 1/8? Three independent fair binary choices are required to reduce the probability to 1/8, so observing the outcome conveys 3 bits. Changing the logarithm base changes the numerical unit. \(-\log_{2}(1/8)=3\) bits. Let X be fair Bernoulli and \(Y=X\). What are \(H(X)\), \(H(X|Y)\), and \(I(X;Y)\)? Once Y is known, X is known exactly and conditional uncertainty is zero. High entropy in Y does not imply low redundancy between the two variables. \(H(X)=1\) bit, \(H(X|Y)=0\), and \(I(X;Y)=1\) bit. Let \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), with every term zero-mean and the noises independent. How should \(C_{y}\) be written? Signal and input noise both pass through A, whereas output noise is added afterward. The two noise sources therefore cannot be placed at the same point in the model. \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\); for isotropic noise, \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+\sigma _{x}^2I)A^\mathrm{T}+\sigma _{y}^2I\). After whitening makes covariance I, why does left multiplication by any orthogonal U leave output covariance equal to I? Second-order decorrelation requires normalized orthogonal axes but does not uniquely specify their spatial form. Center-surround filters require translation or rotation symmetry, locality, or other constraints. Because \(U I U^\mathrm{T}=UU^\mathrm{T}=I\). Why does negative differential entropy not mean probability theory has failed? A continuous density is not the probability of one outcome; it may exceed 1, and its entropy contains the coordinate bin size or units. Rescaling a variable adds a log-scale term. Shared scale contributions cancel in MI, which remains nonnegative and retains its dependence interpretation. This is the distinction tested in Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory. Worked example — Binary Entropy and Predictability: Compute the entropy of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli} p=0.5\) and \(p=0.9\) using \(\log 2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Compute the entropy of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli} p=0.5\) and \(p=0.9\) using \(\log 2\). \(H(0.5)=-0.5log2(0.5)-0.5log2(0.5)=1\) bit. \(H(0.9)=-0.9log2(0.9)-0.1log2(0.1)\approx 0.137+0.332=0.469\) bit. At \(p=0.9\) the outcome is more predictable, so expected surprise is lower. This has nothing to do with the numerical mean of the random variable. As \(p\to 1\), \(H\to 0\). Exchanging p with 1-p leaves entropy unchanged because it merely swaps outcome labels. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory”? Efficient coding is constrained optimization, not the unique mechanism behind every sensory feature. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory”? The logarithmic form of surprise follows because independent probabilities multiply while their information adds. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Efficient coding is constrained optimization, not the unique mechanism behind every sensory feature. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Equivalent Forms of Mutual Information and Independence”? Probabilities and their ratios are dimensionless, making the logarithm valid. A differential density has reciprocal units, which is why a standalone differential entropy depends on coordinate units. A deterministic continuous relation can yield infinite MI in the ideal zero-noise limit. Finite measurement noise and discretization alter the numerical estimate. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can the idea that a sensory system should not waste spikes on predictable content be converted into quantitative measures of uncertainty and dependence? The source notes retain three ideas from Barlow: detect “passwords” of critical significance, filter signals for other nervous-system regions, and recode sensory messages to reduce redundancy. This lecture focuses on the third. Efficient coding explains why a code is advantageous under specified input statistics, noise, and cost. It is a normative hypothesis; the same receptive field may also have developmental, biophysical, or task-specific explanations. Surprise for one outcome should increase as its probability decreases, and surprises for independent events should add. Because their joint probability is pq, the continuous monotone solution of \(S(pq)=S(p)+S(q)\) is \(S(p)=-\log_{bp}\). Base 2 gives bits and base e gives nats; an event of probability 1 has zero surprise. Why does moving input and output noise into one term before A change the optimization? A reshapes input noise, so increasing gain at one frequency also amplifies its input noise. Output noise does not pass through A, and increasing gain can improve signal relative to output noise. Their effects on the gain tradeoff differ and cannot be merged. This is the distinction tested in The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation. Worked example — Transforming Signal and Noise Together in a Two-Dimensional Encoder: Let \(C_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)\), input noise \(C_\eta x=I\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)\), and output noise \(C_\eta y=0.25I\). Find \(C_{y}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)\), input noise \(C_\eta x=I\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)\), and output noise \(C_\eta y=0.25I\). Find \(C_{y}\). \(C_{x}=C_{s}+I=\operatorname{diag}(10,2)\). \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}((1/2)^2\times 10,2^2\times 2)=\operatorname{diag}(2.5,8)\). \(C_{y}=\operatorname{diag}(2.5,8)+\operatorname{diag}(0.25,0.25)=\operatorname{diag}(2.75,8.25)\). For \(A=0\), only 0.25I remains in \(C_{y}\). The output appears decorrelated but contains no s, showing that decorrelation alone is not a valid objective. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation”? Input noise is added before encoder A and is filtered; output noise is added afterward. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation”? Covariance propagates as \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive noises enter at their respective stages. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Covariance propagates as \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive noises enter at their respective stages. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving Output Covariance Step by Step”? If s and x are dimensionless contrast and A has units output/contrast, then \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\mathrm{output}^2\) units and can be added to \(C_{\eta _{y}}\). When \(\eta _{x}\) correlates with s or noise depends on the stimulus, cross-terms do not vanish and the simple independent additive model fails. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What crucial conditions are missing from the statement “decorrelation produces center-surround filters”? Decorrelation requires only a diagonal or whitened output covariance, and any subsequent orthogonal rotation satisfies it equally well. Translation and rotation symmetry, locality, wiring, noise, or cost constraints are needed to select center-surround filters from the equivalent solutions. This is the distinction tested in Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters. Worked example — Rotation Ambiguity in Two-Dimensional Whitening: Let \(C_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), and 45° rotation \(U=(1/\sqrt 2)[[1,-1],[1,1]]\). Compare the pre-output-noise code covariances of V and UV, then state when MI is also invariant. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), and 45° rotation \(U=(1/\sqrt 2)[[1,-1],[1,1]]\). Compare the pre-output-noise code covariances of V and UV, then state when MI is also invariant. \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}((1/2)^2\times 4,1)=I\). With \(A'=UV\), \(A'C_{x}A'^\mathrm{T}=U I U^\mathrm{T}=I\). The outputs of V align with the original axes, whereas those of UV are 45° mixtures of the two whitened coordinates. Before output noise, both have decorrelated unit variance. If subsequent noise is \(\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), adding it also contributes the same \(\sigma _{y}^{2}\) on both output axes. If U is not orthogonal—for example, if its first row is multiplied by 2—the pre-noise covariance is no longer I. If output-noise covariance is anisotropic, orthogonal U alone also does not imply invariant MI. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters”? The determinant ratio in Gaussian MI compares total output covariance with conditional noise covariance. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters”? Whitening and decorrelation are nonunique under orthogonal rotations. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A unique center-surround form requires symmetry, locality, or other additional constraints; redundancy reduction alone does not imply it. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From Gaussian Entropy to an Information Constraint and Rotation Ambiguity”? \(\det C_{y}\) and \(\det C_{y|s}\) share units output-units^{2d}, so their ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless. Whitening usually standardizes outputs to unit variance; retaining physical units requires an additional scale matrix. For singular covariance, restrict the log determinant to the supported subspace or regularize it. Non-Gaussian components can remain dependent even when covariance is I, allowing higher-order objectives to break the rotational degeneracy. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints”? Encoder A transforms signal and input noise together, whereas output noise enters after A. A diagonal output covariance alone therefore does not guarantee useful coding. In the Atick–Redlich framework, redundancy is reduced subject to retained-information and output-power or dynamic-range constraints. Whitening removes second-order correlations, but any orthogonal rotation preserves whitened covariance; localized center-surround filters require additional assumptions such as symmetry and locality. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “efficient coding” mean in this lecture? efficient coding: A normative principle for optimizing an information representation under resource and noise constraints. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “redundancy” mean in this lecture? redundancy: Structure that is predictable from other components and transmitted repeatedly. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “surprise” mean in this lecture? surprise: The −log probability of an event. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “entropy” mean in this lecture? entropy: Average surprise or uncertainty. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “conditional entropy” mean in this lecture? conditional entropy: Residual uncertainty after another variable is given. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. title: Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory
subtitle: Lecture 15 · Lecture15-EfficientCoding.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture15-EfficientCoding.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture15-EfficientCoding.pdf, p. 3
text: How can the idea that a sensory system should not waste spikes on predictable content be converted into quantitative measures of uncertainty and dependence? The source notes retain three ideas from Barlow: detect “passwords” of critical significance, filter signals for other nervous-system regions, and recode sensory messages to reduce redundancy. This lecture focuses on the third. Efficient coding explains why a code is advantageous under specified input statistics, noise, and cost. It is a normative hypothesis; the same receptive field may also have developmental, biophysical, or task-specific explanations. Surprise for one outcome should increase as its probability decreases, and surprises for independent events should add. Because their joint probability is pq, the continuous monotone solution of \(S(pq)=S(p)+S(q)\) is \(S(p)=-\log_{bp}\). Base 2 gives bits and base e gives nats; an event of probability 1 has zero surprise. Entropy \(H(X)=E[-\log p(X)]\) is expected surprise before observation. Conditional entropy \(H(Y|X)\) averages the remaining uncertainty in Y at each x. Mutual information \(I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)\) is the average reduction in uncertainty about Y after observing X, equivalently \(\sum p(x,y)\log(p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y)))\). It detects every statistical dependence, not only linear correlation. If X and Y are independent, the joint ratio equals 1, \(\log 1=0\), and \(I=0\). Under standard discrete or continuous definitions, the converse also holds almost everywhere. For a continuous variable, differential entropy \(h=-\int f \log f\) uses density \(f(x)\); it can be negative and changes with measurement units. Mutual information is an entropy difference whose coordinate-scaling terms cancel, making it more stable than differential entropy alone. Efficient coding is constrained optimization, not the unique mechanism behind every sensory feature. The logarithmic form of surprise follows because independent probabilities multiply while their information adds. Entropy is average uncertainty; mutual information is the average reduction in one variable's uncertainty provided by another. Compute the entropy of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli} p=0.5\) and \(p=0.9\) using \(\log 2\). A uniform binary distribution has maximum uncertainty; biasing it toward one outcome lowers entropy. Why does negative differential entropy not mean probability theory has failed? A continuous density is not the probability of one outcome; it may exceed 1, and its entropy contains the coordinate bin size or units. Rescaling a variable adds a log-scale term. Shared scale contributions cancel in MI, which remains nonnegative and retains its dependence interpretation. Equating high entropy directly with high useful information while ignoring the receiver, task, noise, and conditional structure. Replacing independence with correlation=0, even though nonlinear dependent variables can have zero linear correlation and \(MI>0\).

title: The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation
subtitle: Lecture 15 · Lecture15-EfficientCoding.pdf, p. 4
text: How can a linear retinal encoder transform natural signals and input noise together while preserving decodable information in the presence of output noise? Atick and Redlich conceptualize the retina as a noisy channel. Photoreceptor or input noise \(\eta _{x}\) is first added to world signal s, giving \(x=s+\eta _{x}\). Retinal processing A acts on x, and RGC or output noise \(\eta _{y}\) is then added, giving \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\). A is both a spatial filter and a linear recoding from photoreceptor coordinates to output channels. Assuming signal and noises are zero-mean and mutually independent, \(C_{x}=C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}}\). A linear transformation yields \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\), after which output noise adds: \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\). Input noise is amplified or attenuated together with the signal, while output noise never passes through A; optimal gain therefore cannot be based on signal covariance alone. Natural-image signals are highly correlated at nearby positions, so \(C_{s}\) typically has long spatial scales. Isotropic white noise can be written \(\sigma _{x}^2I\) and \(\sigma _{y}^2I\). A high-pass or center-surround A can reduce low-frequency redundancy but may relatively amplify high-frequency input noise. Setting A to zero eliminates output redundancy but also removes all signal information, so an information constraint is essential. The Gaussian assumption makes covariance sufficient to specify the distribution and yields a closed-form mutual information. Real natural images contain edges, heavy tails, and nonstationarity, so the theory is a second-order approximation. Its value is a precise prediction: the optimal spatial profile should vary with the signal-to-noise ratio and channel cost, rather than being an unconditionally optimal fixed center-surround. Input noise is added before encoder A and is filtered; output noise is added afterward. Covariance propagates as \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive noises enter at their respective stages. Redundancy reduction must be constrained jointly by retained information and output cost. Let \(C_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)\), input noise \(C_\eta x=I\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)\), and output noise \(C_\eta y=0.25I\). Find \(C_{y}\). A suppresses the first coordinate and amplifies the second, while output noise adds the same 0.25 variance on both axes. Why does moving input and output noise into one term before A change the optimization? A reshapes input noise, so increasing gain at one frequency also amplifies its input noise. Output noise does not pass through A, and increasing gain can improve signal relative to output noise. Their effects on the gain tradeoff differ and cannot be merged. Omitting \(A^\mathrm{T}\) in covariance propagation, producing a nonsymmetric result or incorrect output shape. Treating a Gaussian second-order model as the full natural-image distribution and ignoring edges and higher-order dependencies.

title: Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters
subtitle: Lecture 15 · Lecture15-EfficientCoding.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture15-EfficientCoding.pdf, p. 6
text: Why does retaining fixed information while reducing output redundancy favor whitening yet fail to determine a unique receptive-field shape? For a d-dimensional Gaussian z, \(h(z)=1/2 \log[(2\pi e)^d \det C_{z}]\). In \(y=As+A\eta _{x}+\eta _{y}\), conditioning on s turns As into a known shift, leaving \(C_{y|s}=AC_{\eta _{x}}A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\); unconditional \(C_{y}\) also includes \(AC_{s}A^\mathrm{T}\). Substitution into \(I(y;s)=h(y)-h(y|s)\) cancels the two factors \((2\pi e)^d\) and gives \(I(y;s)=1/2 \log[\det C_{y}/\det C_{y|s}]\). The determinant is the product of covariance eigenvalues, so this ratio compares total output uncertainty volume with noise-only volume rather than any single variance. Atick and Redlich first require retained information \(I(y;s)=I^{*}\le I(x;s)\), then reduce redundancy under fixed output power or dynamic range. Let \(w=Ax\) denote the encoder signal before output noise and \(y=w+\eta _{y}\). The source notes therefore write output-channel capacity as \(C_{\mathrm{out}}=\max_{p(w)}\) \(I(y;w)\). The objective \(R=1-I(y;s)/C_{\mathrm{out}}\) penalizes spending channel capacity to retransmit the same information. A basis with diagonal output covariance has no second-order correlations; with fixed total power and isotropic output noise, distributing variance more evenly can increase Gaussian channel capacity. The aim is not unconstrained entropy maximization but code optimization under information, noise, and output-range constraints. A whitening transform V satisfies \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=I\). For any orthogonal U, \((UV)C_{x}(UV)^\mathrm{T}=UIU^\mathrm{T}=I\), so the pre-output-noise whitened code may be rotated without changing covariance. Full Gaussian MI is also unchanged only if output noise is isotropic, \(C_{\eta _{y}}=\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), or absent; then total and conditional-noise covariances undergo the same orthogonal similarity transformation. With anisotropic output noise, rotating the encoder changes signal alignment with the noise axes and generally changes MI. Decorrelation alone therefore identifies a family of solutions, not a unique localized center-surround shape for each neuron. Additional translation invariance, rotational symmetry, local wiring, or identical-channel constraints can select an isotropic center-surround member of that family. This prediction makes center-surround filtering compatible with natural statistics but is not unique causal proof. The real retina must also handle optics, photoreceptor low-pass filtering, adaptation, and non-Gaussian scenes; the next lecture's SNR-dependent filter follows from these constraints. The determinant ratio in Gaussian MI compares total output covariance with conditional noise covariance. Whitening and decorrelation are nonunique under orthogonal rotations. A unique center-surround form requires symmetry, locality, or other additional constraints; redundancy reduction alone does not imply it. Let \(C_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), and 45° rotation \(U=(1/\sqrt 2)[[1,-1],[1,1]]\). Compare the pre-output-noise code covariances of V and UV, then state when MI is also invariant. One covariance objective permits different filter axes. Preferring localized center-surround filters requires additional spatial constraints. What crucial conditions are missing from the statement “decorrelation produces center-surround filters”? Decorrelation requires only a diagonal or whitened output covariance, and any subsequent orthogonal rotation satisfies it equally well. Translation and rotation symmetry, locality, wiring, noise, or cost constraints are needed to select center-surround filters from the equivalent solutions. Claiming that more output entropy or channel capacity is unconditionally better while ignoring fixed information, noise, and firing cost. Treating the normative prediction of center-surround filtering as unique evidence for its anatomical or developmental mechanism.

title: Lecture 16: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
subtitle: How is the correlation structure of natural images represented in the Fourier domain, and how does SNR let an efficient retinal filter adapt between decorrelation and denoising?
text: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis How is the correlation structure of natural images represented in the Fourier domain, and how does SNR let an efficient retinal filter adapt between decorrelation and denoising? SNR → center-surround adaptation → translation invariance → Fourier basis → convolution theorem → power spectrum Explain from the relative strengths of input signal and noise why decorrelating filters are appropriate at high SNR while spatial averaging serves a different objective at low SNR. Express translation-invariant image statistics as a correlation function of displacement alone and explain why complex exponentials are the natural basis of convolution operators. Derive the convolution theorem and output power-spectrum equation step by step, then infer the frequency trend of a whitening filter from the approximate natural-image spectrum \(1/|\xi |^{2}\). Design an LNP comparison across illumination levels or stimulus statistics that separates a change in the linear filter, a change in the static nonlinearity, and a mere response-scale change. The central prediction of Atick–Redlich theory is not one fixed filter but a filter that changes with SNR: high SNR permits strong decorrelation, while low SNR favors spatial averaging and denoising. Approximate translation invariance of natural scenes makes covariance depend only on displacement, allowing Fourier modes to diagonalize convolution and covariance. Natural-image power falls approximately with inverse squared spatial frequency. Perfect whitening would boost high frequencies, but optics, photoreceptors, and noise suppress excessive high-frequency gain. Treating the Fourier transform as a table of physically meaningless formulas. Confusing spatial-frequency magnitude, orientation, and phase. Assuming complex numbers introduce an additional biological variable; they are a representational tool. Using the convolution theorem without a normalization or sign convention. Treating \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) as an exact law for every image. Letting perfect whitening amplify high frequencies without bound while ignoring optics and noise. Comparing only firing rates in an adaptation experiment and not the filter or nonlinearity. Do not teach the Fourier transform as a formula table. Always explain the physical meaning of spatial frequency for an image and receptive field, and state what amplitude and phase each represent. Signal-to-noise ratio SN \(R = S/N\) One frequency and measurement convention Translation-invariant covariance \(C(\rho _{1} , \rho _{2} ) = C(\rho _{1} - \rho _{2} )\) Stationary field Fourier transform \(\hat{s}(\xi ) = e^{-i2\pi \xi }\cdot x s(x)dx\) Chosen normalization Euler's identity ei\(\theta  = \cos \theta  + i \sin \theta \) Complex representation Convolution theorem \ \(K \ast  s = \hat{K}\) \(\hat{s}\) Linear shift-invariant filtering Power spectrum \(P (\xi ) = E[|\hat{s}(\xi )|2 ]\) Ensemble or time average Perfect-whitening magnitude −1/2 |K̂| ∝ Pin No additional noise or cost adaptation A change in response or model parameters with stimulus statistics or state. signal-to-noise ratio, SNR Signal magnitude or power relative to noise. translation invariance Statistics or an operator that do not depend on absolute position. spatial frequency Sinusoidal cycles per unit distance; the vector also encodes direction. Fourier transform A conversion between position and frequency representations. complex \(\operatorname{exponential} A\) unified representation of sine/cosine amplitude and phase. power spectrum Mean squared amplitude of each frequency component. whitening Making an output spectrum or covariance approximately flat or identity. low-pass Preserving low frequencies while suppressing high frequencies. aliasing Undersampling that makes a high frequency appear as a lower one. Four adjacent receptors all receive common signal value 8, and each has independent noise with standard deviation 2. After averaging the four, what are the signal mean and noise standard deviation? Averaging does not attenuate a signal identical across the four channels. Independent-noise variances add and are then divided by \(4^{2}\). This is the quantitative reason spatial pooling can improve readability at low SNR. The common signal remains 8; the average noise variance is \(4/4=1\), so its standard deviation is 1. A two-dimensional grating is \(\cos(\xi \cdot x)\). Are its equal-luminance stripes parallel or perpendicular to frequency vector \(\xi\)? \(\xi\) points along fastest phase increase, not along the stripes themselves. Confusing those directions rotates an orientation-tuning interpretation by ninety degrees. Equal-luminance lines have constant \(\xi \cdot x\), so motion along a stripe must leave the dot product unchanged. The stripe direction is perpendicular to \(\xi\). If \(y(x)=(K*s)(x)\), how is \(\hat{y}(\xi )\) written in the Fourier domain? The multiplication magnitude determines amplification or attenuation at that frequency, and its phase determines spatial shift. Each frequency mode can therefore be analyzed independently. \(\hat{y}(\xi )=\hat{K}(\xi )\hat{s}(\xi )\): spatial convolution becomes complex multiplication at each frequency. Suppose the natural-image input spectrum is \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\). If complete whitening is the sole objective, how should \(|\hat{K}(\xi )|\) vary with \(|\xi |\)? That is the ideal noise-free result. Real retinas are also limited by optical low-pass filtering, receptor noise, and metabolic cost, so gain cannot grow without bound at the highest frequencies. \(|\hat{K}(\xi )|\) should increase approximately linearly with \(|\xi |\), because \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) must be constant across frequencies. Why should a weaker surround in low light not be summarized as the visual system “no longer caring about edges”? Edges can remain behaviorally important. The change means that current high-frequency evidence is unreliable relative to noise and strong differencing would amplify noise. The system temporarily sacrifices resolution for a more stable estimate; the behavioral target need not have changed. This is the distinction tested in SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise. Worked example — Comparing Four-Point Averaging with Neighbor Differencing: A flat region has common signal 10 and independent pixel noise of standard deviation 2. Compute the noise standard deviation after averaging four pixels, then for the difference x1-x2. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A flat region has common signal 10 and independent pixel noise of standard deviation 2. Compute the noise standard deviation after averaging four pixels, then for the difference x1-x2. The four-point average preserves common value 10. Its noise variance is \(2^{2}/4=1\), so standard deviation is 1. Neighbor differencing cancels the common value, \(10-10=0\). Its noise is \(\epsilon _{1}-\epsilon _{2}\), with variance \(2^{2}+2^{2}=8\). The difference-noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt 8\approx 2.83\), larger than that of one pixel. This cost is worthwhile only when the edge signal is strong enough. If both channels contain identical rather than independent noise, differencing cancels it. The result shows why noise correlation structure must be stated. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise”? At high SNR, reliable high-frequency information lets center-surround differencing reduce redundancy across neighboring channels. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise”? At low SNR, spatial averaging preserves common signal and lowers independent-noise standard deviation at the cost of spatial resolution. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? At high SNR, reliable high-frequency information lets center-surround differencing reduce redundancy across neighboring channels. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How Noise Shrinks When n Neighboring Measurements Are Averaged”? x, s, \(\epsilon\), and y share luminance or voltage units. n and SNR are dimensionless; variance has squared signal units. For \(n=1\), noise is unchanged. As n grows, independent noise falls, but signal bias increases if the signal varies within the window, so an infinitely large window cannot produce infinite performance. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why might one visual system strengthen center-surround filtering in bright conditions but behave more like a spatial averager in dim conditions? Page 1 interprets filter shape along an SNR axis. At high SNR, input detail is reliable relative to internal and photon noise. Neighboring pixels are then strongly correlated, and transmitting them unchanged wastes limited output dynamic range on repeated information. An excitatory-center, inhibitory-surround difference kernel suppresses common slow components while retaining edges, reducing output correlations. A strong surround is a normative prediction under specified statistics and costs; it does not alone establish its synaptic implementation. At low SNR, differencing creates another problem: subtracting two channels removes their common signal but imports both independent noise sources into the result. When genuine high-frequency signal is already buried in noise, amplifying high frequencies wastes firing range. Spatial pooling sums or averages nearby measurements. Shared low-frequency structure adds coherently, whereas independent noise adds in variance, raising output SNR. A broad same-sign receptive field is then more useful than a sharp center-surround. Why do Fourier modes “diagonalize” a translation-invariant linear filter? After convolution, each input mode \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) remains the same \(\xi\) and is multiplied only by complex number \(\hat{K}(\xi )\); distinct \(\xi\) never mix. In this basis, the operator is represented by diagonal gains, one per mode. This is the distinction tested in From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization. Worked example — Passing a Sinusoid Through a Filter with Amplitude and Phase: The input is \(s(x)=3\cos(2x)\). At \(\xi =2\) the filter response is \(\hat{K}(2)=0.5e^{-i\pi /4}\). Find the output sinusoid's amplitude and phase shift. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The input is \(s(x)=3\cos(2x)\). At \(\xi =2\) the filter response is \(\hat{K}(2)=0.5e^{-i\pi /4}\). Find the output sinusoid's amplitude and phase shift. The input contains only the conjugate frequency pair \(\xi =+2\) and \(\xi =-2\), with real-space amplitude 3. Multiplying each component by \(\hat{K}\) scales amplitude from 3 to 1.5 because its magnitude is 0.5. The angle \(-\pi /4\) adds phase \(-\pi /4\) to the positive-frequency component, so \(y(x)=1.5\cos(2x-\pi /4)\). A linear translation-invariant filter cannot turn one sinusoid into a new frequency. Obtaining \(\xi =4\) means multiplication was mistaken for a nonlinear square. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization”? Translation-invariant covariance depends only on positional difference, making Fourier modes statistically nonmixing directions. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization”? Frequency vector \(\xi\) is perpendicular to image stripes, and \(|\xi |\) sets spatial oscillation speed. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Frequency vector \(\xi\) is perpendicular to image stripes, and \(|\xi |\) sets spatial oscillation speed. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving the Convolution Theorem Term by Term”? If spatial integral dx' has area units and y and s share units, K must have inverse-area units. Fourier-transform scale units depend on convention but remain consistent on both sides. For a delta-function K, \(\hat{K}=1\) and every frequency passes unchanged. For a broad averaging K, \(\hat{K}\) is concentrated at low frequency, matching the smoothing intuition. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why must an LNP filter's scale convention be fixed before comparing two adaptation conditions? Multiplying k by constant a while dividing the nonlinearity's horizontal axis by a gives identical firing predictions. Without fixing ||k|| or another convention, an apparent gain change can be only parameterization nonuniqueness. This is the distinction tested in Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation. Worked example — Whitening Two Frequencies and Its Noise Cost: Let \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(1)=16\) and \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(4)=1\), and require output signal power 4 at both frequencies. Find both gains. Then assume post-input noise power 1 at each frequency and compute output noise powers. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(1)=16\) and \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(4)=1\), and require output signal power 4 at both frequencies. Find both gains. Then assume post-input noise power 1 at each frequency and compute output noise powers. From \(|K|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}=4\), the low-frequency gain is \(|K(1)|=\sqrt{4/16}=0.5\). The high-frequency gain is \(|K(4)|=\sqrt{4/1}=2\), consistent with a fourfold frequency difference and a fourfold gain difference. Noise is also multiplied by squared gain, so low-frequency output noise is 0.25 and high-frequency output noise is 4. Although signal powers are equalized, high-frequency SNR remains worse. Substitution confirms equal signal powers: \(0.5^{2}\times 16=4\) and \(2^{2}\times 1=4\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation”? Linear filtering yields \(P_{\mathrm{out}}(\xi )=|\hat{K}(\xi )|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation”? For \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\), noise-free whitening gives \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\), but optics and noise force real filters to roll off at high frequency. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Cross-condition LNP comparisons must fix filter scale, estimate each nonlinearity separately, and test parameter swaps on held-out data. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Inferring Whitening Gain from the Input Power Spectrum”? If input and output share signal units, \(|\hat{K}|\) is dimensionless gain. P has \(\mathrm{signal}^{2}\) units, and c has the same units as \(P_{\mathrm{out}}\). As \(|\xi |\to 0\), ideal gain tends to zero, removing the global mean. As \(|\xi |\to \infty\), the formula diverges, exposing its noise-free infinite-bandwidth assumptions; a real system must regularize. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening”? If natural-image power is approximated by \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\) and noise and gain limits are temporarily ignored, flattening \(P_{\mathrm{out}}=|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) requires \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). Real optics attenuate extreme high-frequency signal without eliminating approximately flat output noise, so a noise-aware filter rolls off at high frequencies. When SNR falls further, the reliable band narrows and favors pooling. All three curves are normalized theoretical sketches, not empirical measurements. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Fourier transform” mean in this lecture? Fourier transform: A conversion between position and frequency representations. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. subtitle: Lecture 16 · Lecture16-Adaptation.pdf, p. 1
text: Why might one visual system strengthen center-surround filtering in bright conditions but behave more like a spatial averager in dim conditions? Page 1 interprets filter shape along an SNR axis. At high SNR, input detail is reliable relative to internal and photon noise. Neighboring pixels are then strongly correlated, and transmitting them unchanged wastes limited output dynamic range on repeated information. An excitatory-center, inhibitory-surround difference kernel suppresses common slow components while retaining edges, reducing output correlations. A strong surround is a normative prediction under specified statistics and costs; it does not alone establish its synaptic implementation. At low SNR, differencing creates another problem: subtracting two channels removes their common signal but imports both independent noise sources into the result. When genuine high-frequency signal is already buried in noise, amplifying high frequencies wastes firing range. Spatial pooling sums or averages nearby measurements. Shared low-frequency structure adds coherently, whereas independent noise adds in variance, raising output SNR. A broad same-sign receptive field is then more useful than a sharp center-surround. Intermediate SNR creates a continuous tradeoff, not a hard switch. Distinguish amplitude \(SNR_{\mathrm{amp}}=S/\sigma\) from power \(SNR_{\mathrm{power}}=P_{s}/P_{n}\); for the same linear measurement and bandwidth, \(SNR_{\mathrm{power}}=SNR_{\mathrm{amp}}^{2}\). The pooling derivation below uses amplitude SNR, so averaging n independent noisy measurements improves it by \(\sqrt n\). Spectral analysis uses \(P_{s}(\xi )/P_{n}(\xi )\). Where this ratio is high, the filter can spend gain correcting redundancy; where it is low, gain should shrink. SNR differs across spatial frequencies, so dimmer light can broaden pooling, weaken the surround, and change total gain rather than merely scaling the whole filter. Read the page's graph as a conditional prediction. First establish that the axis or curves denote SNR rather than time; then compare center and surround areas and widths; finally state measurable outcomes, such as reduced high-frequency gain and a broader estimated receptive field in low light. A fall in firing rate alone does not show that the filter broadened, since a higher nonlinear threshold or fewer available spikes can produce the same observation. At high SNR, reliable high-frequency information lets center-surround differencing reduce redundancy across neighboring channels. At low SNR, spatial averaging preserves common signal and lowers independent-noise standard deviation at the cost of spatial resolution. Adaptation should be described as frequency-dependent changes in filter and nonlinearity, not only as a change in mean firing rate. A flat region has common signal 10 and independent pixel noise of standard deviation 2. Compute the noise standard deviation after averaging four pixels, then for the difference x1-x2. Averaging is favored in a low-SNR flat region; strong differencing is justified when SNR is high and reliable edges exist. Why should a weaker surround in low light not be summarized as the visual system “no longer caring about edges”? Edges can remain behaviorally important. The change means that current high-frequency evidence is unreliable relative to noise and strong differencing would amplify noise. The system temporarily sacrifices resolution for a more stable estimate; the behavioral target need not have changed. Equating high SNR with high mean luminance, even though SNR also depends on frequency, internal noise, and stimulus contrast. Comparing only receptive-field peaks and ignoring integrated center-surround strength, width, and estimation uncertainty.

title: From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization
subtitle: Lecture 16 · Lecture16-Adaptation.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture16-Adaptation.pdf, p. 3
text: Why does rewriting an image by spatial frequency allow convolutional filtering to be computed frequency by frequency? Page 2 describes translation statistics of natural scenes. Across many images, or a sufficiently large stationary image, correlation between two positions depends mainly on displacement \(\Delta x\) rather than absolute coordinates: \(C(x,x')=C(x-x')\). This does not mean every photograph is uniform everywhere; it means the statistical ensemble follows the same rule after translation. Such covariance matrices repeat by displacement. Complex exponential modes retain their frequency under convolution or correlation and change only in complex amplitude, making them a natural basis. A two-dimensional component \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) carries frequency direction and phase. The dot product \(\xi \cdot x\) projects position onto the frequency vector. Phase changes fastest along \(\xi\) and remains constant in the perpendicular direction, so visible stripes are perpendicular to \(\xi\). A real image uses paired \(+\xi\) and \(-\xi\) components whose imaginary parts cancel. Near the spectrum center are slow variations; farther away are finer spatial structures. The convolution theorem on page 3 converts \(y(x)=\int K(x-x')s(x')dx'\) into \(\hat{y}(\xi )=\hat{K}(\xi )\hat{s}(\xi )\). Rather than memorizing it, expand the Fourier integral, exchange integration order, and set \(u=x-x'\). The \(\operatorname{exponential} e^{-i\xi \cdot (u+x')}\) then factors into one term in u and one in x', leaving the two integrals \(\hat{K}\) and ŝ. Every \(\xi\) multiplies independently, diagonalizing the large translation-invariant linear operator. \(\hat{K}(\xi )\) is generally complex. Its magnitude \(|\hat{K}|\) is the gain at that frequency and its argument is the phase shift. A symmetric center-surround kernel often has phase near zero or \(\pi\), making its amplitude response prominent. Asymmetric receptive fields and temporal delays carry important phase information. A spatial thumbnail alone makes it difficult to tell whether a receptive field favors slow gradients, edges, or a particular band. Translation-invariant covariance depends only on positional difference, making Fourier modes statistically nonmixing directions. Frequency vector \(\xi\) is perpendicular to image stripes, and \(|\xi |\) sets spatial oscillation speed. Convolution becomes frequencywise complex multiplication; magnitude controls gain and phase angle controls shift. The input is \(s(x)=3\cos(2x)\). At \(\xi =2\) the filter response is \(\hat{K}(2)=0.5e^{-i\pi /4}\). Find the output sinusoid's amplitude and phase shift. The filtered sinusoid still has frequency 2, amplitude 1.5, and phase shifted negatively by \(\pi /4\). Why do Fourier modes “diagonalize” a translation-invariant linear filter? After convolution, each input mode \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) remains the same \(\xi\) and is multiplied only by complex number \(\hat{K}(\xi )\); distinct \(\xi\) never mix. In this basis, the operator is represented by diagonal gains, one per mode. Drawing the frequency-vector direction along the stripe direction and thereby rotating the orientation interpretation by ninety degrees. Using only \(|\hat{K}|\) and discarding phase, even though phase of asymmetric spatial and spatiotemporal kernels controls localization and delay.

title: Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation
subtitle: Lecture 16 · Lecture16-Adaptation.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture16-Adaptation.pdf, p. 5
text: How does the input statistic \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) predict a filter's frequency profile, and how can an LNP experiment test whether the system actually changes with the environment? Page 4 approximates the ensemble power spectrum of natural images as \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\): slow luminance variations at low frequencies usually have greater variance than fine high-frequency detail. Linear filtering gives output coefficient \(\hat{K}\hat{s}\) and power \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\). In an ideal model without noise or gain limits, equal output variance across frequencies requires \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) to be constant, hence \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). In space, this is a difference structure that suppresses low frequency and relatively enhances edges. Ideal whitening cannot continue to arbitrarily high frequency. Ocular optics and photoreceptor integration attenuate extreme frequencies, reducing usable signal power. If output noise is approximately flat across frequencies, gain \(|\xi |\) would strongly amplify noise at the highest frequencies. An effective filter therefore often rises over a reliable midfrequency band and falls again when noise dominates, becoming band-pass. As illumination falls, the reliable band contracts and the optimum shifts from stronger center-surround filtering toward smoother pooling. Page 5 turns this prediction into an LNP measurement. Present sufficiently rich stimuli under high and low light or different spatial correlations, estimate filter \(k_{c}\) separately, and then estimate each condition's nonlinearity \(f_{c}\). Fix a normalization before comparing filters—for example \(||k_{c}||=1\) with signs aligned by the dominant lobe—because multiplying k by a constant and inversely scaling the input axis of f gives identical predictions. Then compare spatial profile, Fourier gain, integrated center-surround ratio, and cross-condition prediction. Strong evidence comes from distinguishable counterfactuals. If only the nonlinearity changes, the filter from condition A paired with condition B's nonlinearity should approximate data in B. If the filter truly changes, this swap systematically misses particular stimulus directions. Match spike counts or use bootstrap confidence intervals to handle noisier low-light estimates. An adaptation claim should report parameter changes and predictive improvement, not treat two visually different kernel plots as sufficient proof. Linear filtering yields \(P_{\mathrm{out}}(\xi )=|\hat{K}(\xi )|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\). For \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\), noise-free whitening gives \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\), but optics and noise force real filters to roll off at high frequency. Cross-condition LNP comparisons must fix filter scale, estimate each nonlinearity separately, and test parameter swaps on held-out data. Let \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(1)=16\) and \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(4)=1\), and require output signal power 4 at both frequencies. Find both gains. Then assume post-input noise power 1 at each frequency and compute output noise powers. Pure whitening uses gains 0.5 and 2, but the latter amplifies equal input noise to 16 times the former's power, so a noise-aware solution must suppress high frequency. Why must an LNP filter's scale convention be fixed before comparing two adaptation conditions? Multiplying k by constant a while dividing the nonlinearity's horizontal axis by a gives identical firing predictions. Without fixing ||k|| or another convention, an apparent gain change can be only parameterization nonuniqueness. Treating \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) as an exact law for every natural image rather than an approximate trend over an ensemble. Directly comparing noisy filter images in a low-spike condition without resampling uncertainty or held-out prediction to rule out estimation variance.

title: Lecture 17: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence
subtitle: How do multilayer LNP cascades and a quadratic energy model produce selectivity and invariance, and how can recurrent E/I dynamics explain surround suppression?
text: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence How do multilayer LNP cascades and a quadratic energy model produce selectivity and invariance, and how can recurrent E/I dynamics explain surround suppression? LNP cascade → simple-cell pooling → complex-cell \(STA=0\)→ quadrature energy → task-optimized models → E/I recurrence Distinguish linear selectivity in simple cells from phase invariance in complex cells, and explain why an even-symmetric response can drive the first-order STA toward zero. Derive phase invariance step by step from the two linear outputs of a quadrature pair while stating the amplitude and orientation dependence that remains. Separate task training of an optimized model from evaluation of neural predictivity, and design a comparison that never leaks test neural data. Write the fixed-point equations and nullclines of an E/I rate network and analyze how surround input can produce suppression without raising inhibitory rate. Use local stability to define an inhibition-stabilized network and avoid reducing ISN to “strong inhibition.” Feedforward cascades can construct selectivity and invariance stage by stage, but descriptive blocks do not automatically identify biological mechanisms. Complex cells are approximately invariant to grating phase, so a single linear STA can be zero; a quadrature-pair square-and-sum energy model is a minimal explanation. Surround suppression likewise is not simply “more inhibition”: recurrent E/I dynamics can make excitation and inhibition fall together, with excitation falling more. Nullclines show the fixed-point shift, while Jacobian stability and an unstable E-only subsystem establish an inhibition-stabilized regime. Treating a descriptive LNP cascade automatically as anatomy or mechanism. Concluding from complex-cell \(STA=0\) that there is no stimulus selectivity. Forgetting that squaring changes sign and phase information. Treating task accuracy and neural predictivity as the same metric. Equating surround suppression with a necessary increase in inhibitory firing or conductance. Reading ISN as meaning that inhibitory rate is always higher. Locating a fixed point without checking its stability. State explicitly that “complex-cell \(STA=0\)” does not mean “no stimulus selectivity”; it is a central counterexample in nonlinear system identification. Motion or orientation energy model \(E = (K_{1} \ast  s)2 + (K_{2} \ast  s)2\) Quadrature filters Phase-invariance identity \(\cos 2 \varphi  + \sin 2 \varphi  = 1\) Ideal pair Linear model-to-neuron mapping \(\hat{r} = Bz\) Fixed features z E/I nullclines \(\dot{r}E = 0\), \(\dot{r}I = 0\) Steady state Rate-network fixed point \(r = F (W r + I)\) Chosen nonlinearities Intuitive ISN criterion E-only unstable + feedback I stable Local effective gain matters cascade Several processing stages composed in sequence. simple cell A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation and sensitive to spatial phase. complex cell A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation but more invariant to phase. quadrature pair Matched filters separated by 90° of phase. energy model A nonlinear model that squares and sums quadrature-filter outputs. neural predictivity How well model features predict neural responses. surround suppression A reduction in center response when the receptive-field surround is stimulated. nullcline A phase-plane curve on which one state derivative equals zero. inhibition-stabilized network, ISN A network whose E subnetwork is unstable alone but stabilized by feedback inhibition. A neuron responds identically to filter projections z and -z. Why can the first-order average of spike-triggered stimuli be nearly zero? A zero STA rules out one signed linear direction as a complete account, not selectivity for |z| or \(z^{2}\). STC or an energy feature can detect the latter. Spikes select large projections on both the positive and negative sides. With a symmetric stimulus distribution, the two trigger means point in opposite directions and cancel. If \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\), does \(L_{1}^{2}+L_{2}^{2}\) depend on phase \(\phi\)? A quadrature pair turns phase into rotation of a two-dimensional vector; the squared sum reads its length and ignores its direction. No. Since \(\cos^{2}\phi +\sin^{2}\phi =1\), the sum of squares is always \(A^{2}\). Must a network with higher classification accuracy predict visual-cortical responses better? Choosing a layer, mapping, or network after inspecting test neural data inflates predictivity through selection bias. The evaluation pipeline must keep these data isolated. No. Task performance constrains only the final behavioral output, while internal representations may differ. Predictivity must be tested separately on held-out neural stimuli. After surround stimulation, both excitatory and inhibitory rates fall. Can recurrent inhibition still contribute to the suppression? A lower I rate does not make inhibition irrelevant. Analyze the recurrent equations, the changed inputs, and the fixed-point shift rather than treating inhibitory firing itself as inhibitory current. Yes. Surround input can first reduce network excitation, causing the inhibitory population to receive less drive. If E falls more, the net outcome remains suppression. Why does the energy model retain orientation tuning after gaining phase invariance? Phase rotates the matched quadrature outputs in their two-dimensional plane. Changing orientation reduces both filter projections' common amplitude A, so \(A^{2}\) still falls with orientation mismatch. This is the distinction tested in From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy. Worked example — Equal Energy at Three Phases: Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\). For \(\phi =0\), \(L_{1}=4\) and \(L_{2}=0\), hence \(E=16\). For \(\phi =\pi /4\), \(L_{1}=L_{2}=4/\sqrt 2\); each square is 8, hence \(E=16\). For \(\phi =\pi /2\), \(L_{1}=0\) and \(L_{2}=4\), hence \(E=16\). Every pair (L1,L2) lies on a circle of radius 4, and the sum of squares is the squared radius. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy”? Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy”? A complex-cell energy model uses the squared sum of a quadrature pair to turn stimulus phase into an ignored two-dimensional angle. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Why Quadrature Energy Is Invariant to Phase”? If linear outputs use drive units of spikes/s, their squared sum has \(drive^{2}\) units. A final output nonlinearity can map it back to firing rate. When \(A=0\), every phase gives \(E=0\). If the second filter has twice the gain of the first, the squared sum varies with \(\phi\) and phase invariance fails. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can two filters separated by one-quarter period retain orientation selectivity while discarding grating phase? Page 1 links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection. The challenge for a complex cell is phase invariance. If it responds strongly to both positive and negative phases of a grating at one orientation, a linear STA averages the two spike-triggered groups toward zero. Page 2 instead uses two filters separated by 90° of spatial phase—a quadrature pair. As input phase changes, their linear outputs carry energy in turn like two coordinates. Squaring and adding reads vector radius rather than angle. Why is it invalid to repeatedly select the most brain-like network layer on test neural stimuli and report its highest correlation on the same data? Repeated layer selection already uses the test responses. The maximum contains positive selection noise and is biased upward. Choose layers and regularization on validation neural data and perform the final evaluation once on an independent test set. This is the distinction tested in Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests. Worked example — A Least-Squares Readout from One Feature: For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\). The one-dimensional normal equation gives \(b=(z^\mathrm{T} r)/(z^\mathrm{T} z)\). \(z^\mathrm{T} r=1\times 2+2\times 4+3\times 5=25\) and \(z^\mathrm{T}z=1+4+9=14\), so \(b=25/14\approx 1.786\). For a new stimulus with \(z=4\), prediction is \(4b=100/14\approx 7.14\). Its reliability must be tested against the actual held-out response. If \(r=2z\) exactly, the formula returns \(b=2\). Here the third point is below 6, so the fitted slope is slightly below 2. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests”? Task training determines the representation; a neural readout and held-out evaluation test its alignment with biological responses. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests”? Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving a Neural Readout from a Least-Squares Objective”? The units of Z depend on network activations. B has neural-response-units per feature-unit so that ZB and R both use spikes/s or trial counts. With only a constant column in Z, the model predicts only each neuron's mean response. If \(d\ge N\) without regularization, training error may be tiny while overfitting is severe. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does lower inhibitory-neuron firing after surround not imply that inhibition did not cause surround suppression? A firing rate is the network fixed-point outcome, while inhibitory current also depends on connectivity and presynaptic rate. Surround can first lower E drive and thereby lower I, even though I feedback still determines the fixed point at which E amplification is contained. This is the distinction tested in E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization. Worked example — Surround Suppression with Simultaneous Decreases in E and I Rates: Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5. Find both fixed points. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5.
