Find both fixed points. Center only: \(r_{E}=(10-2)/0.8=10\) and \(r_{I}=r_{E}+2=12\). Surround: \(r_{E}=(10-5)/0.8=6.25\) and \(r_{I}=r_{E}+5=11.25\). Thus E falls from 10 to 6.25 and I from 12 to 11.25. Although the I population receives more external drive, its steady rate falls slightly because recurrent E input falls more. Substitution verifies the surround E equation: \(-6.25+1.2\times 6.25-11.25+10=0\); and I equation: \(-11.25+6.25+5=0\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization”? Surround suppression is a shift of the full recurrent fixed point and does not require an increase in inhibitory firing rate. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization”? Nullcline intersections give steady states; local vector fields or Jacobian eigenvalues determine stability. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An ISN has an unstable E-only subsystem but a stable complete E/I loop; it is not merely a network with qualitatively strong inhibition. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Fixed Point, Surround Shift, and Local Stability in a Linear E/I Network”? For rates in spikes/s, dimensionless weights map presynaptic rates into drive of the same units, and \(I_{E}\),\(I_{I}\) are equivalent rate drives. Jacobian eigenvalues contain \(1/\tau\) and therefore have reciprocal-time units. Setting \(w_{\mathrm{EI}}\) or \(w_{\mathrm{IE}}\) to zero breaks the stabilizing E/I feedback loop. If E gain exceeds leak, the E-only mode runs away, exposing the ISN condition. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection”? In a locally linear E/I rate model, a nullcline intersection is a steady state. Increasing surround drive to the I population shifts the I-nullcline upward. Its new intersection with the fixed E-nullcline can have both lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\), so surround suppression does not require inhibitory firing to rise. The curves are normalized geometric sketches of the course equations. Full stability still requires Jacobian eigenvalues and cannot be inferred from line intersection alone. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “cascade” mean in this lecture? cascade: Several processing stages composed in sequence. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “simple cell” mean in this lecture? simple cell: A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation and sensitive to spatial phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “complex cell” mean in this lecture? complex cell: A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation but more invariant to phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “quadrature pair” mean in this lecture? quadrature pair: Matched filters separated by 90° of phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “energy model” mean in this lecture? energy model: A nonlinear model that squares and sums quadrature-filter outputs. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “neural predictivity” mean in this lecture? neural predictivity: How well model features predict neural responses. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “surround suppression” mean in this lecture? surround suppression: A reduction in center response when the receptive-field surround is stimulated. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “nullcline” mean in this lecture? nullcline: A phase-plane curve on which one state derivative equals zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “inhibition-stabilized network, ISN” mean in this lecture? inhibition-stabilized network, ISN: A network whose E subnetwork is unstable alone but stabilized by feedback inhibition. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Motion or orientation energy model” be used? Motion or orientation energy model: \(E = (K_{1} \ast  s)2 + (K_{2} \ast  s)2\). Quadrature filters This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Phase-invariance identity” be used? Phase-invariance identity: \(\cos 2 \varphi  + \sin 2 \varphi  = 1\). Ideal pair This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Linear model-to-neuron mapping” be used? Linear model-to-neuron mapping: \(\hat{r} = Bz\). Fixed features z This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “E/I nullclines” be used? E/I nullclines: \(\dot{r}E = 0\), \(\dot{r}I = 0\). Steady state This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Rate-network fixed point” be used? Rate-network fixed point: \(r = F (W r + I)\). Chosen nonlinearities This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Intuitive ISN criterion” be used? Intuitive ISN criterion: E-only unstable + feedback I stable. Local effective gain matters This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy
subtitle: Lecture 17 · Lecture17-VisualNetworks.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture17-VisualNetworks.pdf, p. 2
text: How can two filters separated by one-quarter period retain orientation selectivity while discarding grating phase? Page 1 links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection. The challenge for a complex cell is phase invariance. If it responds strongly to both positive and negative phases of a grating at one orientation, a linear STA averages the two spike-triggered groups toward zero. Page 2 instead uses two filters separated by 90° of spatial phase—a quadrature pair. As input phase changes, their linear outputs carry energy in turn like two coordinates. Squaring and adding reads vector radius rather than angle. For a grating matching orientation and spatial frequency, let the two filter projections be \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\), where A depends on contrast and match quality and \(\phi\) is stimulus phase. Energy \(E=L_{1}^{2}+L_{2}^{2}=A^{2}\) is independent of \(\phi\). The invariance is conditional: changing orientation or frequency lowers the common projection amplitude A, and changing contrast changes A and hence E. The energy model removes phase, not all stimulus information. STC can identify these two feature axes as abnormal directions of spike-triggered covariance because spikes select a large radius in the two-dimensional subspace rather than one signed mean direction. The model is still a descriptive cascade of two linear filters, squaring nonlinearities, summation, and perhaps an output nonlinearity. Reproducing several complex-cell responses does not prove that biological synapses implement four anatomically separate stages. Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity. A complex-cell energy model uses the squared sum of a quadrature pair to turn stimulus phase into an ignored two-dimensional angle. A zero STA can coexist with strong selectivity; examine covariance or a multifilter subspace in that case. Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\). The linear outputs differ at all three phases, but energy equals 16 each time. Why does the energy model retain orientation tuning after gaining phase invariance? Phase rotates the matched quadrature outputs in their two-dimensional plane. Changing orientation reduces both filter projections' common amplitude A, so \(A^{2}\) still falls with orientation mismatch. Concluding from a near-zero complex-cell STA that the stimulus does not drive the cell, while ignoring positive-negative cancellation under an even nonlinearity. Calling square-and-sum invariant to every transformation; it is only approximately invariant to phase rotations within the covered subspace.

title: Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests
subtitle: Lecture 17 · Lecture17-VisualNetworks.pdf, p. 3
text: How can we test whether the internal feature space of a network trained for object classification genuinely resembles a neural representation? The logic on page 3 spans two data domains. A network first learns weights from a task dataset and classification loss; its feature hierarchy reflects both task and architecture. Freeze the network, compute layer features \(z(x)\) for experimental stimuli, and fit a constrained mapping from z to response r using training neural trials—for example, a ridge-regularized linear readout. Report predictive correlation or explained variance only on held-out stimuli or trials. High task accuracy does not define neural similarity. Many internal coordinate systems can implement the same classification boundary; networks that rely on texture or shape may score similarly on labels. Predictivity also depends on mapping flexibility. A nonlinear mapper with far more parameters than observations can fit almost any representation to training responses. Use simple mappings of equal complexity and identical cross-validation for every candidate layer. Let feature matrix \(Z\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times d}\) contain one stimulus per row and one model feature per column, and neural matrix \(R\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times m}\) contain one neuron per column. Fit \(B\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\) by minimizing \(||ZB-R||^{2}\). B aligns coordinate systems but does not change the task representation of the original network. Compare models with the same N, neurons, noise ceiling, and regularization-selection rule. Neural data contain trial noise, so single-trial correlation cannot reach 1 even when a model captures all reproducible stimulus-driven signal. A noise ceiling estimated from split-half reliability approximates the predictable limit. Report uncertainty with raw and ceiling-normalized predictivity. If one layer scores higher, the justified claim is limited to the current stimuli, area, mapping family, and measurement noise—not mechanistic equivalence to the whole visual system. Task training determines the representation; a neural readout and held-out evaluation test its alignment with biological responses. Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately. Mapping complexity, data splits, and the noise ceiling materially affect the comparison. For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\). Training data give \(b\approx 1.786\), and held-out feature 4 maps to \(\mathrm{prediction}\approx 7.14\). Why is it invalid to repeatedly select the most brain-like network layer on test neural stimuli and report its highest correlation on the same data? Repeated layer selection already uses the test responses. The maximum contains positive selection noise and is biased upward. Choose layers and regularization on validation neural data and perform the final evaluation once on an independent test set. Mistaking the fitting power of a flexible nonlinear mapping for similarity between the original representation and neural representation. Comparing raw correlations across datasets without accounting for neural-response reliability.

title: E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization
subtitle: Lecture 17 · Lecture17-VisualNetworks.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture17-VisualNetworks.pdf, p. 5
text: How can a fixed-point shift produce surround suppression, and why might inhibitory-population firing decrease? Page 4 places surround effects in an E/I recurrent rate model. One common form is \(\tau _{E} dr_{E}/dt=-r_{E}+F_{E}(w_{\mathrm{EE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{EI}} r_{I}+I_{E})\) and \(\tau _{I} dr_{I}/dt=-r_{I}+F_{I}(w_{\mathrm{IE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{II}} r_{I}+I_{I})\). The weights are positive magnitudes and inhibition already carries a minus sign. Recurrent excitation, feedback inhibition, and external inputs jointly determine the fixed point. One population's firing rate is not identical to the net current it delivers to a target. Within a piecewise-linear region, temporarily set F to identity. The E-nullcline is \(r_{E}=w_{\mathrm{EE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{EI}} r_{I}+I_{E}\), and the I-nullcline can also be rearranged as a line giving \(r_{I}\) versus \(r_{E}\). Their intersection is the steady state. If surround increases external drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population, it shifts the I-nullcline. In an ISN regime, the added drive initially strengthens inhibition and lowers \(r_{E}\), which then reduces recurrent excitation to I. The new intersection can have lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\). The ISN on page 5 has an excitatory subnetwork that would be unstable in isolation—effective recurrent E gain exceeds leak—but fast inhibitory feedback stabilizes the complete E/I network. The name does not mean that inhibitory firing always rises or that every suppression comes from added I input. Under some perturbations, stronger external drive to I lowers its steady-state rate. This paradoxical response arises from network rebalancing and tests ISN structure more directly than simply measuring whether I is large. Read a nullcline plot in four steps: label both axes and zero-derivative curves; determine where each derivative is positive; locate intersections; and ask whether arrows after a small displacement return to the intersection. An intersection alone does not establish stability. With nonlinear F there may be several intersections, and surround can change gain instead of only shifting input. The linear example exposes causal structure, while realistic fitting must retain nonlinearities and temporal dynamics. Surround suppression is a shift of the full recurrent fixed point and does not require an increase in inhibitory firing rate. Nullcline intersections give steady states; local vector fields or Jacobian eigenvalues determine stability. An ISN has an unstable E-only subsystem but a stable complete E/I loop; it is not merely a network with qualitatively strong inhibition. Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5. Find both fixed points. Both steady-state E and I are lower with surround; this does not exclude a role for recurrent inhibition. Why does lower inhibitory-neuron firing after surround not imply that inhibition did not cause surround suppression? A firing rate is the network fixed-point outcome, while inhibitory current also depends on connectivity and presynaptic rate. Surround can first lower E drive and thereby lower I, even though I feedback still determines the fixed point at which E amplification is contained. Conflating inhibitory-population rate, inhibitory current received by a target, and net suppression. Declaring an intersection stable from the nullclines alone without inspecting the local vector field or Jacobian eigenvalues.

title: Lecture 18: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
subtitle: How can a distributed motor population be written as a linear recurrent dynamical system, and how do eigenmodes distinguish decay, long memory, perfect integration, and instability?
text: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics How can a distributed motor population be written as a linear recurrent dynamical system, and how do eigenmodes distinguish decay, long memory, perfect integration, and instability? Brain-body-environment → feedback control → recurrent rate network → eigendecomposition → mode dynamics → effective time constant Draw the brain, body, and environment as a closed-loop dynamical system and distinguish feedforward commands, sensory feedback, state estimates, and external disturbances. Generalize the first-order equation for one neuron to \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), correctly interpreting the direction of \(W_{ij}\) and every matrix shape. When W is diagonalizable, transform population activity into its eigenbasis and derive mutually decoupled mode equations step by step. From eigenvalue \(\lambda _{i}\), derive effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\) and interpret \(\lambda _{i}<1\), =1, and >1 as decay, integration, and instability. Find the fixed point under constant input and distinguish long memory near an integrator, a perfect integrator, and runaway positive feedback. Motor control consists of closed-loop dynamics among brain, body, and environment, and neural activity is highly distributed. In a linear recurrent network, transforming individual neuronal activities into eigenmode coordinates decouples the system so each mode behaves like an independent first-order process. Eigenvalue \(\lambda\) sets effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\): \(\lambda <1\) decays, \(\lambda \approx 1\) has long memory, \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator, and \(\lambda >1\) grows without bound. Restricting a motor signal to one region and overlooking distributed population activity. Confusing neuronal activity coordinates with eigenmode coordinates. Treating an eigenmode as one neuron. Writing \(V^{-1}WV=D\) without checking the convention that columns of V are right eigenvectors. Using \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\) as a positive decay time when \(\lambda >1\). Assuming \(\lambda =1\) is automatically robust, despite its sensitivity to perturbation. Analyzing neural dynamics without body and environmental feedback. Distinguish individual-neuron activity, population-mode coordinates, and behavioral state; do not turn an eigenmode into one “special neuron.” Linear recurrent rate network \(\tau \) \(\dot{h} = -h + W h + I\) Common \(\tau\) and linearization Diagonalization \(W = V DV -1\) Diagonalizable W Mode coordinates \(\alpha  = V -1 h\) Invertible V Decoupled mode \(\tau \) \(\dot{\alpha }i = -(1 - \lambda _{i} )\alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}\) Eigenbasis Mode time constant \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\) \(\lambda <1\) for stable decay Perfect integrator \(\lambda  = 1 \Rightarrow  \dot{\alpha } = \beta /\tau \) Exact cancellation of feedback and leak feedforward control Control based mainly on a prior model or command rather than current feedback correction. feedback control Online correction of action from sensory or state error. proprioception Sensory feedback about body position or force. recurrent network A network with feedback loops among its units. eigenmode A population activity pattern associated with an eigenvector of W. change of basis Conversion of the same state between neuronal and modal coordinates. effective time constant A mode's decay or integration timescale after feedback. fixed point A state whose derivative is zero. stability Whether a small perturbation returns to a fixed point. perfect integrator A mode that accumulates input without leak. Under convention \((Wh)_i=\sum _j W_{ij}h_{j}\), does \(W_{ij}\) represent a connection from i to j or from j to i? Some texts use the transposed convention. Expanding the matrix multiplication first prevents reversing the connection diagram. It represents source j to target i, because \(W_{ij}h_{j}\) contributes to output component i. If \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and an eigenvalue \(\lambda =0\), what is the mode's effective time constant? \(\lambda =0\) means no recurrent input along that mode, so leak alone sets decay. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )=20 \mathrm{ms}\), equal to the intrinsic time constant without recurrent feedback. Which continuous-time mode decays more slowly, \(\lambda =0.9\) or \(\lambda =-0.5\)? For this continuous-time equation, the stability boundary for a real eigenvalue is 1, not absolute value 1, because the dynamics contain -I+W. \(\lambda =0.9\) is slower, with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=10\tau\); \(\lambda =-0.5\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /1.5\), so negative feedback accelerates decay beyond the intrinsic rate. Is eigenmode amplitude \(\alpha _{i}\) the firing rate of neuron i? A mode coincides with one neuron coordinate only when W is diagonal in the neuronal basis. Treating modes as neurons misreads distributed dynamics. Usually not. \(\alpha _{i}\) is the coordinate of the population vector along eigenvector \(v_{i}\), and one mode generally combines many neurons. Why does larger proportional gain improve disturbance rejection in a delay-free model but not justify infinite gain in a biological system? The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop. This is the distinction tested in Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop. Worked example — Steady Position Error Under a Persistent Velocity Disturbance: For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). The fixed point is \(x^{*}=d/k=0.6/2=0.3\). Error \(e=x-0.3\) obeys \(de/dt=-2e\), so \(e(t)=0.7e^{-2t}\) and the time constant is 1/2 s. At \(t=1\), \(x=0.3+0.7e^{-2}\approx 0.3+0.0947=0.3947\). At initial \(x=1\), derivative=\(-2+0.6=-1.4\), so the trajectory must move downward. The computed result has the correct direction. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop”? Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop”? Feedforward control anticipates; feedback corrects disturbances. Delay, noise, and gain set the stability costs. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How Proportional Feedback Rejects a Constant Disturbance”? x has position units and \(dx/dt\), u, and d have position/time units. Thus kx has position/time units and k has units 1/time. As \(k\to 0\), restoring feedback disappears and constant disturbance makes position drift. Increasing k reduces ideal-model error, but an unmodeled delay can destabilize high gain. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why is a single command arrow from motor cortex to muscle insufficient to explain stability and correction during real movement? Page 1 embeds the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup. A feedforward command acts in advance from a goal and internal model and can compensate for known delays, but it is vulnerable to unexpected disturbances and model error. A feedback controller corrects output using sensed state error and resists disturbances, but excessive gain combined with delay can oscillate. Biological control combines both, with spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and motor cortex contributing on different timescales and representational levels rather than taking over sequentially. For asymmetric W, why can normalized right eigenvectors not justify writing \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\)? Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes. This is the distinction tested in The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition. Worked example — Common and Difference Modes in a Two-Neuron Network: Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations. For common pattern \(v_{+}=(1,1)/\sqrt 2\), \(Wv_{+}=(0.9,0.9)/\sqrt 2\), so \(\lambda _{+}=0.9\). For difference pattern \(v_{-}=(1,-1)/\sqrt 2\), \(Wv_{-}=(0.7,-0.7)/\sqrt 2\), so \(\lambda _{-}=0.7\). The mode equations are \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{+}/dt=-0.1\alpha _{+}\) and \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{-}/dt=-0.3\alpha _{-}\). The common mode decays more slowly. Matrix \(\operatorname{trace} 1.6\) equals eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 0.9+0.7\), and determinant 0.63 equals product \(0.9\times 0.7\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition”? The direction of \(W_{ij}\) follows by expanding \((Wh)_i\); here it is \(j\to i\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition”? \(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From the Recurrent Equation to Decoupled Mode Equations”? If V consists of dimensionless normalized patterns, \(\alpha\) and h have firing-rate units; W and \(\lambda\) are dimensionless, \(\tau\) has time units, and Ĩ has the same units as h. For \(W=0\), choose \(V=I\) and \(\lambda _{i}=0\); every neuronal mode decays independently with \(\tau\). If W is already diagonal, the basis change leaves the coordinates unchanged. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does changing \(\lambda\) from 0.98 to 0.999 create drift risk in addition to longer memory? The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement. This is the distinction tested in Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration. Worked example — Extending an Intrinsic 20 ms Time Constant to 1 s of Memory: A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\). Because \(1-\lambda =0.02\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20 \mathrm{ms}/0.02=1000 \mathrm{ms}=1 \mathrm{s}\). After 1 s, \(\alpha =5e^{-1}\approx 1.84\). Recurrent feedback lengthens but does not eliminate decay. For \(\lambda =1\) without input, \(d\alpha /dt=0\) and the amplitude remains 5 after 1 s. A persistent small bias would be integrated continuously. The incorrect formula \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1+\lambda )\) gives about 10 ms, the opposite of the memory-lengthening effect of positive feedback. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration”? For a real eigenvalue \(\lambda <1\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); decay slows as the eigenvalue approaches 1. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration”? \(\lambda =1\) removes leak and integrates input; \(\lambda >1\) makes the linear mode grow exponentially. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Approaching 1 increases both memory time and constant-input gain, amplifying bias and connectivity error as well. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Mode Solution, Effective Time Constant, and Fixed Point”? \(\lambda\) is dimensionless, while \(\tau\) and \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) are times. \(\alpha\) and Ĩ share units, so \(\int \widetilde I ds/\tau\) retains the units of \(\alpha\). \(\lambda =0\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, both \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and constant gain grow. For \(\lambda >1\), the exponent changes sign and the zero fixed point is unstable. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes”? If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “feedforward control” mean in this lecture? feedforward control: Control based mainly on a prior model or command rather than current feedback correction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feedback control” mean in this lecture? feedback control: Online correction of action from sensory or state error. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “proprioception” mean in this lecture? proprioception: Sensory feedback about body position or force. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “recurrent network” mean in this lecture? recurrent network: A network with feedback loops among its units. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “eigenmode” mean in this lecture? eigenmode: A population activity pattern associated with an eigenvector of W. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “change of basis” mean in this lecture? change of basis: Conversion of the same state between neuronal and modal coordinates. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “effective time constant” mean in this lecture? effective time constant: A mode's decay or integration timescale after feedback. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “fixed point” mean in this lecture? fixed point: A state whose derivative is zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “stability” mean in this lecture? stability: Whether a small perturbation returns to a fixed point. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Linear recurrent rate network” be used? Linear recurrent rate network: \(\tau \) \(\dot{h} = -h + W h + I\). Common \(\tau\) and linearization This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Diagonalization” be used? Diagonalization: \(W = V DV -1\). Diagonalizable W This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Mode coordinates” be used? Mode coordinates: \(\alpha  = V -1 h\). Invertible V This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Decoupled mode” be used? Decoupled mode: \(\tau \) \(\dot{\alpha }i = -(1 - \lambda _{i} )\alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}\). Eigenbasis This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Mode time constant” be used? Mode time constant: \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\). \(\lambda <1\) for stable decay This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Perfect integrator” be used? Perfect integrator: \(\lambda  = 1 \Rightarrow  \dot{\alpha } = \beta /\tau \). Exact cancellation of feedback and leak This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop
subtitle: Lecture 18 · Lecture18-IntroToMotorSystemsAndDynamics.pdf, p. 1
text: Why is a single command arrow from motor cortex to muscle insufficient to explain stability and correction during real movement? Page 1 embeds the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup. A feedforward command acts in advance from a goal and internal model and can compensate for known delays, but it is vulnerable to unexpected disturbances and model error. A feedback controller corrects output using sensed state error and resists disturbances, but excessive gain combined with delay can oscillate. Biological control combines both, with spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and motor cortex contributing on different timescales and representational levels rather than taking over sequentially. A sensory signal is a delayed noisy observation, not the body's exact current state. A state estimate combines recent sensation, copies of motor commands, and a dynamics model to infer current latent position, velocity, and related variables. Feedback commonly computes error around this estimate. A central pattern generator (CPG) shows that a recurrent circuit can generate rhythmic motor output without an external command on every cycle; sensory feedback corrects phase and amplitude rather than generating each cycle from scratch. A minimal scalar example writes body position dynamics as \(dx/dt=u+d\), with neural command u and external disturbance d. Proportional feedback \(u=-kx\) gives \(dx/dt=-kx+d\). Without persistent disturbance, x returns to zero at rate k. Under constant disturbance, fixed error is d/k. Raising k reduces steady error, but sensory delay, actuator limits, and noise constrain gain in real systems, foreshadowing recurrent-stability tradeoffs. Distributed motor-cortical activity need not map one neuron to one muscle. A movement can be represented by a population trajectory: instantaneous activity is the dynamical state, and recurrent dynamics determine how the trajectory continues. The question expands from which neuron encodes which variable to which modes govern population-state evolution and which inputs alter initial conditions or the vector field. A linear network is not a complete motor theory, but it is the first decomposition of temporal structure. Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback. Feedforward control anticipates; feedback corrects disturbances. Delay, noise, and gain set the stability costs. A state estimate infers current latent state from delayed noisy observations, while a CPG demonstrates endogenous rhythm generation by recurrent dynamics. Motor-population activity is a dynamical state; no mode should be assumed to equal one muscle or action variable. For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). The system converges not to zero but to steady error 0.3; at 1 second its position is about 0.395. Why does larger proportional gain improve disturbance rejection in a delay-free model but not justify infinite gain in a biological system? The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop. Treating feedforward and feedback as mutually exclusive, although real actions commonly combine predictive commands with sensory correction. Assigning one function to each motor region from a region list while ignoring circuits, parallel pathways, and the abstraction level of the course diagram.

title: The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition
subtitle: Lecture 18 · Lecture18-IntroToMotorSystemsAndDynamics.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture18-IntroToMotorSystemsAndDynamics.pdf, p. 3
text: How can N coupled rate equations be rewritten as independent scalar equations, one for each eigenmode? Page 2 begins with \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\). Vector \(h\in \mathbb{R}^N\) contains the activities of N units, -h is unitwise leak, Wh is recurrent input, and I is external drive. Here \(W_{ij}\) points from j to i. In neuronal coordinates, each derivative depends on many \(h_{j}\) and the equations are coupled. We seek coordinates in which recurrent multiplication no longer mixes components. Page 3 uses right eigenvectors of W. If \(Wv_{i}=\lambda _{i} v_{i}\), multiplication by W rescales pattern \(v_{i}\) by \(\lambda _{i}\) without rotating it. Put these eigenvectors in the columns of V. If they are linearly independent, \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Expand activity as \(h=V\alpha\), where \(\alpha _{i}\) is the amplitude of population pattern i. This basis change leaves the physical state unchanged, just as a two-dimensional displacement can be expressed in oblique rather than x-y coordinates. Substitute \(h=V\alpha\) into the original equation and take V to be time-independent: \(\tau V d\alpha /dt=-V\alpha +WV\alpha +I\). Using \(WV=V\Lambda\) and left-multiplying by \(V^{-1}\) gives \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-\alpha +\Lambda \alpha +V^{-1}I\). Since \(\Lambda\) is diagonal, row i contains only \(\alpha _{i}\): \(\tau  d\alpha _{i}/dt=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). The complex network's linear dynamics decompose into familiar first-order systems. The limitations matter. Eigenvectors of asymmetric W need not be orthogonal, so \(V^{-1}\) cannot be replaced casually by \(V^\mathrm{T}\). Nearly parallel eigenvectors make mode coordinates noise-sensitive. If W is defective, there is no complete ordinary eigenbasis; use Jordan form or \(e^{(-I+W)t/\tau }\) directly. The diagonalizable case highlights eigenvalue control of timescale but does not claim that cortical connectivity is symmetric. The direction of \(W_{ij}\) follows by expanding \((Wh)_i\); here it is \(j\to i\). \(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns. When W is diagonalizable, \(\Lambda\) does not mix modes and every \(\alpha _{i}\) follows an independent first-order equation. Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations. Population activity decomposes into an aligned common mode with \(\lambda =0.9\) and an opposing difference mode with \(\lambda =0.7\). For asymmetric W, why can normalized right eigenvectors not justify writing \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\)? Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes. Inferring source-target direction of \(W_{ij}\) by habit instead of expanding the matrix product. Assuming every W has an orthonormal eigenbasis, a property restricted to special matrices such as real symmetric ones.

title: Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration
subtitle: Lecture 18 · Lecture18-IntroToMotorSystemsAndDynamics.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture18-IntroToMotorSystemsAndDynamics.pdf, p. 5
text: Why does \(\lambda\) near 1 create long memory, while \(\lambda =1\) and \(\lambda >1 \operatorname{mean}\) perfect integration and instability? Page 4 begins with input-free equation \(\tau  d\alpha _{i}/dt=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}\). For real \(\lambda _{i}<1\), \(\alpha _{i}(t)=\alpha _{i}(0)\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})t/\tau ]\), giving \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\). Positive recurrent feedback pushes \(\lambda\) toward 1, offsets leak, and lengthens memory; negative \(\lambda\) strengthens restoration and accelerates decay. Continuous-time stability requires Re(λ_i)<1, not \(|\lambda _{i}|<1\). At \(\lambda _{i}=1\), restoring force vanishes. Without input \(\alpha _{i}\) holds its initial value; with time-varying input, \(\tau  d\alpha _{i}/dt=\widetilde I_{i}(t)\), so the state accumulates the input integral—a perfect integrator. For \(\lambda _{i}\) slightly below 1 there is long but finite leakage; for \(\lambda _{i}>1\) small perturbations grow exponentially. Under constant input, algebraic fixed point \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\) may still exist, but it is unstable: any initial condition not exactly at that point departs. Nonlinear saturation may create another attractor, beyond the local range of this linear mode. Page 5 also separates fixed point from timescale. For constant transformed input Ĩ_i and \(\lambda _{i}\ne 1\), \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\). The same small denominator creates both long \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and high steady-state gain, so near-integration amplifies constant bias and parameter error. Memory is the benefit and drift the risk. Negative feedback, multiple timescales, and nonlinear bounds can manage that sensitivity. For arbitrary time-varying input, the mode response is the sum of decaying initial condition and input convolution. Kernel \(\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})(t-s)/\tau ]/\tau\) weights only past input. As \(\lambda _{i}\) approaches 1, the kernel decays more slowly and older inputs continue to influence present state. The impulse response therefore exposes \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) directly, while transformed-input magnitude \(\widetilde I_{i}=V^{-1}I\) determines whether external drive enters that slow mode. In population space, \(h(t)=V\alpha (t)\) sums all modal time courses. A slow mode may dominate the late trajectory even with a small initial projection because faster modes vanish first. An input's effect depends on which modes it projects onto, not only its total energy. An eigenvalue account of motor dynamics should report model fit, initial conditions, input projection, and observed timescale; a rotating trajectory alone does not identify an eigenmode as a behavioral command. For a real eigenvalue \(\lambda <1\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); decay slows as the eigenvalue approaches 1. \(\lambda =1\) removes leak and integrates input; \(\lambda >1\) makes the linear mode grow exponentially. Approaching 1 increases both memory time and constant-input gain, amplifying bias and connectivity error as well. A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\). \(\lambda =0.98\) turns an intrinsic 20 ms constant into a 1 s leaky memory; only \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator. Why does changing \(\lambda\) from 0.98 to 0.999 create drift risk in addition to longer memory? The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement. Applying the discrete-time condition \(|\lambda |<1\) directly to continuous-time equation \(\tau dh/dt=(-I+W)h\). Continuing to use \(\alpha *=\widetilde I/(1-\lambda )\) at \(\lambda =1\), despite a perfect integrator having no finite fixed point under constant input.

title: Lecture 19: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis
subtitle: How do recurrent modes in a two-neuron network produce nearly one-dimensional population trajectories, and how does PCA recover maximum-variance dimensions from activity covariance alone?
text: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis How do recurrent modes in a two-neuron network produce nearly one-dimensional population trajectories, and how does PCA recover maximum-variance dimensions from activity covariance alone? two-neuron W → common/difference modes → mode regimes → activity-space trajectory → covariance → PCA top-K Starting from the two-neuron recurrent equation, compute by hand the eigenvalues, normalized eigenvectors, and input coordinates of the common and difference modes. Use each mode's time constant to classify stable decay, leaky integration, perfect integration, and unstable growth, then reinterpret the mode coordinates as trajectories in neural activity space. Derive PCA by maximizing the projection variance of centered data, and work through numerical examples of top-K projection, reconstruction, variance explained, and dimensional truncation. Distinguish rigorously between dynamical modes of a recurrent weight matrix and principal components of a covariance matrix, including when they may align and when no such alignment should be expected. Compare the updated and earlier notes: retain their shared material, then use the new page 6 to add the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative-variance curve. The common and difference eigenmodes of a symmetric two-neuron network can be calculated completely by hand: one receives feedback +w0 and the other −w0. If the difference mode decays rapidly, the neural trajectory collapses toward the common-mode line and becomes approximately one-dimensional. PCA does not require W; it finds maximum projected variance from centered activity covariance. Dynamical eigenvectors of W can relate to principal components of C, but they are not generally identical. Equating eigenvectors of W with covariance PCs without additional assumptions. Omitting \(1/\sqrt 2\) when normalizing the common and difference modes. Using the wrong ± sign in the mode time constants. Misreading a low-dimensional trajectory as activity in only a few neurons. Applying PCA without centering the data. Treating maximum variance as maximum causal or behavioral relevance. Treating the eigenvalue cliff as an objectively unique dimensionality cutoff. The UPDATE is the primary version and adds Page 6. PCA orders directions by variance; it does not automatically discover causal dynamics and can mix signal, noise, and condition structure. common and difference modes \(\xi \pm  = (1, \pm 1)T / 2\) symmetric two-neuron W orthonormal mode coordinates \(\alpha  = V\) Th \(V^\mathrm{T}V=I\) mode time constants \(\tau \pm  = \tau  /(1 \mp  w_{0} )\) \(|w_{0}|<1\) for stability of both modes activity covariance \(C = E[\delta h\delta hT ]\) centered data PC1 v1 = arg \(\max v\) T Cv \(\Vert v\Vert =1 C\) symmetric positive semidefinite PC score and projection pk = vkT \((h - \bar{h})\) orthonormal PCs cumulative variance explained ∑ ∑ VarFrac\((K) = \lambda _{k} / \lambda _{j} k\le K j\) sorted eigenvalues common mode An eigenmode in which both neurons change in the same direction. difference mode An eigenmode in which the two neurons change in opposite directions. neural activity space A state space whose coordinates are the activities of individual neurons. mode space A state space whose coordinates are dynamical eigenmode amplitudes. principal component analysis, PCA A linear method that orders orthogonal directions by the covariance variance they capture. principal component A covariance eigenvector together with the score obtained by projecting data onto it. projection The component of a vector along a specified basis direction. reconstruction An approximation of the original data formed from retained components. scree plot A plot of eigenvalue against component index. variance explained The fraction of the total eigenvalue sum retained by selected components. What is the result of multiplying \(W=[[0,0.6],[0.6,0]]\) by \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\)? Multiply row by row: the first row gives \(0\times 1+0.6\times 1\) and the second gives \(0.6\times 1+0\times 1\). If this calculation is unfamiliar, return to the common/difference-mode module and check each component. The result is \((0.6,0.6)^\mathrm{T}\), so \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.6. For \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\lambda =0.8\), what is the effective time constant of \(\tau d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha\)? The coefficient \(1-\lambda\) sets the decay rate: the smaller this gap, the longer the time constant. Do not mistake \(\lambda\) itself for a time constant measured in milliseconds. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.8)=100 \mathrm{ms}\). Why must each neuron's mean activity be subtracted before computing the covariance? Without centering, the second moment h \(h^\mathrm{T}\) contains both the mean outer product and trial-to-trial variation, so PC1 may primarily track mean activity. Centering makes covariance describe joint fluctuations around the mean firing pattern instead of mistaking the mean response direction for the direction of greatest variability. Does a nearly one-dimensional trajectory mean that only one neuron is active? Dimension counts independent, variable population coordinates; it does not count nonzero neurons. Return to the activity-space reconstruction to see how both neurons participate in the common mode. No. It means that the joint activity of many neurons varies mainly along one population direction, which usually contains nonzero components from multiple neurons. If the PCA eigenvalues are 9, 3, 1, and 1, what cumulative variance is explained by retaining the first two PCs? The denominator of cumulative variance explained must contain every eigenvalue. Dividing only by the retained eigenvalues would incorrectly give 100%. \((9+3)/(9+3+1+1)=12/14\), or approximately 85.7%. If \(I_{1}=1\) and \(I_{2}=-1\), which mode is driven directly? \(\beta _{+}=(1-1)/\sqrt 2=0\) and \(\beta _{-}=(1-(-1))/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\), so only the difference mode is driven directly; the neurons tend to change in opposite directions. This is the distinction tested in Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations. Worked example — Transform a population state into mode coordinates: Given \(h=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(I=(2,2)^\mathrm{T}\), calculate \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then verify that \(\alpha\) reconstructs h without loss. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(h=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(I=(2,2)^\mathrm{T}\), calculate \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then verify that \(\alpha\) reconstructs h without loss. Compute \(\alpha _{+}=(3+1)/\sqrt 2=2\sqrt 2\) and \(\alpha _{-}=(3-1)/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\). Compute \(\beta _{+}=(2+2)/\sqrt 2=2\sqrt 2\) and \(\beta _{-}=(2-2)/\sqrt 2=0\), so the input drives only the common mode. Reconstruct \(\alpha +\xi _{+}+\alpha -\xi _{-}\): the first component is \((2\sqrt 2+\sqrt 2)/\sqrt 2=3\) and the second is \((2\sqrt 2-\sqrt 2)/\sqrt 2=1\). The squared coordinates sum to \(8+2=10\), matching the original vector's squared length \(3^{2}+1^{2}=10\). An orthogonal transform preserves length, providing an arithmetic check. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations”? \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations”? \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Complete solution of the common/difference eigensystem”? \(V^\mathrm{T}h\) has shape \((2\times 2)(2\times 1)=2\times 1\), and every term in the mode ODE has units of a rate coordinate. At \(w_{0}=0\) the original neurons are uncoupled and the two basis directions decay at the same rate. The eigenbasis is then not unique: common/difference coordinates remain valid but are no longer the only choice. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why does replacing h1 and h2 with common and opposing changes decouple the originally coupled network? The source page gives \(W=[[0,w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\) and the rate equations \(\tau dh_{1}/dt=-h_{1}+w_{0}h_{2}+I_{1}\) and \(\tau dh_{2}/dt=-h_{2}+w_{0}h_{1}+I_{2}\). Zeros on the diagonal mean that this teaching example has no self-coupling, while equal off-diagonal entries make the reciprocal coupling symmetric. That symmetry suggests testing \(h_{1}=h_{2}\) and \(h_{1}=-h_{2}\): exchanging the neurons leaves the first pattern unchanged and changes only the sign of the second. Set \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}-w_{0}^{2}=0\) to obtain \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) and \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{+}\) gives \(h_{2}=h_{1}\), so a common eigenvector is \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{-}\) gives \(h_{2}=-h_{1}\), so a difference eigenvector is \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Dividing each by \(\sqrt 2\) produces unit vectors with zero dot product, an orthonormal basis V. Normalization preserves direction and lets coordinates be computed directly by dot products. At \(w_{0}=-0.9\), which mode is slowest, and what is its time constant in units of \(\tau\)? The difference mode is slowest because \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1-0.9)=10\tau\); the common mode has \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1+0.9)\approx 0.526\tau\). Negative coupling near -1 preserves the opposing-change pattern. This is the distinction tested in Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability. Worked example — Compare the speeds of the two modes: Let the single-cell time constant be \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(w_{0}=0.8\). Remove the input, calculate both mode time constants, and predict the fraction remaining after 100 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let the single-cell time constant be \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(w_{0}=0.8\). Remove the input, calculate both mode time constants, and predict the fraction remaining after 100 ms. \(\tau _{+}=20/(1-0.8)=100 \mathrm{ms}\); \(\tau _{-}=20/(1+0.8)=11.11 \mathrm{ms}\). After 100 ms, the common-mode amplitude fraction is \(e^{-100/100}=e^{-1}\approx 0.368\). The difference-mode fraction is \(e^{-100/11.11}=e^{-9}\approx 0.000123\), so it has nearly vanished. Setting w0 to 0 should return both time constants to 20 ms. One long and one short time constant here agrees with the direction of positive reciprocal feedback. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability”? \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1+w_{0})\); the signs cannot be collapsed into a common denominator. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability”? Only \(|w_{0}|<1\) makes both modes stable; \(w_{0}=\pm 1\) produces a perfect integrator in one mode. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Only \(|w_{0}|<1\) makes both modes stable; \(w_{0}=\pm 1\) produces a perfect integrator in one mode. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Read the effective time constant from the mode coefficient”? Because the denominator is dimensionless, \(\tau /(1\mp w_{0})\) retains the time unit of \(\tau\). A unitless 'time constant' signals that \(\tau\) was omitted. As w0→1^-, \(\tau +\to \infty\). Beyond 1 the formula becomes negative; this is not a negative physical time but a sign that the exponent now describes growth. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If a constant input \(\beta _{-}=1\) acts at every moment, must \(\alpha _{-}\) approach zero? No. A stable difference mode approaches the nonzero fixed point \(\alpha _{-}* = \beta _{-}/(1+w_{0})\), so the trajectory can remain away from the common axis. Low-dimensional conclusions depend on input structure. This is the distinction tested in Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory. Worked example — How quickly does the trajectory enter the low-dimensional manifold?: Let \(\alpha +(0)=4\), \(\alpha -(0)=2\), \(\tau _{+}=200 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(\tau _{-}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find both amplitudes and the difference-mode energy fraction after 100 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\alpha +(0)=4\), \(\alpha -(0)=2\), \(\tau _{+}=200 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(\tau _{-}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find both amplitudes and the difference-mode energy fraction after 100 ms. \(\alpha +(100)=4e^{-0.5}\approx 2.426\). \(\alpha -(100)=2e^{-5}\approx 0.0135\). The difference fraction is \(0.0135^{2}/(2.426^{2}+0.0135^{2})\approx 0.000031\), or about 0.0031%. Swapping 20 ms and 200 ms reverses the fast/slow conclusion; first check which denominator is closer to zero. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory”? Activity coordinates and mode coordinates are reversible representations of the same state. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory”? After the fast mode decays, the slow mode dominates the trajectory and produces approximate low dimensionality. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The error from discarding a mode is quantified by the square of that mode's coordinate. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Why the loss of a fast mode yields a nearly one-dimensional trajectory”? \(\alpha \pm\) and h share the same units, while \(\xi \pm\) is dimensionless, so both terms in the reconstruction have compatible units. If \(\tau _{-}=\tau _{+}\), both modes decay at the same relative rate, so timescale separation does not automatically collapse the initial two-dimensional structure to one dimension. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is chiefly mixed in if \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]\) is computed without centering? The mean outer-product term \(\bar{h}\) \(\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\) is included, so the leading direction may represent the mean firing pattern rather than trial or temporal fluctuations. This is the distinction tested in PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors. Worked example — Compute the PC of a two-dimensional covariance by hand: Given \(C=[[5,4],[4,5]]\), find both eigenvectors and eigenvalues, then interpret the long axis of the data cloud. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(C=[[5,4],[4,5]]\), find both eigenvectors and eigenvalues, then interpret the long axis of the data cloud. For common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\), \(C(1,1)^\mathrm{T}=(9,9)^\mathrm{T}\), so the eigenvalue is 9. For difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), \(C(1,-1)^\mathrm{T}=(1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), so the eigenvalue is 1. After normalization, PC1=\((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\) and PC2=\((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\); the variance of PC1 is 9 times that of PC2. The trace of C is 10, equal to the eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 9+1\), which checks the arithmetic. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors”? PCA must be applied to centered activity: \(C=E[\delta h\delta h^\mathrm{T}]\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors”? Under a unit-norm constraint, projected variance is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Maximum variance is not the same as maximum causal or behavioral relevance. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Rayleigh-quotient derivation of PC1”? If h is a firing rate, C and \(\lambda\) have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\); v is dimensionless and projection p retains the rate unit. If every sample is identical, centering gives \(C=0\). Variance is zero in every direction and the PC directions are not unique. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I\) not imply \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}=I\)? When \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) is not square. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}\) is the identity in K-space, while \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space projector onto a K-dimensional subspace. This is the distinction tested in Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations. Worked example — Top-2 reconstruction of a three-dimensional state: Let \(\operatorname{mean}=0\), with PCs equal to coordinate axes \(v_{1}=(1,0,0)\), \(v_{2}=(0,1,0)\), \(v_{3}=(0,0,1)\), and sample \(h=(4,2,1)\). Retain \(K=2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\operatorname{mean}=0\), with PCs equal to coordinate axes \(v_{1}=(1,0,0)\), \(v_{2}=(0,1,0)\), \(v_{3}=(0,0,1)\), and sample \(h=(4,2,1)\). Retain \(K=2\). The scores are \(p_{1}=4\), \(p_{2}=2\), and \(p_{3}=1\). Keeping the first two terms gives \(\hat{h}=4v_{1}+2v_{2}=(4,2,0)\). The residual is \(h-\hat{h}=(0,0,1)\), with squared error 1. The original squared norm is 21, the reconstruction has 20, and the residual has 1, satisfying the orthogonal Pythagorean relation \(21=20+1\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations”? \(V_{K}\) is N×K, scores are K×1, and reconstruction returns to N×1 neuron space. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations”? A complete orthogonal basis transform is lossless; dimensions are discarded only by projection with \(K<N\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(V_{K}\) is N×K, scores are K×1, and reconstruction returns to N×1 neuron space. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Top-K reconstruction and error”? \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) has shape N×N and acts on N×1 centered activity. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I_{K}\), but \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is generally not \(I_{N}\). At \(K=N\), residual and error are zero; at \(K=0\), reconstruction is only the mean and error equals total variance. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does '95% variance explained' not guarantee retention of 95% of behavioral information? Variance measures activity amplitude, whereas behavioral information depends on condition distributions and the decoder. A low-variance direction may reliably distinguish choices, so the two percentages are not generally equivalent. This is the distinction tested in New page: eigenvalue cliff, cumulative variance, and dimensionality selection. Worked example — Different cutoffs produce different values of K: The eigenvalues are \([9,3,1,1]\). Find the smallest K under cumulative-variance thresholds of 80% and 95%. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The eigenvalues are \([9,3,1,1]\). Find the smallest K under cumulative-variance thresholds of 80% and 95%. Total variance is 14; \(F(1)=9/14\approx 64.3\)%. \(F(2)=12/14\approx 85.7\)%, so an 80% threshold selects \(K=2\). \(F(3)=13/14\approx 92.9\)% and \(F(4)=100\)%, so a 95% threshold selects \(K=4\). Cumulative variance should never decrease and must equal 1 at \(K=N\). Violating either condition usually signals an error in sorting or the denominator. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “New page: eigenvalue cliff, cumulative variance, and dimensionality selection”? A scree-plot elbow is a heuristic and usually has no unique location. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “New page: eigenvalue cliff, cumulative variance, and dimensionality selection”? Cumulative variance \(F(K)\) is the partial sum of sorted eigenvalues divided by their total sum. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “New page: eigenvalue cliff, cumulative variance, and dimensionality selection” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Cumulative variance \(F(K)\) is the partial sum of sorted eigenvalues divided by their total sum. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Complementarity of cumulative variance and residual error”? Numerator and denominator both have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\), so the ratio is unitless. K is an integer index, not a continuous parameter. If \(\lambda _{1}=\cdots =\lambda _{N}\), the spectrum has no cliff and \(F(K)=K/N\). Any low-dimensional cutoff then reflects an external tolerance rather than a natural turning point in the data. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance”? Read the two curves in principal-component order: beyond the cliff, each eigenvalue contributes little additional variance, while cumulative variance continues to rise monotonically. The elbow suggests candidate dimensionalities but does not determine a unique cutoff; the plotted coordinates illustrate the normalized relation on page 6 and are not empirical data. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “common mode” mean in this lecture? common mode: An eigenmode in which both neurons change in the same direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “difference mode” mean in this lecture? difference mode: An eigenmode in which the two neurons change in opposite directions. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “neural activity space” mean in this lecture? neural activity space: A state space whose coordinates are the activities of individual neurons. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “mode space” mean in this lecture? mode space: A state space whose coordinates are dynamical eigenmode amplitudes. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “principal component analysis, PCA” mean in this lecture? principal component analysis, PCA: A linear method that orders orthogonal directions by the covariance variance they capture. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “principal component” mean in this lecture? principal component: A covariance eigenvector together with the score obtained by projecting data onto it. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “projection” mean in this lecture? projection: The component of a vector along a specified basis direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “reconstruction” mean in this lecture? reconstruction: An approximation of the original data formed from retained components. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “scree plot” mean in this lecture? scree plot: A plot of eigenvalue against component index. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “common and difference modes” be used? common and difference modes: \(\xi \pm  = (1, \pm 1)T / 2\). symmetric two-neuron W This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “orthonormal mode coordinates” be used? orthonormal mode coordinates: \(\alpha  = V\) Th. \(V^\mathrm{T}V=I\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “mode time constants” be used? mode time constants: \(\tau \pm  = \tau  /(1 \mp  w_{0} )\). \(|w_{0}|<1\) for stability of both modes This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “activity covariance” be used? activity covariance: \(C = E[\delta h\delta hT ]\). centered data This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “PC1” be used? PC1: v1 = arg \(\max v\) T Cv \(\Vert v\Vert =1\). C symmetric positive semidefinite This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “PC score and projection” be used? PC score and projection: pk = vkT \((h - \bar{h})\). orthonormal PCs This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “cumulative variance explained” be used? cumulative variance explained: ∑ ∑ VarFrac\((K) = \lambda _{k} / \lambda _{j} k\le K j\). sorted eigenvalues This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations
subtitle: Lecture 19 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA-UPDATE.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA.pdf, p. 1
text: Why does replacing h1 and h2 with common and opposing changes decouple the originally coupled network? The source page gives \(W=[[0,w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\) and the rate equations \(\tau  dh_{1}/dt=-h_{1}+w_{0}h_{2}+I_{1}\) and \(\tau  dh_{2}/dt=-h_{2}+w_{0}h_{1}+I_{2}\). Zeros on the diagonal mean that this teaching example has no self-coupling, while equal off-diagonal entries make the reciprocal coupling symmetric. That symmetry suggests testing \(h_{1}=h_{2}\) and \(h_{1}=-h_{2}\): exchanging the neurons leaves the first pattern unchanged and changes only the sign of the second. Set \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}-w_{0}^{2}=0\) to obtain \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) and \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{+}\) gives \(h_{2}=h_{1}\), so a common eigenvector is \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{-}\) gives \(h_{2}=-h_{1}\), so a difference eigenvector is \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Dividing each by \(\sqrt 2\) produces unit vectors with zero dot product, an orthonormal basis V. Normalization preserves direction and lets coordinates be computed directly by dot products. The new coordinates are \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\): \(\alpha _{+}=(h_{1}+h_{2})/\sqrt 2\) and \(\alpha _{-}=(h_{1}-h_{2})/\sqrt 2\). Applying the same transformation to the input gives \(\beta _{+}=(I_{1}+I_{2})/\sqrt 2\) and \(\beta _{-}=(I_{1}-I_{2})/\sqrt 2\). Substitute \(h=V\alpha\) into the original equation and left-multiply by \(V^\mathrm{T}\) to obtain \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=-(1-w_{0})\alpha _{+}+\beta _{+}\) and \(\tau  d\alpha _{-}/dt=-(1+w_{0})\alpha _{-}+\beta _{-}\). Each equation now contains only its own coordinate, confirming that the basis change has decoupled the dynamics. Both modes are population patterns, not patterns belonging separately to neuron 1 and neuron 2. Increasing the common mode changes both neurons in the same direction; increasing the difference mode raises one and lowers the other. In an asymmetric network the eigenvectors need not be orthogonal, so \(V^{-1}\) need not equal \(V^\mathrm{T}\). Mode decomposition may still be possible, but the coordinate transform and geometry must use the general inverse rather than the orthogonal formulas on this page. \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). Activity and input must be transformed in the same basis: \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T}h\) and \(\beta =V^\mathrm{T}I\). The eigenvectors of W describe directions of model dynamics; they are not the PCs obtained from data covariance. Given \(h=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(I=(2,2)^\mathrm{T}\), calculate \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then verify that \(\alpha\) reconstructs h without loss. The mode coordinates are \(\alpha =(2\sqrt 2,\sqrt 2)^\mathrm{T}\), the input coordinates are \(\beta =(2\sqrt 2,0)^\mathrm{T}\), and reconstruction returns exactly \((3,1)^\mathrm{T}\). If \(I_{1}=1\) and \(I_{2}=-1\), which mode is driven directly? \(\beta _{+}=(1-1)/\sqrt 2=0\) and \(\beta _{-}=(1-(-1))/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\), so only the difference mode is driven directly; the neurons tend to change in opposite directions. Omitting \(1/\sqrt 2\) makes the coordinate and reconstruction scales inconsistent. Treating the common and difference modes as separate neurons, even though each mode is a joint pattern of both neurons.

title: Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability
subtitle: Lecture 19 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA-UPDATE.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA.pdf, p. 2
text: Why does the same w0 slow the common mode but accelerate the difference mode? The homogeneous mode equations are \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=-(1-w_{0})\alpha _{+}\) and \(\tau  d\alpha _{-}/dt=-(1+w_{0})\alpha _{-}\). Comparing them with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}} d\alpha /dt=-\alpha\) gives \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1+w_{0})\). Page 1 of the source writes \(1/(1\mp w_{0})\), which is valid only after normalizing \(\tau\) to 1; otherwise it loses the time unit. The dimensionally complete expression is \(\tau /(1\mp w_{0})\). Positive coupling supplies positive feedback to common changes and cancels part of the intrinsic leak. For opposing changes it acts as restoring feedback, because a rise in neuron 1 drives neuron 2 upward and reduces their difference.
