When \(|w_{0}|<1\), both 1-w0 and 1+w0 are positive, so both modes decay exponentially after input removal. As w0 approaches 1, \(\tau _{+}\) becomes long and the common coordinate behaves as a leaky integrator. At \(w_{0}=1\) the common equation has no leak: sustained input is integrated and the accumulated \(\alpha _{+}\) remains after the input ends. The same logic moves to the difference mode as w0 approaches -1. Equality marks a perfect integrator and should not be lumped into the ordinary leaky regime. If \(|w_{0}|>1\), at least one coefficient becomes negative. For example, at \(w_{0}=1.2\) the common equation is \(\tau  d\alpha _{+}/dt=+0.2\alpha _{+}\), so a small perturbation grows exponentially. Mathematical instability does not \(\operatorname{mean} a\) real firing rate can increase without bound; neuronal saturation, thresholds, and inhibition change the large-amplitude behavior. Linear analysis nevertheless identifies a direction that leaves the fixed point locally. Read the activity-space sketches as follows. In the h1-h2 plane, the common axis has slope +1 and the difference axis has slope -1. If \(\tau _{-}\) is much smaller than \(\tau _{+}\), an arbitrary initial state rapidly loses its difference component, approaches the common axis, and then moves slowly along it. The drawn axes show eigenvector directions; trajectory speed comes from the eigenvalues and \(\tau\), not from the lengths of the lines. \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1+w_{0})\); the signs cannot be collapsed into a common denominator. Only \(|w_{0}|<1\) makes both modes stable; \(w_{0}=\pm 1\) produces a perfect integrator in one mode. \(|w_{0}|>1\) makes the linear fixed point unstable along at least one mode. An activity-space trajectory decomposes into independent exponential components along the eigenvectors. Let the single-cell time constant be \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(w_{0}=0.8\). Remove the input, calculate both mode time constants, and predict the fraction remaining after 100 ms. At 100 ms the state contains almost only the common component, although both neurons may still have nonzero activity. At \(w_{0}=-0.9\), which mode is slowest, and what is its time constant in units of \(\tau\)? The difference mode is slowest because \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1-0.9)=10\tau\); the common mode has \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1+0.9)\approx 0.526\tau\). Negative coupling near -1 preserves the opposing-change pattern. Judging stability from the sign of an eigenvalue of W while forgetting the -h term in the full ODE. Using \(\tau /(1-w_{0})\) for both modes and thereby losing the negative sign of the difference eigenvalue.

title: Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory
subtitle: Lecture 19 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA-UPDATE.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA.pdf, p. 3
text: Precisely what does 'nearly one-dimensional population dynamics' mean, and what does it not claim? Activity space uses (h1,h2) to describe the state of both neurons at each moment; mode space uses \((\alpha _{+},\alpha _{-})\) to describe the same point. An invertible V connects the two, so they are not distinct datasets. Activity space corresponds directly to recorded firing rates, whereas mode space exposes the dynamics because each \(\alpha\) coordinate evolves with its own time constant. A coordinate change removes no information; dimensionality reduction occurs only when coordinates are later discarded. Any state can be written \(h(t)=\alpha +(t)\xi _{+}+\alpha -(t)\xi _{-}\). If \(\tau _{-}\) is much smaller than \(\tau _{+}\) and no persistent difference input acts during the delay, \(\alpha -(t)\) decays much faster than \(\alpha +(t)\). After several \(\tau _{-}\), \(h(t)\approx \alpha +(t)\xi _{+}\) and subsequent states lie near the common axis. 'One-dimensional' means that \(\alpha _{+}\) is the main free coordinate needed for the trajectory, not that only one neuron participates. Approximation quality can be measured by residual energy. Because the basis is orthonormal, \(||h||^{2}=\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2}\). Discarding the difference mode gives squared reconstruction error exactly \(\alpha -^{2}\). An analyst may set a tolerance, for example calling the state 95% common-mode when \(\alpha -^{2}/(\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2})<0.05\). This criterion is chosen for the analysis; it is not an absolute boundary that appears automatically in a sketch. This reasoning also states the conditions for a low-dimensional conclusion. Strong drive to \(\beta - at\) every moment or trial-specific fast transients keep the difference coordinate away from zero. If nonlinear dynamics rotate directions with state, no fixed V describes the entire trajectory. Near-one-dimensionality is a property of a particular data distribution and time window, not a claim that the network can access only one line forever. Activity coordinates and mode coordinates are reversible representations of the same state. After the fast mode decays, the slow mode dominates the trajectory and produces approximate low dimensionality. The error from discarding a mode is quantified by the square of that mode's coordinate. Persistent input, transients, or a nonlinear curved manifold can invalidate a fixed straight-line approximation. Let \(\alpha +(0)=4\), \(\alpha -(0)=2\), \(\tau _{+}=200 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(\tau _{-}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find both amplitudes and the difference-mode energy fraction after 100 ms. After 100 ms, well over 99.9% of the state energy lies on the common axis, so a one-dimensional approximation is safe. If a constant input \(\beta _{-}=1\) acts at every moment, must \(\alpha _{-}\) approach zero? No. A stable difference mode approaches the nonzero fixed point \(\alpha _{-}* = \beta _{-}/(1+w_{0})\), so the trajectory can remain away from the common axis. Low-dimensional conclusions depend on input structure. Calling a coordinate transform itself dimensionality reduction; true reduction begins only when a coordinate is discarded. Interpreting low dimensionality as activity in only a few neurons instead of coordinated variation of many neurons through a few population patterns.

title: PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors
subtitle: Lecture 19 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA-UPDATE.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA.pdf, p. 4
text: Why must the direction of maximum variance be the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue of the centered covariance? Now suppose W is unknown and we observe only T population vectors \(h_{t}\in \mathbb{R}^N\). First compute the \(\operatorname{mean} \bar{h}\) and define \(\delta h_{t}=h_{t}-\bar{h}\). The covariance \(C=(1/T)\sum _t \delta h_{t}\delta h_{t}^\mathrm{T}\) is an N×N symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix; \(C_{ij}\) describes centered cofluctuation between neurons i and j. For a chosen unit direction v, each sample has scalar projection \(p_{t}=v^\mathrm{T}\delta h_{t}\). The projection variance is \((1/T)\sum  p_{t}^{2}=(1/T)\sum  v^\mathrm{T}\delta h_{t}\delta h_{t}^\mathrm{T}v=v^\mathrm{T}Cv\). Without a constraint on ||v||, scaling v arbitrarily would make the variance arbitrarily large, so require \(v^\mathrm{T}v=1\). Maximize \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv-\lambda (v^\mathrm{T}v-1)\) with a Lagrange multiplier. Differentiating with respect to every component of v gives \(2Cv-2\lambda v=0\), or \(Cv=\lambda v\). The candidate directions are therefore covariance eigenvectors. Along eigenvector \(v_{k}\), projected variance equals \(\lambda _{k}\) because \(v_{k}^\mathrm{T}Cv_{k}=v_{k}^\mathrm{T}(\lambda _{k}v_{k})=\lambda _{k}\). Choosing \(v_{1}\) for the largest eigenvalue gives PC1. The derivation establishes only maximum data variance. A small but reliable task signal or a large measurement artifact can make PC1 poor for decoding, nor is it automatically a causal circuit direction. Modes of W and PCs of C align only under additional conditions. For example, in a linear network driven by isotropic noise at stationarity, with W normal or symmetric, slow dynamical modes often accumulate more variance. Structured input, unequal noise, trial conditions, and nonlinear observations can all rotate the covariance. Similar axes motivate a hypothesis; statistical collinearity does not identify recurrent weights by itself. PCA must be applied to centered activity: \(C=E[\delta h\delta h^\mathrm{T}]\). Under a unit-norm constraint, projected variance is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\). A stationary point satisfies \(Cv=\lambda v\), and the eigenvector with the largest \(\lambda\) is PC1. Maximum variance is not the same as maximum causal or behavioral relevance. Given \(C=[[5,4],[4,5]]\), find both eigenvectors and eigenvalues, then interpret the long axis of the data cloud. The data cloud is elongated along the common axis, where h1 and h2 vary together. Retaining PC1 explains \(9/(9+1)=90\)% of the variance. What is chiefly mixed in if \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]\) is computed without centering? The mean outer-product term \(\bar{h}\) \(\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\) is included, so the leading direction may represent the mean firing pattern rather than trial or temporal fluctuations. Calling covariance eigenvectors recurrent modes. Forgetting to constrain \(||v||=1\), which leaves variance maximization unbounded.

title: Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations
subtitle: Lecture 19 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA-UPDATE.pdf, p. 5 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA.pdf, p. 5
text: When K PCs are retained, exactly what is preserved, and at what step is information lost? Order the covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda _{1}\ge \lambda _{2}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{N}\) with orthonormal eigenvectors v1,...,vN. PC one uses v1. PC two must be orthogonal to v1 and maximize variance in the remaining subspace, so it uses v2. Continuing gives \(V_{K}=[v_{1},\cdots ,vK]\), an N×K matrix. For one centered sample, score vector \(p=V_{K}^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\) has K coordinates. If all N components are retained, V is an orthogonal square matrix and \(h=\bar{h}+VV^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\); the transform is reversible and loses no information. With \(K<N\), reconstruction \(\hat{h}=\bar{h}+V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\) is the sample's orthogonal projection onto the top-K subspace. The discarded residual \(e=(I-V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T})(h-\bar{h})\) is orthogonal to the retained subspace. Mean squared reconstruction error equals the sum of discarded eigenvalues \(\sum _{k>K}\lambda _{k}\). This is why PCA minimizes squared reconstruction error among all K-dimensional linear subspaces. Calling the reconstruction denoised requires an extra assumption: noise primarily occupies low-variance directions and signal occupies high-variance directions. A rare but important movement command on a low-variance axis would be treated as residual by PCA. The practical algorithm has five steps: center across the neuron dimension; compute the N×N covariance or apply SVD to the data matrix; sort eigenpairs; project to obtain scores; and reconstruct or analyze for the task. Training and test data must use the training-set mean and PCs. Recomputing them separately and then comparing coordinates can turn a basis change into an apparent condition difference. \(V_{K}\) is N×K, scores are K×1, and reconstruction returns to N×1 neuron space. A complete orthogonal basis transform is lossless; dimensions are discarded only by projection with \(K<N\). PCA residual error equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues. 'Denoising' assumes high-variance signal and low-variance noise; the name of the algorithm does not establish that assumption. Let \(\operatorname{mean}=0\), with PCs equal to coordinate axes \(v_{1}=(1,0,0)\), \(v_{2}=(0,1,0)\), \(v_{3}=(0,0,1)\), and sample \(h=(4,2,1)\). Retain \(K=2\). Top-2 reconstruction keeps the first two coordinates and discards the third component. Whether this is denoising depends on whether the third axis is predominantly noise. Why does \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I\) not imply \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}=I\)? When \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) is not square. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}\) is the identity in K-space, while \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space projector onto a K-dimensional subspace. Fitting PCA separately in each condition and comparing PC1 coordinates directly, despite possible rotation of the axes. Assuming that a smoother reconstruction means the discarded activity was noise, without behavioral or held-out validation.

title: New page: eigenvalue cliff, cumulative variance, and dimensionality selection
subtitle: Lecture 19 · Lecture19-PopulationActivity-PCA-UPDATE.pdf, p. 6
text: How should K be selected from the eigenvalue spectrum without treating a convenient cutoff as a natural constant? Update page 6 is a substantive addition absent from the earlier notes. A scree plot graphs sorted \(\lambda _{k}\) against component index k. If the first few eigenvalues are large and the curve then enters a flat tail, the transition is called an eigenvalue cliff or elbow. Directions before the cliff capture stronger coordinated variation; each direction after it contributes little additional variance. Real spectra often decline continuously, however, so different readers may place the elbow differently. Cumulative variance explained \(F(K)=\sum _{k=1}^K\lambda _{k}/\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\) increases monotonically from \(F(0)=0\) to \(F(N)=1\). The handwritten expression at the bottom of page 6 omits the total-variance denominator and writes the summand as \(\lambda _{i}\). The cumulative definition requires numerator \(\sum _{j=1}^K\lambda _{j}\) divided by \(\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\), which is used throughout this module. Thresholds of 80%, 90%, or 95% give reproducible rules but need not be optimal for a particular scientific question. Measurement noise can raise the tail, condition means can create large PCs, and trial averaging can change the spectrum. Report preprocessing and the selection criterion together with K. A stronger dimensionality choice uses held-out data. Fit PCs on training trials and compare reconstruction error on test trials, or evaluate behavioral decoding, likelihood, or downstream model performance as K changes. A low-variance component may still deserve retention if it materially improves held-out behavior prediction. PCA dimensionality depends on both the data and the purpose of the analysis. Finally separate three meanings of dimension. The number of slow dynamical modes of W follows from model stability; PCA dimension follows from the observed covariance spectrum; task dimension follows from behaviorally relevant variables. Carefully designed experiments can relate them, but no general identity equates them. Pages 1-5 of the earlier notes and the first five update pages are substantively the same, so this module cites only the newly added page 6 rather than inventing a counterpart in the earlier version. A scree-plot elbow is a heuristic and usually has no unique location. Cumulative variance \(F(K)\) is the partial sum of sorted eigenvalues divided by their total sum. A dimensionality choice should report preprocessing, threshold, and held-out criterion. PCA dimension, dynamical dimension, and task dimension should not be used interchangeably. The eigenvalues are \([9,3,1,1]\). Find the smallest K under cumulative-variance thresholds of 80% and 95%. The same data give \(K=2\) or \(K=4\) solely because the threshold changes. The cutoff is an analysis decision and must be reported explicitly. Why does '95% variance explained' not guarantee retention of 95% of behavioral information? Variance measures activity amplitude, whereas behavioral information depends on condition distributions and the decoder. A low-variance direction may reliably distinguish choices, so the two percentages are not generally equivalent. Treating a hand-drawn elbow as the one true neural dimensionality. Reporting only a cumulative-variance threshold while omitting centering, trial averaging, noise treatment, and held-out validation.

title: Lecture 20: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations
subtitle: Is the rhythm cell-intrinsic or network-generated, and how do linear complex modes, Morris–Lecar fast–slow geometry, and half-center inhibition each produce oscillatory behavior?
text: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations Is the rhythm cell-intrinsic or network-generated, and how do linear complex modes, Morris–Lecar fast–slow geometry, and half-center inhibition each produce oscillatory behavior? pacemaker vs follower → half-center → complex eigenvalues → Morris–Lecar → nullclines/limit cycle → release vs escape Use synaptic-block logic to distinguish a cell-intrinsic pacemaker, a follower, and a network-generated half-center rhythm, while stating the limits of this experimental diagnosis. Solve for the complex eigenvalues of a two-neuron rotation matrix, using the real and imaginary parts to assess envelope stability and oscillation frequency, respectively. Explain every term in the Morris–Lecar voltage and recovery equations, then reconstruct the relaxation cycle from nullclines, fixed points, and fast–slow separation. Distinguish intrinsic release from intrinsic escape in a reciprocally inhibitory half-center, identifying whose intrinsic transition triggers each phase switch. Transfer the phase-plane geometry of a conductance model to a firing-rate model with adaptation while respecting the difference in model level. Whether rhythm persists after synaptic block can distinguish candidate intrinsic-pacemaker and network-generated mechanisms. Complex eigenvalues in a linear two-neuron system produce only damped or growing oscillatory components; a stable autonomous limit cycle requires nonlinearity. Fast voltage and slow recovery nullclines in Morris–Lecar generate a relaxation oscillation, while a mutually inhibitory half-center can alternate through intrinsic release or escape. Calling every rhythmic activity pattern a CPG. Assuming complex eigenvalues automatically imply sustained oscillation. Ignoring the real part of the full eigenvalue. Treating a nullcline as a trajectory. Assuming a fixed point is stable merely because a nullcline intersection exists. Distinguishing release from escape by superficial firing order rather than the intrinsic transition that triggers the switch. Excluding sensory feedback from real locomotor rhythms. Avoid classifying all rhythmic activity as a CPG, and do not conflate a damped linear oscillation with an autonomous nonlinear oscillator. complex mode \(\lambda  = a \pm  ib\) a controls the envelope; b controls frequency Euler decomposition e(a+ib)t = eat (cos bt + i sin bt) complex representation two-dimensional conductance model \(\dot{V} = F (V, N )\), \(\dot{N} = G(V, N )\) fast–slow variables V-nullcline \(F (V, N ) = 0\) \(dV/dt=0\) N-nullcline \(G(V, N ) = 0\) \(dN/dt=0\) sharp synaptic-threshold approximation \(S_{\infty } (V ) = H(V - VT )\) idealized switch central pattern generator, CPG A neural circuit that can generate a rhythmic motor pattern without periodic sensory drive. pacemaker neuron A neuron that oscillates spontaneously through intrinsic dynamics. half-center oscillator A network oscillator in which two mutually inhibitory units alternate activity. complex eigenvalue An eigenvalue that encodes both an exponential envelope and oscillatory phase. Morris-Lecar model A reduced, conductance-based neuron model with two variables. phase plane The trajectories and nullclines in a two-dimensional state space. relaxation oscillation A limit cycle that alternates slow drift with fast jumps. intrinsic release Removal of inhibition when the active neuron terminates its activity. intrinsic escape A transition in which the inhibited neuron recovers first and escapes inhibition. limit cycle A closed periodic orbit that attracts nearby trajectories. A neuron's linear mode has eigenvalue -2+6i s^-1. Does its amplitude grow or decay over time? Read the real part first to determine the envelope and the imaginary part second to determine oscillation. If you equated a complex eigenvalue with a sustained rhythm, review linear complex modes. The amplitude decays as \(e^{-2t}\); 6 rad/s specifies only the angular frequency of rotation. What does an intersection of the V-nullcline and N-nullcline represent? Stability still depends on the nearby vector field; an intersection alone does not tell you whether the point is stable, a saddle, or unstable. It simultaneously satisfies \(dV/dt=0\) and \(dN/dt=0\), so it is a fixed point of the two-dimensional system. After synapses are blocked, one cell continues at approximately its original rhythm. Which candidate mechanism does this most directly support? This is supporting evidence, not a logical proof; the diagnosis assumes a complete block that does not alter intrinsic currents. It supports a cell-intrinsic pacemaker mechanism in that cell, although drug side effects and residual coupling must still be controlled. What is the central criterion for distinguishing release from escape? Do not look only at which cell spikes first. Track the intrinsic variable and nullcline crossing that trigger the transition. Ask whether the active cell stops and lifts inhibition, or the inhibited cell recovers intrinsically, crosses a threshold, and escapes inhibition. If both cells stop alternating after the block but continue to oscillate at different frequencies, is this a purely network-generated rhythm? No. Coordinated alternation depends on network coupling, but each cell retains intrinsic oscillatory capacity; the full mechanism is coupled intrinsic oscillators. This is the distinction tested in Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center. Worked example — Diagnose a candidate network from block results: In the intact preparation, cells A/B alternate at 2 Hz. After the block, A still oscillates at 1.8 Hz and B fires constantly. Give the minimal mechanism and the next control. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: In the intact preparation, cells A/B alternate at 2 Hz. After the block, A still oscillates at 1.8 Hz and B fires constantly. Give the minimal mechanism and the next control. Because A's rhythm is approximately preserved, first classify A as an intrinsic-pacemaker candidate. B loses its modulation, consistent with a follower candidate. The intact alternation could arise from periodic drive from A to B or from more complex inhibition. Next inject periodic current into B to verify that it can follow, measure synaptic current to confirm a complete block, and check whether the drug altered A's waveform. 1.8 Hz is close to but not identical to 2 Hz, reasonably suggesting that removing coupling changed the pacemaker frequency slightly rather than requiring exact equality. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center”? Persistence of intrinsic rhythm after a block supports a pacemaker; loss of alternation supports network dependence. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center”? A synaptic-block result requires checks for block completeness and side effects on intrinsic currents. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Persistence of intrinsic rhythm after a block supports a pacemaker; loss of alternation supports network dependence. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Compare mechanistic hypotheses with intervention outcomes”? Measure frequency in Hz and period in s, with \(f=1/T\); when comparing after a block, use a sufficiently long recording window. If both cells combine intrinsic oscillation with reciprocal inhibition, the block reveals a mixed mechanism rather than forcing the system into one category. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How does persistence or loss of rhythm after synaptic block narrow the mechanisms, and why is it not sufficient proof by itself? The source pages first distinguish two origins. A cell-intrinsic pacemaker continues to generate a rhythm from its own voltage-gated currents even without periodic synaptic input; a follower does not oscillate on its own and simply tracks synaptic drive from a pacemaker. The second origin is a network-generated rhythm: individual cells may remain tonic or silent in isolation, but reciprocal inhibition makes the pair alternate activity as a half-center oscillator. Respiration and alternating muscles during walking are the functional examples used in the course. Synaptic block is an intervention, not a labeling exercise. If neuron 1 retains its rhythm after the block while neuron 2 becomes tonic or silent, the result is consistent with 1 as pacemaker and 2 as follower. If the pair alternates naturally but both lose rhythmicity under the block, the result supports a network-generated candidate. The key observation is each cell's time series in intact and blocked conditions, not a comparison of average frequency across different animals. What happens if the full eigenvalues are \(0.2\pm 5i s^{-1}\)? The trajectory rotates while its envelope grows as \(e^{0.2t}\), producing an outward spiral. The linear model is unstable; whether a limit cycle subsequently forms depends on nonlinear saturation. This is the distinction tested in Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system. Worked example — Read the waveform from the full eigenvalue: Given \(\tau =0.2 \mathrm{s}\) and \(w_{0}=4\), find the envelope time constant, angular frequency, frequency in Hz, and amplitude fraction after one period. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(\tau =0.2 \mathrm{s}\) and \(w_{0}=4\), find the envelope time constant, angular frequency, frequency in Hz, and amplitude fraction after one period. The full eigenvalues are \((-1\pm 4i)/0.2=-5\pm 20i s^{-1}\). The envelope time constant is \(1/5=0.2 \mathrm{s}\); \(f=20/(2\pi )\approx 3.18 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the period is ≈0.314 s. After one period, the amplitude fraction is \(e^{-0.314/0.2}=e^{-1.57}\approx 0.208\). The period comes from the imaginary part and the envelope from the real part; using \(|\lambda |\) for both gives inconsistent results. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system”? The full-system eigenvalues are \((-1\pm iw0)/\tau\); the ±iw0 eigenvalues of W alone are insufficient. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system”? The real part determines the envelope, and the imaginary part determines angular frequency. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The real part determines the envelope, and the imaginary part determines angular frequency. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Solve the complex modes and recover a real oscillation”? \(\omega\) has units rad/s and f has units Hz; the exponent in \(e^{-t/\tau }\) must be dimensionless. When \(w_{0}=0\), \(\omega =0\) and the system only decays exponentially without oscillating; as \(\tau \to \infty\), both decay and rotation slow in this model. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is a nullcline not the neuron's actual trajectory? A nullcline is only the set of points where one derivative is instantaneously zero. The other variable usually continues to change, so the state crosses or moves nearby; only an intersection of both nullclines can remain stationary. This is the distinction tested in Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points. Worked example — Use signs to determine motion at a phase-plane point: At a point above the V-nullcline, substitution gives \(dV/dt<0\); the same point lies below the N-nullcline. Determine its initial direction of motion. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At a point above the V-nullcline, substitution gives \(dV/dt<0\); the same point lies below the N-nullcline. Determine its initial direction of motion. \(dV/dt<0\) means that V moves leftward. Below the N-nullcline, \(N<N_{\infty }(V)\), so \(dN/dt>0\) and N moves upward. The combined vector points up and left. If the trajectory crosses a nullcline at the next moment, reassess the signs. Only the corresponding derivative is zero on a nullcline. Merely being 'above the V-nullcline' does not establish the sign of dV; the problem supplies the test-point sign. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points”? The V equation balances leak, Ca, K, and external currents. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points”? The V-nullcline satisfies \(dV/dt=0\); the N-nullcline satisfies \(N=N_{\infty }(V)\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion.
