title: Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center
subtitle: Lecture 20 · Lecture20-CentralPatternGenerators.pdf, p. 1
text: How does persistence or loss of rhythm after synaptic block narrow the mechanisms, and why is it not sufficient proof by itself? The source pages first distinguish two origins. A cell-intrinsic pacemaker continues to generate a rhythm from its own voltage-gated currents even without periodic synaptic input; a follower does not oscillate on its own and simply tracks synaptic drive from a pacemaker. The second origin is a network-generated rhythm: individual cells may remain tonic or silent in isolation, but reciprocal inhibition makes the pair alternate activity as a half-center oscillator. Respiration and alternating muscles during walking are the functional examples used in the course. Synaptic block is an intervention, not a labeling exercise. If neuron 1 retains its rhythm after the block while neuron 2 becomes tonic or silent, the result is consistent with 1 as pacemaker and 2 as follower. If the pair alternates naturally but both lose rhythmicity under the block, the result supports a network-generated candidate. The key observation is each cell's time series in intact and blocked conditions, not a comparison of average frequency across different animals. The experiment cannot eliminate every alternative explanation. A blocker may alter intrinsic conductances, the block may be incomplete, electrical coupling may remain, and sensory feedback may contribute in an intact preparation. A stronger design records membrane potential, verifies that synaptic current disappears, uses washout or a second blocking method, and tests whether current injection into an isolated cell can re-evoke the rhythm. State that the result supports a candidate mechanism, not that it proves a unique one. A CPG is a central neural circuit capable of organizing patterned motor output without an external command at the same periodicity. The definition does not require real behavior to be independent of sensory feedback: sensory input can reset phase, adjust speed, or stabilize gait. Calling all rhythmic neural activity a CPG confuses an oscillator with sensory entrainment and downstream follower responses. Persistence of intrinsic rhythm after a block supports a pacemaker; loss of alternation supports network dependence. A synaptic-block result requires checks for block completeness and side effects on intrinsic currents. The basic half-center motif is reciprocal inhibition with alternating phases. A CPG can be modulated by sensory feedback; it does not imply open-loop behavior. In the intact preparation, cells A/B alternate at 2 Hz. After the block, A still oscillates at 1.8 Hz and B fires constantly. Give the minimal mechanism and the next control. The minimal account is that A supplies intrinsic rhythmic drive and B follows it; this does not yet exclude feedback contributions from both A/B. If both cells stop alternating after the block but continue to oscillate at different frequencies, is this a purely network-generated rhythm? No. Coordinated alternation depends on network coupling, but each cell retains intrinsic oscillatory capacity; the full mechanism is coupled intrinsic oscillators. Interpreting disappearance of the rhythm after a block as cell death without testing excitability. Describing a CPG as a fully autonomous system unaffected by sensory feedback.

title: Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system
subtitle: Lecture 20 · Lecture20-CentralPatternGenerators.pdf, p. 2
text: Why does an imaginary eigenvalue component create back-and-forth variation, while intrinsic leak makes that variation decay? The source page uses \(W=[[0,-w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\), with excitation in one coupling direction and inhibition in the other, so W formally resembles a two-dimensional rotation generator. The full rate equation remains \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), so continuous-time stability is set not by the ±iw0 eigenvalues of W alone, but by the eigenvalues \((-1\pm iw0)/\tau\) of \(A=(-I+W)/\tau\). Their real part is fixed at \(-1/\tau\), so the unforced envelope must decay. The characteristic polynomial \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}+w_{0}^{2}=0\) gives λ_W=±i|w0|. A complex-mode solution contains \(e^{(-1\pm iw0)t/\tau }=e^{-t/\tau }[\cos(|w_{0}|t/\tau )\pm i \sin(|w_{0}|t/\tau )]\). Combining the conjugate pair yields real sine–cosine trajectories for h1 and h2. The angular frequency is \(\omega =|w_{0}|/\tau  \mathrm{rad}/s\), and the ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega /(2\pi )\). In the phase plane, the trajectory rotates about the fixed point while its radius contracts as \(e^{-t/\tau }\), producing an inward spiral. A positive full real part instead produces an expanding outward spiral. With a real part exactly equal to zero, a linear system has neutrally stable closed orbits but no amplitude selection, so noise makes the radius drift. A stable autonomous limit cycle generally requires a nonlinearity that expands small amplitudes and contracts large ones. Thus, having complex eigenvalues is not equivalent to having a sustained CPG rhythm. A complex pair means that the transient response to a perturbation may oscillate. Long-term rhythm additionally depends on the real part, nonlinear saturation, external drive, and noise. The notes turn next to Morris–Lecar precisely to introduce fast–slow geometry capable of producing a stable nonlinear cycle. The full-system eigenvalues are \((-1\pm iw0)/\tau\); the ±iw0 eigenvalues of W alone are insufficient. The real part determines the envelope, and the imaginary part determines angular frequency. A negative real part produces an inward spiral and damped oscillation. A stable limit cycle requires amplitude regulation; complex eigenvalues alone are not enough. Given \(\tau =0.2 \mathrm{s}\) and \(w_{0}=4\), find the envelope time constant, angular frequency, frequency in Hz, and amplitude fraction after one period. After one revolution the trajectory retains only about 20.8% of its initial amplitude, so this is a strongly damped transient, not a sustained oscillator. What happens if the full eigenvalues are \(0.2\pm 5i s^{-1}\)? The trajectory rotates while its envelope grows as \(e^{0.2t}\), producing an outward spiral. The linear model is unstable; whether a limit cycle subsequently forms depends on nonlinear saturation. Writing rad/s directly as Hz and forgetting to divide by \(2\pi\). Reporting only the imaginary part while ignoring the -h leak in the full equation.

title: Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points
subtitle: Lecture 20 · Lecture20-CentralPatternGenerators.pdf, p. 3
text: How do ionic-current equations generate a two-dimensional phase plane, and how can that plane identify resting and oscillatory candidates? Morris–Lecar compresses conductance dynamics into two state variables, V and N. Its voltage equation is C dV/dt=-gL(V-EL)-gCa M∞(V)(V-ECa)-gK \(N(V-E_{K})+I_{e}\). Each \(g(V-E)\) is conductance times driving force; the preceding minus signs follow the outward-current convention. \(M_{\infty }(V)\) assumes fast Ca activation and therefore takes its voltage-dependent steady-state value immediately, whereas N follows \(N_{\infty }(V)\) on a slower time scale. The recovery equation can be written \(\tau N dN/dt=N_{\infty }(V)-N\). When \(N<N_{\infty }\), \(dN/dt>0\) and K activation increases; when \(N>N_{\infty }\), it decreases. The N-nullcline is therefore the \(\operatorname{sigmoid} N=N_{\infty }(V)\). The V-nullcline is obtained by setting net membrane current to zero and is often cubic-like or N-shaped. Their intersection makes both derivatives zero and is a candidate equilibrium. Read a phase plane by determining signs in each region. Whether \(dV/dt\) is positive on a given side of the V-nullcline must be checked with a test point, not guessed from the curve's appearance. Below the N-nullcline, usually \(N<N_{\infty }\) and arrows point upward; above it, arrows point downward. A fixed point is stable if nearby arrows converge, a saddle if one direction converges and another diverges, and unstable if the flow departs overall. Fast–slow separation comes from the difference between the voltage time scale C/g and \(\tau N\). When V is fast, a trajectory quickly approaches an attracting branch of the V-nullcline, then N slowly carries it along that branch. If the fixed point lies in an unstable middle region, the state may not settle and instead jump between the two stable branches, forming a relaxation oscillation. The particular bifurcation depends on parameters; a hand-drawn nullcline diagram conveys mechanism, not universal numerical values. The V equation balances leak, Ca, K, and external currents. The V-nullcline satisfies \(dV/dt=0\); the N-nullcline satisfies \(N=N_{\infty }(V)\). Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability still requires the vector field. Fast voltage and slow recovery permit slow motion along a branch and a fast jump at a fold. At a point above the V-nullcline, substitution gives \(dV/dt<0\); the same point lies below the N-nullcline. Determine its initial direction of motion. The instantaneous trajectory points up and left; it does not run along either nullcline. Why is a nullcline not the neuron's actual trajectory? A nullcline is only the set of points where one derivative is instantaneously zero. The other variable usually continues to change, so the state crosses or moves nearby; only an intersection of both nullclines can remain stationary. Treating a reversal potential as a fixed current and ignoring the driving force V-E. Assigning arrows from the cubic curve's shape alone instead of checking regional signs in the equations.

title: Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center
subtitle: Lecture 20 · Lecture20-CentralPatternGenerators.pdf, p. 4
text: How does slow recovery carry the state to a fold, and how does reciprocal inhibition organize this intrinsic geometry into alternating output? When the fixed point is unstable and the V-nullcline has two attracting outer branches, a trajectory can cycle through four stages. On the low-V branch, V rapidly approaches the branch while N slowly decreases. At the lower fold, no nearby stable voltage solution remains, so V jumps rapidly to the high branch. Along the high branch, N slowly rises and strengthens hyperpolarizing K current. At the upper fold, V jumps rapidly back to the low branch. Repeating this sequence creates an autonomous relaxation oscillation. Slow portions of the voltage trace correspond to motion along phase-plane branches; steep rises and falls correspond to fast jumps. The period is governed mainly by slow N evolution, whereas the duration of spike-like transitions is governed by fast V dynamics. Changing Ie or the conductances moves the nullclines and can place the fixed point on a stable branch, terminating the cycle. An oscillator is therefore a parameter-dependent attractor, not a single waveform. A half-center couples two Morris–Lecar cells through mutual inhibition. For cell i, write the synaptic current as \(-gS_{\infty }(V_{j})(V_{i}-Es)\), with a relatively negative Es. When presynaptic cell j is in the high state, \(S_{\infty }\approx 1\) and pushes i's V-nullcline into its inhibited position. When j is low, \(S_{\infty }\approx 0\) and i regains its free nullcline. Alternation follows because each change in synaptic state rearranges the partner's geometry. Even if the fixed point of each isolated cell is stable, mutual inhibition plus recovery can make the pair oscillate; conversely, not every mutually inhibitory pair oscillates. The system needs an intrinsic variable that evolves slowly in active and inhibited phases, a suitable synaptic threshold, and the right ordering of transitions. A sensory pulse can push one cell across a separatrix and reset phase without generating the rhythm itself. A relaxation cycle has four stages: slow motion on the low branch, an upward jump, slow motion on the high branch, and a downward jump. Slow recovery largely determines period; fast jumps determine the waveform edges. An active presynaptic cell moves the partner's effective V-nullcline through inhibitory current. A half-center rhythm requires cooperation between intrinsic recovery and synaptic switching. Keep the nullcline shapes fixed and increase \(\tau N\) from 100 ms to 300 ms. Predict the main changes in period and fast-jump duration. Frequency should decrease and waveform plateaus should lengthen, with comparatively small changes in the edge of each fast jump. Why can two mutually inhibitory cells generate a network rhythm even when neither oscillates in isolation? Inhibition switches each partner's effective nullcline between active and inactive conditions. Slow recovery makes the cells reach their transitions in turn, so coupling creates periodic state switching. Treating the fast jump as motion along a nullcline; the state leaves the slow manifold during a jump. Assuming mutual inhibition alone is sufficient without checking the recovery variable and threshold ordering.

title: Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?
subtitle: Lecture 20 · Lecture20-CentralPatternGenerators.pdf, p. 5
text: When two cells alternate firing, how can we tell whether the active cell lets go or the inhibited cell escapes? The source page simplifies the synapse with a sharp threshold: \(S_{\infty }(V)=0\) when \(V<VT\) and 1 when \(V>VT\). While the active cell's V exceeds VT, it inhibits its partner; once V falls below VT, inhibition shuts off rapidly. A free neuron follows the \(F(V,N)=0\) nullcline, whereas an inhibited neuron follows a shifted nullcline that includes synaptic current. Switching between these two geometries makes the identity of the first threshold-crosser an observable mechanistic criterion. In a release mechanism, N rises while the active cell occupies the upper branch until that cell can no longer sustain high V. It jumps first to the low branch and falls below VT, closing the synapse; only then is the partner released to jump into its own high state. The trigger is intrinsic adaptation in the active cell. Clamping its recovery variable should delay or prevent the phase switch. In an escape mechanism, N in the inhibited cell gradually recovers during the low state. Eventually that cell crosses the fold or separatrix of the inhibited nullcline and jumps high even while inhibition remains on. Its rise then inhibits the formerly active cell. The trigger is intrinsic recovery in the inhibited cell, so changing that recovery speed should strongly alter phase duration. Real circuits can occupy a mixed regime: the active cell may be nearing release while its partner is nearing escape, leaving noise or sensory input to decide which occurs first. Experimentally, track both cells' voltage and a proxy for recovery before the transition, and use brief pulses to push the active cell down or the inhibited cell up. An alternating spike raster alone does not reveal causal order. A sharp \(S_{\infty }\) threshold approximates the synapse as an on/off switch. Release is triggered by intrinsic termination of the active cell. Escape is triggered when intrinsic recovery in the inhibited cell crosses a boundary. In mixed regimes, noise can make both mechanisms contribute to phase timing. A is active. At \(t=500 \mathrm{ms}\), B suddenly depolarizes while inhibition remains strong; at \(t=507 \mathrm{ms}\), A is inhibited; at \(t=512 \mathrm{ms}\), A falls below VT. Which mechanism dominates? The event order supports intrinsic escape rather than release by the active cell. If the active cell falls below VT and its partner jumps 20 ms later, does that delay refute release? No. Release requires only that removal of inhibition be the upstream trigger. The partner still takes finite time to leave its low state according to its own membrane and recovery dynamics. Naming the mechanism solely from which cell spikes first, without measuring synaptic state. Treating release and escape as mutually exclusive and ignoring mixed regimes and stochastic switching.

title: From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center
subtitle: Lecture 20 · Lecture20-CentralPatternGenerators.pdf, p. 6
text: After removing ion-channel detail, what is the smallest set of rate-level variables that preserves half-center geometry? Page 6 gives only the direction of the extension: replace V with firing rate h and N with an adaptation or recovery variable a while retaining similar nullcline geometry. A minimal pair can be written \(\tau _{h} dh_{i}/dt=-h_{i}+F(I_{i}-w h_{j}-a_{i})\), \(\tau a da_{i}/dt=-a_{i}+b h_{i}\). F is a thresholding, saturating nonlinearity; \(w>0\) denotes reciprocal inhibition; and b controls how activity accumulates adaptation. While cell i is active, high \(h_{i}\) slowly raises \(a_{i}\). Increasing adaptation lowers effective drive until the active rate falls. Inhibition of the partner then weakens, allowing it to rise and subsequently inhibit the original cell. This is release-like switching. If \(a_{j}\) falls during the inhibited cell's low-activity phase, restoring its effective excitability until it crosses threshold first, switching is escape-like. The rate model preserves state-dependent feedback, slow recovery, and threshold geometry; it does not preserve particular Ca/K currents, spike waveforms, or reversal potentials. It is suited to population rhythm, phase relations, and parameter effects, but one rate variable cannot establish a particular ionic mechanism. Parameters also change meaning across levels: \(\tau _{h}\) is a rate-response time, not a time constant obtained directly from membrane capacitance. Validate the model by plotting \(h_{i}-a_{i}\) nullclines, simulating both rates, varying w, b, and \(\tau a\), and testing phase resetting. If F is fully linear and lacks saturation, strong feedback may produce only decay or divergence. Nonlinearity limits amplitude and permits a stable cycle. A rate-level fit can show compatibility with a computational mechanism but cannot uniquely identify cellular conductances. A rate–adaptation model needs at least fast activity, slow recovery, reciprocal inhibition, and a nonlinearity. Accumulating adaptation can trigger release; recovery during low activity can support escape. A rate variable and a voltage or gating variable are not the same biological quantity. Test the model through predictions of phase, frequency, resetting, and perturbations. The model initially has \(\tau _{h}=20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\tau a=400 \mathrm{ms}\). Double only \(\tau a\) to 800 ms, keeping all else fixed and assuming the cycle persists. Predict frequency and phase relation. Alternation should persist with a longer period and lower frequency. The exact ratio requires numerical simulation because the switching threshold and nonlinear F also matter. Why are two linear rate variables h1 and h2 usually insufficient for a stable half-center limit cycle? A linear system can only decay, rotate neutrally, or grow; it lacks a slow state and amplitude regulation. Adaptation or recovery plus nonlinear F supplies phase switching and a bounded cycle. Naming a in the rate model as a particular K channel without additional evidence. Inferring a half-center from one rate trace without verifying antiphase activity and perturbation responses in the partner.

title: Lecture 21: Oculomotor Integrator, Degeneracy, and Sloppy Models
subtitle: How does a recurrent network integrate an eye-velocity command into persistent position, why can many parameter combinations implement the same function, and how does the Hessian reveal stiff and sloppy directions?

title: Eye-velocity integration, persistent position, and the bilateral circuit
subtitle: Lecture 21 · Lecture21-OculomotorIntegrator.pdf, p. 1
text: How does a brief saccade command become an eye-position code that persists after the command disappears? Moving the eye requires phasic motor drive to generate velocity and tonic drive to oppose orbital restoring forces and hold the new position. The course abstracts the distributed brainstem and cerebellar network as a neural integrator: its input is the eye-velocity command \(v(t)\), and its output state approximates \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). Ideally, x retains its latest value when v returns to zero; if the network leaks, position slowly drifts back toward center. The source diagram contains excitatory populations EL and ER and inhibitory populations IL and IR in the left and right hemispheres. Their position-tuning curves have opposite directions: at rightward positions, firing rises in one population and falls in the other. Mutual excitation can prolong the memory mode, while crossed inhibition organizes the left–right push–pull pattern into a signed coordinate. This is a functional architecture; arrows alone do not reveal the strength of each real synapse. Linear tuning lets a weighted difference of population rates encode eye position. If a right-preferring neuron has \(hR\approx b+kx\) and a left-preferring one \(hL\approx b-kx\), then \(hR-hL\approx 2kx\), while the common baseline \(hR+hL\approx 2b\). The integrator can store signed position in a difference-like mode while keeping the common mode stable. Real neurons have thresholds, saturation, and heterogeneity, so these linear relations hold only over an operating range. Test the integrator by asking whether firing persists after a velocity pulse, whether the persistent level scales with the pulse integral, and how a network perturbation changes the drift time constant. Position-tuning correlations alone cannot separate sensory eye-position feedback from recurrent memory; comparisons in darkness, feedback perturbations, or circuit interventions are needed. The time integral of velocity gives position change. Recurrent positive feedback sustains a persistent state after the command ends. Opponent tuning in left and right populations can encode signed eye position. Position-tuning correlations alone do not prove recurrent integration. Start at \(x=0 \mathrm{deg}\). Move right at 30 deg/s for 0.08 s, then left at -20 deg/s for 0.05 s. Ignoring leak, find the final position. After the second command ends, an ideal integrator should hold +1.4 deg rather than return to zero. If position returns to center after the velocity command with a time constant of 5 s, is this still an integrator? It is a leaky rather than perfect integrator. Behavior may appear persistent for periods shorter than 5 s, but a long delay reveals measurable drift. Conflating velocity tuning and position tuning as the same population signal. Treating the bilateral arrows in the schematic as the one measured connectomic implementation.

title: General \(2\times 2\) weights, eigenvalue one, and a compensating family
subtitle: Lecture 21 · Lecture21-OculomotorIntegrator.pdf, p. 2
text: Why does retaining one mode impose only one weight constraint, allowing many different circuits to implement the same integration? Let \(W=[[W_{11},W_{12}],[W_{21},W_{22}]]\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda ^{2}-(W_{11}+W_{22})\lambda +(W_{11}W_{22}-W_{12}W_{21})=0\), and the quadratic formula gives both eigenvalues. For \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh\), perfect integration requires an eigenvalue of W equal to 1 because that mode's coefficient \(-(1-\lambda )\) is exactly zero. Substituting \(\lambda =1\) directly is more robust than manipulating the square root and gives \(\det(I-W)=0\). Expanding gives \(\det(I-W)=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})-W_{12}W_{21}=0\). If \(W_{12}\ne 0\), solve \(W_{21}=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})/W_{12}\). Once three weights are chosen, the fourth compensates; increasing a self-weight can be offset by changing cross-coupling while preserving \(\lambda =1\). This is a many-to-one functional mapping: different parameter points share the same integrator eigenvalue. Do not hide special cases with division. When \(W_{12}=0\), the formula is invalid and the condition becomes \((1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})=0\), so at least one self-weight equals 1. The other eigenvalue must also be checked. Since the sum of the eigenvalues is \(\operatorname{trace}(W)\), if \(\lambda _{1}=1\) then \(\lambda _{2}=W_{11}+W_{22}-1\). Transverse stability of the continuous rate equation requires \(\lambda _{2}<1\). If \(\lambda _{2}\) is also very close to 1, the network acquires another slow mode and may fail to encode position uniquely. Algebraic satisfaction does not guarantee biological feasibility. Excitatory and inhibitory cell types constrain weight signs, conductance and firing ranges constrain magnitudes, noise makes exact \(\lambda =1\) difficult to maintain, and nonlinear saturation changes large-state dynamics. Study the region of parameter space that gives adequate integration and its robustness, rather than treating a one-parameter relation as a complete circuit solution. A perfect linear integrator satisfies \(\det(I-W)=0\). When \(W_{12}\ne 0\), \(W_{21}=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})/W_{12}\). The other eigenvalue must be stable; \(\lambda _{2}=\operatorname{trace}(W)-1\). Parameter compensation is not measurement noise and does not guarantee biophysical feasibility. Let \(W_{11}=0.8\), \(W_{22}=0.7\), and \(W_{12}=0.2\). Find W21 so that one mode is a perfect integrator, then check the other mode. \(W=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]]\) has eigenvalues 1 and 0.5, giving one memory mode and one stable transverse mode. What happens if the same constraint gives \(\lambda _{2}=1.1\)? The memory mode still has \(\lambda =1\), but the transverse mode's full growth rate is \((1.1-1)/\tau >0\). Any small error grows, so the full network is not a stable, usable integrator. Replacing the general matrix with the symmetric two-neuron special case and missing asymmetric compensation. Checking \(\det(I-W)=0\) without checking \(\lambda _{2}\), input projection, and readout.

title: Biological variability and reparameterizing a nonlinear circuit fit
subtitle: Lecture 21 · Lecture21-OculomotorIntegrator.pdf, p. 3
text: Once nonlinear F–I and synaptic transfer functions are fixed, how can a model containing them become linear in its fitted weights? Following work by Goldman, Marder, and others, the source page emphasizes that different parameter settings can produce similar voltage or behavioral dynamics; variability across animals need not destroy function. Approximately linear position tuning in the oculomotor integrator lets researchers measure rates at several eye positions and ask which sets of synaptic weights reproduce those states. This variability concerns model or individual parameters, not recording noise. For postsynaptic neuron i, measure the target rate \(h_{i}(p\mu )\) at position \(p\mu\) and use the measured inverse F–I curve to convert it into the required net current \(Y_{i}\mu =F_{i}^{-1}(h_{i}(p\mu ))\). For each presynaptic neuron j, pass its rate through a fixed synaptic nonlinearity \(S_{E}\) or \(S_{I}\) to obtain feature \(X_{j}\mu\). Add a row of constant 1 values for bias current. The complicated biophysics is thereby precomputed into Y and X. With the nonlinear functions fixed, the prediction is \(\hat{Y}_{i\mu }=\sum _j W_{ij} X_{j}\mu\), linear in the unknown weights Wij and bias. Each output neuron i can fit one row of weights independently. If M sample positions are columns, X has shape D×M, Y is N×M, W is N×D, and \(\hat{Y}=WX\) is dimensionally consistent. State this orientation explicitly, because placing samples in rows yields a transposed formula. The boundary of this reparameterization matters. If the inverse F–I estimate is wrong, the synaptic threshold is fitted jointly, features are highly correlated, or noise is heteroscedastic, simple OLS gives unreliable uncertainty. Different nonlinear assumptions can yield different weight ensembles that fit the rates equally well. 'Linearized fitting' is a conditional computational convenience, not a claim that the native circuit lacks nonlinearities. First use \(F_{i}^{-1}\) to convert each target rate into required current. Once synaptic nonlinearities are fixed, their outputs become design-matrix features. With samples as columns, \(Y=N\times M\), \(X=D\times M\), and \(W=N\times D\). Linear in the weights does not mean that the entire biological model is linear. At two positions, an output has features \(x_{1}=[1,2]\) and \(x_{2}=[3,1]\), with an additional bias 1 at both. The weights are \([w_{1},w_{2},b]=[0.5,-1,2]\). Find both predictions. The target-current predictions at the two positions are 0.5 and 2.5; matrix and term-by-term calculations agree. Why does fitting become linear after fixing the nonlinearities even though the neuron response itself remains nonlinear? \(S_{j}\) and \(F_{i}^{-1}\) already apply nonlinear transformations to the data. Only the unknown weights linearly combine those transformed features; the full input–output mapping remains nonlinear. Treating parameter variability and observation noise as the same source. Applying \(YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\) without stating sample orientation and obtaining incompatible shapes.

title: Least squares, the closed-form solution, and the Hessian
subtitle: Lecture 21 · Lecture21-OculomotorIntegrator.pdf, p. 4
text: Why does a squared-error fit form a quadratic surface, and how does the Hessian arise from the data design? With samples as columns, write the loss \(L(W)=1/2||Y-WX||_F^{2}\). The Frobenius norm sums squared residuals across all outputs and samples. Output rows are independent, so begin with one weight row w and target row y: \(L(w)=1/2(y-wX)(y-wX)^\mathrm{T}\). Expanding gives the constant \(yy^\mathrm{T}\), the linear term \(-yX^\mathrm{T}w^\mathrm{T}\), and the quadratic term wXX^\(Tw^\mathrm{T}\). Differentiating with respect to w gives gradient \((wX-y)X^\mathrm{T}\). Setting it to zero gives the normal equation wXX^\(T=yX^\mathrm{T}\). If \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is invertible, \(\hat{w}=yX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\); stacking all rows gives \(\hat{W}=YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\). If features are collinear, \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is singular and requires a pseudoinverse, regularization, or redesigned samples. Near the optimum, let \(\Delta w=w-\hat{w}\). The normal equation eliminates the cross term, leaving \(L=L\min+1/2 \Delta w H \Delta w^\mathrm{T}\) with \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\). The same feature Hessian applies row by row to the full W, or appears in blocks after vectorizing the parameters. H depends only on design features for this local curvature; changing the noise model or constraints changes the effective Hessian. This connects fitting with experimental design. If one feature combination barely changes across positions, X contains little information along that direction and H has a small eigenvalue. Conditions that selectively activate that combination can increase curvature and tighten parameter uncertainty. Sloppiness need not be accepted passively; perturbations and improved sampling can reduce it. The OLS loss is \(1/2||Y-WX||^{2}\). When the inverse exists, \(\hat{W}=YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\). \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\) describes parameter curvature supported by the features. Collinear features make H singular or nearly singular, requiring regularization or new experiments. Let \(X=[[1,0,1],[0,1,1]]\). Compute \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\) and determine whether it is invertible. Both parameter combinations are identifiable, but curvature along the common-feature direction is 3 and exceeds the difference-direction curvature of 1. How does adding a ridge penalty \(\lambda ||w||^{2}/2\) change the Hessian? H becomes \(XX^\mathrm{T}+\lambda I\). Every eigenvalue increases by \(\lambda\), stabilizing the inverse, but the estimate is biased toward zero; regularization must not be mistaken for additional data. Treating existence of a closed-form inverse as proof that the biological parameters are unique. Ignoring feature scaling; different units directly alter Hessian eigenvalues and comparisons of stiffness.

title: The Hessian eigenbasis, stiff/sloppy directions, and model ensembles
subtitle: Lecture 21 · Lecture21-OculomotorIntegrator.pdf, p. 5
text: Why can many individual weights vary widely while the data tightly constrain a few parameter combinations? A Hessian is symmetric positive-semidefinite, so \(H=VDV^\mathrm{T}\), where columns \(v_{k}\) are orthonormal parameter directions and D contains \(\lambda _{k}\ge 0\). Let \(z=V^\mathrm{T}(w-\hat{w})\); then the quadratic loss increase is \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\). A large \(\lambda _{k}\) gives a large loss for the same displacement and defines a stiff direction. A small \(\lambda _{k}\) permits farther movement within the adequate-fit contour and defines a sloppy direction. The fit shown on the source page has about 4 stiff and 46 sloppy dimensions. Those counts belong to that model, dataset, and parameterization; they are not universal constants of oculomotor circuits. In a two-direction example, the error contour is an elongated ellipse: its short axis corresponds to large \(\lambda\) and its long axis to small \(\lambda\). Each axis is generally a mixture of many weights, so calling one parameter sloppy is often imprecise. Sloppiness can reflect genuine functional compensation, but also failure of an experiment to excite certain modes, large measurement noise, collinear features, or poor parameter scaling. It does not make the associated biology irrelevant. A direction that is sloppy for the current eye-position dataset may matter during perturbation, development, or another behavior. New conditions are needed to distinguish biological degeneracy from insufficient data. Reporting one best-fit W hides this structure. Instead, collect all models with loss below a prespecified adequacy threshold, compare their common predictions, and identify experiments on which they disagree most. A perturbation outcome predicted by every model is robust; divergence along a sloppy valley identifies an experiment that can narrow the ensemble. Sloppiness in parameter space is distinct from low dimensionality of neural states in Lecture19. \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\) decomposes curvature along parameter eigen-directions. Large \(\lambda\) is stiff; small \(\lambda\) is sloppy. A sloppy direction usually combines multiple parameters and does not mean that one synapse is irrelevant. An adequate-model ensemble expresses uncertainty and robust predictions better than a single best fit. The Hessian eigenvalues are 100 and 0.01, and the allowed \(\Delta L\) is 0.5. Find the maximum displacement along each axis and their ratio. The adequate-fit ellipse is extremely long along the small-eigenvalue direction, directly visualizing parameter compensation or weak constraint. Why can sloppy not be translated as 'this parameter is unimportant'? A Hessian direction usually combines parameters, and small curvature means only that the current data and loss are insensitive to it. The combination may still be crucial for an unmeasured behavior, a perturbation response, or biological viability. Comparing Hessian eigenvalues of unstandardized parameters and creating artificial sloppiness through unit differences. Interchanging parameter-space Hessian eigenvectors with neural-activity PCs or dynamical modes.

title: Lecture 22: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces
subtitle: How are high-dimensional motor-cortex activities organized by a few latent trajectories, how can preparatory activity occupy output-null space, and how can these ideas support a stable closed-loop BMI?
text: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces How are high-dimensional motor-cortex activities organized by a few latent trajectories, how can preparatory activity occupy output-null space, and how can these ideas support a stable closed-loop BMI? center-out tuning → PCA low dimension → latent vs activity space → GPFA → preparatory trajectories → output-null readout Distinguish three levels of description—single-neuron directional tuning, low-dimensional population trajectories, and latent dynamics—and explain how all three can hold simultaneously. Explain each component of GPFA from high-dimensional neural activity to low-dimensional factors, including the observation model, temporal covariance, matrix shapes, and non-identifiability. Use a delayed-reach timeline to explain how preparatory states enter movement-potent and output-null subspaces without misrepresenting graphical correlations as causal conclusions. Compute the null space and rank–nullity of a linear readout by hand, construct a simple decoder, and apply the results to closed-loop BMI and cross-day alignment. Compare the UPDATE and earlier edition: interpret their shared pages using the UPDATE while retaining citations to the old edition, and attribute Page 5 only to the new UPDATE material. Directional tuning is a classic description of motor cortex, whereas the modern population view asks whether low-dimensional trajectories generate movement dynamics. GPFA embeds smooth latent factors into noisy neural activity with a Gaussian observation model and explicitly models temporal covariance. A preparatory state can vary within the null space of muscle readout U without causing movement. BMI decodes neural or latent state into device commands and uses feedback and cross-day latent alignment to improve stability. Conflating a single-neuron tuning curve with a latent trajectory. Using PCA components, GPFA factors, dynamical modes, and decoder axes interchangeably. Assuming that a K-dimensional model means only K neurons matter. Ignoring non-identifiability of \(C-\alpha\) scale and rotation. Inferring \(r=0\) from \(Ur=0\). Ignoring user feedback and learning in a feedforward BMI account. Describing cross-day latent stability as absolute invariance. Tuning curves, principal components, latent factors, dynamical modes, and decoder axes must be distinguished explicitly. They may be related, but they are not interchangeable. GPFA observation model rt |αt ∼ N (Cαt + d, Σ) Gaussian approximation GP temporal covariance ′ 2 \(K(t, t' ) = \sigma s_{2} e-(t-t ) /(2\tau  ) + \sigma n_{2} \delta tt'\) 2 stationary smooth kernel linear motor readout \(m = Ur\) local approximation output-null space Null(U ) = {r : U r = 0} linear algebra rank–nullity dim N ull\((U ) = N - \operatorname{rank}(U )\) U: M×N latent decoder \(\hat{v} = B\alpha \) aligned latent coordinates center-out reach task A reaching paradigm from a central location to multiple radial targets. direction tuning Variation of the mean response with reach direction. latent factor A low-dimensional hidden variable that explains shared population variability. embedding A mapping from latent coordinates into high-dimensional activity. Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA A latent-factor model with a temporal Gaussian-process prior. preparatory activity A target-dependent population state before movement. output-null space Neural directions that do not change the current readout. output-potent space Directions that change muscle or device output. brain-machine interface, BMI A system that controls an external device from neural activity. closed-loop control Online control that includes sensory or device feedback. If 100 neurons are recorded and 6 latent factors are retained, what is the shape of the GPFA loading matrix C? Check matrix multiplication from output dimension back to input dimension; do not mix trials or time bins into the neuron axis of C. C is \(100\times 6\); it maps a \(6\times 1\) latent vector to a \(100\times 1\) mean neural-activity vector. Does a directional tuning curve prove that the neuron directly encodes force in one muscle? A causal encoding claim additionally requires control of confounders and tests of perturbations and decoder generalization. No. Tuning establishes a statistical association between firing rate and reach direction; it may arise from input, shared dynamics, task covariates, or a readout. If U is \(2\times 5\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(U)=2\), what is the dimension of its linear output-null space? Null-space dimension is input dimension minus rank, not output dimension minus rank. By rank–nullity, the dimension is \(5-2=3\). As \(\tau\) in a GP kernel increases, do neighboring latent values usually become smoother or more abrupt? Substitute both limits into the kernel: with very large \(\tau\), the exponential approaches 1; with very small \(\tau\), covariance at a nonzero lag falls rapidly. Smoother. A fixed temporal separation becomes smaller relative to \(\tau\), making kernel covariance closer to its maximum. Why should a cross-day decoder not require exact correspondence of individual neuron identities every day? Cross-day stability is a hypothesis about population structure. It must be tested on held-out days and cannot be confirmed by an attractive two-dimensional plot. Electrode drift changes which units are visible. If the stable computation lies in a latent subspace, align each day's latent coordinates before decoding. Why does a PC explaining 70% of neural variance not necessarily explain 70% of behavioral variance? Behavior depends on a separate readout map, which may ignore high-variance directions or amplify low-variance directions; there is no fixed ratio between the two variances. This is the distinction tested in Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories. Worked example — Compute tuning at four directions: A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\). At \(\theta =0\), \(\cos 0=1\), giving 28 Hz. At \(\pi /2\) and \(3\pi /2\), the cosine is 0, giving 20 Hz in both cases. At \(\pi\), cos\(\pi =-1\), giving 12 Hz. The maximum and minimum are symmetric around the 20 Hz baseline, and their mean remains 20 Hz. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories”? Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories”? Single-cell tuning can be a coordinate projection of a low-dimensional population trajectory. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Directional tuning as a linear projection of a two-dimensional movement vector”? The direction vectors in the dot product are dimensionless; multiplying by k yields Hz, which can be added to baseline b. When \(k=0\), every direction gives b. At \(\theta =\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) the rate is b+k, and in the opposite direction it is b-k. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why can the same center-out data support directional tuning curves and also be viewed as projections of a low-dimensional dynamical system? A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded. Stack all neuronal rates at one moment into \(r(t)\), so each reach condition traces an N-dimensional trajectory. If most variance lies on a few PCs, the trajectory is close to a low-dimensional subspace. A single-neuron curve is the shadow of the high-dimensional trajectory on one coordinate axis. Multiple phase-shifted shadows can arise from one rotating or curved population trajectory, so tuning and dynamics are compatible observations. If one latent factor is multiplied everywhere by 2 without changing C, is it still the same GPFA model? No; the predicted mean changes. It is an equivalent coordinate reparameterization only if the corresponding column of C is also divided by 2. This is the distinction tested in Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model. Worked example — Reconstruct two neurons from one factor: Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates. The first neuron's mean is \(2\times 3+10=16 \mathrm{Hz}\). The second neuron's mean is \(-1\times 3+20=17 \mathrm{Hz}\). A negative loading means that as the latent increases, the second neuron falls below baseline; it does not imply a negative firing rate. Setting \(\alpha\) to 0 should recover the baseline \((10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model”? C is N×K and links latent space with neural activity space. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model”? \(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Shapes in the observation model and reparameterizing its conditional mean”? \(C\alpha\) and d must share the units of r. If \(\alpha\) is dimensionless, entries of C have units of rate or count. \(\Sigma\) uses squared observation units. When \(K=N\) and C is invertible, there is no dimensionality reduction. If all latent factors share an identical kernel, an orthogonal rotation can preserve the prior form; different kernels generally preclude arbitrary rotation. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does the smooth kernel on Page 3 of the UPDATE not prove that the true cortical trajectory is intrinsically smooth? Some smoothness comes from the prior. Compare held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolutions to determine whether the data support that time scale. This is the distinction tested in GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories. Worked example — Compare correlation strength at two time lags: Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms. At \(\Delta t=100\), the exponent is -1/2 and \(K=e^{-1/2}\approx 0.607\). At \(\Delta t=200\), the exponent is \(-4/2=-2\) and \(K=e^{-2}\approx 0.135\). The second lag is twice as long, but covariance falls by more than a factor of four because distance is squared. At \(\Delta t=0\) the value should be 1; the kernel decreases monotonically as \(|\Delta t|\) grows. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories”? \(\tau\) is a temporal correlation scale, not trial duration. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories”? A kernel family is a modeling assumption that must be tested with held-out data. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Target, go, and movement events must delimit the epochs of a delayed-reach trajectory. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Two limits of the squared-exponential kernel”? The numerator and denominator of the exponent both have units of time squared, so their ratio is dimensionless; K retains units of latent variance. As \(\tau \to \infty\), the factor is nearly constant within a finite window. As \(\tau \to 0\), between-bin covariance vanishes and the smooth prior degenerates. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If the downstream readout changes to \(U'\), must the original output-null vector remain null? No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable. This is the distinction tested in Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space. Worked example — Compute an output-null vector: Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector. \(m=1\times 2+2\times (-1)=0\), so r is a nonzero null vector. Choose rpotent=\((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\), giving \(m=1\). Adding the two vectors gives \((3,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), whose output remains \(3+2\times (-1)=1\). A null vector of U has zero dot product with the row vector (1,2), so the two are geometrically orthogonal. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space”? \(Ur=0\) can hold with \(r\ne 0\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space”? Null-space size is determined by input dimensionality and rank. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(Ur=0\) can hold with \(r\ne 0\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Rank–nullity and the potent/null decomposition”? If r is in Hz and m in command units, U has units of command units/Hz; the zero vector carries the corresponding output units. If U has full column rank and \(N\le M\), its null space contains only the zero vector. If N≫M, the null space has at least N-M dimensions. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can an improvement in closed-loop performance not be attributed entirely to more accurate decoder parameters? The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes. This is the distinction tested in Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment. Worked example — Swap the axes of a two-dimensional latent space: On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\). Use \(A=[[0,1],[1,0]]\) to swap the coordinates, giving \(\widetilde{\alpha }=(1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Apply B: \(\hat{v}=2\times 1-1\times 3=-1\). Without alignment, the result is \(2\times 3-1\times 1=5\), showing how a coordinate-convention change can seriously disrupt the decoder. A is a permutation matrix, so \(A^\mathrm{T} A=I\) and latent-vector length is unchanged. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment”? A closed-loop BMI is a joint brain–decoder–feedback system. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment”? Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Mapping chain of a cross-day latent decoder”? If velocity is in cm/s and the latent is dimensionless, B is in cm/s; squared error is in \(\mathrm{cm}^{2}/s^{2}\). \(A_{d}=I\) means that no rotation is required. If latent subspaces do not overlap at all, linear alignment should not be expected to recover an accurate decoder. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From population activity to closed-loop BMI”? Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “center-out reach task” mean in this lecture? center-out reach task: A reaching paradigm from a central location to multiple radial targets. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “direction tuning” mean in this lecture? direction tuning: Variation of the mean response with reach direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “latent factor” mean in this lecture? latent factor: A low-dimensional hidden variable that explains shared population variability. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “embedding” mean in this lecture? embedding: A mapping from latent coordinates into high-dimensional activity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA” mean in this lecture? Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA: A latent-factor model with a temporal Gaussian-process prior. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “output-null space” mean in this lecture? output-null space: Neural directions that do not change the current readout. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term.
