title: Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories
subtitle: Lecture 22 · Lecture22-MotorCortex-UPDATE.pdf, p. 1 · Lecture22-MotorCortex.pdf, p. 1
text: Why can the same center-out data support directional tuning curves and also be viewed as projections of a low-dimensional dynamical system? A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded. Stack all neuronal rates at one moment into \(r(t)\), so each reach condition traces an N-dimensional trajectory. If most variance lies on a few PCs, the trajectory is close to a low-dimensional subspace. A single-neuron curve is the shadow of the high-dimensional trajectory on one coordinate axis. Multiple phase-shifted shadows can arise from one rotating or curved population trajectory, so tuning and dynamics are compatible observations. PCA orders dimensions by variance; it does not know which dimension drives muscles. A low-variance dimension may carry a small but behaviorally crucial output, especially if the readout has high gain along it. Conversely, a large-variance dimension may be output-null preparation. Judging usefulness requires both neural covariance and the behavioral readout, not explained variance alone. The two-dimensional loops or clusters in teaching figures are projections. Overlap may result from truncation, while separation may be exaggerated by normalization. Record the time axis, condition colors, whether trials were averaged, and whether PCs were fitted jointly across conditions. If PCA is fitted separately per condition, the trajectories no longer share coordinates and cannot be compared for target-specific preparation. Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code. Single-cell tuning can be a coordinate projection of a low-dimensional population trajectory. PCA variance and motor potency are different criteria. A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\). The four rates are 28, 20, 12, and 20 Hz, respectively. Why does a PC explaining 70% of neural variance not necessarily explain 70% of behavioral variance? Behavior depends on a separate readout map, which may ignore high-variance directions or amplify low-variance directions; there is no fixed ratio between the two variances. Treating a cosine-fit preferred direction as an immutable causal label. Mistaking the smoothness of a trial-averaged projection for noise-free single trials.

title: Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model
subtitle: Lecture 22 · Lecture22-MotorCortex-UPDATE.pdf, p. 2 · Lecture22-MotorCortex.pdf, p. 2
text: How does GPFA map a few smooth latent functions into many neurons, and what does each matrix dimension represent? Let \(r_{t}\) be the observed vector from N neurons in time bin t and \(\alpha _{t}\) contain K latent factors. Conditional on \(\alpha _{t}\), \(r_{t}\) follows a multivariate Gaussian with \(\operatorname{mean} C\alpha _{t}+d\) and covariance \(\Sigma\). Rows of C correspond to neurons, columns to factors, and d is each neuron's baseline. For spike counts, the Gaussian is an approximation; with very narrow bins or low rates, a Poisson observation model may be more appropriate. A K-dimensional trajectory in latent space is embedded by C into N-dimensional activity space. The column span of C is the shared-activity subspace allowed by the model, while \(\Sigma\) usually absorbs neuron-specific residuals. Shared variation does not require neuron pairs to have identical waveforms: positive and negative loadings allow one factor to produce different amplitudes and directions across cells. The conditional observation mean has a coordinate reparameterization. For any invertible K×K matrix A, define \(\alpha '=A\alpha\) and \(C'=CA^{-1}\); then \(C'\alpha '=C\alpha\). This proves only that the conditional mean is unchanged. Preserving the full GPFA marginal likelihood also requires transforming the latent prior covariance to \(A K A^\mathrm{T}\). Standard GPFA usually assumes independent factors that may have different temporal kernels; arbitrary rotation generally introduces between-factor covariance and leaves that model family. Sign flips, factor permutations, and paired scale changes are common ambiguities. More general rotational equivalence requires extra conditions such as identical kernels or an allowed correlated prior. The GP prior supplies the temporal structure of \(\alpha\), while the observation model supplies the spatial relationship between r and \(\alpha\). Their roles cannot be reversed: C does not smooth time, and the kernel does not specify each neuron's loading. If \(\Sigma\) is diagonal, residual neurons are conditionally independent given the latent state. Strong remaining residual correlations may indicate too few factors K, a poor kernel, or an oversimplified noise model. C is N×K and links latent space with neural activity space. \(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data. Conditional observation coordinates can be reparameterized; equivalence of the full GPFA also depends on the latent prior. Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates. The predicted mean is \((16,17)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\). If one latent factor is multiplied everywhere by 2 without changing C, is it still the same GPFA model? No; the predicted mean changes. It is an equivalent coordinate reparameterization only if the corresponding column of C is also divided by 2. Treating a latent factor as a directly measured neuron. Concluding from diagonal \(\Sigma\) that real neurons are independent; independence applies only to residuals conditional on the latent state.

title: GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories
subtitle: Lecture 22 · Lecture22-MotorCortex-UPDATE.pdf, p. 3 · Lecture22-MotorCortex.pdf, p. 3
text: How does a squared-exponential kernel encode smoothness, and how should target preparation, go cue, and movement be separated in delayed reaches? The squared-exponential kernel \(K(t,t')=\sigma s^{2}\) \(\exp[-(t-t')^{2}/(2\tau ^{2})]+\sigma n^{2}\delta tt'\) gives covariance between two times for one factor. \(\sigma s^{2}\) controls smooth signal variance, \(\tau\) controls the correlation-decay time, and \(\sigma n^{2}\) adds independent variability only in the same time bin. The original Page 3 notes a global scale ambiguity between \(\alpha\) and loading C and uses \(\sigma n^{2}+\sigma s^{2}=1\) as a normalization convention. That constraint fixes scale; it is not a new biological law. Nor is this the only GP kernel: for rapid switching or oscillation, Matérn or periodic kernels may better match the hypothesis. Fitting jointly estimates latent trajectories, loadings, baselines, noise, and kernel hyperparameters, commonly by marginal likelihood or an EM-like procedure. Increasing K always increases in-sample flexibility, so choose dimensionality with cross-validation, held-out likelihood, or reconstruction prediction. Training explained variance alone can mistake noise dimensions for meaningful factors. Read a delayed-reach plot along its timeline. The interval after target onset but before the go cue is the preparatory epoch; movement begins only after go. Preparatory activity for different targets may approach different latent locations without producing obvious movement. After the cue, trajectories depart from those initial states along target-specific movement paths. The plot supports the idea that an initial condition influences later dynamics, but trajectories alone cannot exclude sustained common input. Trial averaging clarifies preparatory trajectories but conceals single-trial onset jitter and variability. To claim that trajectory geometry predicts behavior, use the pre-go latent state to predict reaction time, directional error, or muscle activity on held-out trials. A post-go divergence may reflect alignment and condition averaging, so compare it with shuffled labels and alternative alignments. \(\tau\) is a temporal correlation scale, not trial duration. A kernel family is a modeling assumption that must be tested with held-out data. Target, go, and movement events must delimit the epochs of a delayed-reach trajectory. Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms. The two values are approximately 0.607 and 0.135. Why does the smooth kernel on Page 3 of the UPDATE not prove that the true cortical trajectory is intrinsically smooth? Some smoothness comes from the prior. Compare held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolutions to determine whether the data support that time scale. Mistaking \(\tau\) for the number K of latent factors. Interpreting divergence after the go cue as recurrent causality without testing a sustained-input model.

title: Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space
subtitle: Lecture 22 · Lecture22-MotorCortex-UPDATE.pdf, p. 4 · Lecture22-MotorCortex.pdf, p. 4
text: How can a linear readout produce zero motor output despite strong neural activity during preparation? Write a locally linear readout as \(m=Ur\), where r is an N-dimensional neural state and m an M-dimensional motor command; U must therefore be M×N. The original Page 4 labels U as N×M, which is incompatible with \(m=Ur\), so we correct it to M×N. Any nonzero r satisfying \(Ur=0\) lies in the null space of U; the neurons need not be silent. Preparatory activity can move the network along null directions without changing output in this approximation. After the go cue, the state enters potent directions and the readout becomes nonzero. Rank–nullity gives dim Null\((U)=N-\operatorname{rank}(U)\). This simplifies to the source page's N-M only when U has full row \(\operatorname{rank} M\); if \(\operatorname{rank}(U)<M\), the null space is larger. When recording dimension greatly exceeds motor-output dimension, a large null space is theoretically possible. But recorded r samples only some neurons, and the true downstream map may be nonlinear, state-dependent, or delayed. The null space of a fitted U is therefore relative to a model, not an anatomically absolute no-output pathway. Use the singular value decomposition of U to write r=rpotent+rnull. Row-space directions change output, while their orthogonal complement belongs to the null space. Test whether preparatory activity is output-null by fitting U on independent trials, measuring pre-go projections, and checking EMG or kinematics. Choosing a direction and reporting zero output on the same data is circular. Output-null does not mean computation-null. Activity along a null direction can set a recurrent initial condition, suppress an erroneous movement, or prepare multiple candidates. The same neural vector may also affect unrecorded downstream populations. The course diagram is a linear framework that separates the existence of activity from the existence of current output; it does not justify calling null activity biologically functionless. \(Ur=0\) can hold with \(r\ne 0\). Null-space size is determined by input dimensionality and rank. Output-null is a model statement relative to a specified readout U. Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector. The null component changes the neural state without changing the original potent output of 1. If the downstream readout changes to \(U'\), must the original output-null vector remain null? No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable. Incorrectly inferring \(r=0\) from \(Ur=0\). Defining and testing the null space on the same training trials, thereby overfitting.

title: Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment
subtitle: Lecture 22 · Lecture22-MotorCortex-UPDATE.pdf, p. 5
text: When recorded units change from day to day, how can closed-loop feedback and latent alignment keep a decoder working? A BMI decoder maps neural features to cursor velocity, position, or a discrete action. During open-loop calibration, the participant observes prescribed movement or attempts an action while the system fits a mapping offline. In closed loop, decoder output immediately changes visual feedback, so participant and decoder coadapt. Closed-loop performance is therefore not a passive measure of a fixed encoding; the brain, decoder, and feedback form a new dynamical system. Suppose the observation on day d is \(r_{d}=C_{d}\alpha +d_{d}+\mathrm{noise}\). Different electrode samples change \(C_{d}\) while similar latent dynamics may persist. A cross-day method first estimates daily subspaces and then finds \(A_{d}\) to make their \(\alpha\) coordinates comparable; it finally applies \(\hat{v}=B\alpha\) in the aligned latent space. Stability here means that a transferable low-dimensional relationship exists, not that each neuron's loading is constant. Alignment can manufacture false stability. If behavior labels from the current day rotate latent space and the decoder is then tested on that same day, the answer has leaked into the analysis. A strict evaluation uses calibration data alone to estimate \(A_{d}\) and B, tests on held-out blocks or future days, compares no alignment, random alignment, and a direct neuron-space decoder, and reports adaptation time and failure days. The BMI and cross-day material newly added on Page 5 of the UPDATE has no corresponding page in the earlier edition. It connects the first four pages: PCA/GPFA supplies a shared subspace, a linear readout supplies the behavioral map, closed-loop feedback changes the data distribution, and alignment handles coordinate drift. Every step has assumptions; 'stable latent structure' must not be expanded into permanent invariance of single-neuron representations. A closed-loop BMI is a joint brain–decoder–feedback system. Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity. Holding out future days prevents behavior labels from leaking into the alignment result. On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\). The aligned prediction is -1; the unaligned prediction is 5. Why can an improvement in closed-loop performance not be attributed entirely to more accurate decoder parameters? The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes. Mislabeling the newly added UPDATE page as content already present in the older edition. Using test-day behavior to choose an alignment and then reporting those same data as cross-day generalization.

title: Lecture 23: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions
subtitle: How do long-time-scale recurrent modes, evidence accumulation, and nonlinear attractor dynamics implement short-term memory and perceptual decision-making, and how do those mechanisms relate to behavior?
text: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions How do long-time-scale recurrent modes, evidence accumulation, and nonlinear attractor dynamics implement short-term memory and perceptual decision-making, and how do those mechanisms relate to behavior? cognition/decoupling → DMS/Romo → persistent activity → long recurrent mode → drift-diffusion → psychometric/chronometric/LIP Organize decision-making, working memory, and long-term learning around the working definition that current brain state is not determined solely by current input, while recognizing that this is not an exhaustive definition. Reconstruct DMS and Romo parametric working-memory tasks through sample, delay, comparison, and choice, specifying what information must be retained during the delay. Derive the effective time constant of graded persistent activity from a recurrent eigenmode and classify leaky, perfectly persistent, and unstable regimes. Explain the evidence, noise, bias, bounds, and reaction time of a leaky drift-diffusion process, and predict its psychometric and chronometric curves. Use the Wong–Wang phase plane to distinguish fixed points, separatrices, and stochastic choice while keeping model predictions separate from correlations in LIP. This lecture provisionally defines cognition as a brain state not determined solely by present input. Short-term memory can preserve a past sample in persistent population modes without immediately modifying synapses. Perceptual decisions can be described behaviorally by noisy evidence accumulation and bounds; LIP ramps are correlated neural variables, not automatic proof of mechanism. A reduced Wong–Wang attractor model uses two-dimensional nonlinear nullclines to connect integration, competition, and discrete choice. Treating the working definition of cognition as a complete philosophical or psychological definition. Assuming that STM requires immediate synaptic plasticity. Conflating persistent single-cell activity with a stable population mode. Treating the DDM decision variable as a directly observed neuron. Fitting only the psychometric function and not testing the chronometric function. Equating an LIP correlation directly with a causal accumulator. Conflating a descriptive DDM with a biophysical attractor model at the same explanatory level. Distinguish working-memory content, neural correlates, persistent modes, and synaptic memory; also distinguish a descriptive DDM from a biophysical attractor model. persistent memory mode \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\) \(\lambda <1\) but close to 1 leaky evidence accumulator \(\tau a\) \(\dot{a} = -a + e(t) + \gamma (t)\) white or colored noise specified decision bias \(a(0) = b\) initial-condition interpretation absorbing decision bounds \(a = \pm B\) first-passage rule psychometric function \(P (\mathrm{choice}|c)\) signed stimulus strength chronometric function \(E[RT |c]\) state whether nondecision time is included Wong–Wang nullclines \(G_{1} = 0\), \(G_{2} = 0 2D\) reduced dynamics cognition This lecture's working definition: a brain state partly decoupled from present input and shaped by past events or future goals. short-term memory The ability to retain recently encountered information briefly. working memory Information retained for use in a current computation. delayed match-to-sample A sample–delay–test memory task. persistent activity Neural activity that remains after the stimulus ends. drift-diffusion model, DDM A decision model that accumulates noisy evidence to bounds. psychometric curve Choice or accuracy as a function of stimulus strength. chronometric curve Reaction time as a function of stimulus strength. separatrix A boundary separating different attractor basins. attractor A state or set toward which nearby states converge under the dynamics. DMS needs only a memory that the sample was seen. What additional information must the Romo task preserve? A one-bit 'sample occurred' label cannot explain graded comparison errors between nearby frequencies. The Romo parametric task must retain the continuous or graded value of the first vibration frequency so it can be compared with the second. For a recurrent mode with \(\lambda =0.9\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), what is the effective time constant? First compute the eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\), then divide the intrinsic time constant by it; \(\lambda\) has no time units. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.9)=200 \mathrm{ms}\). If only decision bound B is increased, how do accuracy and reaction time usually change in a DDM? A farther bound permits more evidence collection but requires a longer first-passage time. With other parameters fixed and informative trials, accuracy usually increases and reaction time lengthens. Both LIP firing rate and the model decision variable ramp. Is that enough to conclude that LIP implements a DDM? The claim additionally requires trial-level covariation, perturbations, parameter-linked predictions, and comparison with alternative models. No. Similar temporal shapes are correlational and can arise from common input, urgency, condition averaging, or other dynamics. What happens when a phase-plane trajectory lies exactly on a separatrix? A separatrix is not a broad third choice region; it is the boundary between attractor basins. In an ideal deterministic system it follows the boundary toward a saddle; a minute noise fluctuation or bias pushes it into one of the two choice basins. Why does continued brain activity with the eyes closed not by itself prove cognition in this lecture's sense? Persistent activity may be spontaneous fluctuation or an unmeasured input. It must carry task-relevant history and predict later behavior. This is the distinction tested in A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input. Worked example — Identify history dependence: Two trial groups share a current comparison stimulus of 20 Hz. The first sample is 10 Hz in one group and 30 Hz in the other. Animals predominantly choose 'comparison larger' and 'comparison smaller,' respectively. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Two trial groups share a current comparison stimulus of 20 Hz. The first sample is 10 Hz in one group and 30 Hz in the other. Animals predominantly choose 'comparison larger' and 'comparison smaller,' respectively. Because the current comparison is identical, a current-input-only model predicts the same choice distribution. Different sample histories change both the correct relation and actual choice. The internal state must carry at least the sample's relation to 20 Hz to explain the difference. First rule out confounds if motor cues or rewards also differ systematically between the groups. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input”? The working definition emphasizes a history-dependent internal state. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input”? The key experimental control holds current input fixed while varying the past. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The working definition emphasizes a history-dependent internal state. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Express 'current input is insufficient' with conditional probability”? These are probabilities, dimensionless and between 0 and 1; the conditioning variables themselves may have different units. If a history effect vanishes after all observable current inputs are included, no additional cognitive state is needed to explain that effect. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can the course's definition of cognition become a testable state dependence rather than an abstract label? This lecture adopts a working definition: cognition makes brain state or behavior incompletely determined by present sensory input. The same current stimulus can produce different responses under different memories, goals, or beliefs; conversely, an internal decision variable can keep evolving while the outside world is unchanged. This definition is useful for modeling, but it is not a complete philosophical definition of consciousness, language, or intelligence. A test presents the same current input after different histories. If sample identity, previous reward, or instruction changes delay activity and choice, the system requires a history-dependent state. Control current stimulus, movement preparation, and arousal; otherwise an apparent internal state may simply be an omitted external or bodily variable. Why does monotonic delay-period firing with f1 not by itself prove that this is the memory used for behavior? The correlated signal could be a passive readout. Functional evidence is stronger when its trial fluctuations, selective perturbation, or downstream coupling affect comparison behavior. This is the distinction tested in Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory. Worked example — Make a comparison from noisy memory: The internal memory value is \(m_{1}=18 \mathrm{Hz}\), the comparison estimate is \(m_{2}=22 \mathrm{Hz}\), and the rule is to choose 'second is larger' when \(m_{2}-m_{1}>0\). Ignoring decision noise, find the choice variable. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The internal memory value is \(m_{1}=18 \mathrm{Hz}\), the comparison estimate is \(m_{2}=22 \mathrm{Hz}\), and the rule is to choose 'second is larger' when \(m_{2}-m_{1}>0\). Ignoring decision noise, find the choice variable. Compute \(d=m_{2}-m_{1}=22-18=4 \mathrm{Hz}\). Since \(d>0\), the result lies on the 'second is larger' side. If memory error overestimates m1 beyond 22 Hz, the choice reverses, showing that an error need not arise from comparison sensation. Swapping the two estimates should produce -4 Hz and the opposite choice. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory”? DMS can be supported by categorical or identity memory. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory”? The Romo task must preserve a comparable magnitude for f1. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Romo task must preserve a comparable magnitude for f1. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Why does increasing \(\lambda\) from 0.99 to 1.01 not simply lengthen memory a little? It crosses the stability boundary. The linear mode changes from slow decay to exponential growth and needs another nonlinearity to limit amplitude. This is the distinction tested in Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one. Worked example — Predict drift during a delay: Let \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.99\), and \(\alpha _{0}=10\) after the sample. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and estimate the amplitude after 1 s. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.99\), and \(\alpha _{0}=10\) after the sample. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and estimate the amplitude after 1 s. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.99)=2000 \mathrm{ms}=2 \mathrm{s}\). After 1 s, \(\alpha =10e^{-1/2}\approx 6.07\). Although \(\lambda\) is very close to 1, a 1 s delay still loses about 39%, so 'near one' does not mean perfect memory. After one \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=2 \mathrm{s}\), the amplitude should fall to \(e^{-1}\approx 36.8\)% of its initial value. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one”? The eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\) amplifies \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one”? \(\lambda =1\) is the ideal persistence boundary, not a necessary condition for every memory network. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Directions outside the memory mode must also be stable. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive the effective time constant from a recurrent eigenvalue”? The exponent must be dimensionless, as \((1-\lambda )t/\tau\) is. For \(\lambda =0\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) diverges. When \(\lambda >1\), the formula becomes negative, indicating growth rather than a decay time constant. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why do identical coherence values yield different choices and RTs? Each trial has a different noise path, which changes both the first-passage time and which boundary is reached first. This is the distinction tested in Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage. Worked example — Determine a deterministic first-passage time: Let \(\tau a=1 \mathrm{s}\), \(b=0\), \(\mu =2\), and \(B=1\). Ignoring noise, find the time to +B. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau a=1 \mathrm{s}\), \(b=0\), \(\mu =2\), and \(B=1\). Ignoring noise, find the time to +B. The solution is \(a(t)=2(1-e^{-t})\). Set \(a=1\) to get \(1=2(1-e^{-t})\), hence \(e^{-t}=1/2\). Taking the natural logarithm gives \(t=\ln 2\approx 0.693 \mathrm{s}\). The steady state 2 exceeds bound 1, so the trajectory must cross. If \(\mu \le 1\) and \(b=0\), a deterministic leaky trajectory never reaches +B. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage”? This lecture's accumulator includes leak and must be distinguished from a perfect DDM. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage”? Choice and decision time are determined jointly by the first boundary crossing. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? This lecture's accumulator includes leak and must be distinguished from a perfect DDM. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “A leaky accumulator under constant evidence”? \(da/dt\) has units of state/time; dividing every state term on the right by \(\tau a\) gives the same units. The no-leak limit requires \(\tau a\to \infty\) together with appropriate input scaling. As \(t\to \infty\), \(a\to \mu\); if \(|\mu |<B\), a deterministic trajectory never reaches a boundary. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can mean LIP ramp slopes alone not distinguish accumulation from averaged discrete steps? Both forms of single-trial dynamics can yield similar smooth curves when different onset or choice times are averaged, requiring single-trial model comparison. This is the distinction tested in Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping. Worked example — Identify bias from simplified psychometric data: At signed coherences -10, 0, and +10%, the probabilities of a right choice are 0.15, 0.65, and 0.93. Does the pattern suggest a rightward bias? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At signed coherences -10, 0, and +10%, the probabilities of a right choice are 0.15, 0.65, and 0.93. Does the pattern suggest a rightward bias? An unbiased model generally predicts about 0.5 at 0 coherence. The observed 0.65 exceeds 0.5, suggesting a starting-point or choice-rule bias toward the right. A confidence interval and lapse model are still needed; one proportion cannot identify the source of bias. At strong evidence on the two sides, probabilities approach 0 and 1 respectively, so the sign convention for direction is consistent. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping”? Psychometric and chronometric functions should be interpreted jointly. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping”? A condition-averaged ramp does not uniquely imply a single-trial ramp. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A condition-averaged ramp does not uniquely imply a single-trial ramp. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Why do two choice attractors generally require a saddle or basin boundary between them? Distinct basins of attraction in a continuous dynamical system must be separated by a boundary that flows to neither attractor. In two dimensions, that boundary is commonly the stable manifold of a saddle. This is the distinction tested in Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries. Worked example — Classify two points from their Jacobians: Point A has Jacobian eigenvalues -2 and -0.5 s^-1; point B has +1 and -3 s^-1. Classify them. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Point A has Jacobian eigenvalues -2 and -0.5 s^-1; point B has +1 and -3 s^-1. Classify them. Both real parts at A are negative, so every small perturbation decays. At B, one direction grows and the other decays. A is therefore a local attractor and B a saddle; B's stable manifold can form a separatrix. The eigenvalue units match the given s^-1; positive and negative signs denote growth and decay, respectively. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries”? Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability requires a separate test. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries”? A separatrix is the boundary between choice basins. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Evidence biases one attractor by changing input and geometry. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Classify fixed-point stability from the local Jacobian”? The derivative \(G_{i}/\partial S_{j}\) has units 1/time, matching a local exponential growth or decay rate. Recovery slows as an eigenvalue's real part approaches 0; a positive eigenvalue destabilizes the fixed point. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “First-passage paths in drift–diffusion”? Each path begins at bias b, accumulates noisy evidence step by step, and stops the first time it reaches +B or −B. The endpoint determines choice and the horizontal coordinate determines decision time. Under identical task parameters, noise can carry the two trajectories to different boundaries; a trajectory must not be averaged further after crossing before a decision is assigned. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “cognition” mean in this lecture? cognition: This lecture's working definition: a brain state partly decoupled from present input and shaped by past events or future goals. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “short-term memory” mean in this lecture? short-term memory: The ability to retain recently encountered information briefly. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “working memory” mean in this lecture? working memory: Information retained for use in a current computation. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “delayed match-to-sample” mean in this lecture? delayed match-to-sample: A sample–delay–test memory task. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “persistent activity” mean in this lecture? persistent activity: Neural activity that remains after the stimulus ends. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. title: A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input
subtitle: Lecture 23 · Lecture23-Intro-ShortTermMemory-PerceptualDecisions.pdf, p. 1
text: How can the course's definition of cognition become a testable state dependence rather than an abstract label? This lecture adopts a working definition: cognition makes brain state or behavior incompletely determined by present sensory input. The same current stimulus can produce different responses under different memories, goals, or beliefs; conversely, an internal decision variable can keep evolving while the outside world is unchanged. This definition is useful for modeling, but it is not a complete philosophical definition of consciousness, language, or intelligence. A test presents the same current input after different histories. If sample identity, previous reward, or instruction changes delay activity and choice, the system requires a history-dependent state. Control current stimulus, movement preparation, and arousal; otherwise an apparent internal state may simply be an omitted external or bodily variable. Decision-making, short-term memory, learning, and generalization operate on different time scales but can all be written as state updates. A decision state accumulates evidence over hundreds of milliseconds; working memory retains a sample for a delay of seconds; learning changes parameters across trials; long-term memory retrieves information over much longer intervals. A shared mathematical language does not imply a shared brain area or cellular mechanism. Use a Markov-state question while learning: if present input alone does not predict the next event, which added internal variable improves prediction? The variable may be accumulated evidence, a remembered frequency, or a task rule. A good model explains how state is written, maintained without input, read, and cleared; it does more than draw a high firing trace during a delay. The working definition emphasizes a history-dependent internal state. The key experimental control holds current input fixed while varying the past. A shared state-space language does not imply a shared biological mechanism. Two trial groups share a current comparison stimulus of 20 Hz. The first sample is 10 Hz in one group and 30 Hz in the other. Animals predominantly choose 'comparison larger' and 'comparison smaller,' respectively. This design supports a history-dependent state, but recording or intervention is still needed to identify its particular neural code. Why does continued brain activity with the eyes closed not by itself prove cognition in this lecture's sense? Persistent activity may be spontaneous fluctuation or an unmeasured input. It must carry task-relevant history and predict later behavior. Treating a working definition as the only definition of cognition. Failing to measure eye movements or body state and misattributing their effects to internal memory.

title: Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory
subtitle: Lecture 23 · Lecture23-Intro-ShortTermMemory-PerceptualDecisions.pdf, p. 2
text: After the sample disappears, must memory preserve only a categorical label or a continuously comparable quantity? Delayed match-to-sample presents a sample, a delay, and a test in order, followed by a match or nonmatch report. The minimum memory content may be sample identity or category. Because no sample is directly available during the delay, above-chance behavior shows that past information remains accessible. The strategy could nevertheless use a verbal label, familiarity, or a rule-specific code and does not automatically imply an exact sensory trace. In the Romo vibration task, frequency f1 is delivered to a fingertip, followed after a delay by f2; the animal judges whether f2 is greater or less than f1. Comparing neighboring frequencies requires a graded magnitude, not merely a 'stimulus occurred' marker. If the delay representation is noisy, f1 and f2 become harder to discriminate as they approach each other, and psychometric slope can estimate their combined sensory and memory uncertainty. Align neural data to each event. The sample epoch tests encoding; the delay tests maintenance; the comparison epoch asks how remembered f1 and current f2 combine into a decision variable; and the choice epoch also contains motor preparation. A cell whose delay firing is ordered by f1 is a candidate memory signal, but trial-to-trial fluctuations should predict comparison errors rather than relying only on condition means. DMS and parametric memory differ chiefly in readout demands. A DMS classifier may only need to separate finitely many patterns, whereas a Romo comparison must preserve ordering and distance. Poor performance cannot be assigned directly to maintenance failure; it may arise in sample encoding, comparison sensation, the decision rule, or motor report. Perturbations must be restricted to a particular epoch to separate these stages. DMS can be supported by categorical or identity memory. The Romo task must preserve a comparable magnitude for f1. Epoch-specific recording and perturbation separate encoding, maintenance, and readout. The internal memory value is \(m_{1}=18 \mathrm{Hz}\), the comparison estimate is \(m_{2}=22 \mathrm{Hz}\), and the rule is to choose 'second is larger' when \(m_{2}-m_{1}>0\). Ignoring decision noise, find the choice variable. The decision variable is +4 Hz, predicting the choice 'second is larger.' Why does monotonic delay-period firing with f1 not by itself prove that this is the memory used for behavior? The correlated signal could be a passive readout. Functional evidence is stronger when its trial fluctuations, selective perturbation, or downstream coupling affect comparison behavior. Attributing every drop in accuracy to forgetting without checking other task epochs. Extending a mechanism for discrete DMS directly to continuous frequency memory.

title: Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one
subtitle: Lecture 23 · Lecture23-Intro-ShortTermMemory-PerceptualDecisions.pdf, p. 3
text: How can recurrent feedback maintain a population mode for seconds when individual neurons have time constants of only tens of milliseconds? Linearized population dynamics can be written \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\). Project activity onto an eigenvector v of W. If \(Wv=\lambda v\), the corresponding mode amplitude \(\alpha\) obeys \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha +\beta\). After sample input writes \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is removed, \(\alpha\) decays with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); as \(\lambda\) approaches 1, recurrent excitation cancels intrinsic leak. \(\lambda =1\) is the linear condition for an ideal line attractor: any amplitude of that mode persists without input. \(\lambda <1\) produces drift toward baseline, while \(\lambda >1\) produces growth in the linear model and requires nonlinear saturation. Real working memory may tolerate slight leak, correct itself with sensory feedback, or rely on nonlinear discrete attractors; persistent firing does not require connections exactly equal to mathematical 1. Persistent activity of individual neurons may change over time while a population projection remains stable. Conversely, a condition-averaged cell may look flat because different trial dynamics cancel. Examine decoding across the delay, population trajectories, single-trial drift, and behavioral error together. Short-term memory need not alter synaptic weights online on every trial; the existing recurrent network state can store it. All modes require stability analysis. One \(\lambda \approx 1\) mode can retain memory, while the remaining eigenvalues should define decaying transverse directions; otherwise noise spreads into irrelevant coordinates. Nonorthogonal eigenvectors can also produce transient amplification. Reporting the longest \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) alone does not establish reliable memory; assess noise accumulation, input selectivity, readout, and reset mechanisms. The eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\) amplifies \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\). \(\lambda =1\) is the ideal persistence boundary, not a necessary condition for every memory network. Directions outside the memory mode must also be stable. Let \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.99\), and \(\alpha _{0}=10\) after the sample. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and estimate the amplitude after 1 s. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=2 \mathrm{s}\), and after 1 s \(\alpha \approx 6.07\). Why does increasing \(\lambda\) from 0.99 to 1.01 not simply lengthen memory a little? It crosses the stability boundary. The linear mode changes from slow decay to exponential growth and needs another nonlinearity to limit amplitude. Using the \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) formula for \(\lambda >1\) and still calling it a positive decay time constant. Examining only condition-averaged persistent firing and ignoring single-trial drift.

title: Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage
subtitle: Lecture 23 · Lecture23-Intro-ShortTermMemory-PerceptualDecisions.pdf, p. 4
text: How does random-dot evidence become a choice process with leak, bias, noise, and absorbing bounds? Random-dot motion provides noisy evidence at every moment. Define \(a>0\) as support for right and \(a<0\) as support for left, and write \(\tau a da/dt=-a+e(t)+\gamma (t)\). The conditional mean of \(e(t)\) varies with signed coherence, while \(\gamma\) is zero-mean noise. The -a term is leak and discounts old evidence; a classic perfect DDM often omits it, whereas this lecture uses the more general leaky accumulator. The initial condition \(a(0)=b\) represents starting bias; absorbing boundaries \(a=\pm B\) determine first-passage choice and decision time. Positive b puts +B closer, usually making that choice more frequent and faster. Raising B typically increases accuracy and RT; increasing drift magnitude raises accuracy and shortens RT; increasing noise broadens trajectories, changes both, and may create more fast-error trials. Reaction time also contains nondecision time: sensory encoding and motor execution occur outside accumulator passage. Attributing all RT to evidence accumulation misestimates the bound or drift. Leak, collapsing bounds, urgency, and across-trial variability can produce similar distributions, so constrain parameters with the full choice–RT likelihood and model comparison. In simulation, update a with a small step \(\Delta t\) and stop at the first boundary crossing; do not average after crossing and then decide. Noise scaling must vary with the square root of \(\Delta t\). Adding a fixed-variance noise term each step makes the model change when the time step changes. Begin numerical self-study with deterministic constant evidence, then add randomness to understand the distribution. This lecture's accumulator includes leak and must be distinguished from a perfect DDM. Choice and decision time are determined jointly by the first boundary crossing. Nondecision time and time-step-dependent noise scaling cannot be omitted. Let \(\tau a=1 \mathrm{s}\), \(b=0\), \(\mu =2\), and \(B=1\). Ignoring noise, find the time to +B. The decision time is about 0.693 s, and the positive boundary is chosen. Why do identical coherence values yield different choices and RTs? Each trial has a different noise path, which changes both the first-passage time and which boundary is reached first. Treating the leaky equation as a classic no-leak DDM. Changing \(\Delta t\) in a simulation without rescaling the noise and thereby creating a time-step artifact.

title: Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping
subtitle: Lecture 23 · Lecture23-Intro-ShortTermMemory-PerceptualDecisions.pdf, p. 5
text: Which aspects of an accumulator can behavioral curves and LIP firing constrain, and what can they not prove? A psychometric function plots P(choice|signed coherence). Choice is nearly uncertain around zero coherence and saturates toward the correct option as coherence magnitude grows. Horizontal displacement suggests bias, while slope reflects overall sensitivity but also depends on sensory noise, integration, and lapses. An accuracy curve alone often cannot distinguish drift, bound, and noise. A chronometric function plots \(E[RT|coherence]\), typically with slower responses to weak evidence and faster responses to strong evidence. Report correct and error RTs, distribution quantiles, and nondecision time rather than the mean alone. Different models can share a mean curve while differing in tails, fast errors, or conditional accuracy; joint fitting supplies stronger constraints. During motion decisions, LIP neurons often show choice-selective ramps that approach a similar firing level before response, consistent with accumulation to bound. Yet condition averaging can make step-like single trials appear as a smooth ramp, and urgency or motor plans can also increase over time. Ramping is a neural correlate, not a unique cellular implementation. Stronger tests map parameter changes to neural predictions: coherence should change ramp slope, prior bias can shift the starting point, and speed instructions can alter bound-like termination. Trial-level neural fluctuations should predict choice and RT. Even if all hold, LIP could read rather than generate the decision variable; temporally precise perturbation and network-wide recording are needed to distinguish these roles. Psychometric and chronometric functions should be interpreted jointly. A condition-averaged ramp does not uniquely imply a single-trial ramp. Quantitative parameter-to-neural-curve predictions are stronger than shape analogy. At signed coherences -10, 0, and +10%, the probabilities of a right choice are 0.15, 0.65, and 0.93. Does the pattern suggest a rightward bias? The data suggest a right-choice bias but cannot distinguish initial-state, reward, or motor bias. Why can mean LIP ramp slopes alone not distinguish accumulation from averaged discrete steps? Both forms of single-trial dynamics can yield similar smooth curves when different onset or choice times are averaged, requiring single-trial model comparison. Equating psychometric slope directly with one sensory-noise parameter. Using resemblance to a ramp-to-threshold plot in place of a causal test.

title: Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries
subtitle: Lecture 23 · Lecture23-Intro-ShortTermMemory-PerceptualDecisions.pdf, p. 6
text: How does a nonlinear recurrent two-population model amplify a weak bias into one of two stable choices? The reduced Wong–Wang model uses two population variables for recurrent pools supporting the two choices. Self-excitation maintains an activated pool, cross-inhibition suppresses its competitor, and slow synaptic gating supplies an accumulation time scale. Write the dynamics as \(dS_{1}/dt=G_{1}(S_{1},S_{2})\) and \(dS_{2}/dt=G_{2}(S_{1},S_{2})\); the transfer function and parameter values determine the nullcline shapes. Intersections of \(G_{1}=0\) and \(G_{2}=0\) are fixed points. Under absent or weak evidence, a common topology contains a low-activity undecided state, two choice attractors, and a saddle on the basin boundary. Other parameter settings produce other topologies, so the schematic is not a universal theorem. A separatrix through the saddle assigns initial states and noise paths to the two attractor basins. Signed evidence makes the two inputs asymmetric, shifts the nullclines, and expands the correct-choice basin. Strong evidence drives trajectories away from the boundary more quickly, usually increasing accuracy and lowering RT; at zero evidence, noise determines the basin. Unlike a DDM with explicit absorbing bounds, choice termination can be defined by entry into an attractor neighborhood, with nonlinear recurrent feedback itself stabilizing the outcome. Read a phase portrait by inserting test points on both sides of each nullcline to determine arrows and then following trajectories; intersection count alone is insufficient. Keep experimental links at the proper level: the model can generate behavioral curves, population recordings can test competitive dynamics, and perturbing one pool predicts a basin shift. These results show compatibility, not that cortex implements this exact reduced equation. Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability requires a separate test. A separatrix is the boundary between choice basins. Evidence biases one attractor by changing input and geometry. Point A has Jacobian eigenvalues -2 and -0.5 s^-1; point B has +1 and -3 s^-1. Classify them. A is stable, and B is a saddle. Why do two choice attractors generally require a saddle or basin boundary between them? Distinct basins of attraction in a continuous dynamical system must be separated by a boundary that flows to neither attractor. In two dimensions, that boundary is commonly the stable manifold of a saddle. Treating a nullcline itself as a trajectory. Mapping a reduced-model attractor one-to-one onto a single anatomical population.

title: Lecture 24: Learning from Rewards
subtitle: How does reward-gated plasticity avoid unconditional weight growth and produce matching, and how do value prediction and temporal-difference error explain blocking and dopamine responses?
text: Learning from Rewards How does reward-gated plasticity avoid unconditional weight growth and produce matching, and how do value prediction and temporal-difference error explain blocking and dopamine responses? stimulus/action/reward → three-factor plasticity → reward baseline/covariance → matching law → Rescorla–Wagner → TD/RPE Organize stimulus, action, reward, and synaptic eligibility into a three-factor learning rule, explaining why naive reward-gated Hebbian learning remains excessively strong. Derive the reward-baseline covariance update and matching equilibrium, stating assumptions such as stationary reward and the choice rule at each step. Derive Rescorla–Wagner learning from squared prediction error and use blocking to explain why an already predicted reward produces no further learning. Express delayed reward as a temporal-difference error and distinguish state value, action value, reward-prediction error, and dopamine response. Read dopamine timelines for early reward, cue transfer, and omission while preserving the evidential boundary for alternatives such as salience. Learned decisions must connect stimulus/action activity to delayed reward. A simple reward-gated Hebbian rule keeps strengthening when reward is common; subtracting the expected-reward baseline turns it into a covariance rule. Under a specified choice model and assumptions, the stationary covariance condition produces matching behavior. Rescorla–Wagner learns cue value from current reward-prediction error, while TD extends error to future value. Dopamine cue-transfer and omission patterns resemble RPE, though dopamine signals may also mix salience and movement. Failing to subtract a baseline from reward-gated Hebbian learning, so every rewarded coactivity continues to strengthen. Treating matching as an unconditional law of rational optimality. Explaining blocking by claiming that S2 did not coincide with reward. Conflating RPE, value, and salience. Omitting \(\gamma\) or next value from TD error. Treating dopamine as the only third factor in all reward learning. Prematurely treating this lecture's simplified Q concept as a complete Q-learning algorithm. Lecture 24 is a biological and reward-learning bridge; Lecture 25 introduces MDP/RL systematically. Do not let Bellman equations or Q-learning obscure this lecture's plasticity and dopamine logic. reward-baseline three-factor update ∆\(w = \eta e(R - \bar{R})\) eligibility e defined covariance learning E[∆w] = \(\eta \operatorname{Cov}(e, R)\) stationary average matching law \(CA /CB \approx  RA /RB\) specific foraging assumptions linear value predictor \(V = w_{\mathrm{T}} x\) features x Rescorla–Wagner update ∆\(w = \eta x(R - V )\) immediate or represented reward TD/RPE \(\delta  = R + \gamma V_{\mathrm{next}} - V\) Markov or state representation implicit state–action value \(Q(s, a) = E[G|s, a]\) policy and future behavior specified reward learning Adjustment of stimulus–action associations by outcomes. eligibility \(\operatorname{trace} A\) variable marking recent pre/post or action activity for modification by a later reward. reward baseline Expected reward used to compute a signal above or below expectation. matching law Approximate matching of choice proportions to obtained-reward proportions. value Expected discounted future reward from the current state or cue. Rescorla-Wagner rule A rule that updates cue value using reward-prediction error. blocking Failure of a new cue to learn because an existing predictor leaves zero error. temporal-difference error, TD error Reward plus discounted next value minus current value. reward-prediction error, RPE The difference between an actual or updated target and predicted value. Q value Expected return conditioned on a state–action pair. If reward is always 1 and the naive update is \(\Delta w=\eta Rxy\), with x and y often positive, what happens? A baseline, prediction error, normalization, or another stabilizing mechanism is needed. The weight keeps increasing whenever the activities coincide; correctly predicting the reward supplies no natural stopping point. For \(R=0\), baseline \(b=0.4\), eligibility \(e=2\), and \(\eta =0.1\), what is the covariance update? Failing to receive reward is negative relative to a positive baseline, so the eligible connection weakens on this trial. \(\Delta w=0.1\times (0-0.4)\times 2=-0.08\). At a matching equilibrium, what do the choice-conditioned expected rewards of two selected actions generally satisfy? This condition depends on the relevant stochastic-choice and learning assumptions and need not hold exactly in every environment. Their marginal or choice-conditioned expected rewards are equal; otherwise choice probability continues moving toward the action with higher return. In blocking, an old cue already predicts reward completely and a new cue is presented beside it. Why does the new cue acquire little learning? This is the key prediction that separates an error-correcting rule from pure reward-gated coactivity. The total prediction is already close to reward, so prediction error is nearly zero; even though the new cue is active, it receives almost no update signal. After a cue predicts reward, does a smaller dopamine response at reward time mean that the reward has lost value? Keep the time series for value, received reward, and prediction error separate. No. The cue now predicts value, so RPE transfers to the cue; at reward time, outcome matches prediction and \(\delta\) is nearly zero. Why should a dopamine pulse without preceding eligibility not selectively strengthen one stimulus–action synapse? The third factor broadcasts the outcome, but local eligibility identifies the synapse that participated in the action; without eligibility, there is no correct credit address. This is the distinction tested in Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit. Worked example — Eligibility under delayed reward: At the action, \(e_{0}=1\). With no new coactivity, \(\tau e=2 \mathrm{s}\); after 1 s, \(M=0.6\) and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the instantaneous update magnitude \(\eta Me\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At the action, \(e_{0}=1\). With no new coactivity, \(\tau e=2 \mathrm{s}\); after 1 s, \(M=0.6\) and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the instantaneous update magnitude \(\eta Me\). The trace decays to \(e=e^{-1/2}\approx 0.607\). Multiplying by the third factor gives \(Me\approx 0.364\). After multiplying by \(\eta\), the update magnitude is approximately 0.0364. With a delay of 0, the update would be 0.06; the smaller delayed update is consistent with trace decay. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit”? Eligibility identifies candidate synapses; the third factor specifies the sign of the outcome. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit”? A naive nonnegative reward gate lacks error-driven stopping and weakening. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Eligibility identifies candidate synapses; the third factor specifies the sign of the outcome. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “A three-factor update with an eligibility trace”? If x and y are treated as rates, the trace equation must normalize them consistently; \(\eta\) balances units on the two sides of the weight derivative. As \(\tau e\to 0\), a delayed outcome can barely credit the earlier action. When \(b=R\), \(M=0\) and updating stops. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: When reward arrives, how can learning modify only the connections that participated in the preceding choice? A foraging animal selects an action from a sensory cue and receives reward. Learning must establish the stimulus–action–outcome relation rather than strengthen every recently active synapse. Let x be a presynaptic stimulus feature and y postsynaptic or action activity, so xy creates eligibility. A third factor M arrives after the outcome, giving update \(\Delta w=\eta Mxy\). An eligibility trace can bridge the delay from action to reward. If M is simply the nonnegative reward R, every rewarded coactivity grows. A mastered action continues to strengthen, and the common offset of frequent reward contaminates credit; weights stop only through saturation rather than a correct equilibrium. If \(R=0\), an unrewarded choice merely receives no update and the wrong association cannot actively weaken. Why does an underestimated baseline produce systematic positive drift? The mean of R-b becomes positive. If mean eligibility is also positive, an offset update appears that is unrelated to genuine reward–eligibility covariance. This is the distinction tested in Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium. Worked example — Compute a covariance update over four trials: For four trials, \(R=[1,0,1,0]\), \(e=[2,1,0,1]\), \(b=0.5\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the average update. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For four trials, \(R=[1,0,1,0]\), \(e=[2,1,0,1]\), \(b=0.5\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the average update. Across trials, (R-b)e is 1, -0.5, 0, and -0.5. The average of the four terms is 0. After multiplying by \(\eta\), the average \(\Delta w\) is 0 even though individual trials have positive and negative updates. \(E[R]=0.5\) matches the stated baseline. Direct calculation gives \(E[Re]=0.5\) and \(E[R]E[e]=0.5\), so the covariance is again zero. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium”? An average baseline turns expected updating into reward–eligibility covariance. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium”? A state-dependent baseline can reduce error in heterogeneous environments. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A state-dependent baseline can reduce error in heterogeneous environments. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From a baseline update to covariance”? R-b has the same units as R; \(\eta e\) must convert it into a dimensionless or otherwise specified weight change. If e is constant, covariance is zero. If b is not \(E[R]\), the update also contains a baseline-mismatch term. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does a matching curve not prove that the animal explicitly computes RA/RB? A long-run ratio can emerge automatically from local prediction-error updates and stochastic choice; the behavioral equality does not uniquely identify the internal algorithm. This is the distinction tested in Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging. Worked example — Check matching: Across 100 choices, A is selected 60 times and earns 30 rewards; B is selected 40 times and earns 20 rewards. Check the conditional returns and both ratios. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Across 100 choices, A is selected 60 times and earns 30 rewards; B is selected 40 times and earns 20 rewards.
