title: Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit
subtitle: Lecture 24 · Lecture24-LearningFromRewards.pdf, p. 1
text: When reward arrives, how can learning modify only the connections that participated in the preceding choice? A foraging animal selects an action from a sensory cue and receives reward. Learning must establish the stimulus–action–outcome relation rather than strengthen every recently active synapse. Let x be a presynaptic stimulus feature and y postsynaptic or action activity, so xy creates eligibility. A third factor M arrives after the outcome, giving update \(\Delta w=\eta Mxy\). An eligibility trace can bridge the delay from action to reward. If M is simply the nonnegative reward R, every rewarded coactivity grows. A mastered action continues to strengthen, and the common offset of frequent reward contaminates credit; weights stop only through saturation rather than a correct equilibrium. If \(R=0\), an unrewarded choice merely receives no update and the wrong association cannot actively weaken. Replacing M with reward prediction error or reward minus baseline makes an unexpectedly good outcome strengthen, an unexpectedly bad outcome weaken, and an expected outcome produce nearly zero change. Dopamine is a canonical candidate third factor because phasic responses often correspond to RPE, but different dopamine neurons, time scales, and tasks can also encode components of movement, novelty, or salience. Experimental tests must control the timing of pre/post eligibility and the third factor. A dopamine pulse should not cause the same task-specific update at synapses lacking relevant eligibility, and a pulse delayed beyond the eligibility window should weaken learning. Co-occurring reward, dopamine, and behavioral change alone do not demonstrate a local three-factor product. Eligibility identifies candidate synapses; the third factor specifies the sign of the outcome. A naive nonnegative reward gate lacks error-driven stopping and weakening. Dopamine–RPE is a powerful framework but not the only explanation of every signal. At the action, \(e_{0}=1\). With no new coactivity, \(\tau e=2 \mathrm{s}\); after 1 s, \(M=0.6\) and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the instantaneous update magnitude \(\eta Me\). The reward updates this connection by approximately +0.0364. Why should a dopamine pulse without preceding eligibility not selectively strengthen one stimulus–action synapse? The third factor broadcasts the outcome, but local eligibility identifies the synapse that participated in the action; without eligibility, there is no correct credit address. Equating dopamine with a pure reward scalar. Ignoring eligibility decay and claiming that any arbitrarily long delay can be assigned locally.

title: Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium
subtitle: Lecture 24 · Lecture24-LearningFromRewards.pdf, p. 2
text: How does baseline subtraction remove an uninformative reward offset and make choices above and below average update in opposite directions? For eligibility e of a choice, let \(\Delta w=\eta (R-b)e\). If \(b=E[R]\), then \(E[\Delta w]/\eta =E[Re]-E[R]E[e]=\operatorname{Cov}(R,e)\). Only covariation between reward and that eligibility drives average learning; adding the same constant to every reward does not change the covariance. A baseline may be a global running average or depend on state or choice. A global baseline has lower variance but can be biased when reward scales differ across states. A state-dependent value baseline is more precise but requires additional parameters. For its expected conditional dependence to remain valid, the baseline must not improperly inspect the outcome of the current action. In a stochastic two-choice learner, selecting A raises its preference when RA exceeds baseline and lowers it when RA falls below baseline. An interior long-run equilibrium requires equal expected advantage for both actions that continue to be sampled; otherwise preference keeps drifting toward one side. An action whose probability falls to zero no longer updates, so exploration remains important for detecting environmental change. Baseline subtraction does not guarantee bounded weights. Eligibility, choice nonlinearity, learning rate, and reward nonstationarity all affect stability. Short-term lag in the baseline can cause transient overshoot after reward probability changes. Plot reward, baseline, advantage, and choice probability together; one weight curve cannot identify a unique mechanism. An average baseline turns expected updating into reward–eligibility covariance. A state-dependent baseline can reduce error in heterogeneous environments. At an interior equilibrium, the expected advantages of actions that remain selected are equal. For four trials, \(R=[1,0,1,0]\), \(e=[2,1,0,1]\), \(b=0.5\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the average update. The mean update is 0. Why does an underestimated baseline produce systematic positive drift? The mean of R-b becomes positive. If mean eligibility is also positive, an offset update appears that is unrelated to genuine reward–eligibility covariance. Treating the baseline as removing the learning signal from reward. Using the current outcome itself as a baseline that leaks action information while still claiming an unbiased estimate.

title: Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging
subtitle: Lecture 24 · Lecture24-LearningFromRewards.pdf, p. 3
text: When does the choice ratio track the obtained-reward ratio, and which behavioral and learning assumptions support that relationship? A common form of the matching law is \(CA/CB\approx RA/RB\), where C counts choices and R counts obtained rewards over a time window. It describes allocation, not a deterministic rule for each choice. If scheduled rewards accumulate while an option is unchosen, the next payoff opportunity on the neglected side rises, creating negative feedback that draws choices back. At an interior equilibrium, choice-conditioned expected rewards \(qA=E[R|A]\) and \(qB=E[R|B]\) are equal; otherwise an advantage rule keeps increasing preference for the better side. If obtained reward rate on each side is approximated by total rewards divided by choice count, \(qA\approx RA/CA\) and \(qB\approx RB/CB\). Equating them gives \(CA/CB\approx RA/RB\). The derivation assumes continued sampling of both sides, an approximately stationary reward schedule, comparable cost per choice, and negligible changeover delay, satiety, and risk sensitivity. When reward magnitudes differ, match obtained value rather than raw count. Undermatching, overmatching, and bias can be described by generalized matching: \(\log(CA/CB)=a \log(RA/RB)+\log b\). A fly mushroom-body model can connect odor features, action channels, dopaminergic outcome signals, and stochastic choice. On original Page 3, \(Y=\sum _iW_{i}X_{i}\) and approach probability decreases as Y rises, so the reward-modulated rule is ΔW_i=-ηX_i(R-⟨R⟩): reward above baseline lowers Y and therefore raises approach probability. The minus sign follows from the convention for Y. If the postsynaptic variable is defined instead as approach drive, the same covariance logic takes a positive sign. Reproducing matching does not mean that a fly explicitly computes a ratio; local covariance updates and choice competition can generate the aggregate relationship. Matching relates long-run choice allocation to obtained-reward allocation. Equal choice-conditioned return is the core equilibrium condition. A local learner can generate a ratio law without an explicit division neuron; interpret the update sign together with the direction convention of the choice readout. Across 100 choices, A is selected 60 times and earns 30 rewards; B is selected 40 times and earns 20 rewards. Check the conditional returns and both ratios. Conditional returns are equal and both ratios are 1.5, consistent with matching. Why does a matching curve not prove that the animal explicitly computes RA/RB? A long-run ratio can emerge automatically from local prediction-error updates and stochastic choice; the behavioral equality does not uniquely identify the internal algorithm. Counting only reward occurrences even when reward magnitudes differ. Ignoring an unexplored action and forcing the interior-equilibrium derivation onto a boundary solution.

title: Rescorla–Wagner, blocking, and the temporal-difference bridge
subtitle: Lecture 24 · Lecture24-LearningFromRewards.pdf, p. 4
text: Why does prediction error stop learning once reward is predicted, and how does this naturally produce blocking? Use features x to predict value linearly as \(V=w^\mathrm{T} x\), with target reward R. The squared error \(L=1/2(R-V)^2\) has negative-gradient update \(\Delta w=\eta (R-V)x\). An active cue increases in weight when R exceeds prediction and decreases when R falls below prediction. When \(V=R\), prediction error is zero and learning stops. Blocking first trains cue A→reward until wA predicts R. Then A and novel cue B appear together, so total prediction \(V=wA+wB\approx R\), the error is nearly zero, and wB changes little. A pure reward-gated Hebbian rule notices only that B is active and rewarded and incorrectly predicts strong learning to B. Blocking is therefore important behavioral evidence for error correction. When reward is delayed, the target for the current state includes not only immediate R but next-state value. The temporal-difference error \(\delta t=Rt+1+\gamma V(st+1)-V(st)\) compares predictions at consecutive times. A predictive cue can back up value before reward arrives, shifting the reward response toward the cue. Rescorla–Wagner and TD both depend on feature representation. Blocking changes if A and B are highly similar or a hidden context shifts; zero error may also reflect reduced attention. A model account should state alternative mechanisms and distinguish them with unblocking, reward revaluation, and trial-level learning curves. The negative gradient gives a prediction-error × feature update. Blocking occurs because the total prediction from the compound cue already equals reward. TD error propagates delayed reward backward through next-state value. Reward is \(R=1\). After A-alone training, \(wA=0.9\) and novel B has \(wB=0\). On a compound trial, \(xA=xB=1\) and \(\eta =0.2\). Find both weight updates. wA becomes 0.92 and wB becomes 0.02, showing strong but incomplete blocking. If reward is unchanged but the prediction from old cue A is removed, why does B begin learning again? The total prediction falls and positive prediction error returns. Because B is active, it now receives an update—the logic of unblocking. Explaining blocking only from co-occurrence of B and reward. Excluding an attentional alternative without a corresponding experiment.

title: Temporal features, state–action value, and choice
subtitle: Lecture 24 · Lecture24-LearningFromRewards.pdf, p. 5
text: Why does the same physical cue need different features and Q values at different times and for different actions? In a delayed task, expand a sustained cue into time-specific features x1,x2,… so the learner knows which interval follows the cue. TD updates begin with features near reward and propagate to earlier features across trials. One time-invariant feature cannot easily represent when reward will arrive or predict a negative error at omission time. State value \(V(s)\) is expected future return from state s under a policy. Action value \(Q(s,a)\) additionally specifies the first action. Choice compares Q values for multiple actions in the same state using a greedy, softmax, or other stochastic rule. A high V does not identify the best action; Q assigns credit to an action channel. Greedy \(\operatorname{argmax}_{a}\) Q exploits current knowledge but may never try an action that was initially undervalued. Temperature or \(\epsilon\) exploration supplies sampling. Biological choice also depends on effort, uncertainty, and habit, so correlation of a neural signal with Q does not prove an exact maximization operation. Features determine generalization. A shared feature transfers learning from one state–action pair to similar situations, improving sample efficiency but potentially causing erroneous transfer. To test a Q-like signal, manipulate state, action, and future reward together and verify that immediate reward, movement vigor, or state value alone cannot explain it. Temporal features represent different time positions after a cue. Q includes an explicit action condition absent from V. Feature sharing trades useful generalization against misgeneralization. In one state, \(QA=2\), \(QB=1\), and inverse temperature \(\beta =\ln 3\). Find \(P(A)=\exp(\beta QA)/[\exp(\beta QA)+\exp(\beta QB)]\). The choice probability of A is 0.75. Why does equal state value not imply that two actions are equally good? V is a policy-weighted average. One action may have high Q and another low Q while producing the same aggregate V under a particular policy. Conflating \(Q(s,a)\) with immediate reward. Ignoring the decisive role of feature representation in the transfer of learning.

title: Dopamine RPE timelines and the boundary with action selection
subtitle: Lecture 24 · Lecture24-LearningFromRewards.pdf, p. 6
text: How can one TD error explain early reward, a predictive cue, and omitted reward? Before learning, reward is unexpected: Rt+1 is positive at reward time while prior V is low, so \(\delta\) has a positive transient. After cue–reward pairing, state value following the cue rises; cue onset causes a positive \(\Delta V\) and \(\delta\) transfers to the cue. When reward arrives as predicted, Rt+1 is offset by the drop in value and \(\delta\) at reward time is nearly zero. If predicted reward is omitted at its expected time, \(Rt+1=0\) and next value collapses, making \(\delta\) negative at that moment and producing a dip. Accurate dip timing requires a temporal representation of when reward should arrive; a one-state-per-trial model cannot place the negative error precisely. Together, the three timelines constrain a prediction-error account rather than a pure reward response. Keep value, RPE, and action signals separate. Value may persist after a cue, \(\delta\) marks a change or surprise, and action selection compares Q. Dopamine populations are heterogeneous, and movement and salience also influence responses. The course figure supports a canonical RPE pattern, but any single-cell response must be interpreted alongside task events, expected value, and movement controls. For plasticity, dopamine-like \(\delta\) acts as a third factor on synapses whose eligibility persists. For choice, learned Q changes the policy. These are distinct stages: a dopamine perturbation may affect both learning and performance. Testing choice only after training cannot tell whether the perturbation altered an update or momentary vigor. RPE is jointly determined by actual reward and successive value predictions. Cue transfer and an omission dip require a temporal state representation. Effects of dopamine perturbation on learning and performance must be separated. Before the reward deadline, \(V_{\mathrm{current}}=0.8\); afterward \(V_{\mathrm{next}}=0\), with \(R=0\) and \(\gamma =0.95\). Find \(\delta\). \(\delta =-0.8\) value units. Why does an omission dip support prediction error more strongly than merely observing no burst at reward time? It is a negative signal below baseline timed to the expected reward. A purely nonnegative reward detector cannot naturally generate this timed negative response. Writing that the cue itself contains physical reward because it evokes a response. Labeling every dopamine change an RPE without controlling movement and salience.

title: Lecture 25: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning
subtitle: How can an MDP formalize agent–environment interaction, how does recursively decomposing discounted return yield the Bellman equation, and how do Q-learning and a generative model learn an action policy?
text: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning How can an MDP formalize agent–environment interaction, how does recursively decomposing discounted return yield the Bellman equation, and how do Q-learning and a generative model learn an action policy? agent/state/action/reward → Markov property → discounted return → V/Q/policy → Bellman backup → Q-learning/exploration Define an MDP completely in terms of agent, state, action, reward, and a transition distribution, and use counterexamples to test whether a state satisfies the Markov property. Derive discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\) from a reward sequence, computing both a finite chain and an infinite geometric series by hand. Derive the Bellman expectation and optimality equations by splitting return after its first step, making explicit that the maximum ranges over actions in the next state. Carry out tabular Q-learning and ε-greedy exploration update by update, distinguishing the behavior policy, target, and off-policy update. Compare model-free learning, model-based learning, generative representations, and replay while rigorously separating algorithmic variables from hippocampal evidence. The central MDP claim is not that the environment has no history, but that the chosen state representation makes the future conditionally independent of earlier history given current state and action. Discounted return decomposes recursively into immediate reward plus \(\gamma\) times future return, yielding the Bellman optimality equation. Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman error for an off-policy bootstrap update. Model-based RL also learns a transition/reward model and can improve sample efficiency with simulated experience or replay. Equating the Markov property with an environment that has no history. Confusing \(V_{\pi }\), \(Q_{\pi }\), \(V^{*}\), and \(Q^{*}\). Omitting the transition expectation from the Bellman equation. Using the behavior action in a Q-learning target and inadvertently writing SARSA. Assuming that the random branch of ε-greedy samples only nongreedy actions without stating that convention. Equating model-free learning with an absence of internal representation. Equating hippocampal replay directly with an exact Bellman backup. Q-learning is not a synonym for every TD-learning method, and hippocampal replay is not directly equivalent to an exact Bellman backup; evidence and inference must be distinguished explicitly. MDP transition/reward model \(p(s' , r|s, a)\) Markov state discounted return Gt = \(\gamma \) k Rt+k+1 \(k\ge 0\) \(0\le \gamma <1\) or a finite episode state value \(V_{\pi } (s) = E_{\pi } [G_{t} |s_{t} = s]\) policy \(\pi\) state-action value \(Q_{\pi } (s, a) = E_{\pi } [G_{t} |s_{t} = s, a_{t} = a]\) first action fixed Bellman optimality \(Q\ast  = E[R + \gamma  \max Q\ast  ]\) optimal continuation tabular Q-learning Q ← Q + α(R + γ max Q′ − Q) sampled transition ε-greedy exploration \(\pi \epsilon  = (1 - \epsilon )\)greedy \(+ \epsilon \mathrm{random}\) finite action set reinforcement learning A framework that learns a policy or value through interaction and rewards. agent A learner that selects actions and updates an internal policy or model. state An environment representation used to predict the future and select an action. Markov property The conditional independence of the future from earlier history given the current state and action. policy A mapping from states to action probabilities. return The discounted sum of future rewards. Bellman equation A recursive self-consistency relation for value. Q-learning A model-free, off-policy TD control algorithm. exploration-exploitation The tradeoff between gathering new information and selecting the currently best action. model-based reinforcement learning A reinforcement-learning approach that learns or uses an environment model for planning. replay A neural or computational process that reinstates or simulates state sequences offline. At the same maze location, available routes differ depending on whether a door is open. Is location alone a Markov state? The Markov property requires the next transition and reward to be independent of earlier history once current state and action are given. Usually not. Include the door state or sufficient history to predict it. If every step forever gives reward=1 and \(\gamma =0.9\), what is the return? This sum is bounded only when \(\gamma <1\) or the episode is finite. The infinite geometric sum is \(1/(1-0.9)=10\). Which variable does the maximum in the Bellman optimality equation range over? Do not maximize again over the already executed current action or over the random reward itself. It maximizes Q over the available next action \(a'\) in the next state \(s'\). Given \(Q=2\), \(R=1\), \(\gamma =0.9\), \(\max Q_{\mathrm{next}}=4\), and \(\alpha =0.5\), what is Q after one update? The update moves an \(\alpha\) fraction toward the target; it does not replace Q directly with reward. The target is 4.6, TD error is 2.6, and new \(Q=2+0.5\times 2.6=3.3\). Hippocampal replay resembles simulated experience. Does that prove that every replay event performs Q-learning? Replay may supply sequences for offline updating or planning, but a reinstated sequence alone cannot distinguish Q-learning, a model-based backup, memory consolidation, or another computation. No. Reinstated content is compatible with planning, but the particular update rule, target, and causal role require further experiments. Why might adding the trial number to state improve training prediction but still be a poor representation? It may memorize samples without capturing generalizable, future-relevant structure and will perform poorly in held-out contexts. This is the distinction tested in MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state. Worked example — Repair a non-Markov state: An agent is at the same room location x. If it previously collected a key, opening the door gives 10; otherwise hitting the door gives 0. Give a minimal state extension. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? title: MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state
subtitle: Lecture 25 · Lecture25-ReinforcementLearning.pdf, p. 1
text: What information must enter the state so that a one-step transition model no longer depends on earlier history? An MDP is defined by states, actions, reward, and the transition–reward distribution \(p(s',r|s,a)\). The Markov property says that, conditioned on current s and a, the next outcome does not change with earlier trajectory. It does not require a deterministic environment: one s,a pair may lead randomly to several \(s'\) values, provided the probabilities are determined fully by current state. State representation is a modeling choice. Location may be insufficient in a Tolman maze because door status, food depletion, or latent context changes the future. Omitting such variables aliases states, causing Q values to average conflicting outcomes and making learning appear unstable. Including the complete history always restores prediction but sacrifices compression and generalization. The goal is a state that is sufficient without being excessive. Policy \(\pi (a|s)\) specifies a choice distribution. Environmental transitions and policy are distinct sources of randomness: one determines where an action leads and the other which action is selected in a state. Separate them in causal tests. Changing choice frequency changes the observed transition distribution but does not imply that physical \(p(s'|s,a)\) changed. Test the Markov assumption by comparing held-out likelihood under a state-only predictor and a history-augmented predictor. If past events still predict \(s'\) or r after conditioning on s,a, the state is insufficient. With finite data, failure to detect a history effect is not proof; task design should deliberately probe identical observations under different hidden contexts. The Markov property permits stochastic transitions but requires conditional independence from history. State aliasing incorrectly averages distinct futures. Policy randomness and environmental randomness must be separated. An agent is at the same room location x. If it previously collected a key, opening the door gives 10; otherwise hitting the door gives 0. Give a minimal state extension. Use the pair of location and key status as the state. Why might adding the trial number to state improve training prediction but still be a poor representation? It may memorize samples without capturing generalizable, future-relevant structure and will perform poorly in held-out contexts. Misunderstanding Markov as requiring a unique next state. Equating the visible screen directly with a sufficient state.

title: Discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\)
subtitle: Lecture 25 · Lecture25-ReinforcementLearning.pdf, p. 2
text: How can a sequence of future rewards be compressed into one value while preserving the distinction between policy and the first action? Return from time t is \(G_{t}=\sum _{k=0}\infty \gamma ^kR_{t+k+1}\). The first term is undiscounted, the following reward is multiplied by \(\gamma\), and so on. \(\gamma\) is not a learning rate; it changes temporal preference and mathematical convergence of the objective. A finite episode can use \(\gamma =1\), whereas continuing positive reward generally requires \(\gamma <1\). \(V_{\pi }(s)=E_{\pi }[G_{t}|s_{t}=s]\) averages over environmental randomness and future policy actions. \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)=E_{\pi }[G_{t}|s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a]\) fixes only the first action, after which \(\pi\) is followed. Consequently, \(V_{\pi }(s)=\sum _{a}\pi (a|s)Q_{\pi }(s,a)\); under a deterministic policy, only the selected action contributes. Value scale varies with reward units and \(\gamma\). If reward normalization differs across animals or sessions, V magnitudes cannot be compared directly. The rough time horizon associated with \(\gamma\) is about \(1/(1-\gamma )\) steps, but episodic termination and transition structure alter the actual influence. When relating a neural signal to V or Q, control immediate reward, state identity, and action. State value may appear before several actions, whereas Q should vary with the candidate action. Greater firing on high-reward trials alone cannot distinguish received reward, expected return, and movement vigor. Return is the discounted sum of future rewards. V fixes the state; Q additionally fixes the first action. \(\gamma\) sets the temporal weighting of the objective, not the update step size. Future rewards are 2, 0, and 4, after which the episode terminates; \(\gamma =0.5\). Find Gt. \(G_{t}=3\). Why does a in \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)\) fix only the first step? The definition conditions on \(a_{t}=a\). Future actions are sampled from \(\pi\) beginning in the next state, so Q evaluates 'take a first, then follow \(\pi\).' Treating \(\gamma\) as learning rate \(\alpha\). Conflating a single-trial return with expected value.

title: Bellman recursion: from the entire future to a one-step backup
subtitle: Lecture 25 · Lecture25-ReinforcementLearning.pdf, p. 3
text: How is the Bellman equation derived from return without placing the maximum over the wrong variable? Return decomposes as \(G_{t}=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}\). Conditioning on s,a and taking the expectation gives \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)=E[R+\gamma \sum _{a'}\pi (a'|s')Q_{\pi }(s',a')|s,a]\). This follows only from total expectation and the return decomposition; it does not assume deterministic transitions. Optimal Q assumes the best action is selected after the next state, replacing the policy-weighted average with \(\max_{a'}Q^{*}(s',a')\). The maximum lies inside the expectation because each random next state has its own best action. In general, one cannot average Q across all \(s'\) first and then select a single common action. The Bellman operator maps one Q table to another. In the tabular discounted setting with \(\gamma <1\) it is a contraction, so repeated backups approach a unique fixed point. As \(\gamma\) approaches 1, information reaches farther but contraction slows. Function approximation and off-policy sampling can invalidate this simple convergence guarantee. A 'backup' does not imply that the biological brain scans a table cell by cell; it is a computational relation. Neural data can test successor value, RPE, and revaluation, but naming a brain region the Bellman operator requires additional mechanistic evidence. Keep the algorithmic derivation separate from biological mapping. Bellman recursion follows from the one-step decomposition of Gt. The optimal maximum ranges over the next action separately for each next state. A tabular contraction guarantee does not automatically extend to arbitrary function approximation. After an action, with probability 0.5 the agent receives \(R=1\) and reaches s1, where maxQ\((s_{1})=4\); with probability 0.5 it receives \(R=3\) and reaches s2, where maxQ\((s_{2})=2\). Let \(\gamma =0.9\). The Bellman target for this state–action pair is 4.7. Why can the maximum not be moved outside the expectation while fixing the same \(a'\)? Different random next states can have different best actions. Averaging first would force one action across states and change the optimal-continuation problem. Applying the maximum to the current action that has already been executed. Extending a tabular convergence theorem unconditionally to a deep network.

title: Tabular Q-learning and exploration
subtitle: Lecture 25 · Lecture25-ReinforcementLearning.pdf, p. 4
text: How does one sampled transition update one Q entry, and why does exploration not conflict with a greedy target? Q-learning observes \((s,a,R,s')\), constructs target \(y=R+\gamma maxa'Q(s',a')\), computes error \(\delta =y-Q(s,a)\), and updates \(Q\leftarrow Q+\alpha \delta\). Only the visited (s,a) entry changes directly. Across repeated random samples, its mean target approaches the Bellman expectation. The future term is zero on a terminal transition. Q-learning is off-policy: behavior can explore with ε-greedy while the target still uses the greedy maximum. ε-greedy selects a current greedy action with probability \(1-\epsilon\) and samples uniformly from the action set with probability \(\epsilon\). If the random branch can also select the greedy action, total greedy probability includes \(\epsilon /|A|\). Exploration discovers undervalued options, although a fixed large \(\epsilon\) sacrifices reward indefinitely. If \(\alpha\) is too large, new samples overwrite old knowledge and cause oscillation; if too small, adaptation is slow. Tabular convergence requires sufficient visitation and suitable decreasing steps. Maximizing noisy estimates also creates positive maximization bias, which Double Q methods can reduce. The course equation is the basic tabular form and does not imply that function approximation is always stable. In behavioral analysis, exploration should not simply be labeled random error; animals may direct exploration toward uncertain actions. Fitting ε-greedy to systematic uncertainty seeking misattributes it to value or temperature. Model comparisons should include alternatives such as softmax and directed exploration. Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman target to update one state–action entry. The behavior policy can explore while the target policy remains greedy. The convergence conditions for the tabular equation differ from those for function approximation. Initially \(Q=0\), with \(\gamma =0.5\) and \(\alpha =0.5\). The first transition has \(R=2\) and next maxQ=4; the second visit to the same entry has \(R=0\) and next maxQ=2. After both updates, \(Q=1.5\). Why can the random branch of ε-greedy still select the greedy action? The random branch samples uniformly from all actions, including the greedy action, so total greedy probability exceeds \(1-\epsilon\). Setting Q directly to immediate reward. Assuming that off-policy learning removes the need for data covering unvisited actions.

title: Tolman mazes, latent state, and generative maps
subtitle: Lecture 25 · Lecture25-ReinforcementLearning.pdf, p. 5
text: Why can a map-like model adapt immediately after reward revaluation or route closure while cached values may fail? Tolman-style maze results suggest that animals can learn environmental structure rather than a single stimulus–response chain. When reward location changes or a familiar route closes, an agent with a transition map and reward model can plan before traversing every route again. A purely cached model-free Q estimate generally needs new prediction errors to change gradually. A generative model \(p(s',r|s,a)\) can simulate candidate futures. State representation must distinguish locations, contexts, and goals while allowing similar routes to share structure. Hippocampal place or state coding and the cognitive-map hypothesis provide a biological bridge, but place activity also depends on movement, sensory, and task variables. Planning can use tree search, dynamic programming, or sampled trajectories, with computational cost growing with horizon and branching. Model-based flexibility costs memory and computation; habitual cached values are fast. Behavior often mixes both, so one detour result should not assign an animal to a pure algorithmic category. A key experiment revalues an outcome or transition, then tests choice without direct reward experience on the new path. Immediate adjustment supports model-based use of information, but instruction, sensory cues, and simple heuristics must still be ruled out. A neural perturbation that selectively impairs revaluation while preserving a well-trained habit strengthens the circuit-level account. A generative model can simulate a future before it is experienced. Model-based learning is flexible but computationally costly; model-free learning is fast but updates with delay. A hippocampal map bridges evidence and theory; it is not a one-to-one mapping onto an algorithm. In state s, action A deterministically reaches terminal state s1 with reward 5; B reaches terminal state s2 with reward 3. Outcome devaluation then informs the agent that reward at s1 has changed to -1, while transitions are unchanged. Compare model-based and cached model-free choice. Model-based choice switches to B, whereas cached model-free choice may initially remain unchanged. Why is immediate sensitivity to revaluation not sufficient proof of a complete internal map? Other rules, instructions, or direct cues can also alter choice rapidly; constrain the explanation with multiple novel transitions and control conditions. Calling a place field a transition model. Forcing behavior generated by a mixed strategy into a purely model-free or model-based category.

title: Simulated experience, hippocampal replay, and sample efficiency
subtitle: Lecture 25 · Lecture25-ReinforcementLearning.pdf, p. 6
text: How can offline replay turn one real experience into multiple internal backups, and what are the evidential limits? A model-based agent can sample an imagined transition from its learned model and apply the same Bellman or Q update used for a real transition. The Dyna framework uses real experience to update both model and value, then performs simulated backups between interactions to improve sample efficiency. An inaccurate model repeatedly propagates bias and can be exploited by the planner. Hippocampal replay reinstates place-cell sequences during rest or sleep. Sequences may run forward or backward, be temporally compressed, and favor reward or future paths. Replay is compatible with memory consolidation, planning, and credit propagation, but detecting a sequence does not show that downstream circuitry performs a particular numerical update; replay may serve several functions. A causal test selectively disrupts task-relevant sequences while preserving overall sleep, arousal, and firing, then measures later planning or learning. One can also ask whether replay content predicts the next choice, reorganizes after reward relocation, and precedes model-consistent changes in cortical or striatal value signals. Real and simulated samples come from different distributions. Prioritizing transitions with large prediction error or policy relevance can improve efficiency but also introduces sampling bias. An off-policy update may tolerate some bias; estimating behavioral averages requires importance correction. Calling replay merely 'repeated memory' misses the computationally crucial selection rule. Simulated transitions can repeatedly drive value backups. Evidence of a replay sequence does not specify the downstream learning rule. Prioritized replay increases efficiency and changes the sample distribution. One Q estimate starts at 0 with \(\alpha =0.5\) and \(\gamma =0\). A real reward is 2; the model then simulates rewards 2 and 0. Update in order. After three backups, \(Q=0.75\), showing that simulated samples also alter the estimate. Why is more replay not always better? If the learned model has systematic error, repeated simulation amplifies its bias; coverage, priority, and model uncertainty must be balanced. Equating a compressed sequence directly with a Bellman backup. Reporting sample efficiency without measuring planning failures caused by model bias.

title: Lecture 26: Hopfield Associative Memory
subtitle: How do symmetric Hebbian recurrent weights turn random binary patterns into attractors, and how do energy descent, crosstalk noise, and loading \(\alpha\) determine pattern completion and capacity?
text: Hopfield Associative Memory How do symmetric Hebbian recurrent weights turn random binary patterns into attractors, and how do energy descent, crosstalk noise, and loading \(\alpha\) determine pattern completion and capacity? Hebbian assembly → binary asynchronous dynamics → energy → stored attractors/basins → spurious mixtures → signal+crosstalk From Hebbian cell assemblies to the binary Hopfield abstraction, distinguish the biological hypothesis, state variable, encoding rule, and retrieval dynamics. Execute asynchronous sign updates by hand, compute overlap, and explain how symmetric weights and a zero diagonal support energy descent. Derive the energy change from flipping one neuron and the local field for a \(P=1\) stored pattern, identifying aligned, antialigned, and spurious attractors. Separate a multi-pattern local field into signal and crosstalk, estimating variance, error probability, and loading \(\alpha =P/N\). title: Explicit memory, Hebbian assemblies, and pattern completion
subtitle: Lecture 26 · Lecture26-Memory-HopfieldModel.pdf, p. 1
text: How can a shared-activity cell assembly yield a testable encoding–cue–retrieval chain? The Hebbian assembly hypothesis proposes that cells jointly active in an experience develop stronger mutual connections. Encoding changes the connections, a partial cue reactivates some members, and recurrent excitation recruits the missing members to complete the pattern. An engram is a cellular ensemble causally involved in memory storage and expression; activation correlation alone is insufficient for that label. The Hopfield abstraction represents an assembly by binary pattern \(\xi\) and sets \(W_{ij}=(1/N)\sum \mu \xi _{i}^{\mu }\xi _{j}^{\mu }\), with \(W_{ii}=0\). Same-sign pairs receive positive weights and opposite-sign pairs negative weights. Real synapses obey Dale's law and constraints from sparse connectivity and spiking; the classic dense matrix first illustrates a computational principle. Retrieval cue \(S(0)\) has overlap \(m=(1/N)\sum i\xi iS_{i}\) with the target pattern. \(m=1\) is an exact match, \(m=0\) is uncorrelated on average, and \(m=-1\) is the global antipattern. If the cue lies in the target basin, asynchronous dynamics correct errors progressively. Basin size measures tolerated corruption, not merely whether the fixed point exists. A causal engram experiment must test sufficiency and necessity separately: does artificial activation of a tagged ensemble trigger memory-like behavior, and does its suppression selectively impair retrieval? Even if both hold, binary Hopfield units and Hebbian weights remain a model mapping; behavior does not identify the exact W directly. A cell assembly supplies a hypothesis for pattern completion. The Hopfield outer-product rule is an abstract encoding rule. Overlap measures cue similarity, whereas a basin measures retrieval robustness. A 100-bit pattern has 20 flipped bits. Find its overlap with the original pattern. The overlap is 0.6. Why does \(m>0\) not guarantee successful retrieval? It measures only similarity at the start. The basin also depends on memory load, the particular crosstalk, update order, and network parameters. Automatically calling activation-tagged cells a causal engram. Treating positive overlap as a sufficient condition for success.

title: Binary asynchronous dynamics and stored random patterns
subtitle: Lecture 26 · Lecture26-Memory-HopfieldModel.pdf, p. 2
text: When one unit is updated at a time, how is the algorithm executed precisely and convergence determined? At each step choose i, compute local field \(h_{i}=\sum _j W_{ij} S_{j}\), and set \(S_{i}\leftarrow \operatorname{sgn}(h_{i})\). \(W_{ii}=0\) prevents the unit's own state from voting directly. A tie rule for \(h_{i}=0\) must be specified in advance, such as retaining the old value or choosing a fixed sign. Update order may be random or sequential; different orders can reach different basins, but every step uses the latest state. One sweep commonly means an average of N updates and does not imply convergence. Stop only after a full check finds no unit that would change or when both state and energy reach a fixed point. A finite deterministic asynchronous system under strict energy descent cannot visit new states forever, although arbitrary flipping on zero-field ties can create degeneracy. Stored patterns are often independent, unbiased random ±1 vectors for tractable capacity analysis. This is not a statistical model of natural memory: real patterns are correlated and sparse. Correlation increases structured crosstalk but may also support category structure, so randomness is a baseline assumption rather than a fact. A synchronous update computes every new state from the old state at once and may produce a two-cycle; the classic single-flip energy proof does not apply directly. Code and hand calculations must say whether updates occur in place. Disguising a synchronous vectorized multiplication as asynchronous changes the dynamical conclusion. An asynchronous update immediately writes back one unit. Convergence requires a fixed-state check, not a preset number of sweeps. Unbiased random patterns are an analytical assumption. Let \(h_{i}=-0.7\) and current \(S_{i}=+1\), with the rule that \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)\) retains the current value. What are the new state and flip indicator? The new \(S_{i}=-1\) and \(\Delta S_{i}=-2\). Why does updating every neuron once not guarantee a fixed point? After an early unit is updated, later unit changes can alter its local field, so another complete sweep without changes is required. Updating all units at once from the old state and calling it asynchronous. Ignoring the tie convention at \(h=0\).

title: Energy descent and the \(P=1\) stored attractor
subtitle: Lecture 26 · Lecture26-Memory-HopfieldModel.pdf, p. 3
text: Why do symmetric weights make a single-unit update lower energy, and why are both a stored pattern and its antipattern stable? Define energy \(E=-(1/2)\sum _i\sum _{j\ne i}W_{ij}S_{i}S_{j}\). The factor 1/2 prevents double-counting a symmetric pair. When only unit i flips, all other pairs are unchanged. Using \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\) reduces the energy change to \(\Delta E=-\Delta S_{i} h_{i}\). If new \(S_{i}\) aligns with \(h_{i}\), then a flip gives \(\Delta E<0\) and no flip gives 0. For \(P=1\), let \(W_{ij}=\xi _{i}\xi _{j}/N\). Substituting \(S=\xi\) gives \(h_{i}=(\xi _{i}/N)\sum _{j\ne i}\xi _{j}^{2}=((N-1)/N)\xi _{i}\), so \(\operatorname{sign}(h_{i})=\xi _{i}\) and the pattern is a fixed point. Substituting \(S=-\xi\) gives \(h_{i}=-((N-1)/N)\xi _{i}\), aligned with \(S_{i}=-\xi _{i}\), so the antipattern is stable too. Nonincreasing energy guarantees arrival at some local minimum, not the global minimum or target memory. A noisy cue may cross a basin boundary and reach a spurious state. Symmetric W is central to the proof. Asymmetric plasticity or delays can generate cycles, chaos, or sequential dynamics, so the same Lyapunov function cannot still be used to claim convergence. \(W_{ii}=0\) removes self-coupling and subtracts one term from the \(P=1\) field. For large N, (N-1)/N approaches 1, but a small-N example cannot replace it directly by 1. Keeping the finite term teaches the distinction between a finite-size calculation and a large-N approximation. Symmetric asynchronous dynamics makes energy nonincreasing. For \(P=1\), \(\xi\) and \(-\xi\) are both stable because of global sign symmetry. Energy descent does not guarantee retrieval of the desired memory. Let \(N=5\) and pattern \(\xi =(1,-1,1,-1,1)\), with the network in \(\xi\). Find the local field of unit1. \(h_{1}=0.8\), so unit1 remains +1. Why does the derivation of \(\Delta E\) fail when W is asymmetric? Pair terms with i as the first and second index cannot be combined into the same local field, so one scalar energy need not decline under updating. Omitting the energy factor 1/2 and then double-counting pairs. Automatically calling every local minimum a stored pattern.

title: Spurious mixtures and the signal-plus-crosstalk decomposition
subtitle: Lecture 26 · Lecture26-Memory-HopfieldModel.pdf, p. 4
text: When several patterns are stored, how does the local field contain both target signal and interference from other memories? While retrieving pattern1, set \(S\approx \xi ^{1}\). After substituting Hebbian W, the \(\mu =1\) term of \(h_{i}\) aligns with \(\xi _{i}^{1}\) and is the signal; terms with \(\mu >1\) contain random overlaps and form crosstalk. Even when every interference pattern is orthogonal to the target on average, finite-N overlap is nonzero, and many small terms can flip individual bits. An odd mixture can be written \(S_{i}=\operatorname{sgn}(\xi _{i}^{1}+\xi _{i}^{2}+\xi _{i}^{3})\). A component-wise vote among three patterns has no tie and can be self-consistent under the Hebbian field. The mixture is not any one input training pattern but can be a fixed point, shrinking usable basins and causing erroneous combinatorial recall. A two-pattern mixture has component ties, so stability depends more strongly on the tie rule and bias; odd mixtures are more typical in the dense unbiased model. Pattern correlations produce structured mixtures, so not every false memory should be attributed to independent Gaussian noise. Identify a spurious state by comparing its overlap with every stored pattern, not by low energy alone. Basin boundaries shrink as P increases. A cue can have its highest overlap with the target and still flow to a mixture because all stored patterns jointly shape the energy landscape. Any analogy to experimental 'memory blending' is only a hypothesis; real memory distortion also depends on semantic inference, overlap during encoding, and systems consolidation. A local field separates into target-aligned signal and crosstalk from multiple memories. An odd component-wise majority can form a spurious attractor. Neither the lowest energy nor the highest initial overlap guarantees target retrieval. At one unit, three patterns have bits (+1,+1,-1). Find the odd-mixture bit. What if they are (+1,-1,-1)? The two mixture bits are +1 and -1, respectively. Why does low mixture energy not make it a correct memory? Correctness is defined by the training target and behavioral identity; energy determines dynamical stability and does not know which patterns were designated as memories. Mistaking a near-zero mean crosstalk for zero crosstalk in every instance. Using a spurious attractor to explain every human false memory directly.

title: Gaussian crosstalk, loading, and classic capacity
subtitle: Lecture 26 · Lecture26-Memory-HopfieldModel.pdf, p. 5
text: Why does \(\alpha =P/N\) control the scale of random interference, and why is 0.138 not a universal constant for every associative memory? For independent unbiased patterns, one nontarget overlap \(\sum _j\xi _{j}^{\mu }\xi _{j}^{1}\) has \(\operatorname{mean} 0\) and variance approximately N. After multiplication by 1/N, one pattern contributes field variance of about 1/N. Summing P-1 nearly independent terms gives crosstalk variance \((P-1)/N\approx \alpha\). This motivates a Gaussian-noise approximation through the central limit theorem. A target bit is stable when \(\xi _{i}^{1}h_{i}>0\): unit-aligned signal 1 plus noise remains positive. If \(\mathrm{noise}\approx N(0,\alpha )\), the single-step error is approximately \(\Phi (-1/\sqrt \alpha )\) and rises with \(\alpha\). Unit errors feed back into the fields, so full self-consistency gives the classic dense-model retrieval threshold \(\alpha c\) of about 0.138 rather than the simple single-step tail alone. P can grow linearly with N, but 'capacity=Pmax' depends on the retrieval criterion, acceptable error, and basin size. The value 0.138 assumes symmetric dense connectivity, unbiased independent random ±1 patterns, Hebbian weights, and classic dynamics. Sparse codes, correlated patterns, alternative rules, or finite N change the number. A spin-glass regime still has many stable states but little overlap with any stored pattern; the network converges without retrieving. Checking energy convergence alone misclassifies success. Also measure target overlap, bit error, basin volume, and trial-to-trial outcomes. Crosstalk variance is approximately the loading \(\alpha\). The Gaussian tail gives an error tendency; the complete critical value requires self-consistency. Convergence and retrieval are distinct evaluation criteria. Let \(\alpha =0.25\), \(\mathrm{signal}=1\), and noise standard deviation \(\sqrt \alpha =0.5\). An error requires \(\mathrm{noise}<-1\), equivalent to standard \(\operatorname{normal} Z<-2\). The rough bit-error rate is about 2.28%. Why does \(\alpha =0.1\) below 0.138 still not guarantee success for every cue? The threshold is a large-N typical statistic under a particular retrieval criterion. Finite patterns, poor cues, basin differences, and random instances can still fail. Treating 0.138 as the capacity ratio of every biological memory. Passing off a one-step Gaussian tail calculation as the full critical derivation.

title: Sparse stochastic associative memory and global inhibition
subtitle: Lecture 26 · Lecture26-Memory-HopfieldModel.pdf, p. 6
text: When a dense ±1 code becomes sparse \({0,1}\) activity, why must threshold, inhibition, and capacity analyses be rewritten? Real ensembles often activate only a fraction a of their units. With \(\xi _{i}\in {0,1}\) and \(P(active)=a\), pattern mean is nonzero. The Hebbian rule should center \(\xi _{i}-a\) to prevent a large positive bias shared by all units. Retrieval can use a probabilistic logistic output rather than a hard sign, with temperature controlling stochasticity. Original Page 6 places global inhibition directly in every weight by subtracting \(\gamma /(aN)\) after the centered Hebbian term. In the local field, this uniform negative term becomes \(-(\gamma /(aN))\sum _jS_{j}\), so a larger active population imposes stronger inhibition on every unit. Together with stochastic threshold u, it constrains total activity near aN. It is not one particular inhibitory neuron; rewriting it as an adaptive threshold requires an explicit mapping to population activity. Sparse codes reduce active overlap between patterns and can improve information per synapse or some capacity measures. Any claim of 'near-optimality' must say whether it measures patterns/neuron, bits/synapse, or retrieval error. A dense-model \(\alpha c=0.138\) cannot be compared directly with one sparse-model number without matching activity and metrics. As temperature \(T\to 0\), a probabilistic update approaches a deterministic threshold. With large T, states become more random and may escape shallow minima. Stochasticity can aid sampling but also impairs stable recall. Evaluate an alternative model with false-positive and false-negative rates, overlap distributions, and capacity as a function of a, T, and inhibition, not only maximum P. Sparse patterns require mean subtraction or threshold control. Global inhibition stabilizes population activity. Capacity comparisons must use the same information and error metrics. Let sparsity \(a=0.1\). What are the centered values of an active bit and an inactive bit, and what is their product? The centered values are 0.9 and -0.1, with product -0.09. Why does an uncentered 0/1 Hebbian rule produce a global positive bias? Only jointly active bits contribute positively, while inactivity supplies no canceling term. Across many patterns, most weights become positive and drive excessive activity. Applying the dense sign rule unchanged to a sparse 0/1 code. Claiming higher sparse capacity without stating the units of comparison.

title: Lecture 27: Systems Consolidation and Generalization
subtitle: How does episodic memory transfer from the hippocampal one-shot notebook to the neocortical predictive student, why can standard consolidation overfit unpredictable details, and why must Go-CLS stop according to predictability?
text: Systems Consolidation and Generalization How does episodic memory transfer from the hippocampal one-shot notebook to the neocortical predictive student, why can standard consolidation overfit unpredictable details, and why must Go-CLS stop according to predictability? Recent versus remote memory → hippocampal replay → Teacher–Student–Notebook → pattern separation and completion → memory error → generalization error Distinguish changes over time in memory's anatomical dependence from changes in its psychological character, and interpret patient E.P. and recent-versus-remote evidence cautiously. Define the Teacher, Student, and Notebook and their information flows one by one, separating environmental generation, one-shot storage, replay, and slow cortical learning. Explain how pattern separation, pattern completion, and Hebbian Student↔Notebook links support rapid encoding and replay from a partial cue. Calculate memory error and population generalization error by hand in a linear Teacher/Student model, and identify overfitting to noise. Use predictability and SNR to reason about the Go-CLS stopping condition and lesion predictions without presenting formal-model outputs as established biological facts. Systems consolidation changes both the anatomical dependence and the psychological character of memory: recent memories tend to be more vivid and episodic, whereas remote memories tend to be more gist-like and semantic. In the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework, the environment or Teacher is a generative source, the neocortical Student slowly learns predictive structure, and the hippocampal Notebook rapidly stores and replays one-shot episodes. Continuous standard transfer can also write unpredictable noise into the Student and thereby impair generalization. Go-CLS instead controls transfer according to signal predictability/SNR and stops at the optimum, so unpredictable episodic detail remains hippocampus-dependent. A single case such as patient E.P. cannot establish every mechanism of consolidation. Recent memory is not absolutely equivalent to hippocampal storage, nor is remote memory absolutely equivalent to neocortical storage. A correlation with replay does not by itself demonstrate causal synaptic transfer. Teacher, Student, and Notebook are formal roles rather than one-to-one anatomical labels. Memory error and generalization error are distinct metrics. Lower training error does not necessarily mean that consolidation is better. Go-CLS predictions are not established facts. Empirical observations, standard theory, the Teacher–Student–Notebook formal model, and Go-CLS predictions must be distinguished clearly, and model predictions must not be presented as established facts. Linear teacher model y = wTT \(x + \epsilon \) The target contains signal plus unpredictable noise. Student predictor ŷ = wST x The model is linear. Memory/training error em = P −1 (yµ − ŷµ )2 The patterns are stored. Population generalization error eg = \(E[(y - \hat{y})2 ]\) The experiences are new. Predictability/SNR λs = V ar(signal)/V ar(noise) The variances are finite. Optimal stopping t∗ = arg min eg (t) The learning curve is measurable. Consolidation channel replay → student updates This channel is a formal-model hypothesis. systems consolidation The time-dependent change in a memory's dependence on or representation across brain systems. episodic memory Memory for a particular event, including its time, place, and details. semantic memory Memory for abstract, generalized knowledge. replay The reactivation of experience-related neural sequences during rest or sleep. complementary learning systems, CLS A framework that combines fast hippocampal learning with slow cortical learning. Teacher-Student-Notebook A set of formal roles comprising a generative source, a slow predictor, and a one-shot associative memory. pattern separation A process that maps similar experiences onto more distinct memory codes. pattern completion A process that recovers a stored episode from a partial cue. memory error The reconstruction or prediction error measured on stored examples. generalization error The expected prediction error on new samples. overfitting The fitting of sample-specific noise that worsens performance on new data. generalization-optimized complementary learning systems, Go-CLS A model that controls consolidation according to generalization and predictability. Can remote-memory findings from a patient such as E.P. alone prove that all remote episodic memories are independent of the hippocampus? It should be treated as important evidence, not an exhaustive law. No. A single case, lesion extent, memory age, semanticization, and related factors limit any universal conclusion. Does the Teacher represent the hippocampus in the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework? The framework names computational roles: the Teacher supplies the training world, the Student learns generalizable regularities, and the Notebook preserves sample-specific information. These names must not be treated as direct brain-region labels. No. The Teacher is the environment or generative process that produces inputs and targets; the Notebook is the abstraction of rapid hippocampal memory. Do pattern separation and pattern completion conflict? They act at different stages of memory. Separation reduces storage interference between similar events, whereas completion uses an incomplete cue to recover the correct event from an existing attractor. No. Encoding maps similar episodes to distinguishable codes, and retrieval reconstructs the corresponding complete code from a partial cue. What does it mean when training error keeps falling while test error rises? Training error measures only observed samples. A rise in test error shows that the additional fit is memorizing incidental deviations in the training set rather than extracting transferable regularities. The Student has begun fitting sample-specific noise and is overfitting; stopping or regularization should be considered. Why might a low-predictability episode remain hippocampus-dependent for a long time in Go-CLS? When shared structure cannot let the Student reconstruct an episode's unique details, forcing those details into the slow system creates systematic error. Retaining the Notebook trace supports accurate recall. Its details are difficult to predict from cross-episode regularities. Forced transfer would raise generalization error, so retaining them in the Notebook is preferable. Why does correct recall of facts from a remote memory not show that the original episode was preserved intact? Facts can be reconstructed from semantic knowledge, rehearsal, or schemas; spatiotemporal and perceptual details must be tested separately. This is the distinction tested in Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation. Worked example — Decompose a remote-memory score: For a patient's remote event, gist accuracy is 90% and episodic-detail accuracy is 30%; control values are 95% and 80%, respectively. Calculate both deficits. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For a patient's remote event, gist accuracy is 90% and episodic-detail accuracy is 30%; control values are 95% and 80%, respectively. Calculate both deficits. The gist deficit is 95%-90%=5 percentage points. The detail deficit is 80%-30%=50 points. Reporting only 'remote memory 70%' would conceal the large difference between the two dependencies. Each score is compared with its own control. The 30% and 90% values cannot be compared directly as if their difficulty were identical. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation”? Systems consolidation reorganizes dependence across systems. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation”? E.P. is important case evidence but cannot be generalized without limit. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Systems consolidation reorganizes dependence across systems. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Express temporally graded evidence as competing predictions”? If H is a performance difference, it is usually a dimensionless proportion; \(dH/dt\) is change per unit time. Near \(t=0\), effects on encoding and retrieval can be confounded, so the design should perturb the system after encoding. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: As memory changes over time, does its storage location, retrieval dependence, content quality, or some combination of the three change? The standard systems-consolidation account holds that recent memory initially depends on hippocampal indexing. Through replay and reactivation, neocortical connections gradually become able to support retrieval. Temporally graded amnesia, hippocampal lesions, and remote knowledge provide evidence. This is not the movement of a physical memory file from one place to another; it is a reorganization of network dependence. Cases such as patient E.P. show that severe medial-temporal damage impairs new episodic learning and has different effects on recent and remote memories. Such cases have great theoretical value but are limited by their single-case nature, lesion spread, test materials, premorbid exposure, and semantic support. One autobiographical score cannot be generalized to every memory type. Why need Notebook replay not reproduce the original experience pixel for pixel? It can serve as a training sample as long as it reconstructs the task-relevant statistics or targets required for Student learning; the required fidelity is a modeling assumption. This is the distinction tested in Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel. Worked example — Compare interleaved and blocked replay: The Student has learned old pattern A, and new experience B arrives. Each gradient step halves the current target error. If only B is replayed twice, A is not updated; if A and B are replayed once each, which schedule better preserves A? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The Student has learned old pattern A, and new experience B arrives. Each gradient step halves the current target error. If only B is replayed twice, A is not updated; if A and B are replayed once each, which schedule better preserves A? Two blocked B replays correct only B; A receives no rehearsal against interference through shared weights. The interleaved schedule includes one A replay, which can pull A's error back after it is perturbed by the B step. Exact values depend on feature overlap, but rehearsal of old samples mechanistically constrains catastrophic forgetting. If A and B use completely separate weights, the two schedules affect A identically, showing that interference is a prerequisite. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel”? The Teacher is the environmental distribution. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel”? The Notebook rapidly stores episodes; the Student slowly learns regularities. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Notebook rapidly stores episodes; the Student slowly learns regularities. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Information flow in complementary learning with the source notation”? The units of the loss and gradient depend on the model definition; \(\eta _{S}\) makes the parameter update have the same units as wS. When \(\eta _{S}=0\), there is no cortical transfer. If replay reconstruction is entirely wrong, the Student learns a bias. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is stronger pattern separation not always better? If similar partial cues are mapped with no continuity, retrieval addresses become fragile; stronger separation also consumes finite code space. This is the distinction tested in The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections. Worked example — Compare code overlap: Consider three binary sets of active Notebook units: \(\xi _{1}={1,2,3,4}\), \(\xi _{2}={3,4,5,6}\), and, after separation, \(\xi _{2}'={5,6,7,8}\). Count the active units each of the latter two shares with \(\xi _{1}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Consider three binary sets of active Notebook units: \(\xi _{1}={1,2,3,4}\), \(\xi _{2}={3,4,5,6}\), and, after separation, \(\xi _{2}'={5,6,7,8}\). Count the active units each of the latter two shares with \(\xi _{1}\). The original \(\xi _{1}\) and \(\xi _{2}\) share \({3,4}\), for a count of 2. \(\xi _{1}\) and \(\xi _{2}'\) share no unit, for a count of 0. Separation reduces overlap, but retrieval from a partial cue must still be tested for the correct code. Each code still has 4 active units, so the change is not caused by altered sparsity. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections”? Separation reduces overlap between episode codes. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections”? Completion recovers a stored code from a partial cue. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? J within the Notebook performs pattern completion; V replays \(\xi\) to the Student according to the sparse centered rule on the source page. U provides reverse seeding, but the source page does not specify its update. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Reconstruct Student activity with the source page's sparse centered Hebbian rule”? If \(\xi\) is dimensionless, V inherits the activity units of z; (N×M)(M×1) returns N×1 Student activity. If \(\xi\) codes are independent and sparse, crosstalk is relatively small. If the codes are identical, the Notebook address cannot distinguish the two episodes. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can the minimum generalization error remain above zero? The Teacher target contains unpredictable noise \(\epsilon\). Even if the Student recovers the true weight, it cannot predict \(\epsilon\) in a new episode. This is the distinction tested in The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error. Worked example — Calculate the difference between training and test error: Consider a one-dimensional Teacher with \(w_{\mathrm{T}}=2\) and a Student with \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=3\). For fresh \(x=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\), find the expected squared generalization error. A stored sample has \(\epsilon =1\) and \(y=3\), and the Notebook recalls x tilde=1 exactly. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Consider a one-dimensional Teacher with \(w_{\mathrm{T}}=2\) and a Student with \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=3\). For fresh \(x=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\), find the expected squared generalization error. A stored sample has \(\epsilon =1\) and \(y=3\), and the Notebook recalls x tilde=1 exactly. The weight mismatch is \(2-3=-1\), whose square at \(x=1\) is 1. Adding irreducible noise variance 1 gives an expected test error of 2. For the stored sample, the Student receives x tilde=1, so \(\hat{y}=3\) and \(y=3\), giving memory error 0. If \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=2\), expected test error falls to 1, but prediction on this stored sample is 2 and memory error is 1. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error”? Memory error is evaluated on stored samples using Notebook-recalled inputs x tilde. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error”? Generalization error is evaluated on new Teacher samples. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Memory error is evaluated on stored samples using Notebook-recalled inputs x tilde. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The boundary between memory error and generalization error”? Both terms have units \(y^{2}\). Whether the cross term vanishes depends on independence and zero mean. When \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=w_{\mathrm{T}}\), generalization error still contains irreducible noise \(E[\epsilon ^{2}]\) and does not fall to zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does 'stopping consolidation' not mean deleting the Notebook memory? What stops is further Student fitting of that component; the Notebook can still preserve it and support retrieval of episodic detail. This is the distinction tested in Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions. Worked example — Compare two types of memory component: Assume that signal and noise are both zero mean. Component A has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=9\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\); B has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=4\). Calculate \(\lambda\) and predict their relative stopping points. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Assume that signal and noise are both zero mean. Component A has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=9\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\); B has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=4\). Calculate \(\lambda\) and predict their relative stopping points. \(\lambda _{A}=9/1=9\). \(\lambda _{B}=1/4=0.25\). A is highly predictable and permits longer Student training. B is noise-dominant, so it should stop earlier and retain Notebook dependence. A higher ratio means that repeatable structure is stronger relative to noise. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions”? Go-CLS determines the extent of transfer from the minimum of generalization error. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions”? Different components of the same episode can have different dependencies because their predictability differs. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Different components of the same episode can have different dependencies because their predictability differs. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The formal chain from SNR to optimal stopping”? The second-moment ratio is dimensionless; argmin returns the same units as t. As the noise second moment→0, \(\lambda\) increases and pressure to overfit weakens. As the signal second moment→0, transfer cannot improve prediction on new samples. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook”? During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.
