title: Recent and remote memory, E.P., and evidence for systems consolidation
subtitle: Lecture 27 · Lecture27-SystemsConsolidation-Generalization.pdf, p. 1
text: As memory changes over time, does its storage location, retrieval dependence, content quality, or some combination of the three change? The standard systems-consolidation account holds that recent memory initially depends on hippocampal indexing. Through replay and reactivation, neocortical connections gradually become able to support retrieval. Temporally graded amnesia, hippocampal lesions, and remote knowledge provide evidence. This is not the movement of a physical memory file from one place to another; it is a reorganization of network dependence. Cases such as patient E.P. show that severe medial-temporal damage impairs new episodic learning and has different effects on recent and remote memories. Such cases have great theoretical value but are limited by their single-case nature, lesion spread, test materials, premorbid exposure, and semantic support. One autobiographical score cannot be generalized to every memory type. The psychological character of memory may also change: rich episodic detail can gradually become semanticized, preserving gist while losing context. Better remote performance may reflect repeated retrieval and schema support rather than complete transfer of the original episode. Accuracy, vividness, spatiotemporal detail, and confidence should be measured separately. Compressed hippocampal sequences occur during rest and sleep, and cortical patterns can reactivate alongside them, supporting a hypothesis of information exchange. Association does not show that replay is the sole cause of consolidation. Selective sequence disruption followed by remote-memory testing offers stronger causal evidence, provided sleep architecture is controlled. Systems consolidation reorganizes dependence across systems. E.P. is important case evidence but cannot be generalized without limit. Anatomical dependence and memory quality require separate measurement. For a patient's remote event, gist accuracy is 90% and episodic-detail accuracy is 30%; control values are 95% and 80%, respectively. Calculate both deficits. Gist is nearly preserved while detail is markedly impaired, supporting separate reporting. Why does correct recall of facts from a remote memory not show that the original episode was preserved intact? Facts can be reconstructed from semantic knowledge, rehearsal, or schemas; spatiotemporal and perceptual details must be tested separately. Treating one patient's pattern as a universal law. Treating a correlation with replay as evidence for the sole causal mechanism.

title: Teacher–Student–Notebook: three roles and the replay channel
subtitle: Lecture 27 · Lecture27-SystemsConsolidation-Generalization.pdf, p. 2
text: Why can a fast memory system and a slow learning system jointly reduce catastrophic interference while extracting regularities? Following the notation on original Pages 2–3, the Teacher generates Student activity patterns \(z\sim P(z|\theta _{T})\). In a particular prediction task, input x and output y can be extracted from z, and the Student slowly learns \(\hat{y}=f_{S}(x;\theta _{S})\) using finite-capacity parameters. The Notebook creates a sparse code \(\xi ^{\mu }\) for each \(z^{\mu }\) and rapidly stores the pair \({z^{\mu },\xi ^{\mu }}\). Here z always denotes Student activity and \(\xi\) Notebook activity; the names describe computational roles, not three entities at one anatomical level. With only a slow Student, a rare experience may disappear before it is learned. With only a fast Notebook, episodes can be recalled accurately, but population regularities are difficult to extract and both capacity and interference remain limiting. Complementary timescales first write online experiences into the Notebook; later, interleaved replay mixes old and new samples for the Student and reduces the overwriting of old structure by new learning. Replay is a consolidation channel: Notebook pattern completion produces an approximate experience, and the Student updates on the replayed target. If the replay distribution favors salient or recent events, the Student learns a weighted environment rather than the original frequencies. The selection rule therefore affects generalization and bias directly. The formal model and its empirical mapping must remain separate. The Teacher is not a 'teacher brain region,' the Notebook need not store raw sensory pixels, and the Student is not the entire neocortex. Tests should derive role-specific predictions: rapid hippocampal lesions affect one-shot recall, slow cortical learning affects regularities across episodes, and replay disruption affects later transfer. The Teacher is the environmental distribution. The Notebook rapidly stores episodes; the Student slowly learns regularities. Replay selection determines the Student's effective training distribution. The Student has learned old pattern A, and new experience B arrives. Each gradient step halves the current target error. If only B is replayed twice, A is not updated; if A and B are replayed once each, which schedule better preserves A? Interleaving A and B has a better chance of preserving old performance. Why need Notebook replay not reproduce the original experience pixel for pixel? It can serve as a training sample as long as it reconstructs the task-relevant statistics or targets required for Student learning; the required fidelity is a modeling assumption. Mistaking the Teacher for a particular brain region. Ignoring how replay-selection bias changes the Student's objective.

title: The autoassociative Notebook: separation, completion, and bidirectional connections
subtitle: Lecture 27 · Lecture27-SystemsConsolidation-Generalization.pdf, p. 3
text: How are similar episodes separated during encoding yet restored as complete training signals from partial cues? Pattern separation maps similar Student patterns \(z^{\mu }\) to low-overlap Notebook codes \(\xi ^{\mu }\), reducing the chance that a new episode overwrites an old one. The instructional approximation on the source page treats \(\xi ^{\mu }\) as a sparse random code independent of \(z^{\mu }\); a real system must also retain enough addressability for a partial cue to select the correct code. Structures such as the dentate gyrus are often associated with this function, but the formal model first specifies an input–output transformation. Pattern completion uses autoassociative weights J within the Notebook to drive a partial or noisy Notebook state toward stored attractor \(\xi ^{\mu }\). The completed \(\xi ^{\mu }\) then reconstructs Student activity z tilde through Notebook→Student weights V. The diagram denotes reverse Student→Notebook seeding by U, but the source page gives no learning rule for U, so transposing V cannot be presented as the source formula. Separation and completion operate at different stages: encoding increases distances among episodes, whereas retrieval decreases the distance between a cue and a stored pattern within one basin. Excessive separation can prevent a partial cue from generalizing to the right address; excessive completion can force an ambiguous cue into the wrong episode. The two processes must balance capacity, specificity, and robustness. The Notebook need not preserve every sensory detail independently forever; it may index distributed cortical components. Lesion predictions depend on the model variant. Disrupting the Notebook should particularly impair recent one-shot memories and unpredictable details, whereas shared structure already learned by the Student should be relatively spared. The term pattern completion alone does not imply a particular clinical temporal gradient. Separation reduces overlap between episode codes. Completion recovers a stored code from a partial cue. J within the Notebook performs pattern completion; V replays \(\xi\) to the Student according to the sparse centered rule on the source page. U provides reverse seeding, but the source page does not specify its update. Consider three binary sets of active Notebook units: \(\xi _{1}={1,2,3,4}\), \(\xi _{2}={3,4,5,6}\), and, after separation, \(\xi _{2}'={5,6,7,8}\). Count the active units each of the latter two shares with \(\xi _{1}\). The shared count falls from 2 to 0. Why is stronger pattern separation not always better? If similar partial cues are mapped with no continuity, retrieval addresses become fragile; stronger separation also consumes finite code space. Describing separation and completion as opposing operations at the same instant. Replacing the source page's V rule with an uncentered symmetric outer product, or measuring code overlap without testing retrieval from a partial cue.

title: The linear Teacher/Student model: memory error and generalization error
subtitle: Lecture 27 · Lecture27-SystemsConsolidation-Generalization.pdf, p. 4
text: Why can reproducing Notebook samples accurately reduce training error yet impair predictions on new experiences? The linear Teacher generates \(y=w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x+\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is episode noise that x cannot predict; the Student predicts a new input with \(\hat{y}=w_{\mathrm{S}}^\mathrm{T} x\). Memory error on original Page 4 does not feed a perfect x directly to the Student. Instead, for P stored samples it uses the Notebook-recalled input x tilde: \(e_{m}^{2}=(1/P)\sum _\mu (y_\mu -w_{\mathrm{S}}^\mathrm{T} \widetilde{x}_{\mu })^{2}\), with \(\widetilde{x}_{\mu }\approx x_\mu\) identified as the limit of ideal recall. Generalization error \(e_{g}^{2}\) is the expectation over entirely new (x,y) pairs from the Teacher distribution. Early learning moves wS toward wT, reducing signal error, so both training and test errors fall. Continued fitting of \(\epsilon\) in a finite sample can pull wS away from the population-optimal direction; training error continues to fall while test error may rise. This is overfitting. It does not mean that memory itself has deteriorated; reproducing sample details and predicting a new example are conflicting objectives. The Notebook can retain sample-specific \(\epsilon\) for episodic recall, whereas the Student should primarily learn the stable cross-episode structure wT. If standard CLS replays every noisy target uniformly without limit, a finite Student may eventually encode the noise. Regularization, early stopping, or predictability-weighted replay can protect generalization. Experiments must assess training memory and generalization on different stimuli. Testing on the same episodes used for training measures only memory error and cannot establish schema learning. P, input dimensionality, noise variance, and learning time should also be reported because they determine when overfitting occurs. Memory error is evaluated on stored samples using Notebook-recalled inputs x tilde. Generalization error is evaluated on new Teacher samples. The Notebook can remember unpredictable \(\epsilon\), but the Student should not treat it as a regularity. Consider a one-dimensional Teacher with \(w_{\mathrm{T}}=2\) and a Student with \(w_{\mathrm{S}}=3\). For fresh \(x=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\), find the expected squared generalization error. A stored sample has \(\epsilon =1\) and \(y=3\), and the Notebook recalls x tilde=1 exactly. Memory error can be 0 while expected generalization error is 2. Why can the minimum generalization error remain above zero? The Teacher target contains unpredictable noise \(\epsilon\). Even if the Student recovers the true weight, it cannot predict \(\epsilon\) in a new episode. Using a fall in training error to claim improved generalization, or omitting recalled x tilde when calculating memory error. Forgetting the lower bound set by irreducible noise.

title: Go-CLS: predictability, stopping consolidation, and lesion predictions
subtitle: Lecture 27 · Lecture27-SystemsConsolidation-Generalization.pdf, p. 5
text: When does further replay extract signal, and when does it begin writing unpredictable episodic noise into the Student? Go-CLS defines the goal of consolidation as generalization, not complete copying of Notebook contents. Original Page 5 defines the signal-to-noise-style quantity \(\lambda =E[(w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x)^{2}]/E[\epsilon ^{2}]\). It can be simplified to a variance ratio only when predictable signal and noise have both been centered. With high \(\lambda\), cross-episode regularity is strong and the Student benefits from replay for longer. With low \(\lambda\), sample-specific detail dominates, the generalization optimum occurs earlier, and transfer should stop or weaken. The formal stopping time is \(t*=\operatorname{argmin}_{t} eg^{2}(t)\). A real system does not know population eg, but validation-like signals, uncertainty, replay agreement, or learning-curve curvature can serve as proxies. The model's central claim is that stopping or gating exists, not that the brain must calculate argmin explicitly. Different features can have different predictability, so consolidation may stop separately by component rather than uniformly for an entire episode. Lesion predictions depend on memory content. High-predictability structure gradually enters the Student, making remote retrieval more resistant to a Notebook lesion. Unpredictable episodic detail remains supported by the Notebook and can be impaired even when remote. Neither component has transferred fully in recent memories, so recent memory is more fragile overall. This yields finer predictions than one age cutoff. Go-CLS is a formal model and a set of predictions, not a settled empirical conclusion. A test can manipulate training-set regularity and noise, match age and exposure, and then measure how hippocampal disruption affects gist and detail. Comparisons of naturally recent and remote memories alone confound predictability with rehearsal, emotion, and schema differences. Go-CLS determines the extent of transfer from the minimum of generalization error. Different components of the same episode can have different dependencies because their predictability differs. Model-based lesion predictions require tests that manipulate regularity and noise. Assume that signal and noise are both zero mean. Component A has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=9\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=1\); B has signal \(\mathrm{variance}=1\) and noise \(\mathrm{variance}=4\). Calculate \(\lambda\) and predict their relative stopping points. \(\lambda _{A}=9\) and \(\lambda _{B}=0.25\), predicting more complete consolidation for A than for B. Why does 'stopping consolidation' not mean deleting the Notebook memory? What stops is further Student fitting of that component; the Notebook can still preserve it and support retrieval of episodic detail. Treating t* as a fixed age threshold without considering predictability. Treating the Go-CLS lesion curve as an established clinical fact rather than a prediction to be tested.
